mcq.explain: Collecting and analysing data with AI and machine learning to detect anomalies and emerging risks is the data analytics and monitoring tool within risk identification. Dashboards only present risk data that has already been identified.

mcq.q: A company deploys an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and a SIEM platform that continuously generate real-time alerts whenever suspicious network activity is detected. This is an example of ICT's role in:
mcq.explain: IDS and SIEM providing real-time alerts on suspicious activity are the real-time monitoring tool of risk identification. Post-incident analysis reviews an incident after it has happened.

mcq.q: A logistics company uses historical shipment delay data and predictive algorithms to forecast the likelihood of future supply chain disruptions before they occur. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: Using historical data and predictive algorithms to forecast future risks before they occur is predictive modelling. Automated risk scanners look for weaknesses in IT infrastructure instead.

mcq.q: An organisation runs automated vulnerability scanning tools, such as Nessus or OpenVAS, across its IT infrastructure to identify unpatched software and configuration weaknesses before attackers can exploit them. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: Vulnerability scanners and penetration testing tools that find unpatched software and misconfigurations are automated risk scanners. Incident response systems act after a threat is detected.

mcq.q: A cybersecurity dashboard displays real-time metrics such as the number of phishing attempts, unresolved vulnerabilities, and incident resolution status using charts and heat maps, allowing executives to quickly assess the organisation's security posture. This is an example of ICT's role in:
mcq.explain: Presenting risk metrics visually with charts and heat maps so executives can decide quickly is the dashboards and visualisation tool of risk reporting. Scanners and predictive models identify risks rather than report them.

mcq.q: A financial institution's system automatically compiles reports on key risk indicators (KRIs), such as liquidity metrics, on a scheduled basis and distributes them to senior management without requiring manual compilation. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: Generating and distributing scheduled risk reports, such as KRI reports, without manual compilation is an automated reporting system. Automated risk scanners identify technical weaknesses instead.

mcq.q: A multinational corporation implements a cloud-based platform where all regional teams log operational risks in one place, creating a single, unified view of global risk exposure accessible across the organisation. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: A cloud-based platform holding all risk data in one place, accessible across the organisation, is a centralised risk repository. Regulatory compliance tools focus on producing reports for regulators.

mcq.q: A bank's compliance management software automatically tracks evolving regulations, generates the necessary reports to demonstrate compliance, and creates audit trails documenting each step taken. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: Tracking regulatory changes, generating compliance reports and creating audit trails is the role of regulatory compliance tools. A centralised repository stores risk data but does not produce regulatory filings.

mcq.q: A company deploys firewalls, encryption, and antivirus software to protect its systems and data from cyber threats and unauthorised access. This is an example of ICT's role in:
mcq.explain: Firewalls, encryption and antivirus software are risk mitigation tools that protect assets and reduce exposure to threats. Scanning tools only identify weaknesses.

mcq.q: Upon detecting a malware infection, a company's automated system immediately isolates the affected devices from the network and notifies relevant stakeholders, without requiring manual intervention at each step. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: Automatically isolating affected devices and notifying stakeholders through predefined protocols is an incident response system, which minimises damage and downtime. Predictive modelling forecasts risks before they occur.

mcq.q: Following a natural disaster that damages its primary data centre, a company restores operations within hours using cloud-based disaster recovery and redundant network infrastructure. This demonstrates ICT's role in:
options: Regulatory compliance reporting and audit tools
mcq.explain: Restoring operations quickly after a disruption using cloud-based recovery and redundant networks is business continuity and disaster recovery. Predictive modelling forecasts risks rather than restoring systems.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST explains why data accuracy is described as vital to ICT-driven risk management?
options: Flawed data leads to inaccurate risk assessments and poor decisions
Data accuracy matters to IT specialists but not really to risk managers
Risk tools work equally well whatever the quality of the data
Manual data entry is always more accurate than automated systems
mcq.explain: ICT systems that rely on poor-quality or incomplete data produce inaccurate risk assessments, exposing the organisation to unanticipated threats or unnecessary interventions.

mcq.q: A company uses collaboration platforms and a shared, unified risk management system so that IT, Legal, HR, and Operations departments can share risk information with each other in real time. This practice reflects which best practice in ICT-driven risk management?
mcq.explain: Using shared platforms so several departments exchange risk information in real time is the 'foster collaboration across teams' best practice. Leveraging automation is about replacing manual work.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST reflects the concept of "continuous improvement" in ICT-based risk management?
options: Implementing controls once and never reviewing them again
Relying only on manual reports instead of automated ones
Using feedback and post-incident lessons to refine controls
Removing monitoring tools so that operations become simpler
mcq.explain: Continuous improvement uses feedback loops and post-incident analysis to refine models, responses and controls over time, rather than treating implementation as a one-time event.

mcq.q: After a security incident, an organisation conducts a formal post-incident analysis to understand what happened and refine its risk strategies and predictive models accordingly. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this analysis?
options: To assign blame to the staff involved and close the matter
To prepare evidence for the external auditors only
To decide whether to stop future system updates
To learn lessons that improve models and responses
mcq.explain: Post-incident analysis assesses how an incident occurred so that predictive models, response strategies and controls can be refined, supporting continuous improvement.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST describes how blockchain technology can enhance an organisation's risk management processes?
options: By giving immutable, tamper-proof records for a reliable audit trail
By slowing processing so that staff can manually review each transaction
By removing the need for any risk identification activities
By replacing the need for encryption of sensitive data entirely
mcq.explain: Under the data accuracy and integrity best practice, blockchain can provide immutable records that give a tamper-proof audit trail. It does not remove the need for risk identification or encryption.

mcq.q: A company implements "self-healing networks" that automatically detect and reroute traffic around a failed component without human intervention, restoring service before most users even notice a disruption. This is an example of:
mcq.explain: Self-healing networks that reroute traffic around a fault without human intervention are automated risk control systems. A centralised repository only stores risk data.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST explains why employee training is considered an important component of ICT-based risk management, even though it is not itself a technology?
options: Training replaces the need for SIEM systems
Human error is a weak link that tools alone cannot fully close
Training removes the need for organisational security policies altogether
mcq.explain: The effectiveness of ICT tools depends on how well people use them, and human error is often the weak link, so training reduces human-related risks that technology alone cannot remove.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five risk categories that the chapter says ICT helps modern organisations manage?
mcq.explain: The five categories are cybersecurity, operational, compliance, financial and strategic risks. Staff training is a best practice for using ICT in risk management, not a risk category.

mcq.q: A regional bank wants earlier detection of fraud, cyberattacks, and operational anomalies, and is considering implementing AI-based analytics, SIEM, and vulnerability scanning together. Which combination of ICT capabilities does this reflect?
mcq.explain: AI-based analytics, SIEM real-time monitoring and vulnerability scanning are all risk identification tools aimed at earlier detection. Reporting tools communicate risks once they are identified.

mcq.q: A CRO complains that risk information reaches management late and is inconsistent across departments. Which combination of ICT solutions would MOST directly address this specific complaint?
options: Dashboards, automated reports and a central repository
Incident response and disaster recovery systems
mcq.explain: Late and inconsistent risk information is a reporting problem, addressed by dashboards, automated reporting systems and a centralised risk repository. Firewalls and encryption are mitigation tools.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST distinguishes ICT's role in "Risk Identification" from its role in "Risk Reporting"?
options: They are the same activity described in two ways
Identification applies to physical risks; reporting applies to digital ones
Identification detects and forecasts risks; reporting communicates them
Reporting always takes place before identification
mcq.explain: Risk identification detects and forecasts risks through analytics, monitoring, predictive modelling and scanners; risk reporting then communicates that information to stakeholders through dashboards, reports and repositories.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST distinguishes ICT's role in "Risk Reporting" from its role in "Risk Management and Mitigation"?
options: They are the same activity described in two ways
Good reporting removes the need for any mitigation
Mitigation must always take place before any risk reporting can begin
Reporting communicates risk; mitigation reduces or responds to it
mcq.explain: Risk reporting communicates risk information to stakeholders, while risk management and mitigation actively reduces or responds to risk through protective tools, incident response and disaster recovery.

mcq.q: A company's automated compliance system tracks changing regulations, generates the required reports, and produces audit trails — all without requiring risk teams to manually track every regulatory update. What is the PRIMARY benefit of this ICT capability?
options: It cuts manual effort and supports timely, provable compliance
It removes the obligation to comply with regulations at all
It replaces the compliance team, with no oversight needed
It benefits external auditors only, with no internal value
mcq.explain: Compliance management systems automate report generation and audit trails, reducing manual effort while helping show timely adherence to regulations. The obligation to comply and the need for oversight remain.

mcq.q: A manufacturing and e-commerce group faces cybersecurity threats, system downtime, changing regulations, fraud risk and pressure for faster strategic decisions at the same time. The board asks why risk management has 'expanded' beyond traditional approaches. Which explanation is BEST?
options: Traditional approaches remain fully sufficient for these risks
Wider, interconnected risks now need an ICT-supported approach
Risk management has narrowed as technology use has declined
ICT has made formal risk management unnecessary
mcq.explain: Globalisation, digital transformation, regulatory complexity and governance expectations mean organisations face a wider, interconnected range of risks, which ICT helps identify, report and mitigate.

mcq.q: A bank wants to combine (i) earlier fraud/cyberattack detection, (ii) faster and more consistent risk reporting to the board, and (iii) rapid automated response to contain detected incidents. Which combination of ICT capabilities addresses ALL THREE needs together?
options: Firewalls alone, as they address all three needs
Regulatory compliance tools alone, as they cover all three
Identification tools, reporting tools and incident response
Employee training alone, as people drive all three needs
mcq.explain: Earlier detection needs identification tools (AI analytics, SIEM, scanning), board reporting needs reporting tools (dashboards, automated reports), and containment needs incident response systems.

mcq.q: Which of the following BEST reflects a proactive (rather than reactive) approach to ICT-driven risk management, as described in the chapter's best practices?
options: Waiting for an incident before installing monitoring tools
Reviewing controls once at implementation and never again
Excluding historical data from all risk assessments
Using predictive analytics to address risks before they arise
mcq.explain: A proactive approach uses predictive analytics, real-time monitoring and AI-driven detection to anticipate and mitigate risks before they escalate, instead of reacting after they occur.

mcq.q: A company implements strong ICT-based risk identification and reporting tools but neglects employee training, resulting in repeated incidents caused by staff falling for phishing emails despite technical safeguards being in place. What does this scenario BEST illustrate?
options: Strong ICT tools cannot fully replace training to address human risk
Technology alone is sufficient, whatever the human factors
Training is irrelevant once SIEM and firewalls are deployed
The incidents show a failure of physical security controls, not of training
mcq.explain: Untrained staff remain a weak link even with strong technical safeguards, so the 'train employees on ICT tools' best practice is still needed, for example through phishing simulations.

mcq.q: A regulator evaluating a bank's overall ICT-enabled risk management framework wants to see that it addresses the full risk management lifecycle. Which combination of capabilities BEST demonstrates a complete, end-to-end ICT-supported risk management framework?
options: Risk identification tools only, as detection matters most
Identification, reporting and mitigation, plus continuous improvement
Risk reporting tools only, as communication matters most
Business continuity tools only, as recovery is the final goal of the lifecycle
mcq.explain: An end-to-end framework combines risk identification, risk reporting and risk management and mitigation tools, supported by best practices such as continuous improvement; no single stage is enough.

mcq.q: A chain of department stores in Lahore is steadily losing shoppers to a fast-growing online marketplace. From the chain's point of view, this is BEST classified as a:
mcq.explain: Competitive disruption that threatens the long-term position of the business is a strategic risk. Operational risk concerns processes or systems that simply fail to work.

mcq.q: Ravi Leasing Ltd misses its deadline for filing a return with SECP and is fined. Applying the chapter's classification test, this is a:
mcq.explain: Regulatory violations and penalties for failing to follow laws and standards are compliance risks. Although a fine costs money, the root issue concerns a regulator and a legal obligation.

mcq.q: A Sialkot sports goods exporter's margins swing sharply with movements in the PKR exchange rate and global commodity prices. This exposure is BEST classified as a:
mcq.explain: Market volatility and economic downturns fall under financial risks, which ICT helps manage through financial modelling and forecasting. Strategic risk concerns long-term competitive position.

mcq.q: The ERP system at Mehran Steel crashes and the production line stands idle for a shift. No attacker was involved. This is BEST classified as a:
mcq.explain: A system simply not working and causing downtime is an operational risk. It would be a cybersecurity risk only if it involved a digital break-in or data loss.

mcq.q: For which risk category does ICT mainly help by providing competitive intelligence, market analytics and scenario-planning tools?
mcq.explain: Competitive intelligence, market analytics and scenario planning help manage strategic risk. For operational risk, ICT instead provides real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance and process automation.

mcq.q: Which ICT contribution does the chapter link MOST directly to managing operational risks?
options: Tracking changes in regulation and keeping audit trails
mcq.explain: For operational risk, ICT enables real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance and process automation. Tracking regulatory change supports compliance risk instead.

mcq.q: A mobile network operator uses machine learning to analyse billions of call records and spot unusual patterns that suggest SIM-card fraud. Which ICT risk identification tool is this?
mcq.explain: Collecting and analysing vast amounts of data with AI and machine learning to detect anomalies is data analytics and monitoring. Automated risk scanners look for weaknesses in IT infrastructure, not fraud patterns.

mcq.q: A sugar mill in Rahim Yar Khan uses ten years of crop and rainfall data to forecast a likely shortfall in sugarcane supply next season. Which risk identification tool is this?
mcq.explain: Using historical data and predictive algorithms to forecast risks before they materialise is predictive modelling. Real-time monitoring flags suspicious activity as it happens rather than forecasting.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ICT tools for risk identification described in the chapter?
options: Automated risk scanners such as Nessus
mcq.explain: Centralised risk repositories are a risk reporting tool that stores risk data in one place. Predictive modelling, scanners and real-time monitoring are identification tools.

mcq.q: The board of Hunza Bank Ltd now views risks on an interactive, colour-coded screen where directors can click into any branch's figures during the meeting. Which risk reporting tool is this?
mcq.explain: Interactive dashboards present risk data visually in an easily understood format for faster decisions. Regulatory compliance tools focus on producing filings for regulators.

mcq.q: A listed modaraba's system automatically compiles its SECP returns from the accounting ledger, tracks filing deadlines and keeps a clear audit trail. Which risk reporting tool is this?
mcq.explain: Automating compliance reporting to meet regulatory deadlines with a clear audit trail is the role of regulatory compliance tools. An automated risk control system is a mitigation tool such as a self-healing network.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT one of ICT's tools for risk reporting?
mcq.explain: Automated risk scanners such as Nessus or OpenVAS identify infrastructure weaknesses, so they belong to risk identification. The other three are reporting tools.

mcq.q: Sensors on the kilns of Margalla Cement feed an analytics model that warns when a kiln is likely to overheat, so maintenance is booked before a breakdown. This is ICT's role in:
options: Risk identification, for an operational risk
Risk reporting, for a compliance risk
Risk mitigation, for a strategic risk
Risk reporting, for an operational downtime risk
mcq.explain: Forecasting a breakdown before it occurs is predictive modelling within risk identification, and equipment failure halting production is an operational risk.

mcq.q: A Pakistani bank's software pulls data from its core banking system and produces the liquidity risk report in the exact format SBP requires. This BEST illustrates ICT's role in:
options: Risk identification, for a financial risk
Risk mitigation, for an operational risk
Risk reporting, for a compliance risk
Risk identification, for a compliance risk
mcq.explain: Producing regulator-required reports is a regulatory compliance tool under risk reporting, addressing compliance risk. Identification tools detect or forecast risks rather than report them to a regulator.

mcq.q: Before its credit risk model runs, Indus Microfinance applies validation and quality checks that reject duplicate and incomplete borrower records. Which best practice is this?
mcq.explain: Risk decisions are only as good as their data, so validation and quality checks support data accuracy and integrity. Updating and testing systems concerns patching and penetration testing.

mcq.q: A hospital group replaces separate departmental risk spreadsheets with one cloud GRC platform on which finance, legal, HR and IT update the same risk information in real time. Which best practice is this?
mcq.explain: A shared GRC platform used by several departments to remove information silos illustrates fostering collaboration across teams. Automation concerns replacing manual work, not shared visibility.

mcq.q: Each year an independent firm attempts to break into Chenab Bank's systems so the bank can confirm its controls actually work, and patches are applied automatically. Which best practice does this BEST illustrate?
mcq.explain: Penetration testing and automated patch management keep systems current and verify that controls work, which is regularly updating and testing systems. Continuous improvement is driven by post-incident analysis.

mcq.q: After rolling out a new GRC platform, Rohtas Insurance gives each user role-specific training and runs regular phishing simulations. Which best practice is this?
mcq.explain: Role-specific training and ongoing awareness such as phishing simulations make up the 'train employees on ICT tools' practice, because tools are only as effective as their users.

mcq.q: A leasing company deploys software robots (RPA) to perform routine compliance checks and risk data entry that clerks previously did by hand. Which best practice is this?
mcq.explain: Using RPA for repetitive risk-related tasks such as data entry and routine compliance checks is leveraging automation. A proactive approach is about anticipating risks before they escalate.

mcq.q: After a warehouse fire, Bolan Foods reviews exactly how its recovery failed and uses the findings to revise its response strategy and early-warning model. Which best practice is this?
mcq.explain: Post-incident analysis that feeds back into refining models and response strategies is continuous improvement. A proactive approach anticipates risks before an incident rather than learning after one.

mcq.q: A Karachi pharmaceutical company analyses shipping and supplier data to anticipate delays in imported raw materials, and places orders early before production is affected. Which best practice is this?
mcq.explain: Using predictive analytics to anticipate and act on a risk before it escalates is the proactive approach; the giveaway is the verb 'anticipate'.

mcq.q: According to the chapter, combining data analytics, real-time monitoring, automation and incident response systems changes risk management from:
options: A continuous process into an annual review
A reactive exercise into a continuous one
An automated process into a manual one
An organisation-wide task into an IT task
mcq.explain: These ICT capabilities turn risk management from a reactive, after-the-fact exercise into a continuous, largely automated discipline. The other options reverse the direction of change.

mcq.q: A switch failure in a bank's ATM network leaves customers in Peshawar unable to withdraw cash for six hours. No intrusion or data loss occurred. This is BEST classified as a:
mcq.explain: A system failure causing downtime with no break-in or data loss is an operational risk. The scenario names banking technology, but classification follows what went wrong, not the technology mentioned.

mcq.q: A disgruntled employee of a Faisalabad courier company copies the customer database to a USB drive and sells it to a competitor. Under the chapter's five risk categories, this is a:
mcq.explain: Data breaches and insider threats are listed under cybersecurity risks; the test is whether data was lost. Financial risk covers fraud, market volatility and economic downturns.

mcq.q: A Lahore printing house that relies on equipment for paper catalogues finds that clients are moving to digital formats, making its core technology obsolete. This is a:
mcq.explain: Technological obsolescence threatening long-term competitiveness is a strategic risk. Operational risk would involve the existing equipment failing or processes breaking down.

mcq.q: Which ICT capability does the chapter link MOST directly to managing financial risks?
mcq.explain: For financial risks, ICT supports real-time transaction monitoring, fraud detection, financial modelling and forecasting. Scenario planning and market analytics are linked to strategic risk.

mcq.q: For compliance risks, the chapter says ICT mainly helps by:
options: Tracking regulatory change and audit trails
mcq.explain: ICT addresses compliance risk by tracking regulatory change and automating compliance reporting and audit trails. Fraud detection relates to financial risk.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT one of ICT's tools for risk management and mitigation?
mcq.explain: Predictive modelling forecasts risks and so belongs to risk identification. Incident response, BC/DR and automated risk control systems are the mitigation tools.

mcq.q: The CRO of Seher Takaful complains that every department compiles its risk report by hand, so reports arrive late and in different formats. Which ICT tool MOST directly fixes the timing and consistency problem?
mcq.explain: Automated reporting systems generate and distribute reports without manual compilation, giving timely and consistent updates. Automated scanners identify technical weaknesses and do not produce risk reports.

mcq.q: How does the chapter describe ICT's relationship with cybersecurity risk?
options: ICT is both its main target and main defence
ICT is its target but offers no defence
ICT defends against it but is never itself targeted
ICT has little bearing on this risk area
mcq.explain: For cybersecurity risks, ICT is both the primary target and the primary defence; it creates the risk category and also resolves it, reflecting ICT's dual role.

secb.scenario:
Okara Milk Growers Cooperative (OMGC) collects milk every morning from around 2,000 member farmers in Okara, Sahiwal and Pakpattan. To improve payments and planning, OMGC has designed a farmer delivery record. A sample of the fields captured in the new record is shown in Table 1.
OMGC's operations manager has made the following proposals for the monthly management report:
(i) Convert the milk quality grades A, B and C into the numbers 1, 2 and 3, calculate an average grade for each district, and report that a district with an average of 2.0 has milk 'twice as bad' as a district with an average of 1.0.
(ii) Calculate the average membership number of farmers in each district, since membership numbers are already stored as numbers.

tables.caption: Table 1: Farmer delivery record (sample)
rows: Milk quality grade (A = best, C = lowest)
Number of late deliveries this month
Satisfied (scale: Very dissatisfied, Dissatisfied, Neutral, Satisfied, Very satisfied)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the eight fields in Table 1 as nominal, ordinal, discrete or continuous data, giving a brief reason for each classification.
parts.answer:
1. Farmer's district: Nominal (qualitative). It is a label such as Okara or Sahiwal with no natural order; one district is not 'higher' than another.
2. Milk delivered (litres): Continuous (quantitative). It is a measurement that can take any value in a range, including decimals such as 18.5 litres.
3. Number of milking cows owned: Discrete (quantitative). It is a count of whole units; a farmer cannot own 12.5 cows.
4. Fat content (%): Continuous (quantitative). It is a measured value that can be a decimal, such as 4.2%.
5. Milk quality grade: Ordinal (qualitative). The grades are labels, but they have a clear ranking (A is better than B, which is better than C); the gaps between grades are not measurable or equal.
6. Preferred payment method: Nominal (qualitative). Cash, bank transfer and mobile wallet are labels with no ranking.
7. Number of late deliveries this month: Discrete (quantitative). It is a whole-number count; 2.5 late deliveries is meaningless.
8. Farmer satisfaction: Ordinal (qualitative). The scale from Very dissatisfied to Very satisfied has an order, but we cannot say by exactly how much 'Satisfied' exceeds 'Neutral'.
(1 mark per field correctly classified with a valid reason, max 8. Classification without a reason earns 1/2 mark.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate each of the operations manager's two proposals, explaining whether the calculation would produce meaningful information.
parts.answer:
Proposal (i): Not meaningful. Milk quality grade is ordinal data. Converting A, B and C into 1, 2 and 3 only records the order; it does not create equal gaps between the grades. We know B is worse than A, but not by how much, so arithmetic such as averaging and statements like 'twice as bad' are invalid and could mislead management. OMGC should instead report the count or percentage of deliveries falling in each grade for each district (for example, 60% grade A in Okara versus 40% in Pakpattan), which describes the ranking correctly.
Proposal (ii): Not meaningful. A membership number is nominal data even though it is written in digits. It is simply a label that identifies a farmer, like a CNIC number. Applying the two-step test, meaningful arithmetic cannot be performed on it, so it is qualitative; the 'average membership number' of a district tells management nothing. Useful quantitative measures would be the average litres delivered or average fat content per district, which are continuous data.
(2 marks per proposal: 1 for correct conclusion linked to the data type, 1 for explanation or better alternative, max 4.)

secb.scenario:
Swift Parcel Services Limited (SPS) is a courier company based in Karachi with delivery riders in 30 cities. SPS's management wants to build a single analytics platform and has listed the data it currently holds:
(i) Shipment bookings held in SPS's booking database, with fields for booking number, sender, receiver city, weight and charges.
(ii) Photographs taken by riders at the customer's door as proof of delivery.
(iii) Voice notes and text complaints sent by customers to SPS's WhatsApp business number.
(iv) Flight status messages received from a partner cargo airline in XML format.
(v) Rider route logs generated by the rider mobile app in JSON format.
(vi) The monthly payroll register for riders.
The IT manager has warned that most of the new data SPS generates is of the type that 'our current reporting tool cannot read'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the six data items listed above as structured, unstructured or semi-structured data, giving a reason for each.
parts.answer:
(i) Shipment bookings: Structured. The data sits in rows and columns with fixed fields (booking number, city, weight, charges), so it can be searched and totalled easily using tools such as SQL.
(ii) Proof-of-delivery photographs: Unstructured. Images have no fixed format or predefined fields and cannot be queried by ordinary database tools.
(iii) WhatsApp voice notes and text complaints: Unstructured. Free text and audio messages have no fixed structure; their meaning must be extracted with specialised techniques.
(iv) Airline flight status messages in XML: Semi-structured. XML uses tags that label each piece of data, giving it some organisation, but it is not a neat table of rows and columns.
(v) Rider route logs in JSON: Semi-structured. JSON contains markers (keys and values) that organise the data, but the records do not follow a fixed relational table format.
(vi) Rider payroll register: Structured. It is held as a table with fixed fields such as rider ID, days worked and net pay.
(1 mark per item correctly classified with reason, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why the data that the IT manager refers to is difficult to analyse, and how SPS could extract value from it.
parts.answer:
The IT manager is referring to unstructured data such as the delivery photographs and WhatsApp voice notes and complaints.
1. No fixed format: unstructured data has no predefined fields, so it cannot be sorted, filtered or totalled by an ordinary reporting tool or SQL query. A tool cannot, for example, count how many complaints relate to late delivery because the reason is buried in free text or speech.
2. Needs advanced tools: meaning has to be extracted using artificial intelligence techniques such as natural language processing (NLP). For SPS, NLP could read the complaint texts (and transcribed voice notes) and tag each one by theme, such as late delivery, damaged parcel or rude rider, and by city.
3. Converting to structured outputs: once tagged, the results can be stored as structured fields alongside the booking data, so management can report complaints per 1,000 shipments by city and link them to specific riders or routes.
4. Advanced techniques for images: the delivery photographs likewise cannot be read by an ordinary reporting tool; they would need advanced techniques such as machine learning before they could be searched, for example when resolving a delivery dispute.
(1 mark per well-explained point applied to SPS, max 4.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Discuss the significance, for SPS's analytics plans, of the fact that most data generated today is unstructured.
parts.answer:
Roughly 80 percent of all data generated today is unstructured. For SPS this has three implications:
1. If SPS's analytics platform can only handle structured data such as bookings and payroll, it will ignore the majority of its data, including the customer voice captured in complaints and the evidence in delivery photographs, and its picture of service quality will be incomplete.
2. This is precisely why Big Data platforms and artificial intelligence have become important: SPS should choose a platform that can store unstructured and semi-structured data (photos, voice notes, XML and JSON feeds) alongside structured tables.
3. SPS will need investment in suitable tools and skills (for example NLP) and should plan for the cost, rather than assuming its current reporting tool is enough.
(1 mark per relevant point linked to SPS, max 3.)

secb.topic: Sources of data: origin and purpose
secb.scenario:
Margalla Foods Limited (MFL), an Islamabad-based food company, plans to launch a new mango juice in Peshawar next summer. The marketing team has gathered the following data sets to prepare the launch plan:
(i) MFL's own sales records for its existing juices in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa over the last three years, originally recorded by the accounts department for invoicing.
(ii) Household income and expenditure statistics published by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics.
(iii) A taste and price-preference questionnaire designed by MFL's marketing team and completed by 800 shoppers in Peshawar specifically for this launch.
(iv) A beverage market share report purchased from a market research consultancy.
The marketing director believes that 'since we paid for item (iv), it is our own primary data'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the four data sets by origin (internal or external) and by purpose (primary or secondary), giving reasons. Also comment on the marketing director's view.
parts.answer:
The two pairs answer different questions: internal versus external asks where the data comes from and who owns it; primary versus secondary asks who collected it and why. Each data set takes one label from each pair.
(i) Own sales records: Internal, because they were created inside MFL by its accounts department. Secondary, because they were originally recorded for invoicing and are now being reused for a different purpose (launch planning).
(ii) Pakistan Bureau of Statistics data: External, because it comes from a government body outside MFL. Secondary, because it was collected by someone else for their own purpose and is simply reused by MFL.
(iii) Shopper questionnaire: Primary, because MFL collected it first-hand, directly from shoppers, for the specific purpose of this launch. It is internal data in the sense that MFL generated and owns it (a survey you run yourself is internal and primary); the respondents being outside MFL does not change who collected it.
(iv) Purchased market share report: External, because it was prepared outside MFL by a consultancy. Secondary, because it was collected by the consultancy for its own general research purpose before MFL bought it.
Comment on the director's view: The director is wrong. Paying for data does not make it primary. Primary or secondary depends on who collected the data and for what purpose, not on cost. The report was collected by someone else for a different purpose, so it is external and secondary.
(3/4 mark per correctly justified label, eight labels in total, max 6; 2 marks for explaining why the director is wrong; max 8. For (iii), 'external' origin is also acceptable if the student explains that the respondents are outside MFL, provided it is classified as primary.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to MFL of relying on primary data compared with secondary data for this launch.
parts.answer:
Primary data (the Peshawar shopper questionnaire):
1. Advantage: very accurate and relevant for the purpose. It tells MFL exactly what Peshawar shoppers think of mango flavour and price points, which no published report will show.
2. Advantage: it is current, because it is collected now for next summer's launch.
3. Disadvantage: it is slow and expensive to collect. Designing the questionnaire, reaching 800 shoppers and analysing responses costs time and money, and a larger sample would cost more.
Secondary data (PBS statistics and the purchased report):
4. Advantage: cheaper and faster to obtain. MFL can immediately understand household spending power and competitor market shares without running its own research.
5. Disadvantage: it may not be exactly what MFL needs (for example, it may cover all beverages nationally rather than mango juice in Peshawar) and it may be out of date, so its quality must be checked before relying on it.
Conclusion: MFL should combine both, using secondary data for the broad market picture and primary data for launch-specific decisions such as flavour and price.
(1 mark per valid point applied to MFL, max 5.)

secb.scenario:
Mehran Agri Credit Limited (MACL) is a lender in Hyderabad that provides crop loans to farmers in interior Sindh. MACL is designing a new credit-scoring approach for the coming Rabi season. An internal review of the data collection process has found the following:
(i) Loan officers are estimating expected crop yields using district yield figures from 2019, as no later figures were gathered.
(ii) The data team spent two months collecting details of each farmer's mobile phone brand, favourite television channels and number of social media followers, none of which has any link with repayment ability.
(iii) Information about canal water availability in each area was copied from an anonymous online blog with no named author or source.
(iv) Field officers entered land holdings manually; several farmers with 5 acres were recorded as holding 50 acres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Briefly explain the three qualities of good data collection.
parts.answer:
1. Relevance: the data collected must fit the question being asked and the organisation's objectives. Collecting data that does not help the decision wastes time and money.
2. Accuracy: the data must come from reliable and valid sources and be free from error. Inaccurate data leads to false conclusions and bad decisions.
3. Timeliness: the data must reflect the current state of affairs. Old data describes a situation that may no longer exist, so decisions based on it may be wrong.
(1 mark per quality correctly explained, max 3.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the four findings, identify the quality of data collection that has been compromised and explain the likely consequence for MACL.
parts.answer:
(i) 2019 yield figures: Timeliness is compromised. Yields seven years ago reflect different weather, seed varieties and water conditions. Consequence: MACL may overestimate or underestimate farmers' expected income, approving loans that cannot be repaid or rejecting good borrowers.
(ii) Phone brands, TV channels and followers: Relevance is compromised. This data does not answer the credit question of whether the farmer can repay. Consequence: two months of staff time and cost were wasted, and the irrelevant variables could even distort the scoring model and delay the Rabi season launch.
(iii) Water availability from an anonymous blog: Accuracy is compromised, because the source is not reliable or valid. Consequence: if the blog is wrong, MACL may lend heavily in areas facing water shortage, where crops fail and defaults rise, or avoid areas that are actually viable.
(iv) 5 acres recorded as 50 acres: Accuracy is compromised, because the data contains errors. Consequence: the farmer appears ten times larger than reality, so loan limits are set far too high and MACL's exposure and expected losses are understated.
(1 mark for correctly identifying the quality and 1 mark for a relevant consequence, per finding, max 8.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Recommend two measures MACL should take to improve the quality of its data collection.
parts.answer:
Any two of the following:
1. Define the credit question first and list only the data items that relate to repayment ability (land size, crop type, yields, water, past repayment), so that only relevant data is collected.
2. Obtain yield and water data from reliable, named and current sources (for example official agriculture department or irrigation authority releases for the latest season) and record the source and date of every external data set.
3. Verify land holdings against supporting documents and apply checks at entry, such as a reasonable range for land size, with supervisor review of unusual values.
(1 mark per relevant measure, max 2.)

secb.scenario:
Safar Go (Private) Limited (SGL) operates a ride-hailing app in Lahore and Islamabad. A recent internal audit of SGL's data practices reported the following:
(i) The app continues to record passengers' live location even after a trip ends and the app is closed. This is mentioned only in paragraph 47 of the terms and conditions.
(ii) The full passenger database, including names, phone numbers and home addresses, is kept on an unencrypted laptop, and the login password is shared by the whole marketing team.
(iii) To set surge prices, SGL collected demand data only from wealthy neighbourhoods. As a result, passengers in lower-income areas are consistently charged higher fares and shown fewer available cars.
(iv) SGL sold passengers' phone numbers to a real estate developer, which now sends them promotional messages. Passengers were never asked for consent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the four findings, identify the ethical principle(s) of data collection that are at risk and explain how SGL's practice breaches them.
parts.answer:
(i) Location tracking after the app is closed: Transparency and privacy. Disclosure hidden in paragraph 47 of terms that nobody reads is not clear communication of what is collected and why, so transparency is breached. Tracking a person's movements outside any trip, without their real knowledge, takes away their control over highly personal data, breaching privacy.
(ii) Unencrypted laptop with a shared password: Security. The security principle requires collected data to be protected from unauthorised access or misuse. An unencrypted device can be read by anyone who steals it, and a shared password means access cannot be restricted or traced to an individual.
(iii) Demand data collected only from wealthy neighbourhoods: Fairness. The fairness principle requires collection to avoid bias that could lead to discrimination or unfair treatment. Because the data was collected from one group only, the pricing outcome unfairly penalises passengers in lower-income areas with higher fares and poorer service.
(iv) Sale of phone numbers without consent: Privacy and transparency. Passengers' right to control their personal data was ignored by disclosing it to a third party without explicit consent, and they were never told their numbers would be sold. This also destroys customer trust.
(1 mark for the correct principle and 1 mark for linking it to the fact in the scenario, per finding, max 8. Naming the principle without linking it to the scenario earns 1 mark only.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend measures that SGL should implement to collect and use passenger data ethically.
parts.answer:
1. Stop collecting location data when no trip is in progress, and ask passengers in a clear, separate in-app message whether location may be used and why (transparency and privacy).
2. Obtain explicit, separate consent before sharing any personal data with a third party, and give passengers an easy way to opt out at any time; stop the sale to the developer until consent exists (privacy).
3. Move the passenger database off the laptop to a secured system, encrypt the data, and give each marketing user an individual login with access limited to what their role requires (security).
4. Collect demand data from all service areas so the pricing model is not biased, and review fares regularly for unfair differences between neighbourhoods (fairness).
5. Publish a short, plain-language privacy notice explaining what data SGL collects, why, who it is shared with and how long it is kept (transparency).
(1 mark per relevant, specific measure, max 5.)

secb.scenario:
Pindi Steel Fabricators Limited (PSFL) is a family-owned manufacturer of steel doors and racks in Rawalpindi. Its managing director takes decisions on 'gut feeling' and regards data collection as 'paperwork'. Sales invoices and job cards are kept as loose paper files and are rarely summarised. The following problems have arisen:
(i) Several large customers stopped ordering last year and nobody knows why.
(ii) The board set a target of reducing material wastage by 10%, but no one can say whether it has been achieved.
(iii) Tax authorities have asked for supporting records for sales declared in the last two years, and staff are struggling to produce them.
(iv) The managing director wants to start exporting racks to the Middle East but has no basis for choosing which market to enter.
(v) Production schedules are prepared from memory, causing frequent overtime and idle time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how systematic data collection would support PSFL, relating your answer to each of the five problems.
parts.answer:
1. Understanding customer behaviour (problem i): Collecting data on what each customer buys, when and how often, together with complaints and feedback, would show when ordering patterns changed and why customers left (for example delivery delays or price). PSFL could then act to win them back or prevent further losses.
2. Performance measurement (problem ii): Recording material issued and scrap generated for each job would allow PSFL to calculate the actual wastage rate and compare it with the 10% reduction target, so the board knows whether the target is being met and where corrective action is needed.
3. Regulatory compliance (problem iii): Systematic, organised records of invoices and sales would allow PSFL to produce the records that regulators and auditors demand quickly and completely, reducing the risk of penalties and disputes.
4. Strategy development (problem iv): Collecting internal data (capacity, costs, margins) and external data (market reports, trade statistics, competitor prices in Middle Eastern countries) would help PSFL identify the most attractive new market and the risks involved before committing to exports.
5. Decision-making (problem v): Data on orders in hand, machine capacity and labour hours per job would let management schedule production on evidence rather than intuition, reducing costly overtime and idle time.
(1 mark for each area of importance correctly identified and 1 mark for applying it to the related problem, max 10.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Using PSFL's paper files as an example, explain the difference between data and information, and why relying on 'gut feeling' increases PSFL's risk.
parts.answer:
Data is raw, unprocessed facts; information is data that has been organised, summarised and interpreted so it is useful for decisions. PSFL's loose sales invoices and job cards are data: each one records a single fact, such as one door sold to one customer, and on its own tells management very little. When they are sorted and totalled into, for example, a monthly sales report by customer, or a wastage report by job, they become information that management can act on.
Without data, decisions are purely speculative. The managing director's 'gut feeling' is guesswork; good data grounds decisions in evidence, which lowers risk and improves the chances of success, for example in choosing the right export market.
(1 mark for the distinction, 1 for the PSFL example, 1 for the risk point, max 3.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the three measures that currently form Pakistan's framework for the protection of data, giving an example of a situation in which each would be relevant to a business.
parts.answer:
Pakistan does not yet have a comprehensive data-protection law; it is still developing. The current framework rests on three measures:
1. Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016: makes unauthorised access to data and other cyber offences a criminal offence. Example: if a former employee of a Lahore retailer logs into the customer database without permission and copies customer records, the act can be prosecuted under PECA 2016.
2. National Cyber Security Policy: a national policy that promotes secure digital infrastructure and the protection of data. Example: a company building its information security programme can align its controls with the policy's objectives of secure infrastructure and data protection.
3. Electronic Transactions Ordinance (ETO) 2002: gives legal validity to electronic documents and transactions. Example: a distributor that accepts orders and contracts electronically, rather than on paper, can rely on those electronic records being legally valid.
(1 mark for explaining each measure and 1 mark for a relevant example, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify two international data protection laws and discuss why a Pakistani organisation should follow the ethical principles of data collection even though a comprehensive local data-protection law is still developing.
parts.answer:
International laws (2 marks):
1. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) of the European Union, which sets strict rules protecting the personal data of individuals.
2. The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) of the United States, which similarly gives consumers strong rights over their personal data.
Why follow ethical principles anyway (4 marks):
1. Privacy: people have a right to control their own personal data whether or not a specific law requires it; respecting this avoids harm to customers.
2. Transparency: being clear about what is collected and why builds trust. Lost trust, for example after customers discover their phone numbers were sold, is far more expensive to rebuild than any revenue earned from misuse.
3. Security: the duty to protect data from unauthorised access is supported in Pakistan by PECA 2016, and poor security exposes the organisation to cyber crime, losses and reputational damage.
4. Fairness: avoiding bias in collection prevents discrimination and unfair treatment of customer groups.
5. Organisations that deal with customers or partners in jurisdictions with strict laws such as GDPR are expected to meet high standards, and Pakistani regulation is moving in the same direction, so good practice now reduces future compliance cost.
(1 mark per law correctly identified, max 2; 1 mark per well-argued reason, max 4.)

secb.scenario:
Karachi Cotton Exporters Limited (KCEL) exports cotton yarn to buyers in China and Europe. Every morning, two staff members spend about three hours manually copying the following into spreadsheets for the pricing committee:
(i) The PKR/USD exchange rate (for example Rs. 278.32) from a financial news website.
(ii) International cotton prices per pound from a commodity exchange website.
(iii) Posts and comments on social media that mention KCEL or its brand of yarn.
The finance director has suggested using APIs to bring this data in automatically. The pricing committee chairman is concerned that 'outside data cannot be trusted as much as our own ledger'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what an API is and the benefits KCEL would obtain by using APIs instead of manual copying.
parts.answer:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that lets one software system automatically pull data from, or exchange data with, another system without anyone copying it by hand. APIs are one of the most common ways organisations bring in external data.
Benefits for KCEL:
1. Time and cost saving: the three hours of daily manual copying by two staff would be eliminated, freeing them for analysis.
2. Fewer errors: automatic transfer avoids keying mistakes, such as typing Rs. 287.32 instead of Rs. 278.32, which could misprice an export contract.
3. Timeliness: exchange rates and cotton prices can be refreshed automatically and frequently, so the pricing committee always works with current data.
4. Scale: brand mentions on social media are too numerous to copy manually; an API can gather all of them.
(1 mark for the definition, 1 mark per benefit applied to KCEL, max 4.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the three data items, identify its source by origin and purpose, and classify it by type (qualitative or quantitative, with sub-type) and by structure.
parts.answer:
(i) PKR/USD exchange rate: External (from outside KCEL) and secondary (collected and published by others for their own purpose). Quantitative continuous, because it is a measured value that can take decimals (Rs. 278.32). As delivered by an API it would usually be in a tagged format such as JSON, so semi-structured; once loaded into KCEL's spreadsheet or database table it becomes structured.
(ii) International cotton prices: External and secondary, for the same reasons. Quantitative continuous (a price per pound with decimals). Semi-structured when received through the API, structured once stored in KCEL's tables.
(iii) Social media posts and comments: External (generated outside KCEL by social media users) and secondary (written by users for their own purposes, not collected by KCEL for a specific study). Qualitative data, as it is opinions and descriptions, and unstructured, because free text and images have no fixed format and would need tools such as natural language processing to analyse.
(2 marks per item: 1 for source labels, 1 for type and structure, max 6.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Discuss the chairman's concern and explain how KCEL should check external data before relying on it for pricing decisions.
parts.answer:
The chairman is partly right. Internal data, such as KCEL's own ledger, is usually reliable, easy to access and free, because KCEL controls how it is created. External data is useful for market studies and for comparing with industry standards, but KCEL does not control how it is produced, so its quality must be checked. This does not mean it should be avoided; KCEL cannot price exports without external exchange rates and cotton prices.
Checks KCEL should apply:
1. Accuracy: use reliable and valid sources, such as an official or recognised exchange-rate provider and the commodity exchange itself, rather than unverified websites; compare against a second source periodically.
2. Timeliness: check the date and time stamp on each rate or price so the committee never prices on yesterday's figures in a moving market.
3. Relevance: ensure the data fits the decision, for example the cotton grade and market quoted match the yarn KCEL sells, and that social media data is used for brand monitoring rather than pricing.
(1 mark for discussing the concern, 1 mark per check applied, max 4.)

secb.scenario:
Sutlej Pharma Distributors Limited (SPDL) distributes medicines to pharmacies and hospitals across Punjab from its head office in Lahore. SPDL has grown quickly but has never formally organised how it manages its data. A consultant's review has reported the following:
(i) When asked who decides whether sales representatives may see customers' credit limits, the IT manager said it was the sales department's decision, while the sales director said it was an IT matter. Nobody has been formally made accountable for customer data.
(ii) There are no written rules on how long customer and supplier records are retained. Last month, old computers containing customer records were sold to a scrap dealer without the hard drives being wiped.
(iii) The term 'net sales' is calculated after returns in the finance reports but before returns in the sales reports. There is no record of how fields are defined or where they come from.
(iv) About 15% of pharmacy addresses in the customer master file are incomplete and many pharmacies appear more than once.
(v) The server room is unlocked and used as a storeroom, and backup files are copied to an unencrypted USB drive.
(vi) No one has assessed SPDL's obligations under PECA 2016 or the SECP Guidelines for Cyber Security, and there is no register of data risks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (vi), identify the component of data governance that is weak and recommend an appropriate action SPDL should take.
parts.answer:
(i) Component: Data ownership and stewardship. No one has been assigned accountability for customer data. Action: formally appoint a senior business leader (for example the sales director) as data owner for customer data, with authority to decide who may access credit limits, and a data steward to maintain the data day to day; document these roles.
(ii) Component: Data policies and procedures (and data lifecycle management). There are no documented rules on retention and disposal. Action: approve a data retention and disposal policy setting how long each record type is kept, and requiring secure disposal (data wiping, shredding or cryptographic erasure) of devices, with the destruction documented.
(iii) Component: Metadata management. There is no 'data about data' defining fields and their origin. Action: build a data dictionary or metadata catalogue that records the agreed definition, source and calculation of key fields such as net sales, so all departments use the same meaning.
(iv) Component: Data quality management. Completeness and accuracy/consistency are poor. Action: run a data cleansing exercise to complete addresses and merge duplicates, then apply validation at entry (mandatory address fields, duplicate checks) and monitor quality regularly through the data steward.
(v) Component: Data security. Physical and technical controls are missing. Action: lock and restrict access to the server room (physical control), encrypt backups and store them securely (technical control), and train staff on security policy (administrative control).
(vi) Component: Compliance and risk management. Legal obligations and data risks have not been identified. Action: assess SPDL's obligations under PECA 2016 and the SECP cyber security guidelines, set up a data risk register, and assign responsibility for monitoring compliance.
(1 mark for the correct component and 1 mark for a relevant action, per issue, max 12.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between the roles of a data owner and a data steward, using SPDL's customer data as an example.
parts.answer:
A data owner is a senior business leader who is accountable for a data domain and decides how it may be used. At SPDL, the owner of customer data (for example the sales director) would decide whether sales representatives may see credit limits and who may share customer data.
A data steward is an operational custodian who is responsible for keeping the data accurate, available and documented day to day, acting as the liaison between IT and the business. At SPDL, a steward in the sales administration team would remove duplicate pharmacy records each week, complete missing addresses, enforce the data policies and maintain field definitions.
In short, the owner decides; the steward does the daily work.
(1 mark for the owner, 1 for the steward, 1 for application to SPDL, max 3.)

secb.scenario:
Hazara Life Assurance Limited (HLAL) is a life insurer with its head office in Abbottabad. HLAL's internal auditor has reviewed how policyholder data is handled and reported the following:
(i) When new policies are issued, copies of policyholders' CNICs and medical reports are scanned into the system without any classification label, and no one is recorded as responsible for the data.
(ii) The policy administration database is held on a single server with no backups, and the data is not encrypted.
(iii) All sales agents can open any policyholder's file, including medical reports, and there is no record of who viewed which file.
(iv) Policies that matured more than fifteen years ago are still held in the live database, where they slow down the system and can still be edited by staff.
(v) Old laptops used by agents are given to staff for personal use when replaced, without the data being removed, and there is no record of what happened to the data on them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (v), identify the stage of the data lifecycle concerned and recommend the control HLAL should implement at that stage.
parts.answer:
(i) Stage: Creation / Acquisition. At this stage accuracy should be established, ownership defined and classification applied, especially where the data contains personally identifiable information (PII). Control: classify CNIC copies and medical reports as restricted at the point of capture, and record a data owner for policyholder data, so that the right protections follow the data from the start.
(ii) Stage: Storage. Data should be placed in a secure environment with encryption, access controls and backups applied. Control: encrypt the policy database at rest (for example AES-256) and implement regular, tested backups held securely away from the server.
(iii) Stage: Usage. Only authorised users should access data and usage should be logged. Control: implement role-based access so agents can see only their own policyholders' files and medical reports are limited to underwriting staff, and log every access for review.
(iv) Stage: Archiving. Data no longer in active use but still of business, legal or historical value should be moved to long-term, lower-cost storage and is typically read-only. Control: move matured policies to an archive in line with HLAL's retention requirements, make the archive read-only, and remove them from the live system.
(v) Stage: Deletion / Disposal. Data no longer needed should be permanently removed using secure methods, and the destruction documented. Control: wipe laptops (data wiping or cryptographic erasure) before reissue or disposal, and keep a destruction record for each device.
(1 mark for the correct stage and 1 mark for a relevant control, per issue, max 10.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the difference between archiving and disposal of data, and why HLAL should document the destruction of data.
parts.answer:
Archiving moves data that is no longer in active use, but still has business, legal or historical value, to long-term, lower-cost storage, usually read-only, so it can be retrieved if needed (for example for a later claim dispute or regulatory request). Disposal permanently removes data once it is no longer needed and any retention period has expired, using secure methods such as shredding, data wiping or cryptographic erasure.
Documenting destruction provides evidence, for auditors and regulators, that data was disposed of properly, at the right time and by a secure method. It shows HLAL did not lose or leak sensitive policyholder data, and it allows HLAL to answer queries about whether a particular record still exists.
(1 mark for archiving, 1 for disposal, 1 for the reason for documentation, max 3.)

secb.topic: Levels of data governance and operational data issues
secb.scenario:
Kohat Cement Limited (KCL), a listed company, has launched a data governance programme after repeated errors in its management reports. The following activities have taken place during the first year:
(i) The board approved a policy declaring data a strategic asset and aligning data management with KCL's business objectives.
(ii) The CFO agreed to act as executive sponsor and now chairs a newly formed data governance council.
(iii) The IT director prepared a 12-month implementation plan with timelines for each department.
(iv) A standard naming convention and code format for all raw materials and spare parts was introduced.
(v) Data stewards were appointed for the vendor master file and the customer master file.
(vi) A data steward runs a routine every Monday to identify duplicate vendor records.
(vii) The IT helpdesk grants ERP access according to each employee's job role.
(viii) Storekeepers attended training on correct data entry in the inventory module.
The vendor master data steward's first monthly report contained these findings:
(1) The same supplier is spelled differently in the procurement and finance systems.
(2) Dates are recorded as DD/MM/YYYY at the plant but MM/DD/YYYY at head office.
(3) Several employee records have no NTN.
(4) The daily dispatch dashboard does not show the latest dispatches until the following afternoon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain any three objectives of data governance that KCL should expect its programme to achieve.
parts.answer:
Any three of the following, applied to KCL:
1. Minimise risks: identify and mitigate the risks of data breaches, non-compliance and poor data quality, such as the errors in KCL's management reports.
2. Establish internal rules for data use: define who may access, use and share data across KCL's departments.
3. Implement compliance requirements: meet legal and regulatory obligations on privacy and security, including the SECP Guidelines for Cyber Security that apply to a listed company.
4. Improve communication: standardise data practices so everyone means the same thing, for example the same material codes at plant and head office.
5. Increase data value: make data good enough to be genuinely useful for decisions.
6. Facilitate administration and reduce costs: reduce complexity and avoid duplication and inefficiency in managing data.
7. Ensure organisational sustainability: support KCL's long-term viability.
(1 mark per objective explained, max 3.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the activities (i) to (viii) as belonging to the strategic, tactical or operational level of data governance, giving a brief reason.
parts.answer:
(i) Strategic: setting the vision and policy for data as a strategic asset and aligning it with business objectives.
(ii) Strategic: securing executive sponsorship (CFO) and establishing a data governance council are strategic activities that set direction.
(iii) Tactical: developing implementation plans and timelines translates the strategy into actionable plans.
(iv) Tactical: implementing data standards such as naming conventions and formats bridges strategy and execution.
(v) Tactical: defining roles by appointing data stewards for each master file is part of turning strategy into a working structure.
(vi) Operational: running data quality checks such as a weekly duplicate search is day-to-day execution.
(vii) Operational: applying access controls on a role basis (RBAC) is day-to-day execution.
(viii) Operational: user training is an operational governance activity carried out routinely.
(1 mark per activity correctly classified with reason, max 8.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Identify the type of common operational data issue illustrated by each of the steward's four findings, and recommend how each should be resolved.
parts.answer:
(1) Data inconsistency: the same supplier's name differs between procurement and finance. Resolve by agreeing one master vendor record and name standard, and correcting the other system to match.
(2) Data format issue: different date formats between plant and head office. Resolve by adopting a single date format standard across all systems and converting existing records.
(3) Missing / incomplete data: employee records without NTN. Resolve by collecting the missing NTNs and making NTN a mandatory field at entry.
(4) Data latency / timeliness: the dashboard does not reflect the latest transactions. Resolve by increasing the refresh frequency or moving to real-time data feeds from the dispatch system.
(1 mark per finding: 1/2 for the issue type, 1/2 for a relevant resolution, max 4.)

secb.scenario:
Ravi Securities Limited (RSL) is a stock brokerage in Lahore licensed by SECP. RSL is introducing a data classification scheme so that its security controls match the sensitivity of each type of data. The Chief Information Officer (CIO) has listed the following data:
(i) Daily market commentary that RSL publishes on its website.
(ii) The staff leave policy and the office's standard operating procedures.
(iii) Clients' trading account balances and portfolio holdings.
(iv) Clients' CNIC copies and debit card numbers stored for fee collection.
(v) The source code of RSL's proprietary trading algorithm.
(vi) Salaries of RSL's employees.
The CIO has also asked whether RSL should use only the sensitivity-based model, or whether other classification models would help.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Using the sensitivity-based model, classify each of the six types of data listed, giving a reason for each.
parts.answer:
(i) Market commentary on the website: Public. It is intended to be shared openly and disclosure creates no risk.
(ii) Leave policy and SOPs: Internal. They are for use within RSL only, but disclosure would cause little harm.
(iii) Client balances and holdings: Confidential. Customer financial data would harm clients and RSL if disclosed, so access must be restricted.
(iv) CNIC copies and debit card numbers: Restricted. This is personally identifiable information and card data, which is highly sensitive and subject to strict legal and contractual obligations (card data is subject to PCI DSS).
(v) Trading algorithm source code: Confidential. It is a trade secret whose disclosure would damage RSL's competitive position. (Restricted is equally acceptable: the Study Text's sensitivity table places trade secrets under Restricted, while its list of classification types places them under Confidential.)
(vi) Employee salaries: Confidential. Salary data could cause harm if disclosed and access must be restricted to authorised HR and finance staff.
(1 mark per item correctly classified with reason, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain three other data classification models that RSL could use alongside the sensitivity-based model, showing how each would apply to RSL.
parts.answer:
1. Role-based model: classifies data by who needs to know it, such as executive level, departmental level and general staff. At RSL, the trading algorithm would be restricted to senior management and the development team, client portfolios to the relevant dealers and back office, and SOPs to all staff.
2. Compliance-based model: aligns classes with legal and regulatory categories, such as PII, PHI (health information), financial data and sensitive business information. At RSL, CNIC copies would be tagged PII, card numbers and account balances as financial data, and the algorithm as sensitive business information, so the regulatory obligations attached to each category can be applied and evidenced to SECP.
3. Lifecycle-based model: classifies data by its stage, namely draft/temporary, active/in use, historical/archived and expired/ready for deletion. At RSL, draft research notes, current client portfolios, closed client accounts kept for the retention period, and records whose retention period has ended would each be handled differently, supporting archiving and secure disposal.
(1 mark for explaining each model and 1 mark for applying it to RSL, max 6.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain whether the government classification model is appropriate for RSL, and name two frameworks RSL could adopt to guide its classification scheme.
parts.answer:
The government model (Unclassified, Restricted, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) is used in the public sector and defence for national security information. It is not appropriate for a private brokerage, whose needs are better met by the sensitivity, role, compliance and lifecycle models.
RSL could use ISO/IEC 27001 or the NIST Cybersecurity Framework to guide its classification scheme and the controls attached to each level.
(1 mark for the government model point, 1 mark for naming both frameworks, max 2.)

secb.topic: Data storage options and emerging trends
secb.scenario:
Faisalabad Weaving Mills Limited (FWML) has installed 400 IoT-enabled looms. Each loom has sensors that report temperature, vibration and thread tension every second. All data is currently sent to an ageing on-premises server at the head office, which is close to full capacity. FWML has a small IT team of three people.
FWML's management has identified the following needs:
(i) If a sensor detects abnormal vibration, the loom must be stopped within a fraction of a second to prevent damage; delays in sending data to the head office server have already caused two breakdowns.
(ii) A major European buyer requires proof of the origin of the cotton used in each consignment, in a record that cannot be altered after it is created.
(iii) The analytics team wants to keep years of raw sensor readings, together with buyer emails and photographs of fabric defects, for future big data analysis.
FWML's directors are also debating whether to replace the head office server, move to the cloud, or adopt a hybrid approach. Payroll and costing data are regarded as highly sensitive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the on-premises, cloud and hybrid storage options, discussing the trade-offs of each for FWML.
parts.answer:
1. On-premises storage: data is stored on physical servers that FWML owns and manages. Advantages: greater control and customisation, and sensitive payroll and costing data stays within FWML. Trade-offs: high capital cost (FWML would have to buy a new, larger server), ongoing maintenance burden, and the need for in-house IT expertise, which a three-person team may lack as sensor data grows.
2. Cloud storage: data is stored on remote servers run by a third party (for example AWS, Azure or Google Cloud). Advantages: scalable, flexible and cost-efficient; FWML can add capacity as the volume of loom data grows without buying hardware. Trade-offs: FWML becomes dependent on the vendor's security and on internet connectivity, which matters for a mill relying on continuous data flow and for sensitive data.
3. Hybrid storage: a combination of the two, with sensitive data kept on-premises and less critical data in the cloud. It balances control and scalability, but requires FWML to manage two environments and decide carefully which data goes where.
(1 mark for explaining each option and 1 mark for its trade-offs applied to FWML, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate storage option for FWML, justifying your recommendation.
parts.answer:
A hybrid approach is recommended.
1. Sensitive data such as payroll and costing can be kept on-premises (on a modest replacement server), where FWML retains full control.
2. The fast-growing, less sensitive sensor data and analytics data can be stored in the cloud, which scales cost-efficiently without FWML buying ever larger servers.
3. This also suits FWML's small IT team, because the cloud provider manages the infrastructure for the largest data volumes, while internet dependency is limited to the less critical data.
(1 mark for a justified recommendation, up to 2 further marks for reasons linked to the scenario, max 3. A well-argued alternative may earn credit.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: For each of the needs (i) to (iii), recommend an appropriate emerging storage approach and explain why it is suitable.
parts.answer:
(i) Edge storage: storing and processing data close to where it is generated, on or near the IoT looms, rather than sending it to a distant server. This reduces latency and supports real-time processing, so an abnormal vibration reading can trigger an immediate stop of the loom without waiting for a round trip to head office, preventing further breakdowns.
(ii) Blockchain-based storage: decentralised storage that provides security and immutability, and is useful for supply chain tracking. Each step of the cotton's journey, from ginner to spinning to weaving, can be recorded in a ledger that cannot be altered after it is written, giving the European buyer trustworthy proof of origin.
(iii) Data lake: a centralised repository that holds raw structured and unstructured data at massive scale for use with big data analytics. It can store years of raw sensor readings (structured or semi-structured) together with emails and defect photographs (unstructured) in their original form for future analysis.
(1 mark for the correct approach and 1 mark for its justification, per need, max 6.)

secb.scenario:
Indus Valley University (IVU) in Hyderabad maintains a student fee system with two related tables, Students and Fee Payments. Extracts are shown in Table 1 and Table 2. In the Fee Payments table, Student ID is meant to link each payment to a student in the Students table.
The internal auditor has reported the following issues:
(i) Two different students have been given the same Student ID, S-1045.
(ii) A fee payment of Rs. 85,000 is recorded against Student ID S-2210, which does not exist in the Students table.
(iii) The system accepted a fee payment of minus Rs. 40,000 and a payment date of 31-Feb-2026.
