(iv) A power outage during the fee deadline week corrupted part of the database; the server has no backup power supply.
(v) A fee clerk changed a student's scholarship from 25% to 75%. The previous value was overwritten and there is no record of who made the change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (iv), identify the type of data integrity that has been compromised and recommend an appropriate control.
parts.answer:
(i) Entity integrity is compromised: each record must be uniquely identifiable. Control: define Student ID as the primary key of the Students table, so the database rejects any duplicate (and any blank) Student ID; correct the duplicate by issuing one student a new ID.
(ii) Referential integrity is compromised: related tables are inconsistent, because a payment refers to a student who does not exist. Control: define Student ID in Fee Payments as a foreign key referencing the Students table's primary key, so a payment can only be recorded for a valid student; investigate receipt R-502.
(iii) Logical integrity is compromised: the data is not correct and consistent within the database. Control: implement constraints and validation rules, such as a range check that fee amounts must be greater than zero and a format/date check that rejects impossible dates such as 31 February.
(iv) Physical integrity is compromised: data has been damaged by a physical disruption (power outage). Control: install an uninterruptible power supply and backup generator for the server, and take regular backups so the database can be restored after a failure.
(1 mark for the correct integrity type and 1 mark for a relevant control, per issue, max 8.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the five key practices for maintaining data integrity, indicating which practices would have prevented or detected issue (v).
parts.answer:
1. Data validation: checks at entry, such as range and format checks, to ensure accuracy (for example, the scholarship percentage must be within an approved range and above a limit requires approval).
2. Auditing and monitoring: regularly reviewing data processes to catch discrepancies; a periodic review of scholarship changes would have detected the 25% to 75% change.
3. Access controls: limiting who may modify data using role-based access control (RBAC). A fee clerk's role should not allow changes to scholarship percentages, which should be restricted to the scholarship committee or an authorised officer. This would have prevented issue (v).
4. Version control: tracking changes to prevent unintended overwrites and preserve an audit trail. With version control, the previous 25% value, the user who changed it and the time of change would have been recorded, so the change could be detected and reversed.
5. Data backups: enabling recovery from corruption or loss, also relevant to issue (iv).
Issue (v) would have been prevented mainly by access controls, and detected through version control and auditing and monitoring.
(1 mark per practice explained, with credit for correctly linking practices to issue (v), max 5.)

secb.topic: Data security practices and emerging threats
secb.scenario:
Zarq Pay (Private) Limited (ZPL) is an electronic money institution in Islamabad regulated by the State Bank of Pakistan. It operates a mobile wallet used by 1.2 million customers. Following a series of incidents, ZPL's risk committee has listed the following weaknesses:
(i) Customer names, CNIC numbers and wallet balances are stored in the database in plain readable form.
(ii) Staff log in to the back-office system with a password only. Last month an attacker used a password obtained through a fake email to log in as a customer service officer.
(iii) There is no tool that monitors or filters network traffic. Investigators later found that an outsider had been scanning ZPL's systems for several weeks.
(iv) Staff laptops have no antivirus software and are not encrypted. One laptop containing customer data was left in a taxi.
(v) A departing employee emailed a file containing 50,000 customer phone numbers to his personal email address.
(vi) Once remote contractors connect through the VPN, they are treated as trusted and can reach any internal system without further checks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the weaknesses (i) to (vi), recommend the most appropriate data security practice and explain how it would address the weakness.
parts.answer:
(i) Encryption: encode data so that only someone with the correct key can read it, using AES-256 for data at rest and TLS for data in transit. Even if the database is accessed or copied, CNIC numbers and balances would be unreadable without the key.
(ii) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): require two or more forms of verification, such as a password plus an SMS code or biometric. A stolen password alone would no longer allow the attacker to log in as the customer service officer.
(iii) Firewalls and Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS): monitor and filter network traffic to detect and block malicious activity. Weeks of scanning would have been blocked by the firewall or raised alerts through the IDS, allowing ZPL to respond early.
(iv) Endpoint security: secure the devices that access data through antivirus and device encryption. With full-disk encryption, the laptop left in the taxi would not expose customer data, and antivirus would protect laptops from malware.
(v) Data Loss Prevention (DLP): monitor and prevent unauthorised data exfiltration, for example by blocking files containing customer data from being emailed to external addresses. The 50,000 phone numbers would have been blocked and the attempt flagged.
(vi) Zero Trust Architecture: 'never trust, always verify'. Access is granted only after continuous verification of identity and context, regardless of whether the user is already inside the network. Contractors would be verified for each system and given access only to what they need.
(1 mark for the correct practice and 1 mark for explaining how it addresses the weakness, per item, max 12.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the emerging threat illustrated by weakness (v), and explain one other emerging threat that ZPL faces, recommending a mitigation for each.
parts.answer:
Weakness (v) is an insider threat: a risk from an employee or contractor who already has legitimate access. Mitigation: least-privilege access so staff can only reach the data their role needs, and behaviour monitoring to detect unusual activity such as bulk downloads before an employee leaves.
Other emerging threats (either):
1. Ransomware: malicious software that encrypts ZPL's data and demands payment to release it. Mitigation: regular, tested backups kept separately, plus phishing-awareness training, since ransomware often arrives through fake emails like the one in weakness (ii).
2. AI-powered attacks: attackers using AI to create highly convincing phishing messages or to automate the exploitation of vulnerabilities. Mitigation: AI-driven threat detection.
(1 mark for identifying insider threat with mitigation, up to 2 marks for the other threat and its mitigation, max 3.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what is meant by metadata, describe its three types with an example of each, and explain the benefits of metadata management.
parts.answer:
Metadata is 'data about data'. It provides the context, such as definitions, origin, format and relationships, that makes data discoverable and usable.
Three types:
1. Descriptive metadata: describes the content, for example the title, author and keywords of a board report stored in a document system.
2. Structural metadata: defines how data is organised, for example a database schema showing the tables and fields in a payroll database, or a file structure.
3. Administrative metadata: supports management of the data, for example access permissions, creation date and retention policy attached to a customer file.
Benefits of metadata management:
1. Improves discoverability, so users can find and understand the data they need.
2. Supports compliance by documenting data lineage, showing where data came from and how it changed.
3. Gives teams a shared understanding of data assets, so different departments use the same definitions.
(1 mark for the definition, 1 mark per type with example (max 3), up to 2 marks for benefits, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the term data lineage and why it is valuable to an external auditor.
parts.answer:
Data lineage is the history of data, showing how it moves and is transformed from its source system to its final destination, such as a figure in the financial statements.
It is valuable to an auditor because it provides traceability: the auditor can follow a reported number back to the original transactions and see every transformation along the way. This builds trust that the reported figures are complete and accurate, and it is exactly the evidence an auditor asks for.
(1 mark for the definition, 1 mark for its value to the auditor, max 2.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Identify the most relevant Pakistani regulation or framework for each of the following situations, with a brief reason: (i) a commercial bank designing its incident response and technology audit arrangements; (ii) a listed manufacturing company strengthening protection of client and business data; (iii) a former employee who hacks into a company's database; (iv) a company that wishes to sign supply contracts electronically.
parts.answer:
(i) SBP Enterprise Technology Governance and Risk Management Framework (ETGRMF): it mandates robust governance and risk management for financial institutions, including data protection, incident response and technology audits.
(ii) SECP Guidelines for Cyber Security: they direct corporations, such as listed companies, to enhance cybersecurity and protect sensitive business and client data.
(iii) Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016: it criminalises hacking, identity theft and cyber terrorism, so the former employee's unauthorised access is an offence under PECA.
(iv) Electronic Transactions Ordinance (ETO) 2002: it legalises electronic transactions and signatures, giving electronically signed contracts legal validity.
(1 mark per situation correctly matched with reason, max 4.)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Required: Explain homomorphic encryption and federated learning as forms of privacy-enhancing computation, giving an example of how each could be used.
parts.answer:
Privacy-Enhancing Computation (PEC) enables data to be processed without exposing it.
1. Homomorphic encryption allows computation to be performed directly on encrypted data without decrypting it first. Example: a microfinance bank could let an external analytics firm calculate risk scores on encrypted borrower data, without the firm ever seeing the actual borrower values.
2. Federated learning trains a machine-learning model across many decentralised devices or locations that hold their own local data, without the data leaving those locations; only model updates are shared. Example: several hospitals in different cities could build a shared model predicting complications without moving any patient records from their own premises.
(1 mark for explaining each technique and 1/2 mark for each relevant example, max 3.)

secb.topic: Classifying the four stages of analytics
secb.scenario:
Shaheen Freight Services Limited (SFS) operates a fleet of 250 trucks from Karachi, carrying goods to Lahore, Quetta and Peshawar. SFS's new analytics team has started the following work:
(i) A monthly dashboard showing deliveries completed on each route and the percentage delivered on time.
(ii) An investigation into why on-time delivery on the Karachi-Quetta route fell from 90% to 72%, examining breakdown records, road closures and loading delays.
(iii) A model that uses maintenance history and mileage to estimate which trucks are likely to break down next month.
(iv) A system that recommends the allocation of trucks to routes each week so that total fuel cost is minimised while all orders are delivered.
(v) A forecast of freight demand during the wheat harvest season, based on bookings in previous years.
(vi) An analysis of fuel records and tracker data to find the root cause of a sharp rise in fuel cost per kilometre in the last quarter.
(vii) A report ranking SFS's top ten customers by revenue for last year.
(viii) A tool that recommends the number of drivers to roster on each shift so that forecast demand is met at the lowest labour cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the activities (i) to (viii) into the appropriate stage of data analytics, giving a reason for each.
parts.answer:
(i) Descriptive analytics: it summarises historical data (deliveries and on-time percentage) to show what happened.
(ii) Diagnostic analytics: it digs into the data to find why on-time delivery fell, looking for correlations and root causes.
(iii) Predictive analytics: it uses historical data and statistical or machine-learning models to forecast what is likely to happen (future breakdowns).
(iv) Prescriptive analytics: it goes beyond prediction to recommend the best course of action, using optimisation to minimise fuel cost.
(v) Predictive analytics: it forecasts future demand from historical bookings.
(vi) Diagnostic analytics: it seeks the root cause of an anomaly (the rise in fuel cost), answering 'why did it happen?'
(vii) Descriptive analytics: it aggregates last year's data to show what happened, using a simple ranking.
(viii) Prescriptive analytics: it recommends the optimal action (the roster) to meet forecast demand at the lowest cost.
(1 mark per activity correctly classified with reason, max 8. Classification without a reason earns 1/2 mark.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Using examples from SFS, explain how a student can distinguish (1) descriptive from diagnostic analytics and (2) predictive from prescriptive analytics.
parts.answer:
Each stage answers a different question, and the wording of the activity signals the stage.
1. Descriptive versus diagnostic: descriptive answers 'What happened?' and only summarises past data using totals, averages, percentages and charts, such as the on-time dashboard in (i). Diagnostic answers 'Why did it happen?' and uses statistical techniques and data mining to find correlations and root causes, such as the investigation of the Karachi-Quetta decline in (ii). Words such as 'why', 'cause' or 'underlying reasons' indicate diagnostic.
2. Predictive versus prescriptive: predictive answers 'What is likely to happen?' and stops at a forecast, such as the breakdown estimate in (iii). Prescriptive answers 'What should we do about it?' and combines predictions with optimisation and decision-support tools to recommend an action, such as the truck allocation in (iv). Words such as 'recommend', 'optimal' or 'minimise cost' indicate prescriptive.
(2 marks per distinction properly explained with an SFS example, max 4.)

secb.topic: Stages of the data analytics cycle
secb.scenario:
Sheikhupura Sugar Mills Limited (SSML) wants to improve its sugar recovery rate, which has been below the industry average for three seasons. The following activities, listed in random order, were carried out in an analytics project:
A. Charts of recovery rate by cane variety and by grower were plotted, and some unusual values were spotted.
B. Weighbridge records, laboratory test results and a questionnaire completed by growers were gathered.
C. A regression model was built to measure how the delay between cutting and crushing affects recovery.
D. Duplicate weighbridge slips were removed, missing laboratory values were dealt with and cane weights recorded in maunds were converted into kilograms.
E. The team concluded that cane crushed more than 48 hours after cutting gives a noticeably lower recovery, and explained what this means for SSML.
F. Management introduced a token system requiring growers to deliver cane within 24 hours of cutting.
G. Recovery rates were tracked during the following season and the model was refined using the new data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Arrange the activities A to G in the correct order of the data analytics cycle, naming the stage that each activity represents.
parts.answer:
1. B: Data collection. Gathering data from databases (weighbridge, laboratory) and surveys (growers' questionnaire); the data must be relevant, accurate and comprehensive.
2. D: Data cleaning (cleansing or scrubbing). Removing duplicates, handling missing values, correcting errors and normalising formats (maunds into kilograms).
3. A: Data exploration. Creating summary statistics and visualisations to get a feel for the data and identify patterns, outliers and relationships.
4. C: Data modelling. Building a model, here a regression model, to quantify the relationship between delay and recovery.
5. E: Interpretation and insight generation. Translating the model output into meaningful business insight: delays over 48 hours reduce recovery.
6. F: Decision-making and action. Acting on the insight by changing the process (the 24-hour token system).
7. G: Monitoring and optimisation. Tracking the impact of the decision and refining the model, repeating the cycle if necessary.
(1 mark per activity placed in the correct position with the correct stage name, max 7.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why the data analytics cycle is described as iterative, with reference to SSML.
parts.answer:
The cycle is iterative because each stage informs the next and the whole cycle can be repeated to refine understanding, creating a feedback loop for continuous improvement.
At SSML, monitoring next season's recovery (stage 7) feeds back into data collection (stage 1): the new season's weighbridge and laboratory data is collected, cleaned and used to refine the model. If recovery does not improve as expected, the team may find other causes (for example cane variety or mill efficiency) and revise its action. Earlier stages can also be revisited, for example if exploration reveals errors that send the team back to cleaning.
(1 mark for the definition, up to 2 marks for application to SSML, max 3.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between data cleaning and data exploration, and explain why cleaning must come first.
parts.answer:
Data cleaning is about fixing the data: removing duplicates, handling missing values, correcting errors and normalising formats, as SSML did in activity D. Data exploration is about understanding the data: producing summary statistics and visualisations to see distributions, patterns, outliers and relationships, as in activity A.
Cleaning must come first because you cannot sensibly explore data that has not been cleaned. Even small errors distort the outcome: for example, duplicate weighbridge slips would overstate cane received, and weights in mixed units (maunds and kilograms) would make recovery charts meaningless, leading the team to see false patterns.
(1 mark for each correct description, 1 mark for the reason for sequence, max 3.)

secb.scenario:
Rehmat Chemists (Private) Limited (RCL) operates 25 pharmacies in Rawalpindi and Islamabad. RCL built a model to forecast weekly demand for each medicine, but the forecasts have been very poor, causing both stock-outs and expired stock. A review of the sales data used by the model found:
(i) Some outlets record sale dates as DD/MM/YYYY while others use MM/DD/YYYY.
(ii) Some outlets record quantities in strips of tablets, while others record them in boxes of ten strips.
(iii) The same medicine appears under three different product names and codes, for example 'Paracetamol 500mg', 'Paracetamol 500 mg tab' and 'PCM-500'.
(iv) For three weeks, while the point-of-sale system at four outlets was offline, quantity fields were left blank.
(v) One outlet shows a single sale of 50,000 boxes of cough syrup, which is far above its normal weekly sales of about 40 boxes and appears to be a keying error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (v), explain the data cleaning task that RCL should have performed and why it matters for the demand forecast.
parts.answer:
(i) Normalising formats: convert all dates to one standard format. Without this, a sale on 03/04 could be read as 3 April or 4 March, placing sales in the wrong week and distorting the weekly demand pattern the model learns.
(ii) Normalising units: convert all quantities to a single unit, for example strips (one box = ten strips). Otherwise sales at box-recording outlets appear ten times smaller than they are, and the model under-forecasts demand there.
(iii) Removing duplicates and correcting errors: map the three names and codes to a single product master code. Otherwise demand for one medicine is split across three items, each looking smaller than true demand, causing stock-outs.
(iv) Handling missing values: the blank quantity fields should be filled from another source (for example stock movement records), estimated, or excluded from the analysis, with the treatment documented. Leaving blanks or treating them as zero would make demand appear to collapse for three weeks.
(v) Correcting errors: investigate the 50,000 box entry against the invoice and correct it (or remove it if it cannot be verified). Left in place, a single error would inflate the average and cause the model to forecast huge demand and RCL to over-order stock that expires.
(1 mark for the correct cleaning task and 1 mark for its impact on the forecast, per issue, max 10.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the principle of 'garbage in, garbage out' in relation to RCL's model, and why good data governance must come before analytics.
parts.answer:
'Garbage in, garbage out' means that analytics is only as good as the data fed into it: inaccurate, incomplete or inconsistent data produces flawed insights however sophisticated the model is. RCL's forecasts failed not because the mathematics was wrong but because the input data was never cleaned.
Good governance must come first because, without data standards (one date format, one unit, one product master) and a data steward enforcing them at the point of entry, the same problems will recur every week and cleaning becomes an endless manual task. Data quality is the single greatest challenge in analytics, so RCL should fix it at source.
(1 mark for explaining the principle, 1 for applying it to RCL, 1 for the governance link, max 3.)

secb.topic: Applying the four stages to a business problem
secb.scenario:
Margalla Power Distribution Limited (MPDL) distributes electricity to around 900,000 consumers in northern Punjab. Its line losses (electricity supplied but not billed or recovered) have increased from 14% to 19% over two years. At a recent board meeting, the directors raised the following questions:
(i) 'Which feeders and divisions account for the increase, and how has the loss percentage moved month by month?'
(ii) 'Is the increase caused by electricity theft, faulty meters, ageing transformers or billing errors?'
(iii) 'If we change nothing, what will our line losses be next summer, and which feeders are most at risk?'
(iv) 'Given our limited budget, where should we deploy inspection teams and replace meters to reduce losses the most?'
The CEO has suggested skipping the first two questions and buying a software package that 'tells us what to do'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the stage of data analytics needed to answer each of the board's four questions and explain how MPDL would apply each stage.
parts.answer:
(i) Descriptive analytics ('What happened?'): summarise historical billing and supply data using percentages, averages and charts, showing line losses by feeder, division and month, so the board can see where the increase from 14% to 19% is concentrated.
(ii) Diagnostic analytics ('Why did it happen?'): use statistical techniques and data mining to find correlations and root causes, for example comparing losses with meter-fault records, transformer age, inspection findings on theft and billing exception reports, to identify which factor drives the increase on each feeder.
(iii) Predictive analytics ('What is likely to happen?'): use historical data with statistical or machine-learning models to forecast next summer's line losses if nothing changes, and score each feeder by its risk of high losses, taking account of seasonal demand.
(iv) Prescriptive analytics ('What should we do about it?'): combine the predictions with optimisation techniques and decision-support tools to recommend the best allocation of the limited budget, for example which feeders to inspect first and which meters to replace, to achieve the largest reduction in losses per rupee spent.
(1 mark for the correct stage and 1 mark for applying it to MPDL, per question, max 8.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Advise the CEO on his suggestion to skip directly to a tool that 'tells us what to do'.
parts.answer:
1. The four stages build on each other. Prescriptive analytics relies on predictions, and predictions rely on an accurate understanding of past events and their causes; skipping descriptive and diagnostic work means the recommendations rest on an untested understanding of the problem.
2. Without diagnostic analysis MPDL may treat the wrong cause, for example replacing meters on feeders where the real problem is theft or ageing transformers, wasting the limited budget.
3. Descriptive analysis is also the foundation for checking data quality: if billing data is inaccurate or incomplete, any package will produce confidently wrong advice ('garbage in, garbage out').
4. Prescriptive analytics is the most complex stage, and although human input decreases as an organisation moves towards it, management still needs to understand and challenge the recommendations. MPDL should therefore build descriptive and diagnostic capability first, then move to predictive and prescriptive tools.
(1 mark per valid point, max 4.)

secb.topic: Benefits and challenges of data analytics
secb.scenario:
Gujranwala Home Appliances Limited (GHAL) manufactures fans, washing machines and water coolers, selling through 600 dealers across Pakistan. The board is considering a PKR 80 million investment in a data analytics function.
Director A argues that analytics would help GHAL decide which products to make for each season, cut its high warranty repair costs and respond faster than competitors who are introducing inverter fans.
Director B is concerned because:
(i) Dealer sales are reported on spreadsheets in different layouts, and sales figures in the finance system do not agree with those in the sales department's records.
(ii) GHAL's staff are skilled in spreadsheets but nobody has experience of building or interpreting statistical models.
(iii) The analytics plan involves using warranty registration data containing customers' names, CNIC numbers, phone numbers and addresses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain three benefits that GHAL could obtain from data analytics, relating each to Director A's arguments.
parts.answer:
1. Improved decision-making: decisions are based on facts rather than intuition, so they are more accurate and timely. GHAL could use past seasonal sales by region to decide how many fans versus water coolers to produce for each season, instead of relying on managers' judgement, reducing unsold stock and stock-outs.
2. Increased efficiency: analytics makes inefficiencies and areas for improvement visible, leading to streamlined processes and cost savings. Analysing warranty claims by model, component and production batch would reveal which faults drive repair costs, so GHAL can fix the root cause in production.
3. Competitive advantage: faster response to market changes, optimised operations and a better understanding of customer needs. By tracking dealer sales and customer preferences, GHAL could detect the shift towards inverter fans early and respond before competitors take its market share.
(1 mark for each benefit explained and 1 mark for applying it to GHAL, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the challenges of data analytics illustrated by each of Director B's concerns, and recommend how GHAL should address each.
parts.answer:
(i) Data quality: analytics needs high-quality data, and inaccurate, incomplete or inconsistent data produces flawed insights ('garbage in, garbage out'). Dealer spreadsheets in different layouts and conflicting sales figures mean any model will produce unreliable results. Recommendation: standardise dealer reporting (a common template or portal), reconcile and clean the historical data, and appoint a data steward to own sales data before modelling begins.
(ii) Skills gap: organisations often lack staff who can build and interpret models. Without these skills, GHAL may build models that are wrong or misread their output. Recommendation: recruit or contract a small number of analysts, and train existing finance and sales staff to interpret analytics outputs.
(iii) Privacy and ethics: the more data analysed about people, the greater the privacy and regulatory exposure. CNIC numbers, phone numbers and addresses are sensitive personal data. Recommendation: use only the data needed for the analysis, remove or mask identifying fields where possible, restrict and log access, secure the data, and be transparent with customers about how warranty data is used.
(1 mark for explaining the challenge and 1 mark for a relevant recommendation, per concern, max 6.)

secb.topic: Analytics in finance and the maturity model
secb.scenario: Saffron Asset Management Limited (SAML) is an SECP-licensed asset management company in Karachi managing equity and income funds for about 40,000 investors. At present, SAML's research team produces monthly reports showing each fund's past returns and investor inflows and outflows. The chief executive wants SAML to use analytics more extensively in its investment and investor-relations activities. Some fund managers fear that more advanced analytics will 'replace their judgement'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how SAML could apply each of the four stages of data analytics to its business, giving a specific example for each stage.
parts.answer:
1. Descriptive analytics (What happened?): summarising historical data to show past events. SAML already does this, for example reporting each fund's monthly returns, and it could extend it by analysing investor transaction data to identify patterns in investor behaviour, such as when and from which cities redemptions occur.
2. Diagnostic analytics (Why did it happen?): finding the causes of trends or anomalies. SAML could analyse market data to understand why one equity fund outperformed another, for example by examining sector allocation and individual stock selection, or why redemptions spiked in a particular month.
3. Predictive analytics (What is likely to happen?): using historical data and machine-learning or statistical models to forecast outcomes. SAML could use historical financial data to predict share price movements, or predict which investors are likely to redeem in the coming months.
4. Prescriptive analytics (What should we do about it?): recommending the best course of action using optimisation techniques. Based on predicted market conditions, SAML could recommend investment strategies and portfolio allocations that optimise returns within each fund's risk limits, or recommend which investors to contact with retention offers.
(1 mark for explaining each stage and 1 mark for a relevant SAML example, max 8.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the data analytics maturity model and discuss its implications for SAML's fund managers.
parts.answer:
The data analytics maturity model describes what happens as an organisation moves from hindsight (descriptive) towards foresight (prescriptive): the human input into the decision decreases, while both the complexity of the decision and the value of the information derived increase.
Implications for SAML's fund managers:
1. Their role shifts from compiling and reading reports of past returns towards reviewing and challenging forecasts and recommendations produced by models.
2. SAML gains more valuable information, for example earlier warning of redemptions and better-informed allocation decisions, but the models are more complex and need skilled staff to build and interpret them.
3. Reduced human input does not remove the need for judgement: fund managers remain accountable for investment decisions, so they must understand the models' assumptions and limitations (including data quality) before acting on recommendations. Their fear of being 'replaced' is therefore overstated; their judgement is applied at a higher level.
(1 mark for explaining the model, up to 3 marks for implications applied to SAML, max 4.)

secb.topic: Analytics cycle and four stages compared

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Define data analytics and explain each of the seven stages of the data analytics cycle.
parts.answer:
Data analytics is the process of examining datasets to uncover trends, patterns and insights that inform decision-making, using techniques that range from simple summarisation to advanced machine-learning models. The data analytics cycle is a systematic, iterative approach to turning raw data into actionable insight.
1. Data collection: gathering data from databases, surveys, sensors or web scraping; the data must be relevant, accurate and comprehensive, and may be structured or unstructured.
2. Data cleaning (cleansing or scrubbing): removing duplicates, handling missing values, correcting errors and normalising formats, because even small errors distort the outcome.
3. Data exploration: creating summary statistics, visualisations and reports to understand the data, plotting distributions and looking for patterns, outliers and relationships.
4. Data modelling: building models, from basic descriptive statistics to regression, classification, clustering or time-series forecasting.
5. Interpretation and insight generation: translating the model results into meaningful business insight and determining what they mean for the problem.
6. Decision-making and action: acting on the insight by adjusting strategy, refining processes or launching initiatives.
7. Monitoring and optimisation: tracking the impact of the decision and repeating the cycle if necessary, creating a feedback loop for continuous improvement.
(1 mark for the definition/iterative nature, up to 6 marks for the seven stages at roughly 1 mark per stage, max 7.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Compare the four stages of data analytics, stating for each the question it answers, the techniques it typically uses, and an example from a Pakistani business context.
parts.answer:
1. Descriptive analytics. Question: What happened? Techniques: summarising historical data using averages, percentages, charts and graphs (hindsight). Example: a Lahore retail chain aggregates last quarter's sales to identify its top-selling products and best-performing branches.
2. Diagnostic analytics. Question: Why did it happen? Techniques: statistical techniques and data mining to find correlations and root causes of trends or anomalies. Example: a mobile network operator analyses complaint logs and network data to find why dropped calls rose sharply in one city.
3. Predictive analytics. Question: What is likely to happen? Techniques: machine learning and statistical algorithms applied to historical data to forecast future outcomes. Example: a commercial bank forecasts loan default rates using borrowers' credit scores, employment history and repayment behaviour.
4. Prescriptive analytics. Question: What should we do about it? Techniques: optimisation techniques and decision-support tools that go beyond prediction to recommend the best course of action (foresight). Example: a fertiliser manufacturer determines the ideal production level for each product to meet forecast demand without overproducing.
Overall, moving from descriptive to prescriptive, human input decreases while complexity and the value of information increase.
(2 marks per stage: question, technique and relevant example, max 8.)

secb.scenario:
Thar Agritech (Private) Limited (TAL), based in Hyderabad, provides a mobile app that gives farming advice to 60,000 farmers in Sindh. It sells seeds and fertiliser through the app. TAL recently completed an analytics project:
(i) Data was collected from soil sensors on farms and from farmers' app profiles, which include names, CNIC numbers, phone numbers and land locations.
(ii) After cleaning and exploring the data, the data team built a model producing a 'yield risk score' between 0 and 1 for each farmer.
(iii) The scores were emailed to the sales team as a spreadsheet with no explanation of what the scores meant, what drove them or how reliable they were.
(iv) The sales team assumed that every farmer with a score above 0.5 needed TAL's most expensive fertiliser and sent all of them the same promotional offer.
(v) No one has checked whether yields of these farmers changed, whether the offer was taken up, or whether the model's scores were accurate.
(vi) TAL has also agreed to share the farmer data with a fertiliser manufacturer for a fee. Farmers have not been informed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the stages of the data analytics cycle that TAL performed poorly, with reference to issues (iii) to (v), and explain the consequences for TAL.
parts.answer:
1. Interpretation and insight generation (issue iii): this stage translates model output into meaningful business insight. TAL skipped it: raw scores were sent without explaining what they meant, which factors drove them or how reliable they were. Consequence: the sales team could not understand the results and misread a risk score as a need for one specific product.
2. Decision-making and action (issue iv): action should be based on the insight. Instead a single, arbitrary threshold and one generic offer were applied to all flagged farmers, regardless of the actual cause of their yield risk (for example soil nutrients versus water shortage). Consequence: farmers may be sold expensive fertiliser that does not solve their problem, damaging trust in TAL's advice and wasting farmers' money.
3. Monitoring and optimisation (issue v): this stage tracks the impact of the decision and feeds back into the cycle. TAL has not measured yields, offer uptake or model accuracy. Consequence: TAL cannot tell whether the project worked, cannot improve the model, and may keep repeating a flawed approach.
(1 mark for each correctly identified stage and 1 mark for its consequence, max 6.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend how TAL should carry out the monitoring and optimisation stage for this project.
parts.answer:
1. Define measures of success before the next campaign, for example change in yield per acre, offer take-up rate and farmer satisfaction, and record a baseline.
2. Compare actual outcomes with the model's predictions after the season, for example whether high-score farmers actually had lower yields, to test the model's accuracy.
3. Track outcomes continuously during the season, not only at the end, so that if the offer is not working (for example low take-up or no change in yields) TAL can adjust its action early rather than waiting a full season.
4. Feed the results back into the cycle: collect the new season's data, clean it, refine the model and the threshold, and adjust the recommended actions, repeating the cycle each season for continuous improvement.
(1 mark per relevant recommendation, max 4.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain the privacy and ethical challenge raised by issue (vi) and recommend what TAL should do.
parts.answer:
Analytics brings privacy and ethics challenges: the more data an organisation analyses about people, the greater its privacy and regulatory exposure. TAL holds personal data (names, CNIC numbers, phone numbers and land locations). Sharing it with a fertiliser manufacturer without informing farmers breaches transparency (farmers do not know how their data is used) and privacy (they have lost control of their personal data), and once shared TAL cannot secure it. It also risks farmers' trust in the app.
TAL should stop the sharing until it obtains farmers' explicit, informed consent through a clear in-app notice with an option to refuse, share only the minimum data needed (removing CNIC and contact details where possible), and protect any shared data through contractual and security safeguards.
(1 mark for explaining the challenge, 1 for linking it to TAL's facts, 1 for recommendations, max 3.)

secb.scenario:
Karakoram Telecom Limited (KTL) is a mobile network operator with around 40 million subscribers across Pakistan. KTL's Chief Data Officer has listed the following observations in a paper prepared for the board:
(i) Call detail records, internet session records and SMS logs now add about 6 terabytes of new data every day, and the existing storage arrays are already at 85% capacity.
(ii) During a cricket final, traffic on some cell towers in Lahore and Karachi spikes within minutes. The network operations centre must detect congestion and reroute traffic within seconds, otherwise calls drop.
(iii) KTL's data now includes billing tables, recordings of customer service calls, chat transcripts from its self-care app and status messages from network equipment in JSON format.
(iv) KTL's customer churn model uses complaints posted on social media. Many of these posts come from fake accounts and some are sarcastic jokes rather than genuine complaints. In addition, the subscriber master file contains duplicate subscribers with mistyped CNIC numbers.
(v) Despite spending heavily on analytics, KTL's marketing team still sends the same data bundle offer to every subscriber, and the CFO has asked what return the company is earning from the data it holds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the observations (i) to (v), identify the characteristic (V) of Big Data that it illustrates, briefly explain that characteristic and state its implication for KTL.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Volume. Volume is the sheer amount of data an organisation must store and process, typically terabytes or petabytes. KTL adds about 6 TB a day and its storage is at 85% capacity. Implication: KTL's current storage will be exhausted soon; it needs scalable storage (for example cloud storage) and distributed processing rather than simply buying ever larger arrays.
2. (ii) Velocity. Velocity is the speed at which data is generated and must be processed, often in real time. Tower traffic changes within minutes and congestion must be detected within seconds. Implication: batch reports produced the next day are useless here; KTL needs real-time or near real-time processing, otherwise calls are dropped and customers are lost.
3. (iii) Variety. Variety is the range of formats in which data arrives: structured (billing tables), unstructured (call recordings, chat transcripts) and semi-structured (JSON equipment messages). Implication: KTL cannot hold all of this in one rigid table structure; it needs technologies and integration processes that can store and combine different formats.
4. (iv) Veracity. Veracity is the accuracy and trustworthiness of data. Fake accounts, sarcasm and duplicate subscribers with wrong CNICs all reduce trust in the data. Implication: the churn model may target the wrong customers or miss real churners; KTL needs validation and cleansing (for example de-duplicating on verified CNIC, filtering fake accounts) before relying on the model.
5. (v) Value. Value is the actionable insight and business benefit actually extracted from data. KTL holds huge amounts of data but still sends one generic offer, and the CFO cannot see a return. Implication: at present the data is a cost rather than an asset; KTL must use it to change decisions, for example personalised bundle offers based on each subscriber's usage.
(1 mark for each correctly identified V and 1 mark for explanation with implication to KTL, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Students often confuse Variety and Veracity. Distinguish between these two characteristics, using KTL's situation to illustrate your answer.
parts.answer:
Variety is about the TYPES or formats of data. It asks 'how many different kinds of data are arriving?' At KTL, Variety is shown by the mixture of structured billing tables, unstructured voice recordings and chat transcripts, and semi-structured JSON messages from network equipment. A dataset can have high Variety and still be perfectly accurate.
Veracity is about the TRUSTWORTHINESS or accuracy of data. It asks 'can we believe this data?' At KTL, Veracity is shown by the fake social media accounts, sarcastic posts and duplicate subscriber records with mistyped CNICs. Even a single, neatly structured table (such as the subscriber master file) can have poor Veracity.
The two therefore call for different responses: Variety is handled by storage and integration technologies that accept many formats, while Veracity is handled by validation and data cleansing.
(1 mark for each correct distinction and 1 mark for applying both to KTL, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Thal Agro Industries (TAI), based in Multan, manufactures fertiliser and sells certified seed through 900 dealers in Punjab and Sindh. As part of a new analytics initiative, TAI has started to gather the following data:
(1) Readings from soil moisture and temperature probes installed on 60 demonstration farms.
(2) Sales invoices issued by dealers through point-of-sale terminals, and payments received through mobile wallets.
(3) Comments, likes and shares on TAI's Facebook and X pages, including farmers' complaints about seed germination.
(4) Vibration, temperature and run-time readings recorded automatically by the granulation and bagging machinery at TAI's plant.
(5) Location signals from GPS trackers fitted to TAI's delivery trucks.
(6) Orders placed by large farmers through TAI's online ordering portal.
TAI's management also intends to (a) automatically collect competitor fertiliser prices published on agri-input marketplace websites, (b) analyse the records generated by the servers and firewall supporting its farmer mobile app, and (c) send a feedback form through the app to every farmer after each harvest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the data items (1) to (6) into the appropriate source of Big Data, giving a brief reason for each classification.
parts.answer:
1. Soil moisture and temperature probes: Internet of Things (IoT) devices. These are connected sensors placed in the environment that generate readings continuously without human input.
2. Dealer POS invoices and mobile wallet payments: Transactional data. They record business transactions (sales and payments) from point-of-sale and payment systems.
3. Facebook and X comments, likes and shares: Social media data. It is user-generated content on social platforms and can be used to gauge farmer sentiment, for example spotting germination complaints early.
4. Readings from granulation and bagging machinery: Machine-generated data. It is produced automatically by industrial machinery and is the typical input for predictive maintenance.
5. GPS trackers on delivery trucks: IoT devices. Connected trackers on vehicles continuously transmit location data, useful for route and delivery monitoring.
6. Orders through the online ordering portal: Transactional data. Each order is an e-commerce transaction recorded by the portal.
(1 mark per correct classification with reason, max 6. Item 4 may also be accepted as IoT if the student explains the sensors are connected devices; item 5 may be accepted as machine-generated with justification.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the four methods of Big Data collection and, for each method, explain how TAI is (or would be) using it, with reference to the information given.
parts.answer:
1. Web scraping. This is the automated extraction of data from websites so that it can be stored and analysed. TAI's plan (a) to collect competitor fertiliser prices from agri-input marketplace websites is web scraping. It would let TAI keep its price comparison current daily without staff copying prices by hand, and react quickly to competitor price cuts.
2. Data from sensors. IoT devices placed in the environment or on equipment gather data continuously. TAI already uses this method through the soil probes on demonstration farms (data item 1), the plant machinery readings (item 4) and the GPS trackers (item 5). For example, soil moisture and temperature data can show which fertiliser and seed perform best under different conditions.
3. Log files. Log files are records generated by servers, applications and networks, containing details of user interactions, errors, performance and security events. TAI's plan (b) to analyse records from the servers and firewall behind its farmer app uses log files. They would show how farmers use the app, where it crashes or slows down, and any attempted intrusions.
4. Surveys and user-generated data. Polls, feedback forms and content created by users are collected and aggregated at scale. TAI's plan (c) to send a post-harvest feedback form to every farmer is this method. It gives TAI direct feedback on seed and fertiliser performance, complementing the less reliable comments it gathers from social media.
(1 mark for explaining each method and 1 mark for correctly linking it to TAI, max 8)

secb.scenario:
Saadat Holdings (SH) is a diversified group with three subsidiaries:
(i) Saadat Health operates four hospitals in Lahore and Faisalabad and holds electronic patient records, laboratory results and admission data.
(ii) GadgetGhar is an online electronics store that records every customer's browsing history, searches and purchases.
(iii) Saadat Auto Parts manufactures brake and suspension components in Sheikhupura for car assemblers. Its production lines have recently been fitted with sensors.
The group has invested PKR 180 million in data storage and analytics licences over two years. At the latest board meeting the Group CFO remarked: 'We have collected more data than ever, but I cannot point to a single decision in any subsidiary that has changed because of it.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each subsidiary, explain how Big Data could be applied in its sector and the specific business benefit that SH could expect.
parts.answer:
1. Saadat Health (healthcare). Big Data supports early disease detection, improved patient care and personalised treatment. By analysing patient records, laboratory results and admission data together, the hospitals could spot patterns that signal a disease earlier (for example rising blood sugar trends in patients not yet diagnosed with diabetes), tailor treatment to the individual patient, and track seasonal outbreaks such as dengue across admissions so that beds, staff and medicines are deployed where needed. Benefit: better patient outcomes and more efficient use of hospital resources.
2. GadgetGhar (retail and e-commerce). Big Data is used to understand customer preferences, optimise pricing and manage inventory. By tracking browsing history, searches and purchases, GadgetGhar can recommend personalised products to each customer (for example a phone cover to someone who has just bought a phone), set prices in line with demand and keep the right stock of fast-moving items. Benefit: higher conversion rates and basket sizes, and fewer stock-outs or excess stock.
3. Saadat Auto Parts (manufacturing and supply chain). Big Data is used to optimise production, improve quality and enable predictive maintenance. Sensor data from the production lines can reveal which machine settings produce defective components, and can predict when a machine is likely to fail so that it is serviced before it breaks down. Benefit: less unplanned downtime, fewer defective brake parts (critical for safety and for the assemblers' trust) and better delivery reliability.
(1 mark for each correct application, 1 mark for applying it to the subsidiary's data and 1 mark for the business benefit; 3 marks per subsidiary, max 9)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: With reference to the Group CFO's remark, identify the characteristic of Big Data that SH is failing to achieve and explain why this matters.
parts.answer:
The characteristic SH is failing to achieve is Value. Value is the actionable insight and business benefit that is actually extracted from data. Volume, velocity and variety describe the data itself, but Value is the reason for collecting it in the first place.
Why it matters for SH:
1. Data that produces no insight is not an asset but a cost. SH has spent PKR 180 million on storage and licences, and also consumes staff time, power and bandwidth, yet has received no return because no decision has changed.
2. Value only arises when insight is turned into action, for example GadgetGhar actually sending personalised recommendations, or Saadat Auto Parts actually scheduling maintenance from the sensor data. Collecting more data will not fix the problem on its own.
3. The board should therefore require each subsidiary to define the business questions it wants answered and to measure the benefit achieved (for example increase in sales or reduction in downtime), so that future investment is linked to Value.
(1 mark for identifying Value, 1 mark for explaining it, and up to 2 marks for explaining why it matters to SH, max 4)

secb.topic: Challenges of Big Data and solutions
secb.scenario:
Sehat Plus Pharmacies (SPP) operates 120 pharmacy outlets across Karachi, Hyderabad and Sukkur, an online medicine ordering website and a loyalty app. SPP's internal audit department has reported the following issues in its new analytics programme:
(i) The same customer often appears several times with different spellings of the name and missing mobile numbers. Demand forecasts prepared from this data have proved unreliable.
(ii) The nightly loyalty-points analysis on the central SQL server now takes about 14 hours and often has not finished when the outlets open the next morning.
(iii) Scanned prescriptions and customers' CNIC numbers are stored in an unencrypted shared folder which any outlet employee can open.
(iv) Outlet sales are recorded in the POS system, online orders on a separate e-commerce platform and loyalty transactions in the app's own database. Each month management receives three different total sales figures for the same period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (iv), identify the Big Data challenge that SPP is facing, explain why that challenge arises, and recommend an appropriate solution.
parts.answer:
1. Issue (i): Data quality. Why it arises: the volume, velocity and variety of Big Data make it very hard to keep data accurate, complete and consistent; data is captured at 120 outlets by many staff with no standard checks. Poor data produces flawed insights, which is why the demand forecasts are unreliable. Solution: rigorous data validation at the point of entry (for example mandatory mobile number in a valid format, matching against existing customers) and data cleansing techniques to merge duplicate customers and correct inconsistent names.
2. Issue (ii): Storage and processing. Why it arises: traditional databases on a single server were never designed for the scale of Big Data, so as SPP's transaction volume has grown the nightly job has slowed to 14 hours. Solution: move the analysis to a distributed computing platform such as Apache Hadoop or Apache Spark, which splits the job across many machines working in parallel, and/or use cloud storage and processing that scales elastically as volumes grow.
3. Issue (iii): Data privacy and security. Why it arises: the more personal data an organisation holds, the greater its regulatory exposure and the more attractive it is as a target. Prescriptions and CNIC numbers are highly sensitive, and an open, unencrypted folder exposes them to misuse by staff and to attackers. Solution: strong encryption of the stored files, strict access controls so that only authorised staff (for example the pharmacist on duty) can view them, monitoring systems that log and alert on access, and compliance with applicable data protection requirements.
4. Issue (iv): Data integration. Why it arises: data arrives from several disparate systems in incompatible formats, creating silos and conflicting versions of the truth, hence three different sales totals. Solution: ETL processes that extract data from the POS, e-commerce and loyalty systems, transform it into a common format and definitions, and load it into a centralised repository such as a data warehouse or data lake, giving management a single source of truth.
(For each issue: 1 mark for the correct challenge, 1 mark for why it arises in SPP, 1 mark for an appropriate solution, max 12)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: SPP's directors have no technical background. Explain, in simple terms, how distributed computing platforms such as Hadoop and Spark overcome the processing problem described in issue (ii).
parts.answer:
At present one server does all of the loyalty-points calculation on its own, like one clerk trying to count a mountain of receipts. Buying a slightly faster clerk (a bigger server) helps only for a while and becomes very expensive.
Distributed computing takes a different approach. Platforms such as Hadoop and Spark split the large job into many smaller pieces, send each piece to a different machine, let all the machines work on their piece at the same time (in parallel), and then combine the partial results into the final answer. It is like hiring many clerks, giving each a pile of receipts and adding up their totals.
Because the work is shared, a job that takes 14 hours on one server can be completed in a fraction of the time, and as SPP grows it can simply add more machines rather than replacing the server.
(1 mark for splitting the work, 1 mark for parallel processing and combining results, 1 mark for the benefit to SPP, max 3)

secb.topic: Cloud storage, SLAs and data sovereignty
secb.scenario:
Lawn Lane (LL) is a Lahore-based online fashion retailer. For most of the year its website handles about 2,000 orders a day, but during Eid sales and Blessed Friday traffic increases to about twenty times that level. Last Eid the website crashed twice, and order and clickstream data for several hours was lost.
The IT head has proposed buying enough servers to handle the Eid peak. The CEO prefers moving to a cloud service offered by an overseas provider, whose standard contract does not mention uptime, support response times or where LL's data will be stored.
LL also wants to analyse customer reviews, product photographs uploaded by customers and clickstream data alongside its order records. The IT head suggests loading all of this into LL's existing relational database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the IT head's proposal to buy servers for the Eid peak, and explain why cloud storage may be the better solution to LL's storage and processing challenge.
parts.answer:
1. LL's load is highly seasonal. Servers sized for the Eid and Blessed Friday peak (about twenty times normal traffic) would sit largely idle for the remaining weeks of the year. LL would bear the full purchase, maintenance, power and space cost all year for capacity it needs only a few weeks a year, which is a poor use of funds.
2. Even then the servers would only handle the peak LL has predicted; if demand grows faster than expected the site could crash again, as it did last Eid.
3. Cloud storage and processing scale elastically. LL can increase capacity on demand during the sale period and scale back afterwards.
4. LL pays only for the resources it actually uses, converting a large upfront capital cost into a variable cost that follows its sales pattern.
5. Cloud providers can also offer distributed processing, so the higher volume of orders and clickstream data can be processed without the website slowing down or losing data.
Conclusion: the cloud option better matches LL's seasonal pattern, provided the contract risks in part (b) are addressed.
(1 mark per valid point, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the importance of a service-level agreement (SLA) and of data sovereignty to LL, and recommend what LL should do about each before signing the cloud contract.
parts.answer:
1. Service-level agreement (SLA). An SLA is the part of the contract that sets out the level of service the provider commits to, such as uptime, support response times and what happens if the service fails. LL's revenue is concentrated in the Eid and Blessed Friday periods, so an outage at that time would be extremely costly. At present the standard contract is silent on uptime and support.
Recommendation: LL should negotiate a strong SLA specifying guaranteed availability (especially during announced sale periods), support response and resolution times, backup and recovery commitments (so data is not lost as happened last Eid), and penalties or service credits if the provider fails to meet them.
2. Data sovereignty. Data sovereignty is the question of which country the data physically resides in, and therefore which country's laws apply to it. With an overseas provider, LL's customer names, addresses, phone numbers and payment-related data may be stored outside Pakistan and be subject to a foreign jurisdiction, which raises legal, regulatory and privacy concerns.
Recommendation: LL should require the contract to state where its data will be stored, prefer a data location that meets Pakistani legal and regulatory requirements, and ensure that encryption and access controls protect customer data wherever it is held.
(1 mark for explaining each concept, 1 mark for its relevance to LL and up to 1 mark for each recommendation, max 5)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain why LL's existing relational database is not suitable for the analysis of reviews, photographs and clickstream data that LL has in mind.
parts.answer:
1. Variety of data. A traditional relational database is designed for structured data held in fixed rows and columns. Customer reviews and photographs are unstructured and clickstream data is semi-structured, so they do not fit naturally into its tables.
2. Scale. The relational database was sized for LL's order records. Clickstream data in particular is generated for every click by every visitor and, at twenty times normal traffic during Eid, the volume would be far beyond what a traditional database was designed to handle.
3. Processing on a single machine. A traditional database processes data on one server, so it cannot easily provide the fast, large-scale analysis LL needs. Distributed platforms (such as Hadoop or Spark) and repositories that accept raw data in any format, such as a data lake, are better suited.
(1 mark per valid reason, max 3)

secb.topic: Big Data concepts and predictive maintenance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Define Big Data and explain why it is described as more than simply 'a lot of data'.
parts.answer:
Definition: Big Data refers to massive volumes of structured and unstructured data generated at high speed from many different sources, such as social media, sensors and IoT devices, and transaction records. It is so complex that it requires advanced techniques and technologies to capture, store, process and analyse it.
Why it is more than 'a lot of data':
1. Size is only one dimension. Big Data is also characterised by the speed at which it arrives (velocity), the variety of its formats, the doubts over its trustworthiness (veracity) and the need to extract value from it.
2. It is defined by complexity as much as size: data arriving every second, in different formats, from different sources at the same time.
3. Ordinary tools such as Excel or a traditional relational database physically cannot cope with it. It is not enough to use the same tools on a bigger computer; entirely different machinery, such as distributed computing platforms, is required.
(1 mark for definition and up to 3 marks for explanation, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Big Data typically arrives in structured, semi-structured and unstructured formats. Explain each format, giving one example of each from an e-commerce business, and state which characteristic of Big Data this mixture of formats represents.
parts.answer:
1. Structured data is organised in a fixed format of rows and columns with a defined data type for each field, so it fits directly into a relational table. Example: transaction records of each online order (order number, date, customer ID, amount).
2. Semi-structured data does not sit in fixed tables of rows and columns but still has some organisation, as in XML or JSON files. Example: clickstream data recording each visitor's page views and clicks.
3. Unstructured data has no predefined model or organisation. Example: free-text customer reviews, product photographs and videos uploaded by customers.
4. This mixture of formats arriving together represents Variety, one of the 5 Vs. It matters because each format needs different storage and processing, and combining them is a key challenge for Big Data systems.
(1 mark for each format explained with a valid example, and 1 mark for identifying Variety, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Compare reactive maintenance, preventive maintenance and predictive maintenance, and explain how Big Data makes predictive maintenance possible.
parts.answer:
1. Reactive maintenance: the machine is repaired only after it has broken down. It avoids servicing costs until failure, but leads to costly unplanned downtime, lost production and sometimes damage to other equipment.
2. Preventive maintenance: the machine is serviced on a fixed calendar (for example every three months) regardless of its actual condition. It reduces breakdowns, but parts may be replaced too early (wasted cost) or a machine may still fail between scheduled services.
3. Predictive maintenance: data is used to predict when a particular machine is likely to fail, and it is serviced just before that point. This avoids both unplanned downtime and unnecessary servicing.
4. Role of Big Data: predictive maintenance depends on machine-generated data from sensors fitted to the machinery (for example vibration, temperature, wear and engine performance), collected continuously at high volume and velocity. Analysing this data reveals patterns that come before a failure, allowing maintenance to be scheduled before the breakdown occurs. For example, a car manufacturer uses sensor data from production-line machines to service them before failure.
(1 mark for each type correctly explained and 1 mark for the role of Big Data, max 4)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain social media as a source of Big Data and describe two ways in which CNF could legitimately use social media data during a product launch.
parts.answer:
Social media as a source: social media data consists of posts, comments, likes and shares on platforms such as Facebook, X, Instagram and LinkedIn. It is generated by users in very high volume and close to real time, and is used to understand customer sentiment and to personalise marketing.
Two uses during a launch:
1. Spotting problems early. By monitoring the product hashtag and brand mentions, CNF can identify recurring complaints quickly, for example that the chai is too sweet or that bottles leak, and correct the product or its messaging before the problem damages the brand. This is how a consumer goods company tracks hashtags during a launch.
2. Adjusting and personalising the campaign. CNF can see which cities, age groups or messages generate the most engagement and redirect its advertising budget and promotional offers to the audiences and platforms that respond best.
(Up to 2 marks for explaining the source and 1 mark for each valid use applied to CNF, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the characteristic of Big Data that has been compromised in CNF's sentiment analysis. Explain how each of the findings (i) to (iv) affected that characteristic and the consequence for CNF.
parts.answer:
The characteristic compromised is Veracity: the accuracy and trustworthiness of the data. Large volumes of social media data bring inconsistency, bias and error, and here they have made the sentiment score misleading.
1. (i) Sarcasm in Roman Urdu: the analysis counted sarcastic remarks as praise, so comments that were really complaints about sweetness were scored as positive. The true product problem was hidden.
2. (ii) Undisclosed paid influencer posts: these do not represent genuine customer opinion, so they biased the score upwards.
3. (iii) Identical posts from newly created accounts: these are likely fake or bot accounts. They are not real customers and distort both the volume and the tone of opinion.
4. (iv) Each re-share counted as a separate opinion: one view was multiplied thousands of times, so a few popular posts dominated the result.
Consequence for CNF: management believed the launch was succeeding (82% positive) when customers were in fact dissatisfied, so it did not act on the real problem and sales reached only 40% of target. Decisions based on untrustworthy data are flawed, however large the volume of data.
(1 mark for identifying Veracity, 1 mark for each finding explained, up to max 5 including the consequence)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Recommend measures that CNF should take to make its future launch analysis more reliable.
parts.answer:
1. Data validation and cleansing before analysis. CNF should remove duplicates and count each original post once rather than each re-share, filter out posts from newly created or suspicious accounts that post identical text, and exclude or separately tag paid influencer content, so that only genuine customer opinions are scored.
2. Better handling of language. The sentiment rules or model should be tested and adjusted on Roman Urdu and Urdu samples, including common sarcastic expressions, and a sample of comments should be reviewed manually each day to check that the automated scores are reasonable.
3. Use surveys and user-generated data as a second collection method. A short feedback form or poll to verified buyers (for example via a QR code on the bottle) gives more reliable product feedback that can be compared with the social media score.
4. Cross-check against transactional data. Sentiment should be read alongside actual sales and repeat purchases by region; a large gap between a positive score and weak sales, as here, should trigger investigation immediately.
(1 mark per valid, well-explained measure, max 4)

secb.topic: Big Data in financial services and privacy
secb.scenario:
RahPay Limited is a digital wallet company licensed by the State Bank of Pakistan, with 6 million users. It is launching two Big Data projects:
(i) a fraud detection system that scores every wallet transaction, login and device change as it happens and blocks suspicious transactions;
(ii) a credit scoring model that offers small loans to users without a bank account, based on their wallet history, mobile top-ups and the contact list on their phone.
The compliance officer has raised the following concerns:
- When the app was updated, users were asked to tap 'Allow' to continue, without being told that their contact lists would be uploaded and used for credit scoring.
- Transaction data, CNIC images, device identifiers and contact lists are now combined in a single analytics database.
- About 40 employees in the analytics team can download the full analytics database to their laptops.
At present transactions are copied into the analytics database once every night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how Big Data is applied in financial services, with reference to RahPay's two projects.
parts.answer:
1. Fraud detection. Financial institutions use machine-learning models on Big Data to detect suspicious transactions in real time. RahPay's system (i) compares each transaction, login and device change with the user's normal behaviour and with known fraud patterns, for example a new device in another city followed immediately by a large transfer, and blocks it before money leaves the wallet. Benefit: lower fraud losses and greater customer trust.
2. Credit risk assessment. Big Data allows lenders to assess the creditworthiness of customers who have no traditional credit history. RahPay's model (ii) uses wallet history and top-up patterns to estimate whether a user is likely to repay a small loan. Benefit: RahPay can lend to unbanked users and grow its business, while pricing risk more accurately.
Big Data is also used to enhance customer service, for example by identifying users who need help.
(Up to 2 marks for each application explained and linked to RahPay, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the Big Data challenge of data privacy and security, identify the specific privacy and security issues in RahPay's situation, and recommend a control for each issue.
parts.answer:
The challenge: the more personal data an organisation collects and holds, the greater its regulatory exposure and the more attractive a target it becomes for attackers. A regulated wallet company must comply with data protection and regulatory requirements while protecting the data against cyber threats. The recommended solutions are strong encryption, access controls and monitoring.
Issues and controls:
1. Lack of informed consent and transparency. Users tapped 'Allow' without being told their contact lists would be uploaded and used for credit scoring. Contact lists also contain personal data of people who are not RahPay customers. Control: give clear, specific disclosure and obtain explicit consent for each use of data, allow users to refuse, and stop using contact data until valid consent is obtained; review the practice against SBP and data protection requirements.
2. Concentration of sensitive data. Combining transaction data, CNIC images, device identifiers and contact lists in one database creates a very high-value target; a single breach would expose each user's financial and personal life. Control: collect and retain only the data each model needs, encrypt sensitive fields at rest and in transit, and mask or remove CNIC images from the analytics database.
3. Excessive access. Forty analysts can download the entire database to laptops, so data could be lost, stolen or misused. Control: role-based access on a need-to-know basis, block bulk downloads to laptops (analysis to be done within the controlled environment), and monitor and log access with alerts for unusual activity.
(1 mark for explaining the challenge, and for each issue 1 mark for identification and up to 1 mark for the control, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain which characteristic of Big Data is most critical to the fraud detection project and why RahPay's current nightly data copy is inadequate for it.
parts.answer:
1. The most critical characteristic is Velocity: the speed at which data is generated and must be processed, often in real time. With 6 million users, transactions, logins and device changes arrive continuously, and fraud detection only works if each event is scored as it happens.
2. A fraudster who takes over a wallet can empty it within minutes. If transactions reach the analytics database only once a night, the suspicious transfer will be detected the next day, after the money has gone. The system would then be reporting fraud, not preventing it.
3. A nightly copy also means that blocking decisions would be based on stale information about the user's recent behaviour, which increases both missed frauds and wrongly blocked genuine transactions.
4. RahPay therefore needs real-time or near real-time streaming of transaction data into the fraud engine, supported by infrastructure that can process high-speed data at scale (for example distributed processing on scalable cloud resources), rather than a batch copy.
(1 mark for identifying Velocity, up to 2 marks for explaining why the nightly copy fails, 1 mark for the recommendation, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Kohsar Bank Limited (KBL) runs its core banking application on a commercial DBMS. The IT audit team has recorded the following observations:
(i) The month-end loan portfolio report, written in SQL, took more than three hours to run. After the DBA reviewed how the DBMS interprets and plans the query, the same report now runs in eight minutes.
(ii) A teller at the Abbottabad branch was able to sign in using the credentials of a colleague who had resigned two months earlier, and could view the accounts of customers of every branch.
(iii) New deposits could not be saved for 40 minutes one morning because the disk space allocated to the database was full, and no additional space had been assigned.
(iv) A bulk salary upload for a corporate client failed halfway. The DBMS automatically reversed the half-completed upload, so that no employee was credited and the client's account was not debited.
(v) The vendor explained that whenever a teller saves a cash deposit, one core component of the DBMS is responsible for actually storing, retrieving and processing the data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the observations (i) to (v), identify the DBMS component involved and explain the role of that component, relating it to the observation.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Query Processor. The query processor interprets and executes queries written in SQL and optimises them for performance, for example by choosing an efficient way to retrieve the data. The improvement of the month-end report from three hours to eight minutes relates to how the query is interpreted and optimised, which is the query processor's role.
2. (ii) Security Manager. The security manager handles authentication (verifying who the user is) and authorisation (what the user is allowed to see and do). The resigned employee's credentials should have been disabled, so authentication failed to stop the login; and a teller should be authorised to view only the accounts relevant to his role and branch, so authorisation was also too broad.
3. (iii) Storage Manager. The storage manager manages the physical storage of data, allocating disk space and ensuring efficient retrieval. The failure to save deposits because the allocated space was full is a storage management problem; space should be monitored and allocated before it runs out.
4. (iv) Transaction Manager. The transaction manager ensures that transactions obey the ACID properties and protects integrity even when a failure occurs; it is the component that performs a rollback. Treating the salary upload as one unit and reversing it when it failed demonstrates this.
5. (v) Database Engine. The database engine is the core of the DBMS, responsible for storing, retrieving and processing data. Saving the teller's deposit into the database is its basic function.
(1 mark for each correct component and 1 mark for explaining its role in the context of the observation, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: A KBL director refers to 'the Oracle database' when discussing customer records. Distinguish between a database and a DBMS, and explain why the director's description is inaccurate.
parts.answer:
