A database is an organised collection of data stored and accessed electronically, designed so that the data can be easily searched, manipulated and updated. At KBL, the customer, account and transaction records are the database.
A DBMS is the software that enables the creation, management and use of a database. It sits between the applications and the data, controls all access, enforces security and integrity, and allows many users to work concurrently. Oracle, MySQL and SQL Server are examples of DBMSs.
The director's description blurs the two: Oracle is the DBMS (the software, like a librarian controlling the library), while KBL's customer records stored under it are the database (the books). It would be more accurate to say 'our customer database, managed by the Oracle DBMS'.
(1 mark for each correct definition and 1 mark for applying the distinction to the director's statement, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Margalla Airways (MA) is a domestic airline that sells tickets through its website, mobile app and travel agents. Its reservation system runs on a relational DBMS. In a review of complaints received last quarter, the following incidents were identified:
(i) Two travel agents in Karachi and Peshawar each sold seat 12A on the same Islamabad-Skardu flight at the same moment, because each agent's screen showed the seat as available while the other booking was still being processed.
(ii) A passenger's credit card was charged PKR 38,500 but no ticket was issued, because the system stopped after the payment step and before the ticket record was written.
(iii) The system accepted a booking in which the return date was earlier than the departure date, although MA's business rules prohibit this.
(iv) Following a power failure in the data centre, a booking that the system had confirmed to a customer by SMS could not be found when the system restarted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each incident, identify the ACID property that was not properly enforced, explain the property, and explain how its proper enforcement would have prevented the incident.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Isolation. Isolation means that transactions running at the same time do not interfere with each other; each behaves as if it were the only transaction in the system, so no transaction sees another's half-finished result. Properly enforced, the second agent's transaction would not have been able to act on the seat while the first booking was in progress; it would see the seat either as available before the first booking or as taken after it, so the same seat could not be sold twice.
2. (ii) Atomicity. Atomicity means that all operations in a transaction succeed or none of them do ('all or nothing'). Charging the card and issuing the ticket form a single transaction. Properly enforced, when the system stopped before writing the ticket record the whole transaction would have been rolled back, reversing the card charge, so the passenger would not have paid without receiving a ticket.
3. (iii) Consistency. Consistency means that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another and is never allowed to break integrity constraints or business rules. If the rule 'return date must not be earlier than departure date' were defined as a constraint, the booking would have been rejected and could not commit.
4. (iv) Durability. Durability means that once a transaction is committed its effects are permanent and survive crashes, power failures and hardware faults. Properly enforced, a booking that had been committed and confirmed to the customer would still exist when the system restarted after the power failure.
(1 mark for each correct property and 1 mark for explanation and prevention, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the techniques by which a DBMS achieves durability, and how they would apply to incident (iv).
parts.answer:
1. Write-ahead logging. Before changes are applied to the database files, the DBMS first writes them to a transaction log on durable storage (disk). If power fails, on restart the DBMS reads the log: any transaction that had been committed but whose changes had not yet been fully written to the data files is redone, and any transaction that had not reached commit is rolled back. In incident (iv), the confirmed booking would have been recorded in the log before the confirmation SMS was sent, so it would have been recovered automatically after the restart.
2. Replication. The DBMS keeps copies of the data at more than one location, for example on a second server or at a disaster recovery site. If the primary server or its storage is damaged, a replicated copy still holds the committed booking. For MA, replication to a second site would also allow reservations to continue if the main data centre loses power for a long period.
Together these ensure that a booking, once confirmed to a customer, cannot be lost through a crash.
(1 mark for each technique explained and 1 mark for each correct application to incident (iv), max 4)

secb.scenario:
Chenab Mart (CM) is a supermarket chain with 35 stores. Its customer and sales database is used by 14 applications, including the POS system, the loyalty app, the e-commerce website and management reports. This quarter the database administrator plans to make the following changes:
(i) Add a new column, LoyaltyTier, to the Customer table.
(ii) Move the database files from the existing hard disks to a new solid-state storage array.
(iii) Create an index on the CNIC column of the Customer table to speed up customer searches at the tills.
(iv) Split the Customer table into two tables, Customer and CustomerAddress.
(v) Compress the sales history for the years 2018 to 2022 to save storage space.
(vi) Remove the FaxNumber column from the Customer table, which no application uses.
The IT manager is concerned that all 14 applications will need to be rewritten and retested.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the changes (i) to (vi) as relying on logical data independence or physical data independence, giving a brief justification for each.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Adding the LoyaltyTier column: logical data independence. It changes the logical structure (schema) of the Customer table; applications that do not use the new column continue to work unchanged.
2. (ii) Moving files to solid-state storage: physical data independence. Only where and how the data is physically stored changes; the tables and their structure are unchanged.
3. (iii) Creating an index on CNIC: physical data independence. An index is a physical storage structure that improves retrieval performance; it does not change the tables seen by the applications.
4. (iv) Splitting the Customer table into Customer and CustomerAddress: logical data independence. The logical structure of the data is reorganised; with data independence the applications can still obtain customer details as before.
5. (v) Compressing 2018-2022 sales history: physical data independence. Compression changes how the data is stored on disk to save space, not what data exists or how it is structured.
6. (vi) Removing the unused FaxNumber column: logical data independence. Removing a column changes the logical schema; because no application uses it, none is affected.
The test: if the tables or columns change it is logical; if only the disk, indexes or storage format change it is physical.
(1 mark per correct classification with justification, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the benefits to CM of each type of data independence.
parts.answer:
Logical data independence:
1. CM can change the structure of its database, for example adding LoyaltyTier for a new loyalty scheme or improving the design by splitting tables, without rewriting the 14 applications. This lets the database evolve with the business at lower cost and risk.
2. Each application continues to see the data it needs, so new features can be introduced for one application (such as the loyalty app) without disrupting others (such as the tills), reducing testing effort and downtime.
Physical data independence:
3. CM can improve performance and storage efficiency, for example moving to solid-state storage, adding indexes for faster till searches or compressing old data, without any change to application programs.
4. Technical staff can tune and upgrade storage as data volumes grow, or take advantage of cheaper or faster storage technology, without involving application developers or users, so improvements can be made quickly and cheaply.
(1 mark per well-explained benefit, at least one for each type, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain where each type of data independence sits within the three-level (ANSI/SPARC) architecture of a DBMS.
parts.answer:
The ANSI/SPARC architecture has three levels: the external level (individual user views), the conceptual level (the complete logical structure of the database: entities, relationships and constraints) and the internal level (how data is physically stored: files, blocks, indexes and compression).
1. Logical data independence sits between the external and conceptual levels. The conceptual schema can be changed (for example a column added or a table split, as in changes (i), (iv) and (vi)) without having to change the external views and the applications built on them.
2. Physical data independence sits between the conceptual and internal levels. The internal schema can be changed (for example new storage, indexes or compression, as in changes (ii), (iii) and (v)) without having to change the conceptual schema, and therefore without affecting the external views either.
This separation of levels is the reason the three-level architecture exists, and it addresses the IT manager's concern.
(1 mark for describing the levels, 1 mark for each correct placement, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Margalla Medical Centre (MMC) is a 300-bed hospital in Islamabad. It uses one integrated patient database. Different staff groups have different needs:
- Doctors need to see each patient's full clinical record, including diagnoses, test results and prescriptions.
- Pharmacists need to see prescriptions and allergies, but not diagnoses or billing details.
- Billing clerks need to see admissions, procedures performed and charges, but must not see diagnoses or test results.
Meanwhile, the database administrator (DBA) is reorganising how the data files are stored on disk to improve the speed of the system, and the hospital's data architect is redesigning how patients, admissions and procedures relate to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the three levels of the DBMS architecture and how each level applies at MMC.
parts.answer:
The ANSI/SPARC architecture describes a DBMS at three levels of abstraction.
1. External level (user view). This describes how individual users or groups see the data. Each group receives a customised view showing only what it needs. At MMC, doctors have a view of the full clinical record; pharmacists have a view of prescriptions and allergies only; and billing clerks have a view of admissions, procedures and charges, with diagnoses and test results hidden. All three views draw on the same underlying database.
2. Conceptual level (logical view). This describes the complete logical structure of the whole database: the entities (Patients, Admissions, Procedures, Prescriptions, Charges), the relationships between them and the constraints and integrity rules. It is modelled using the entity-relationship model and hides physical storage details. The data architect's redesign of how patients, admissions and procedures relate is work at this level. There is one conceptual schema, which keeps all the external views consistent.
3. Internal level (physical view). This describes how the data is actually stored on disk: file structures, data blocks, indexes, compression and storage allocation. The DBA's reorganisation of the data files to improve speed is work at this level; doctors, pharmacists and clerks are unaware of it.
(1 mark for explaining each level and 1 mark for applying each to MMC, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain how the external level supports security and simplicity at MMC.
parts.answer:
1. Security: the external level allows sensitive fields to be hidden entirely from users who do not need them. Billing clerks simply cannot see diagnoses or test results because those fields do not exist in their view, and pharmacists cannot see billing details. This protects patient confidentiality and reduces the risk of misuse of medical data.
2. Need-to-know access by role: because each view is defined for a staff group, access follows the person's job rather than relying on individuals choosing not to look at data.
3. Simplicity: each user sees only the data relevant to their work, rather than the whole complex hospital database. A pharmacist dispensing medicine is presented with prescriptions and allergies only, which makes the system easier to use and reduces errors.
(1 mark per valid point applied to MMC, max 3)

parts.label: c
parts.answer:
1. (i) Conceptual level. Integrity rules and constraints, such as the relationship between Admissions and Patients, are part of the complete logical structure of the database.
2. (ii) External level. A customised view for a particular user group that hides certain fields is an external (user) view.
3. (iii) Internal level. Data block sizes and compression concern how data is physically stored on disk.
4. (iv) Internal level. Indexes are physical storage structures used to speed up retrieval; adding one does not change the logical structure or the users' views.
(1 mark per correct level with reason, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Sutlej Group is a Lahore-based group of companies. Its IT steering committee must select database models for four systems:
(i) A general ledger and payroll system for the group's 4,000 employees, where every journal and salary payment must be accurate and fully traceable.
(ii) A design library for Sutlej Architects containing complex 3-D building models, together with the routines that render, rotate and modify each model.
(iii) A system for Sutlej Beverages that will collect millions of temperature and stock readings per day from internet-connected vending machines, together with customer comments from social media, in formats that change whenever a new machine model is introduced.
(iv) Documentation of an old system at Sutlej Engineering, which recorded components and suppliers in a graph-like structure in which each component record was linked to several supplier records and each supplier record to several component records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the most appropriate database model for each of the systems (i) to (iv), justifying your choice by reference to the type of data involved.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Relational database (RDBMS). The ledger and payroll data is highly structured (accounts, journals, employees, salaries) and fits naturally into tables of rows and columns linked by primary and foreign keys. Integrity is critical: an RDBMS is fully ACID-compliant, so a salary payment cannot be half-recorded, and its keys and constraints keep records consistent. SQL provides powerful querying for financial reporting and audit trails.
2. (ii) Object-oriented database (OODBMS). The 3-D models are complex data types that do not break down neatly into rows and columns, and the requirement is to store both the data and the routines (methods) that act on it, which is exactly what an object is. An OODBMS stores objects directly, avoiding translation between the design software and tables; CAD and engineering design are typical uses.
3. (iii) NoSQL database. The data is very high in volume and velocity, and is semi-structured or unstructured (sensor readings, social media comments) with formats that change over time. NoSQL has no fixed schema, so new fields from new machine models can be stored without disruptive schema changes, and it scales horizontally by adding more machines, making it suitable for Big Data and IoT streams.
4. (iv) Network model. The graph-like structure in which a record can have many parent records as well as many child records is the defining feature of the network model. It allows the many-to-many relationship between components and suppliers (one component from many suppliers, one supplier providing many components) to be represented directly.
(1 mark for each correct model and 1 mark for a justification related to the data, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the primary characteristics of NoSQL databases and the trade-off they generally make compared with relational databases.
parts.answer:
1. No fixed schema: NoSQL ('Not Only SQL') databases abandon the rigid table structure, so records in the same collection can have different fields. This makes them highly flexible when data formats change.
2. Horizontal scaling: capacity is increased by adding more inexpensive machines rather than buying one larger server (vertical scaling, typical of an RDBMS). This is what allows NoSQL to handle Big Data volumes economically.
3. Four main types: key-value, document, column-family and graph databases.
4. Typical uses: Big Data, social media, IoT sensor streams, real-time web applications and content management, where data is unstructured or semi-structured and arrives fast.
Trade-off: NoSQL databases often give up strict ACID guarantees in exchange for speed and availability. This is why they suit system (iii) but would not be chosen for the general ledger and payroll in system (i), where integrity is paramount.
(1 mark per characteristic explained, including the trade-off, max 4)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Compare the hierarchical model with the network model, explaining why the network model is better able to manage many-to-many relationships. Support your answer with an example.
parts.answer:
1. Structure. The hierarchical model organises records as a strict tree: each child record has exactly one parent. The network model organises records as a graph: records are connected by explicit links and a record can have many parent records as well as many child records.
2. Relationships supported. Because each child has only one parent, the hierarchical model can directly represent only one-to-many (1:N) relationships. The network model, by allowing multiple parents, can represent many-to-many (N:M) relationships directly.
3. Handling many-to-many data. In a hierarchical model, a many-to-many relationship can only be forced into the tree by duplicating records, for example repeating a course record under every student who takes it. This causes redundancy, wastes storage and creates integrity risk, because a change must be made consistently to every copy. The network model stores each record once and links it to all related records, so there is no duplication.
4. Navigation. In the network model the links are stored explicitly, so it is efficient to move in either direction: from a record to all its related records on the other side and back again.
Example: at a university, one student enrols in many courses and one course is taken by many students. In the network model the student Ayesha's record links to her Audit, Tax and Costing course records, while the Audit course record links back to Ayesha, Bilal and Hamza. The course has three parents and the student three children, forming a graph. The same applies to suppliers and parts.
(Up to 4 marks for the comparison and up to 2 marks for a relevant example, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Compare relational databases (RDBMS) with object-oriented databases (OODBMS), covering how each stores data, their strengths and weaknesses, and the types of data each is best suited to manage.
parts.answer:
RDBMS:
1. Storage: data is held in tables of rows and columns, with tables linked by primary and foreign keys, and queried using SQL.
2. Strengths: very strong data integrity, full ACID compliance, maturity and a large skills base, and powerful standardised querying.
3. Weaknesses: a rigid schema, so structural change is disruptive; difficulty handling unstructured data; and vertical scaling (buying a bigger machine), which becomes expensive.
4. Best suited to: structured data where integrity is critical, such as banking, accounting, ERP and payroll (examples of RDBMS: Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server).
OODBMS:
5. Storage: data is held as objects, as in object-oriented programming, with each object bundling together the data and the methods (behaviour) that act on it.
6. Strengths: natural handling of complex data types (images, engineering drawings, multimedia); no awkward translation between the program and the database; support for inheritance.
7. Weaknesses: far less mature than the relational model, a smaller talent pool and weaker standardisation than SQL.
8. Best suited to: complex, richly structured data such as CAD/CAM, engineering design, multimedia and scientific applications.
(1 mark per valid comparative point, covering both models, max 6)

secb.scenario:
Gwadar Traders (GT) imports and distributes industrial chemicals. Its customer, inventory, sales and payroll records are kept in about 60 spreadsheets on a shared network drive. The finance manager has listed the following problems:
(i) When two staff members open and update the same inventory spreadsheet at the same time, one person's changes often overwrite the other's.
(ii) Sales invoices have been recorded against customer codes that do not exist in the customer list, and some customer codes appear twice for different customers.
(iii) Any employee with access to the shared drive can open the payroll spreadsheet and see everyone's salary.
(iv) To answer a question such as 'which customers in Karachi bought more than PKR 1 million of caustic soda last year', staff spend hours filtering and copying across several spreadsheets.
(v) Every time a column is inserted into the sales spreadsheet, a number of linked reports and macros stop working and must be repaired.
(vi) The same kind of data is laid out differently in different spreadsheets, with headings in different places and some sheets containing notes and totals mixed into the data.
GT is considering replacing the spreadsheets with a relational DBMS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the problems (i) to (vi), identify the characteristic of a DBMS that would address it and explain how.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Multiuser access. A DBMS allows many users to work on the data concurrently without conflicts; it controls simultaneous updates (through the transaction manager and isolation) so that one user's change does not overwrite another's.
2. (ii) Consistency and integrity (primary and foreign keys). A primary key on the customer table guarantees that each customer code is unique, so a code cannot be given to two customers. A foreign key from invoices to customers ensures that an invoice can only be recorded against a customer code that exists.
3. (iii) Security. The DBMS's security manager authenticates each user and applies role-based access control (RBAC), so only authorised payroll and HR staff can view salary data; sensitive data can also be encrypted. Ordinary staff simply would not have access to the payroll table.
4. (iv) Query language (SQL). The question can be written as a single SQL query that selects and totals the relevant sales across the related tables, returning the answer in seconds instead of hours of manual filtering and copying, and the query can be saved and rerun.
5. (v) Data independence. With logical data independence, a new column can be added to a table without affecting existing reports and applications that do not use it, so GT's reports would not break each time the structure changes.
6. (vi) Relation-based tables. A DBMS stores each type of data in a defined table of rows and columns with set field names and data types. Every record follows the same structure, without notes or totals mixed into the data, making the data easy to manage and query.
(1 mark for each correct characteristic and 1 mark for explaining how it addresses the problem, max 12)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why, in a DBMS environment, users and applications should access data only through the DBMS, and how this differs from GT's current arrangement.
parts.answer:
1. In a DBMS environment the DBMS stands between the applications and the data, like a librarian between readers and the books. Nothing touches the data except through the DBMS.
2. This lets the DBMS check every request: it verifies that the user is allowed to see or change the data (security), stops two users from changing the same record in conflicting ways (concurrency), enforces integrity rules before accepting a change, retrieves data efficiently and keeps a record of activity.
3. At GT, users open the spreadsheet files directly on the shared drive. There is no gatekeeper, so anyone with drive access can read, change, copy or delete any data, rules are not enforced and conflicting changes go unnoticed. Moving to a DBMS replaces this uncontrolled access with centrally controlled access.
(1 mark per valid point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Kirthar Cement Limited (KCL) is implementing a new ERP system. A software vendor has proposed that KCL should hold ALL of its data, including the general ledger, accounts payable and receivable, and payroll, in a single NoSQL database. The vendor argues: 'NoSQL has no fixed schema, so you will never need to redesign tables, and it scales horizontally, so it can grow with you.'
KCL's operations director also wants to capture readings from about 2,000 sensors on its kilns and grinding mills every few seconds, together with maintenance engineers' free-text notes and photographs.
KCL's CFO is concerned that the ledger must never contain an invoice for a supplier that does not exist, a duplicate supplier code, or a journal entry that is only partly posted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the vendor's proposal to hold KCL's general ledger, payables, receivables and payroll in a NoSQL database.
parts.answer:
1. Nature of the data. Ledger, payables, receivables and payroll data is highly structured and stable (accounts, suppliers, invoices, employees), so it fits naturally into relational tables; the flexibility of having no fixed schema offers little benefit here.
2. Integrity is critical. Financial records must be accurate, complete and consistent. A relational database enforces integrity through primary keys, foreign keys and constraints, which is exactly what the CFO's concerns require. NoSQL databases do not rely on this rigid structure.
3. ACID guarantees. NoSQL databases often trade away strict ACID guarantees in exchange for speed and availability. For a ledger, a journal that is only partly posted, or a payment that is lost after a crash, is unacceptable; an RDBMS is fully ACID-compliant.
4. Scalability argument. Horizontal scaling matters for Big Data volumes, but KCL's financial transaction volumes are modest and well within the capacity of a relational system, so this advantage is not decisive.
5. Reporting and skills. An RDBMS offers mature SQL querying for financial reporting and audit, and a large skills base.
Conclusion: the proposal is not appropriate for the financial modules; these should use a relational database (RDBMS), while NoSQL can be used where its strengths are relevant (part (b)).
(1 mark per valid evaluative point including a conclusion, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain where a NoSQL database would be appropriate within KCL, and why.
parts.answer:
A NoSQL database would be appropriate for the operations director's plant data:
1. Volume and velocity: about 2,000 sensors reporting every few seconds create a continuous, high-speed stream amounting to hundreds of millions of readings. NoSQL scales horizontally by adding more inexpensive machines, so it can absorb this growth economically, whereas a relational database scales vertically and becomes expensive.
2. Variety: the readings are semi-structured, while engineers' free-text notes and photographs are unstructured. NoSQL has no fixed schema, so these different formats can be stored without forcing them into rigid tables.
3. Changing formats: if new types of sensor are installed with different fields, records can simply carry the new fields without a disruptive schema change.
4. Use: IoT sensor streams are a typical NoSQL application, and the data can then support analysis such as predicting equipment failures in the kilns and mills.
(1 mark per valid point, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain how a relational DBMS would address each of the CFO's three concerns.
parts.answer:
1. Invoice for a supplier that does not exist: a foreign key on the invoice table referencing the supplier table ensures that every invoice must quote a supplier code that already exists in the supplier table. Any attempt to record an invoice for a non-existent supplier is rejected.
2. Duplicate supplier code: the supplier code is defined as the primary key of the supplier table. A primary key must be unique (and not blank), so the DBMS will not accept a second supplier with the same code.
3. Partly posted journal: the transaction manager enforces atomicity. All the debit and credit lines of a journal are processed as one transaction; if any line fails, the whole journal is rolled back, so it is either fully posted or not posted at all.
More generally, the consistency property ensures that no transaction can commit if it would break these integrity constraints, so the database always moves from one valid state to another.
(1 mark for each concern correctly addressed and 1 mark for linking to consistency/integrity, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Raavi Pharmacy Limited (RPL) records doctors' prescriptions in a single table, an extract of which is shown in Table 1.
Additional information:
- PrescriptionNo is the primary key.
- A patient is identified by CNIC and may have many prescriptions. A doctor is identified by DoctorCode and may write many prescriptions.
RPL's pharmacists report that they cannot easily find how many units of a particular medicine were dispensed in a month, and that when a doctor's name was misspelt it had to be corrected on hundreds of rows.

tables.caption: Table 1: Prescriptions
rows: Augmentin 625mg x 14; Gaviscon x 1; Panadol 500mg x 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify each normalisation problem in Table 1. For each problem, state the normal form that is breached and explain why, with reference to the data.
parts.answer:
1. Breach of 1NF (atomicity / repeating group). The Medicines column holds several values in one cell, for example 'Augmentin 625mg x 14; Gaviscon x 1; Panadol 500mg x 10' for RX1003. In addition each entry combines two facts, the medicine and the quantity. 1NF requires each cell to hold a single, indivisible value. This is why the pharmacists cannot count units of a medicine dispensed.
2. Breach of 2NF (partial dependency). Once each medicine is put on its own row, PrescriptionNo alone no longer identifies a row; the primary key becomes composite: PrescriptionNo + MedicineName. PrescriptionDate, PatientCNIC, PatientName, DoctorCode and DoctorName depend only on PrescriptionNo (part of the key), not on which medicine was prescribed. These are partial dependencies, which cause the prescription details to be repeated on every medicine line. Only Quantity depends on the whole key.
3. Breach of 3NF (transitive dependencies). PatientName depends on PatientCNIC, and DoctorName depends on DoctorCode. PatientCNIC and DoctorCode are non-key attributes, so PatientName and DoctorName depend on the key only indirectly, through another non-key attribute. This is why the misspelt doctor's name had to be corrected on hundreds of rows (D07 Dr. Asad Mir is repeated for every prescription he writes).
(1 mark for each normal form correctly identified and 1 mark for each explanation referenced to Table 1, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Show how Table 1 should be restructured into Third Normal Form. List each resulting table with its columns, identify the primary key of each table and any foreign keys, and explain how the design resolves the pharmacists' complaints.
parts.answer:
Step 1 (1NF): split the Medicines column so that each medicine is on its own row, with separate MedicineName and Quantity columns.
Step 2 (2NF): move the attributes that depend only on PrescriptionNo into a separate table.
Step 3 (3NF): move the patient and doctor names into their own tables.
Resulting tables:
1. Prescriptions (PrescriptionNo [PK], PrescriptionDate, PatientCNIC [FK to Patients], DoctorCode [FK to Doctors]). Example: RX1003, 04-Mar-2026, 35202-1234567-1, D12.
2. PrescriptionLines (PrescriptionNo [PK, FK to Prescriptions] + MedicineName [PK], Quantity). The composite key is PrescriptionNo + MedicineName. Example rows for RX1003: (RX1003, Augmentin 625mg, 14), (RX1003, Gaviscon, 1), (RX1003, Panadol 500mg, 10).
3. Patients (PatientCNIC [PK], PatientName). Example: 35202-1234567-1, Hina Tariq.
4. Doctors (DoctorCode [PK], DoctorName). Example: D07, Dr. Asad Mir.
(In a fuller design MedicineName could be replaced by a MedicineCode referencing a Medicines table.)
How the complaints are resolved:
- Each medicine and its quantity now sits in its own atomic cells in PrescriptionLines, so units of any medicine dispensed in a month can be totalled with a simple query.
- Each doctor's name is stored once in the Doctors table; correcting a misspelt name means updating a single row, and every prescription that refers to that DoctorCode reflects the correction automatically. The same applies to patient names.
Every non-key attribute now depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
(1 mark per correctly structured table with keys (max 4), 1 mark for correct foreign keys, 1 mark for explaining how complaints are resolved, max 6)

secb.scenario:
Indus School of Accountancy (ISA) is a coaching institute. Its enrolment records are held in the table below.
Additional information:
- StudentID and CourseCode together form the composite primary key.
- Each course is taught by only one tutor, but a tutor may teach several courses.
- EnrolmentDate and MockScore relate to a particular student on a particular course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: State whether Table 1 is in First Normal Form, giving reasons. Then identify each partial dependency and each transitive dependency in the table, explaining why each is classified as it is.
parts.answer:
1. First Normal Form. Table 1 is in 1NF: each cell holds a single atomic value (no lists in any cell), each column holds values of the same type, and each row is uniquely identified by the composite key StudentID + CourseCode.
2. Partial dependency (StudentName). StudentName depends only on StudentID, which is part of the composite key; it is the same whatever course the student takes (Areeba Khan appears twice). This breaches 2NF.
3. Partial dependency (CourseTitle and TutorID). CourseTitle and TutorID depend only on CourseCode, the other part of the key, because each course has one title and one tutor regardless of which student is enrolled (DSR01 always shows Data, Systems and Risks and T05). This breaches 2NF.
4. Transitive dependency (TutorName). TutorName depends on TutorID, which is a non-key attribute, rather than directly on the key. The dependency runs CourseCode to TutorID to TutorName. This breaches 3NF; it is why Faraz Ahmed's name is repeated on every row for T05.
5. Full dependencies. EnrolmentDate and MockScore depend on the whole key (a particular student on a particular course), so they are correctly placed.
Rule of thumb: dependence on part of a composite key is partial (2NF problem); dependence on another non-key attribute is transitive (3NF problem).
(1 mark for 1NF conclusion with reasons, up to 4 marks for the dependencies correctly identified and classified, 1 mark for recognising the fully dependent attributes, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Decompose Table 1 into Third Normal Form. Present each resulting table with its columns and primary key, and show how the tables are linked.
parts.answer:
Step 1 (to 2NF): remove the partial dependencies by moving student-only and course-only attributes to their own tables.
- Students (StudentID [PK], StudentName)
- Courses (CourseCode [PK], CourseTitle, TutorID, TutorName)
- Enrolments (StudentID + CourseCode [composite PK], EnrolmentDate, MockScore)
Step 2 (to 3NF): the Courses table still contains a transitive dependency (TutorName depends on TutorID), so split it.
Final 3NF design:
1. Students (StudentID [PK], StudentName). Rows: ST201 Areeba Khan; ST202 Usman Raza; ST203 Maham Ali.
2. Courses (CourseCode [PK], CourseTitle, TutorID [FK to Tutors]). Rows: DSR01 Data, Systems and Risks, T05; TAX01 Taxation, T09; ECO01 Business Economics, T05.
3. Tutors (TutorID [PK], TutorName). Rows: T05 Faraz Ahmed; T09 Rabia Noor.
4. Enrolments (StudentID [PK, FK to Students] + CourseCode [PK, FK to Courses], EnrolmentDate, MockScore). Rows: ST201/DSR01/02-Feb-2026/68; ST201/TAX01/02-Feb-2026/55; ST202/DSR01/09-Feb-2026/74; ST203/ECO01/11-Feb-2026/61.
Links: Enrolments links to Students through StudentID and to Courses through CourseCode; Courses links to Tutors through TutorID. Each fact (a student's name, a course's title and tutor, a tutor's name) is now stored once.
(1 mark per correct table with key (max 4), 1 mark for correct foreign key links, 1 mark for showing the two-step process, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain the statement that every non-key attribute must depend on 'the key, the whole key and nothing but the key', illustrating each part with ISA's data.
parts.answer:
1. 'The key' (1NF): every non-key attribute must depend on a primary key that uniquely identifies each row, with each cell holding one atomic value. In ISA's table each row is identified by StudentID + CourseCode and no cell contains a list, so this is met.
2. 'The whole key' (2NF): where the key is composite, each non-key attribute must depend on all of it, not part of it. StudentName (depends only on StudentID) and CourseTitle (depends only on CourseCode) fail this test, which is why they were moved to the Students and Courses tables. MockScore passes, since it needs both the student and the course.
3. 'Nothing but the key' (3NF): no non-key attribute may depend on another non-key attribute. TutorName depends on TutorID rather than on CourseCode directly, so it was moved to the Tutors table.
(1 mark for each part correctly explained with ISA's data, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Ravi Insurance Brokers (RIB) records the policies sold by its agents in a single table, an extract of which is shown below. PolicyNo is the primary key.
RIB's operations manager has made the following observations:
- Agent A12 recently changed her mobile number. The table now shows two different mobile numbers for her.
- A new agent, A20 Waqas Butt, joined last week, but his details cannot be entered into the system until he sells his first policy.
- Policy P-503 has been cancelled. If it is deleted, RIB will lose the only record of agent A15's name and mobile number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify and explain the three types of anomaly illustrated by the operations manager's observations, using the data in Table 1.
parts.answer:
1. Update anomaly. An update anomaly occurs when the same fact is stored in several places and a change is made in one place but not the others. Agent A12's mobile number is stored on every policy she has sold (P-501, P-502, P-504). When it changed, only P-502 was updated, so the table now shows 0321-4445566 on one row and 0300-1112233 on two others. The database gives two conflicting answers to 'what is Nadia Hussain's mobile number?'
2. Insertion anomaly. An insertion anomaly occurs when one fact cannot be recorded without also recording another, unrelated fact. Because PolicyNo is the primary key and cannot be blank, a row can only be created for a policy. New agent A20 Waqas Butt cannot be entered until he sells a policy, so RIB cannot record its own staff.
3. Deletion anomaly. A deletion anomaly occurs when deleting one record unintentionally destroys other, unrelated information. P-503 is the only row containing agent A15. Deleting the cancelled policy would also delete the only record of Bilal Akhtar's name and mobile number, although he is still an agent.
(1 mark for each anomaly correctly named and explained, 1 mark for each correct illustration from Table 1, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the highest normal form that Table 1 currently satisfies and the type of dependency causing the anomalies. Recommend how the table should be restructured to remove them.
parts.answer:
1. Current normal form: Table 1 is in Second Normal Form. Every cell holds a single atomic value (1NF), and the primary key PolicyNo is a single column, so a partial dependency cannot arise (2NF).
2. Cause: a transitive dependency. AgentName and AgentMobile depend on AgentCode, which is a non-key attribute, and only indirectly on PolicyNo. This breaches 3NF and is the root cause of all three anomalies, because agent details are tied to policy rows.
3. Restructure into two tables:
- Policies (PolicyNo [PK], CustomerName, PolicyType, Premium, AgentCode [FK to Agents])
- Agents (AgentCode [PK], AgentName, AgentMobile)
4. Effect: each agent's details are stored once. A12's mobile is changed in one row (no update anomaly); A20 can be added to Agents before selling any policy (no insertion anomaly); deleting P-503 from Policies leaves A15 intact in Agents (no deletion anomaly).
(1 mark for the correct normal form with reason, 1 mark for identifying the transitive dependency, 1 mark for the correct redesign, 1 mark for explaining how it removes the anomalies, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: RIB's managing director wants to know whether normalisation has any disadvantages. Explain three trade-offs of normalisation.
parts.answer:
1. Increased complexity: normalisation produces more tables (here Policies and Agents instead of one), and the relationships between them must be maintained correctly through primary and foreign keys. The design is harder to build and maintain.
2. Potentially slower queries: a report showing each policy with the agent's name and mobile now requires joining two tables. As the number of tables grows, joins across many tables make retrieval slower than reading one flat table, which matters at large scale or for heavy reporting.
3. Harder for non-technical users: staff who are used to seeing everything in one sheet may find a multi-table structure difficult to understand and query without help or pre-built reports.
These trade-offs are usually acceptable in a transaction system such as RIB's, where avoiding anomalies matters more.
(1 mark per trade-off explained, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Nayab Dairy Distributors (NDD) distributes milk, yoghurt and juices to retailers across southern Punjab. It is building its first data warehouse. The project charter contains the following requirements:
(i) The warehouse will be organised around sales, inventory and distribution routes. Staff attendance, canteen and vehicle fuel claims data will not be included.
(ii) Data will come from the three source systems shown in Table 1. Product codes and date formats differ between the systems and will be standardised before loading.
(iii) Management wants monthly sales by route from 2016 onwards so that it can compare demand across the last ten Ramadan seasons.
(iv) Once a month's data has been loaded, it must not be changed, so that a report on 2023 sales run today gives the same figures as the same report run next year.
The regional sales managers have asked to be given rights to edit historical sales figures directly in the warehouse whenever they spot an error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the characteristic of a data warehouse reflected in each of the requirements (i) to (iv), and explain each characteristic with reference to NDD.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Subject-oriented. Data in a warehouse is organised around business subject areas rather than operational processes. NDD's warehouse is built around sales, inventory and distribution routes, the subjects management analyses, and deliberately excludes unrelated operational data such as attendance and canteen records.
2. (ii) Integrated. Data from diverse sources is cleaned and unified into one consistent format. NDD's three sources record the same product as 'MLK-1000', 'Milk 1 litre' and '1000' and use three date formats. These will be standardised (through the Transform stage of ETL) so that one product and one date mean the same thing across the whole warehouse.
3. (iii) Time-variant. A warehouse stores historical data over long periods (typically five to ten years), not just a current snapshot. Holding monthly sales by route from 2016 is what makes NDD's comparison of ten Ramadan seasons, and other trend analysis, possible; the operational systems hold mainly current data.
4. (iv) Non-volatile. Once loaded, data in a warehouse does not change; it is effectively read-only. This gives NDD a stable base for analysis, so the 2023 figures remain the same whenever the report is run, unlike an operational database where records are overwritten.
(1 mark for each correct characteristic and 1 mark for each explanation applied to NDD, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the regional sales managers' request to edit historical sales figures directly in the warehouse.
parts.answer:
1. The request conflicts with the non-volatile characteristic. The warehouse is meant to be read-only once data is loaded; allowing direct edits means the same report could give different answers on different days, undermining requirement (iv) and management's trust in the analysis.
2. It also undermines integration. Figures changed only in the warehouse would no longer agree with the source systems from which they were extracted, creating two versions of the truth.
3. Control risk. Giving many managers edit rights over historical data increases the risk of errors and of figures being changed to flatter performance, with no reliable record of what was changed and why.
4. Recommendation: the request should be refused. Managers should be given read-only access. Genuine errors should be reported, investigated and corrected in the source system (or by an approved correcting entry), and the correction should then flow into the warehouse through the controlled ETL process, with an audit trail of who approved it.
(1 mark per valid evaluative point including a reasoned recommendation, max 4)

secb.scenario: Bolan Bank Limited (BBL) is reviewing its systems. The IT director has proposed that all of the workloads in Table 1 should run on the core banking database, so that the bank does not need to maintain a separate data warehouse. The head of strategy disagrees.

tables.caption: Table 1: BBL workloads
rows: A customer withdraws cash from an ATM and the account balance is reduced immediately
Analysis of deposit growth by branch and by product over the last eight years
A customer transfers funds to another bank through internet banking
A board dashboard comparing non-performing loans by region for each quarter since 2018
A teller checks a customer's current balance before encashing a cheque
Identifying seasonal patterns in home remittance inflows around Eid over the last ten years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each workload in Table 1 as an OLTP (transaction processing) workload or a data warehouse (OLAP) workload, giving a brief reason for each.
parts.answer:
1. Workload 1, ATM withdrawal: OLTP. A short, real-time, atomic transaction that updates the account balance immediately.
2. Workload 2, eight-year deposit growth analysis: Data warehouse (OLAP). A complex, read-only analysis of a large volume of historical data.
3. Workload 3, internet banking transfer: OLTP. A real-time transaction that must be processed completely or not at all (debit and credit), with integrity and concurrency control.
4. Workload 4, board dashboard of quarterly NPLs since 2018: Data warehouse (OLAP). Historical, summarised reporting across regions and many periods for decision-making.
5. Workload 5, teller balance check: OLTP. A short, fast query retrieving a small amount of current data.
6. Workload 6, ten-year Eid remittance patterns: Data warehouse (OLAP). Trend analysis over a long timeframe, which depends on time-variant historical data.
(1 mark per correct classification with reason, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Compare OLTP systems with data warehouses across six features, and use your comparison to explain why the IT director's proposal is inappropriate.
parts.answer:
1. Purpose: OLTP processes transactions in real time (workloads 1, 3 and 5); a warehouse supports historical analysis (workloads 2, 4 and 6).
2. Data volume: OLTP works with small, current datasets (one customer's account now); a warehouse holds large historical datasets (eight to ten years of all branches).
3. Data structure: OLTP is highly normalised to avoid redundancy and update anomalies, because it is constantly writing; a warehouse is typically denormalised so that analytical queries avoid slow multi-table joins. One database cannot be optimised both ways.
4. Operations: OLTP performs insert, update and delete; a warehouse is read-only.
5. Performance tuning: OLTP is tuned for fast transactions; a warehouse is tuned for complex queries.
6. Query complexity: OLTP runs simple, short queries ('what is this balance?'); a warehouse runs complex, long-running queries ('NPLs by region by quarter since 2018').
Why the proposal is inappropriate: running long analytical queries over years of data on the core banking database would compete with, slow down or lock the ATM, transfer and teller transactions that customers need instantly, while the normalised OLTP structure would make the analysis slow. The core banking database also keeps mainly current data, whereas the analyses need long, unchanging history. BBL should keep separate systems.
(1 mark per correctly compared feature, max 5, and 1 mark for applying the comparison to the proposal, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain the advantages and the challenges of OLTP systems such as BBL's core banking system.
parts.answer:
Advantages:
1. Real-time data access: balances and transactions are updated immediately, so an ATM withdrawal is reflected at once.
2. High performance and scalability under load: thousands of short transactions can be processed concurrently.
3. Data consistency and integrity: atomic transactions, constraints and concurrency control ensure, for example, that a transfer cannot be half-completed and two users cannot spend the same balance.
Challenges:
4. The highly normalised design is complex to build and maintain.
5. OLTP is poor at analytical queries and historical analysis, which is why workloads 2, 4 and 6 belong in a warehouse.
6. It is resource-intensive, needing powerful infrastructure to maintain performance at peak times such as salary days.
(1 mark per valid point, including at least one advantage and one challenge, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Sindh Snacks Limited (SSL) manufactures crisps and biscuits and is creating a data warehouse to analyse sales by product, channel and region. Table 1 summarises the source data identified by the project team.
The project manager has proposed: 'Let us copy all three sources into the warehouse exactly as they are, and analysts can tidy the data when they use it.' SSL wants the warehouse to hold all sales since January 2021, and to be updated every night after that.

tables.caption: Table 1: Source data
rows: Some rows have a blank amount
Some orders appear twice in the export
Only quantity and unit price are recorded; no sales value

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the Extract and Load stages of the ETL process, applying each to SSL's situation, including the type of load SSL will need at the start of the project and after it.
parts.answer:
1. Extract. Data is collected from the various source systems: databases, APIs, flat files and enterprise systems. For SSL this means pulling the daily CSV files from the outlet tills, querying the online store's PostgreSQL database, and reading the distributors' Excel workbooks. The challenges are handling three different formats, ensuring each source is available when extraction runs (the hand-prepared Excel workbooks may be late), and deciding how often to extract (nightly).
2. Load. The transformed data is transferred into the warehouse.
3. Initial load: at the start of the project SSL will populate the warehouse with all historical sales since January 2021 in one go.
4. Incremental load: after that, each nightly run will add only new or changed records (that day's sales) rather than reloading all the data.
(1 mark for Extract applied, 1 mark for Load explained, 1 mark for initial load and 1 mark for incremental load applied to SSL, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: With reference to Table 1, explain the Transform stage and identify the specific transformations that SSL's data will require.
parts.answer:
The Transform stage cleans, standardises and enriches the raw data in a staging area so that it meets the warehouse's requirements before loading. SSL's data needs the following transformations:
1. Standardise dates. The three sources use MM/DD/YYYY, YYYY-MM-DD and DD-Mon-YY. All dates must be converted to one format (for example YYYY-MM-DD); otherwise a date such as 03/07/2026 could be read as either 7 March or 3 July.
2. Convert currency. Export orders in USD must be converted into PKR (at an agreed rate) so that sales can be totalled and compared meaningfully.
3. Remove duplicates. Orders that appear twice in the online store export must be removed, otherwise online sales will be overstated.
4. Handle nulls / blanks. Till rows with a blank amount must be corrected, completed from another field or excluded, according to an agreed rule, rather than being treated as zero sales without investigation.
5. Apply business rules. For distributor sales, the sales value must be calculated as quantity x unit price, because the workbooks do not record it.
6. Merge and link customers. Customers are identified by mobile number, e-mail address and distributor codes. These must be mapped to a common customer identifier so that a customer's purchases can be linked across channels.
(1 mark per transformation correctly identified from Table 1 and explained, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the project manager's proposal and explain the importance of ETL in data integration.
parts.answer:
1. The proposal skips the Transform stage, which is where the value of a warehouse is created. Loading the data 'as is' would put inconsistent dates, mixed currencies, duplicate orders, blank amounts and unlinked customers directly into the warehouse, so every report drawn from it would be unreliable.
2. Leaving each analyst to tidy the data would mean the same corrections being made many times, in different ways, producing different answers to the same question.
3. Importance of ETL - consistency: it integrates data from heterogeneous sources into one structure with common formats and definitions, so 'sales' means the same thing whichever channel it came from.
4. Importance of ETL - accuracy: cleansing (removing duplicates, handling blanks, applying business rules) produces data that management can rely on.
5. Importance of ETL - efficiency: data arrives in the warehouse ready for fast querying, so analysts spend their time on analysis, not preparation.
Conclusion: the proposal should be rejected and a proper ETL process with a staging area implemented.
(1 mark per valid point, including a conclusion, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Shaheen Motors (SM) operates a network of car showrooms and service workshops in Lahore, Islamabad and Peshawar. Two years ago SM built a corporate data warehouse that integrates data from its sales, finance, inventory and workshop systems.
Two departments now want their own smaller analytical databases, as described in Table 1. The finance director is concerned that 'we will end up with three different versions of the truth'.

tables.caption: Table 1: Departmental proposals
rows: Campaign responses, test-drive bookings and car sales by model and city
Extracted from the corporate data warehouse
Workshop job cards, parts used and customer satisfaction scores
Built by an external contractor directly from the workshop system, bypassing the warehouse

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what a data mart is, and identify the type of data mart proposed by each department, justifying your answer.
parts.answer:
1. A data mart is a subset of a data warehouse that is tailored to a specific business unit or subject area, such as marketing, finance or sales. It gives the unit faster and more focused access for targeted analysis.
2. There are two types. A dependent data mart is built from an existing data warehouse. An independent data mart is created directly from the source systems, bypassing any central warehouse.
3. Marketing: dependent data mart. Its campaign, test-drive and sales data will be extracted from SM's corporate data warehouse, so the mart depends on the warehouse as its source.
4. After-sales service: independent data mart. The contractor will build it directly from the workshop system, bypassing the warehouse.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for explaining the two types, 1.5 marks for each correct classification with justification, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the benefits that the marketing department could obtain from a data mart.
parts.answer:
1. Speed. The marketing mart has a much smaller scope than the corporate warehouse, holding only campaign, test-drive and sales data rather than all finance, inventory and workshop data. Queries such as 'test-drive to sale conversion by model in Islamabad last quarter' therefore run considerably faster.
2. Focus. The mart is customised to marketing's needs: it contains only the subject areas and fields marketing uses and ignores irrelevant data such as payroll or parts inventory. Analysts do not have to navigate the entire warehouse structure to find what they need, which makes the data easier to use and reduces errors.
(Up to 2 marks for each of the two benefits, speed and focus, well explained and applied to SM, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the after-sales service department's proposal in the light of the finance director's concern, and recommend how SM should proceed.
parts.answer:
1. An independent data mart is created directly from the source systems, bypassing the central warehouse. It therefore does not draw on the warehouse's integrated data, that is, data which the warehouse's ETL process has already cleaned, standardised and unified into one consistent format.
2. The contractor would have to build a separate extraction and transformation process. If its Transform rules (for example how workshop revenue is calculated or how customers are identified) differ from those used for the warehouse, workshop revenue, parts usage or customer counts in the after-sales mart may not agree with the same figures in the warehouse, so managers could receive conflicting numbers for the same period. This is the finance director's concern.
3. It also duplicates effort and cost (a second ETL process to build and maintain) and creates another store of customer data to secure.
4. Since the workshop system is already a source of the corporate warehouse, the data the department needs is already available there in integrated form, so there is little reason to bypass it.
Recommendation: SM should build the after-sales mart as a dependent data mart drawn from the corporate warehouse, adding any missing workshop fields to the warehouse's ETL process if required. This gives the department the speed and focus it wants while keeping a single version of the truth.
(1 mark per valid evaluative point and 1 mark for a reasoned recommendation, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Attock Chemicals Limited (ACL) keeps employee and allowance data in the table below. EmpID is the primary key. Each employee belongs to one department, and each department has one department head.
The HR manager complains that when the head of a department changes, every employee row in that department has to be edited, and that it is impossible to calculate the total house rent allowance paid without manually reading every Allowances cell.
Separately, ACL's business intelligence team plans to copy payroll data into the company's data warehouse in a single wide, denormalised table for reporting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain whether Table 1 is in First Normal Form, and identify any other dependency problem in the table.
parts.answer:
1. Not in 1NF. The Allowances column contains several values in one cell, for example 'House rent 20,000; Conveyance 6,000; Shift 5,000' for E102, and each value combines two facts (allowance type and amount). 1NF requires every cell to hold a single, atomic value with consistent data type in each column. Because amounts are buried in text, the total house rent allowance cannot be calculated by a query, which is the HR manager's second complaint.
2. Transitive dependency. DeptName and DeptHead depend on DeptCode, which is a non-key attribute, and only indirectly on the primary key EmpID. This breaches 3NF. It causes the update anomaly the HR manager describes: Tahir Mahmood is repeated on every Finance employee's row, so a change of head must be made on every row, and any missed row leaves conflicting data.
3. Partial dependency is not an issue in the table as given, because the key EmpID is a single column; however, once allowances are split into separate rows the key would become EmpID + AllowanceType, and EmpName and DeptCode would then depend on only part of it.
(1.5 marks for the 1NF analysis, 1.5 marks for the transitive dependency, 1 mark for the comment on partial dependency, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Restructure Table 1 into Third Normal Form, showing each resulting table with its columns, primary key and foreign keys, and sample data.
parts.answer:
Step 1 (1NF): put each allowance on its own row with separate AllowanceType and Amount columns; the key becomes EmpID + AllowanceType.
Step 2 (2NF): EmpName, DeptCode, DeptName and DeptHead depend only on EmpID, so move them to an Employees table, leaving allowances in their own table.
Step 3 (3NF): DeptName and DeptHead depend on DeptCode, so move them to a Departments table.
Final design:
1. Employees (EmpID [PK], EmpName, DeptCode [FK to Departments]). Rows: E101 Saima Rauf FIN; E102 Junaid Iqbal PRD; E103 Omer Shah FIN.
2. Departments (DeptCode [PK], DeptName, DeptHead). Rows: FIN Finance Tahir Mahmood; PRD Production Lubna Sheikh.
3. EmployeeAllowances (EmpID [PK, FK to Employees] + AllowanceType [PK], Amount). Rows: E101 House rent 25,000; E101 Conveyance 8,000; E102 House rent 20,000; E102 Conveyance 6,000; E102 Shift 5,000; E103 House rent 25,000.
Result: a change of department head is made once in Departments, and total house rent can be obtained by summing Amount where AllowanceType = 'House rent' (70,000 in the sample).
(1 mark for each correct table with keys (max 3), 1 mark for foreign keys, 1 mark for correct sample data / atomic amounts, 1 mark for explaining how the complaints are resolved, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: The HR manager asks why the business intelligence team is allowed to denormalise the same data in the warehouse after so much effort has been spent normalising it. Explain.
parts.answer:
1. The two systems have opposite jobs. ACL's payroll system is an OLTP system that is constantly inserting, updating and deleting records, so it must be normalised to avoid redundancy and update anomalies such as the department head problem.
2. The data warehouse is read-only (non-volatile): data is loaded through ETL and then only queried. Because users do not update it, the update anomalies that normalisation prevents do not arise in the same way.
3. In a warehouse the main enemy is slow multi-table joins in complex, long-running reports. A denormalised, wide table accepts some duplication so that analytical queries, such as allowance cost by department over several years, run much faster.
Normalisation is therefore not universally right; it is right for transaction processing, while denormalisation suits analysis.
(1 mark per valid point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Rawal Care Hospital (RCH) is a 300-bed private hospital in Rawalpindi. As part of an IT review, the newly appointed Head of IT has prepared the following inventory of the hospital's IT estate:
(i) Three rack-mounted machines in the basement data room that host the Hospital Management System (HMS) and its patient database.
(ii) The Linux operating system installed on those machines.
(iii) The HMS itself, used by doctors, nurses and the billing desk.
(iv) Switches and a firewall that connect the wards, laboratory and pharmacy and control access from outside.
(v) Barcode scanners and label printers used in the pharmacy.
(vi) A network-attached storage (NAS) device that holds nightly copies of the patient database.
(vii) The network that links all departments inside the hospital building.
(viii) Doctors' personal notes saved only on the hard drives of their own desktop PCs.
RCH has also signed agreements with four health insurance companies. At present, billing staff re-key every insured patient's bill into each insurer's online claims portal, because the HMS cannot exchange data with those portals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the items (i) to (viii) into the relevant component of IT systems architecture (hardware, software, networks or storage), stating the specific type within that component, and briefly explain the role of each.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Hardware - servers. They are powerful computers that handle requests from clients and host the HMS application and patient database; they are the backbone of RCH's infrastructure.
2. (ii) Software - system software. The operating system manages the servers' hardware resources (memory, processing, storage) and provides the platform on which the HMS runs; it is the intermediary between hardware and applications.
3. (iii) Software - application software. The HMS lets users perform specific business tasks such as recording treatment, dispensing and billing.
4. (iv) Hardware - networking equipment. Switches enable communication between devices, and the firewall controls access to the hospital network for security.
5. (v) Hardware - peripheral devices. Scanners (input) and printers (output) are how pharmacy users interact with the system.
6. (vi) Hardware - storage device (and part of the centralised storage layer). The NAS holds data and enables backup for disaster recovery.
7. (vii) Network - Local Area Network (LAN). It covers a limited area (one building), giving fast and secure communication, relying on protocols such as TCP/IP.
8. (viii) Storage - local storage. Data sits on the individual device; it is adequate for small needs but lacks scalability, is not easily accessible to others and is not covered by the central backup.
(1 mark for each item correctly classified with its type and role, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend the type of software that would solve the problem with the insurers' claims portals, and explain how it would work and benefit RCH.
parts.answer:
Recommendation: middleware.
1. Middleware is software that connects different applications and systems so that they can communicate and share data. It acts as a translator sitting between the HMS and each insurer's portal.
2. How it works for RCH: when a bill for an insured patient is finalised in the HMS, the middleware picks up the claim data, converts it to the format each insurer requires and transmits it to the relevant portal, returning acknowledgements to the HMS. It provides messaging, authentication (logging in to each insurer securely) and database access services.
3. Benefits: re-keying is eliminated, so billing staff time is freed and keying errors (wrong amounts, wrong patient) are avoided; claims are submitted faster, improving cash flow; and a record of what was sent supports reconciliation of claims with insurers.
4. RCH does not need to replace the HMS or ask insurers to change their portals, because middleware integrates the existing systems.
(1 mark for identifying middleware, up to 3 marks for explanation of how it works and benefits applied to RCH, max 4)

secb.topic: Interactions and dependencies; LAN, WAN and storage
secb.scenario:
Sarhad Freight Services (SFS) is a transport company with its head office in Peshawar and depots in Islamabad, Lahore and Quetta. The IT manager has received the following complaints in the last month:
(i) A new server was purchased for the Peshawar head office, but the fleet maintenance application, which runs on an old version of its operating system, could not be installed because that operating system does not support the new machine's processor and disk controllers.
(ii) Depot staff in Quetta say that consignment documents saved in the company's cloud storage take several minutes to open, although the same files open quickly in Peshawar. The cloud provider confirms its servers are working normally.
(iii) The online route-tracking application used by dispatchers freezes and drops sessions whenever the depot's internet link is heavily used by staff streaming videos.
(iv) To save cost, the IT manager wants to run the fleet application, the payroll application and the email server on one powerful physical server instead of three separate machines.
At present, each depot has its own office network and the depots exchange files by email. Many depot clerks also keep the only copy of delivery records on their own PCs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (iv), identify the interaction between architecture components that is involved and explain the dependency, stating what SFS should do.
parts.answer:
1. Issue (i) - Hardware and software interaction. Hardware and software must be compatible: the operating system manages the hardware resources and applications use those resources. The old operating system cannot drive the new processor and disk controllers, so the application cannot run. SFS should check compatibility before buying hardware and either upgrade the operating system (and test the fleet application on it) or run the old operating system in a virtual machine supported by the new server. (2 marks)
2. Issue (ii) - Storage and network interaction. With cloud computing, storage is network-dependent: the files sit in a remote data centre and are reached over the network, so network speed governs how quickly they can be retrieved. The storage is fine (the provider confirms this); the Quetta link is the bottleneck. SFS should upgrade bandwidth or reliability of the Quetta connection. (2 marks)
3. Issue (iii) - Software and network interaction. Applications depend on network connectivity to exchange data, and network performance directly determines application performance. The tracking application needs a stable connection; when bandwidth is consumed by streaming, it freezes. SFS should increase capacity and restrict or prioritise traffic so business applications are not starved. (2 marks)
4. Issue (iv) - Hardware and software interaction through virtual machines. A virtual machine environment on powerful hardware lets one physical server run several operating systems and applications at the same time, each isolated in its own VM. This is feasible, but SFS must ensure the server is compatible with all three workloads and should note that consolidation makes the one server a single point of failure, so backup or a failover host is needed. (2 marks)
(2 marks per issue: 1 for the correct interaction, 1 for explaining the dependency and action; max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the types of network that SFS currently uses and the type it needs in order to connect its head office and depots, giving reasons.
parts.answer:
1. LAN: each depot's office network is a Local Area Network, covering a limited area such as one office or building. It allows fast and secure communication between devices in that depot only. (1 mark)
2. Internet: SFS uses the internet (a global network) to send email between depots and to reach its cloud storage. Relying on emailed files leads to multiple versions and delays. (1 mark)
3. Needed - WAN: a Wide Area Network connects devices across a large geographic area, linking remote offices. SFS should link Peshawar, Islamabad, Lahore and Quetta through a WAN so that all sites can share the same applications and data in real time rather than exchanging copies by email. (1 mark)
4. The WAN and LANs should use common protocols such as TCP/IP and be protected by firewalls, and the Quetta link in particular should have sufficient bandwidth given the dependencies identified in part (a). (1 mark)
(1 mark per valid explained point, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Discuss the weakness in the depot clerks' practice of keeping delivery records on their own PCs and recommend an alternative storage approach.
parts.answer:
1. Weakness: this is local storage, where data sits on the individual device. It lacks scalability, the records are not available to head office or other depots, and if a PC fails or is stolen the only copy of the delivery records (evidence of delivery for billing) is lost.
2. Recommendation: move to centralised storage, where data is held in a data centre or in the cloud (for example a shared cloud drive used by all depots).
3. Benefits: centralised storage gives scalability, redundancy (copies are replicated and backed up) and easy access from anywhere, so delivery records can be retrieved by billing staff in Peshawar immediately. Because cloud storage is network-dependent, SFS must make sure each depot's connection is adequate.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Hisaab Online (Private) Limited (HOL) operates a web portal through which salaried individuals and small businesses prepare and submit their income tax returns. Usage is low for most of the year but rises about fifteen-fold in the last three weeks before the FBR filing deadline on 30 September.
The portal has two parts: a web front end that handles user sessions, and a legacy tax-computation engine that was written many years ago as a single monolithic program. The computation engine was not designed to run across more than one machine.
The Chief Technology Officer has received two proposals to cope with next year's peak:

tables.caption: Proposals received by HOL
rows: Purchase additional processors, memory and SSD storage and install them in the existing on-premise server that runs the whole portal.
Move the web front end to a cloud platform where additional virtual servers are added automatically as user numbers rise and removed when they fall, with the load spread across all servers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the scaling approach represented by each proposal and explain the difference between the two approaches.
parts.answer:
1. Proposal A is vertical scaling ('scale up'): more resources (CPU, RAM, storage) are added to an existing machine, making that single machine more powerful. (1 mark)
2. Proposal B is horizontal scaling ('scale out'): more machines or servers are added and the workload is distributed across multiple nodes; existing hardware is not upgraded but added to. This is the model used in cloud environments. (1 mark)
3. The essential difference is one bigger machine versus more machines working together. Vertical scaling avoids coordination between machines; horizontal scaling requires the application to be able to run in parallel across nodes but is not limited by the capacity of a single machine. (2 marks)
(max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the advantages and limitations of each proposal in HOL's circumstances.
parts.answer:
Proposal A - vertical scaling
1. Advantage - simplicity: HOL upgrades what it already has without reconfiguring a fleet of servers. (1 mark)
2. Advantage - fewer dependencies and suitability for monolithic applications: the legacy computation engine cannot run across machines, so giving it a more powerful machine is the approach that suits it. (1 mark)
3. Limitation - single point of failure: the whole portal still runs on one server, so a hardware failure in the deadline week would make the portal unavailable exactly when taxpayers need it. Hardware ceiling and cost: a server can only hold so many processors and so much memory, high-end components are expensive, and HOL would pay for peak capacity that sits idle for 49 weeks of the year. (1 mark)
Proposal B - horizontal scaling
4. Advantage - elasticity: cloud servers are added automatically during the September peak and removed afterwards, so HOL pays for extra capacity only when it needs it. (1 mark)
5. Advantage - fault tolerance and no hardware limit: if one virtual server fails, the workload shifts to the others, minimising downtime, and there is no theoretical limit to the number of servers that can be added as HOL grows. (1 mark)
6. Limitation: horizontal scaling suits distributed workloads; the monolithic computation engine cannot be spread across nodes, so Proposal B alone does not scale that component. Coordination between many servers and the dependence on network connectivity to the cloud also add complexity. (1 mark)
(1 mark per well-applied point, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate approach for HOL, giving reasons.
parts.answer:
1. HOL should adopt Proposal B for the web front end, since user sessions can be distributed and the fifteen-fold seasonal peak is exactly the situation that cloud elasticity addresses, with costs matched to demand and fault tolerance during the deadline period. (1 mark)
2. Because the computation engine is monolithic, it should in the short term be scaled vertically (on a powerful cloud or on-premise instance) and protected by redundancy and failover, so that its failure does not stop the portal. (1 mark)
3. In the longer term HOL should redesign the engine on modular (microservices) lines so that it too can scale horizontally and remove the single point of failure. (1 mark)
(Credit any well-reasoned recommendation that addresses both components; max 3)

secb.topic: Best practices for designing IT architecture
secb.scenario:
Margalla Institute of Management (MIM) is a private university in Islamabad with 9,000 students. Its student portal handles admissions, fee payment, course registration and publication of examination results. An external review of the portal's architecture has reported the following findings:
(i) The portal is a single program. Last semester a change made to the fee module caused the whole portal to crash, and examination results could not be viewed for two days.
(ii) All portal servers are in one server room on campus. A twelve-hour power outage in March made the portal unavailable and there was no alternative site.
