(iii) Students' CNIC numbers, contact details and fee records are stored in plain text, and every member of staff with a portal login can view every student's record.
(iv) Server capacity is fixed. Each August, when admission applications open, the portal slows down severely, while for the rest of the year most of the capacity is unused.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the findings (i) to (iv), identify the architectural best practice that MIM has not followed and recommend how MIM should apply it.
parts.answer:
1. Finding (i) - Modular design. The system should be broken into smaller, independent components, each responsible for one function (a microservices architecture). MIM should separate admissions, fees, registration and results into independent services, so that an upgrade to the fee module can be made and tested while results continue to be available. (2 marks)
2. Finding (ii) - Redundancy and failover. Critical components should have backups, and a failover mechanism should switch automatically to the backup when the primary fails. MIM should host a backup environment at a second location (for example a cloud region or another campus) with automatic failover, giving high availability and business continuity during outages. (2 marks)
3. Finding (iii) - Security by design. Security must be integrated at every layer rather than added as an afterthought. MIM should encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit, apply role-based access control so that, for example, only the finance office sees fee records and teachers see only their own courses, implement intrusion detection and prevention for real-time monitoring, and conduct regular security audits. (2 marks)
4. Finding (iv) - Scalability and flexibility. The architecture should be designed for growth using cloud services that scale dynamically, virtual machines and distributed systems. MIM should use cloud auto-scaling so additional resources are provisioned automatically during the August admissions surge and released afterwards, paying only for capacity actually used. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each correctly identified best practice and 1 for an applied recommendation, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain three benefits that MIM's IT team would obtain from adopting the best practice identified for finding (i).
parts.answer:
1. Flexibility: individual modules can be updated or replaced without touching the rest of the system, so changes to fee rules each semester do not put the results or registration modules at risk. (1 mark)
2. Ease of maintenance: troubleshooting a small independent module is far simpler than debugging one large program, so faults are found and fixed faster and downtime is reduced. (1 mark)
3. Improved collaboration: different teams (for example the finance systems team and the academic systems team) can work on different modules at the same time, shortening delivery times. (1 mark)
4. Containment of failure: because modules operate independently, a fault in one service does not bring down the whole portal, which directly prevents a repeat of the two-day loss of examination results. (1 mark)
(1 mark per explained and applied benefit; three benefits plus application for full marks, max 4)

secb.scenario:
The IT steering committee of Indus Valley Holdings (IVH), a diversified group, is considering four separate initiatives:
(i) IVH's cement plant near Dera Ghazi Khan has sensors on its kilns. The readings must be analysed within milliseconds so that fuel input can be adjusted immediately, but the plant's link to the group data centre in Karachi is slow and occasionally drops.
(ii) IVH's new digital wallet subsidiary wants to launch its application nationally within three months. It owns almost no hardware and wants its software packaged in containers that can be deployed and scaled flexibly.
(iii) Previously anyone connected to the head office network was trusted automatically. Last month a contractor's laptop, plugged into a meeting room socket, was used to browse the payroll database. IVH also now has 1,200 staff working from client sites and home.
(iv) The group's data centre manager wants a system that learns from historical usage to predict demand and allocate server and cooling resources automatically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the emerging trend in IT architecture that is most relevant to each initiative and explain how it would address IVH's need.
parts.answer:
1. Initiative (i) - Edge computing. Processing moves closer to the data source instead of travelling to a distant data centre. Analysing kiln readings on edge servers at the plant gives the low latency needed for real-time fuel adjustment and keeps working even when the link to Karachi is slow or down. (2 marks)
2. Initiative (ii) - Cloud-native architecture. Systems are built for the cloud from the outset, using containerisation and orchestration tools such as Kubernetes for flexible, scalable deployment. The wallet subsidiary can launch nationally with almost no hardware of its own and scale as customer numbers grow. (2 marks)
3. Initiative (iii) - Zero Trust security. Its principle is 'never trust, always verify': there is no trusted perimeter and every access request is continuously verified, whether from inside or outside the network. The contractor's laptop would not have gained access merely by being plugged in, and remote staff are authenticated and authorised each time they access a resource. It also reduces insider risk. (2 marks)
4. Initiative (iv) - AI integration. Machine learning optimises resource allocation and enables predictive analytics, for example predicting load and adjusting cooling, which has been shown to cut data-centre cooling costs significantly. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each correct trend and 1 for applied explanation, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Compare edge computing with centralised cloud computing, and explain why the group data centre should still be used for some of the cement plant's data.
parts.answer:
1. Edge computing processes data at or near the source; its key benefits are low latency and real-time response, and it reduces the volume of data sent over the network. (1 mark)
2. Centralised cloud or data centre computing processes and stores data in a remote location; its strengths are scale, large storage, central management and access from anywhere, but every request involves a round trip over the network, which adds delay and depends on the link. (1 mark)
3. For the kiln, decisions that must be taken in milliseconds should be made at the edge, because the Karachi link cannot guarantee the response time. (1 mark)
4. Summarised readings and historical data should still be sent to the group data centre (when the link allows) for long-term storage, group-wide reporting and analysis such as efficiency trends across plants, where latency does not matter. (1 mark)
(max 4)

secb.scenario:
Ravi Code Labs (RCL) is a Lahore-based software house. It has won five new assignments and the development manager must decide which language each team should use:
(i) Writing the low-level control program for a card-reading chip inside a payment terminal, where the code must directly control memory and the processor.
(ii) Building an Android mobile application for a courier company and its supporting enterprise web services, which must run on many different devices.
(iii) Developing a model that uses machine learning to predict which customers of a telecom client are likely to leave, using numerical computing and machine learning libraries.
(iv) Creating an interactive website for a hotel chain where room availability updates on screen without reloading the page, with server-side code in the same language.
(v) Producing monthly reports for a bank by extracting and summarising data held in its relational database.
RCL is also developing a high-performance 3D driving simulator game for an export client.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate programming language for each of assignments (i) to (v) and the simulator game, justifying each choice.
parts.answer:
1. (i) Low-level language (assembly / machine code). Low-level languages are closely connected to the hardware and give direct control over memory and the processor; they are used for device drivers and embedded systems. They are difficult to write and demand strong hardware knowledge, so RCL must assign specialist staff. (C++ is also acceptable as it is used for embedded systems with control over resources.) (2 marks)
2. (ii) Java. Java is robust and object-oriented and follows 'write once, run anywhere' through the Java Virtual Machine, so the same code runs on many devices. It is widely used for Android apps, large-scale enterprise applications and web services, and has strong typing and an extensive standard library. (2 marks)
3. (iii) Python. Python is known for simplicity and versatility, and is the preferred language for data science and AI. Its library ecosystem (NumPy for numerical computing, TensorFlow for machine learning) and suitability for rapid prototyping fit the churn model. (2 marks)
4. (iv) JavaScript. JavaScript is the backbone of web development and adds interactivity and dynamic content to websites. Frameworks such as React and Angular handle the screen updates, and Node.js allows server-side code, enabling full-stack development in one language. (HTML/CSS would be used alongside for layout.) (2 marks)
5. (v) SQL. SQL is the standard domain-specific language for querying, updating and managing relational databases. It is declarative: the developer specifies what data is wanted rather than how to get it. (1 mark)
6. Simulator game - C++. C++ is known for performance and control over system resources, including manual memory management, and is used for games and simulations. (1 mark)
(Marks as indicated: language identified plus justification, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the four types of programming language, distinguishing scripting languages from other high-level languages.
parts.answer:
1. Low-level languages: closely connected to the hardware, giving direct control over memory and processor; hard to write; examples assembly and machine code; used for operating systems, device drivers and embedded systems. (1 mark)
2. High-level languages: easy to read and understand, allowing the programmer to focus on solving the problem rather than hardware detail, with rich built-in libraries; examples Python, Java and C++; used for websites, applications and business programs. (1 mark)
3. Scripting languages: usually interpreted, meaning the code runs line by line with no separate compilation step; examples JavaScript, Python and PHP; used for web development, automation and rapid development. The absence of a compilation step is what distinguishes them from compiled high-level languages. (1 mark)
4. Domain-specific languages (DSLs): designed for one specialised task, for example SQL for databases, HTML/CSS for web design and R for data analysis. (1 mark)
(1 mark per type correctly explained, max 4)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what is meant by IT systems architecture and why it should be regarded as a strategic framework rather than merely a technical blueprint.
parts.answer:
1. IT systems architecture is the overall design and structure of an organisation's information technology, covering its hardware, software, networks and storage (and the protocols linking them). It decides what sits where, what connects to what, and whether the systems will cope as the organisation grows. (1 mark)
2. It is a strategic framework because it aligns technology with business goals: decisions about architecture determine whether the business can expand to new locations, launch new channels or handle more customers. (1 mark)
3. Architecture choices determine scalability, flexibility and security; for example, a design with a single server creates a single point of failure that threatens business continuity, which is a business risk rather than a wiring issue. (1 mark)
4. Therefore, when advising on architecture, management and accountants are answering business questions about cost, risk, growth and continuity, and architecture decisions should involve business leadership and not only the IT department. (1 mark)
(max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between system software, application software and middleware, giving an example of each.
parts.answer:
1. System software is the operating system and utility programs. It manages hardware resources such as memory, processing power and storage, and provides the platform on which application software runs; it is the intermediary between hardware and applications. Examples: Windows, Linux, macOS, Unix. (2 marks)
2. Application software comprises programs that let users perform specific business tasks such as word processing, accounting or customer relationship management. Examples: Microsoft Office, SAP ERP, Google Chrome. (2 marks)
3. Middleware is software that connects different applications and systems so that they can communicate and share data, providing services such as messaging, authentication and database access. Example: an airline using middleware to integrate its booking system with third-party payment gateways and loyalty programmes. (2 marks)
Key distinction: system software serves the hardware, application software serves the user's task, and middleware serves the connection between applications.
(1 mark for each explanation and 1 for each valid example, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain why storage is treated both as a type of hardware and as a separate component of IT architecture, and compare local and centralised storage.
parts.answer:
1. A physical disk, SSD or NAS device is a piece of hardware. Separately, the way an organisation stores, replicates and retrieves its data is an architectural layer in its own right, which is why storage is also one of the four components. (1 mark)
2. Local storage keeps data on the individual device (such as a PC's own hard drive). It is adequate for small needs but lacks scalability and is not easily shared or protected. (1 mark)
3. Centralised storage keeps data in a data centre or the cloud (for example Google Drive or Dropbox). It provides scalability, redundancy and easy access from anywhere, but cloud-based storage depends on network connectivity for speed of access. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Chenab Foods Limited (CFL) is a food processing company in Gujranwala. Its server room holds twelve ageing physical servers, each running one application (including the ERP, payroll, email, quality laboratory system and the website). Most servers are less than 20% utilised, and maintenance and electricity costs are high.
The IT director has proposed replacing all twelve with two new high-specification servers, each running several virtual machines (VMs). He also plans to move the website to a cloud provider so that capacity can grow during Ramzan promotional campaigns. The Chief Financial Officer supports the cost savings but has asked: 'If we put everything onto two machines, what happens when one of them breaks?'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how virtual machines would allow CFL to consolidate its servers, and identify which interaction between architecture components this relies on.
parts.answer:
1. A virtual machine environment on powerful hardware lets one physical server run several operating systems and applications at the same time. Each application would run in its own VM, isolated from the others, as if it had its own machine. (1 mark)
2. This relies on the hardware and software interaction: the hardware and the software must be compatible, the operating system (and virtualisation layer) manages the hardware resources, and the applications use those resources. (1 mark)
3. CFL's twelve lightly used servers can be replaced by two well-utilised hosts because the spare processing power, memory and storage is shared among the VMs. (1 mark)
4. CFL must confirm that each application (for example the old quality laboratory system) is compatible with the new hardware and virtual environment before migration. (1 mark)
(max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss how the IT director's proposals would improve the scalability and flexibility of CFL's architecture.
parts.answer:
1. Virtual machines are a key enabler of scalability: a new application or test environment can be created as a new VM without buying a new physical server, and resources can be reallocated between VMs as needs change. (1 mark)
2. Cloud services allow resources to be scaled dynamically. Moving the website to the cloud allows capacity to be added during Ramzan campaigns and reduced afterwards, so CFL pays only for capacity it uses (elasticity). (1 mark)
3. Fewer physical machines reduce maintenance, space and electricity costs, and make the estate easier to manage and adapt. (1 mark)
4. Flexibility is improved because CFL can integrate new technologies and adapt as the business changes, for example adding further cloud-based services later without redesigning the server room. (1 mark)
(max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Respond to the CFO's concern, explaining the risk that consolidation creates and recommending the architectural best practice CFL should apply.
parts.answer:
1. The CFO is right: consolidation concentrates many applications on each host, so the failure of one host would stop all the applications on it at once; each host becomes a single point of failure. (1 mark)
2. CFL should apply redundancy and failover: critical components should have backups, and a failover mechanism should automatically switch to the backup when the primary fails. (1 mark)
3. In practice, the two hosts should be configured so that the VMs of a failed host can be restarted on the surviving host (each host sized with enough spare capacity), storage should be replicated and backed up, and the ERP and payroll VMs should be prioritised. (1 mark)
4. This gives high availability, resilience and business continuity; CFL should test failover regularly and could use a cloud or off-site backup in case the whole server room is affected. (1 mark)
(max 4)

secb.topic: ERP modules and the shared database
secb.scenario: Chiniot Woodcraft Limited (CWL) manufactures furniture for the domestic market and for export. It currently uses separate stand-alone packages in each department. The board has approved the implementation of an integrated ERP system and the project manager has listed the following activities that the ERP must support:

tables.caption: Activities to be supported by CWL's ERP
rows: Recording a lead from a hotel chain that has asked for a quotation, and following up with the hotel's buyer.
Scheduling preventive servicing of the CNC cutting machines so that they do not break down during peak orders.
Calculating monthly salaries, deductions and leave balances of 650 workers.
Recording a supplier's invoice for timber and scheduling its payment.
Tracking the stock of finished sofas held in the Chiniot and Karachi warehouses in real time and picking and packing customer orders.
Raising purchase orders for fabric and comparing prices offered by approved suppliers.
Planning the fit-out of a new showroom in Islamabad, with tasks, milestones and a budget.
Arranging shipping and logistics for export containers and monitoring the performance of the freight forwarders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the ERP module that would support each of the activities 1 to 8, giving a brief reason for each.
parts.answer:
1. Activity 1 - Customer Relationship Management (CRM): manages the sales pipeline (leads, prospects, opportunities) and customer interaction history.
2. Activity 2 - Manufacturing and Production Planning: includes maintenance management, scheduling preventive maintenance to avoid breakdowns, alongside production scheduling and capacity planning.
3. Activity 3 - Human Resource Management (HRM): handles employee records, payroll processing, and benefits and leave management.
4. Activity 4 - Financial Management: accounts payable records supplier invoices and payments, posting to the general ledger.
5. Activity 5 - Inventory and Warehouse Management: provides real-time inventory tracking across locations and order fulfilment (picking, packing, shipping).
6. Activity 6 - Procurement: purchase order management, supplier management and cost control (monitoring spend and negotiating better terms). (Supply Chain Management also acceptable.)
7. Activity 7 - Project Management: project planning with tasks and milestones, budgeting, resource allocation and progress tracking.
8. Activity 8 - Supply Chain Management (SCM): covers shipping and logistics and vendor management, tracking supplier performance and contracts.
(1 mark per activity with correct module and reason, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Using an export sales order as an example, explain how sharing one central database across the modules would benefit CWL compared with its present stand-alone packages.
parts.answer:
1. In an ERP all modules write to and read from one shared database, so a transaction is recorded once and every relevant module is updated at the same time. (1 mark)
2. Example: when the export order is confirmed in CRM, the stock of finished goods is reserved in Inventory and Warehouse Management, production is scheduled for any shortfall, a shipment is set up in SCM, and on dispatch the invoice and receivable are posted automatically in Financial Management, without anyone re-keying data. (1 mark)
3. At present each department keeps its own records, which disagree and must be reconciled; with one database there is a single version of the truth, improving data accuracy and consistency. (1 mark)
4. Management obtains real-time information (for example live stock and receivables) for decisions, and processes such as order-to-cash are faster, so revenue is realised sooner. (1 mark)
(max 4)

secb.scenario:
Sialkot Sports Goods Limited (SSGL) is implementing an ERP system. The project manager's draft plan lists the following activities, but not in the correct sequence:
(i) Configure user roles, permissions and access controls.
(ii) Conduct a gap analysis between current processes and future requirements.
(iii) Run hands-on training sessions for end users and prepare user manuals.
(iv) Transfer ongoing transactions from the legacy system to the ERP and monitor performance closely during the first weeks.
(v) Remove duplicate customer records and standardise date formats in the legacy files before loading.
(vi) Confirm that a sales order entered in CRM flows correctly into the finance module.
(vii) Apply vendor patches and provide a helpdesk.
(viii) Establish a cross-functional project team and define the project scope.
To save time, the project manager also proposes that, once the IT department has finished testing, the system should go live without any further testing by business users, because 'IT knows the system better than the users do'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: List the seven phases of the ERP implementation cycle in the correct order, and allocate each of the activities (i) to (viii) to the appropriate phase.
parts.answer:
1. Phase 1 - Planning and requirement analysis: activities (ii) gap analysis and (viii) cross-functional project team and scope. Current processes, challenges and goals are assessed. (2 marks)
2. Phase 2 - System design: activity (i). The ERP is tailored to the organisation's workflows, data structures and workflows are defined, and the user interface and security settings (roles, permissions, access controls) are configured. (1 mark)
3. Phase 3 - Data migration: activity (v). Data is extracted from legacy systems, cleansed and validated (duplicates removed, formats standardised, inaccuracies corrected) and loaded. (1 mark)
4. Phase 4 - System testing: activity (vi), which is integration testing. (1 mark)
5. Phase 5 - Training and change management: activity (iii). (1 mark)
6. Phase 6 - Go-live: activity (iv), the cutover from the legacy system, with close monitoring. (1 mark)
7. Phase 7 - Post-implementation support: activity (vii), ongoing helpdesk support, performance monitoring, patches, enhancements and upgrades. (1 mark)
(Correct order of phases plus correct allocation, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the three kinds of testing performed during ERP implementation and evaluate the project manager's proposal to go live without testing by business users.
parts.answer:
1. Unit testing tests each module on its own to confirm it functions independently, for example that the HR module calculates payroll correctly. (1 mark)
2. Integration testing confirms that the modules work together and data flows correctly between them, for example a sale recorded in CRM flowing through to finance, as in activity (vi). (1 mark)
3. User Acceptance Testing (UAT) lets real business users test the system in a real-world environment to confirm it meets business requirements; the business, not the IT department, signs off. It is the last gate before go-live. (1 mark)
4. Evaluation: the proposal is unsound. IT testing shows that the system works technically, but only users can confirm that it supports SSGL's actual processes, for example export documentation and costing of footballs by order. Skipping UAT means design gaps are discovered after cutover, when they disrupt operations and are more expensive to fix. (1 mark)
5. UAT also builds user ownership and reduces resistance to change. SSGL should keep UAT, with formal sign-off by process owners, and save time elsewhere if needed (for example by phased rollout) rather than by removing a key control. (1 mark)
(max 5)

secb.scenario: Kasur Steel Traders Limited (KSTL) is replacing three ageing systems (a sales package, a stock package and a spreadsheet-based customer list) with a single ERP system. Go-live is planned for 1 July. The data migration lead has profiled the legacy data and reported the following:

tables.caption: Results of legacy data profiling
rows: About 1,400 customers appear two or three times, under slightly different spellings, for example 'Al-Noor Builders' and 'Alnoor Builders Pvt Ltd'.
Invoice dates are held as DD/MM/YYYY in the sales package and MM-DD-YY in the stock package.
Around 9% of customer records have no NTN or have NTNs with the wrong number of digits.
The stock package shows 2,350 tonnes of steel bars, but the physical count in May found 2,190 tonnes; the stock file also contains 600 item codes not used for five years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain why data migration is regarded as the most critical phase of an ERP implementation and describe the steps it involves.
parts.answer:
1. Legacy systems are typically full of duplicates, gaps and inconsistent formats. If this data is loaded directly into the new ERP, the problems are carried across, so the company has simply built a faster and more expensive way to be wrong; every downstream process and report then relies on inaccurate data. (2 marks)
2. Step 1 - Extract data from the existing systems.
3. Step 2 - Cleanse and validate it: remove duplicates, standardise formats and correct inaccuracies, so that only valid and relevant data is carried over.
4. Step 3 - Load the cleansed data into the appropriate ERP modules.
The key principle is that cleansing and validation happen before migration, not after.
(2 marks for why it is critical, 2 marks for the steps, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the findings 1 to 4, recommend the cleansing or validation action KSTL should take before migration.
parts.answer:
1. Finding 1 - Remove duplicates: match records on NTN, address and phone number, merge duplicate customers into one master record and transfer their balances and history to it, with the sales team confirming the correct legal name. (1.5 marks)
2. Finding 2 - Standardise formats: convert all dates to the single format required by the ERP, checking ambiguous dates (for example 03/04) against the source documents, and reject dates that are invalid. (1.5 marks)
3. Finding 3 - Correct inaccuracies and fill gaps: obtain missing or invalid NTNs from customers or FBR records, validate the number of digits, and set the ERP field as mandatory with a format check so incomplete records cannot be loaded. (1.5 marks)
4. Finding 4 - Correct inaccuracies and remove irrelevant data: adjust stock quantities to the verified physical count after investigating and approving the 160-tonne difference, so opening balances in the ERP are demonstrably correct; archive or exclude the 600 obsolete item codes rather than migrating them. (1.5 marks)
(1.5 marks per finding with an appropriate applied action, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Recommend how KSTL should gain assurance that the migration has been performed correctly before go-live.
parts.answer:
1. Perform a trial (test) migration into a non-live environment first, so that problems are identified and resolved before go-live, as part of a comprehensive migration strategy. (1 mark)
2. Reconcile the migrated data with the cleansed source: record counts (customers, items), control totals (receivables, stock tonnage) and sample checks of individual records traced back to source. (1 mark)
3. Have the business owners of the data (sales manager for customers, warehouse manager for stock, finance for balances) review and formally sign off the reconciliations before the final load, and retain evidence for the auditors, since opening balances will be relied on in the audit. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Carewell Pharmacies (Private) Limited (CPL) operates 45 pharmacies in Karachi and Hyderabad. Each branch runs its own point-of-sale package and head office uses a separate accounting package. Payroll is prepared on spreadsheets. The board is considering an ERP system and the finance director has listed the following problems:
(i) Stock figures at head office rarely agree with branch records, and branches run out of fast-moving medicines while others hold excess stock that expires.
(ii) The monthly accounts take fifteen working days to prepare because branch sales must be re-keyed into the accounting package.
(iii) Retail prices of several medicines were changed in branch systems, and nobody can tell who made the change or when.
(iv) When a customer telephones about a home delivery order, staff at the call centre cannot see the order or the customer's previous purchases.
(v) Monthly payroll for 400 staff takes four people a week and contains frequent errors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the problems (i) to (v), explain the benefit of an ERP system that would address it.
parts.answer:
1. Problem (i) - Enhanced data accuracy and consistency, and better collaboration. One central database replaces conflicting branch and head office records, so everyone sees the same up-to-date stock. Real-time inventory tracking and demand forecasting allow stock to be moved or reordered before branches run out, and reduce expired stock (also cost savings from lower inventory). (2 marks)
2. Problem (ii) - Increased efficiency and streamlined processes. Branch sales are posted automatically to the general ledger, eliminating re-keying; routine tasks such as financial reporting are automated, so the month-end close is much faster and staff are freed for analysis. (2 marks)
3. Problem (iii) - Improved compliance and risk management, and data security and integrity. The ERP records an audit trail for every transaction, showing who changed a price and when, and role-based access control restricts price changes to authorised head office staff, reducing the risk of fraud and error. (2 marks)
4. Problem (iv) - Enhanced customer service. Through the integrated CRM, call centre staff have real-time access to customer data, order history and communications, so they can answer queries immediately. (2 marks)
5. Problem (v) - Increased efficiency and productivity. Payroll processing is automated in the HRM module using employee records, attendance and leave data, reducing time and errors and freeing staff for more valuable work. (2 marks)
(2 marks per problem: 1 for the benefit, 1 for application, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain two further benefits of an ERP system that would be of particular interest to CPL's external auditors and to the board, other than those already discussed.
parts.answer:
1. Improved decision-making: real-time insights, customisable dashboards and KPI tracking allow the board to monitor branch profitability, stock days and margins as they happen; for example, the finance director can forecast cash flow from live sales, expense and inventory data. (2 marks)
2. Scalability and flexibility: new branches, users and modules can be added as CPL grows into other cities without separate systems for each, and cloud ERP is particularly flexible. (2 marks)
Alternatively: built-in controls and standardised processes across all 45 branches support a controls-based audit approach, since transactions are handled consistently and evidenced by audit trails; or long-term cost savings from less manual work and lower inventory costs, despite the significant upfront investment.
(2 marks per relevant benefit not already used in part (a), max 4)

secb.scenario:
Gwadar Seafoods Limited (GSL) processes and exports frozen fish. Its processing plant in Gwadar handles production planning, cold storage and quality testing; the plant's internet connection is intermittent and is sometimes unavailable for a full day. GSL's sales and marketing teams work from offices in Karachi and Dubai, and its sales staff travel frequently and need access to customer and order data from anywhere.
The plant runs specialised processes for grading and freezing that are unique to GSL. The company has a small IT team at the plant but none in the sales offices. GSL's export customers require that production and quality testing records be kept under the company's direct control for food safety audits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the three types of ERP deployment, stating two advantages and two disadvantages of each.
parts.answer:
1. On-premise ERP runs on the organisation's own servers on its own premises. Advantages: complete control over data; highly customisable; no reliance on internet connectivity. Disadvantages: high initial investment in hardware, licences and infrastructure; the organisation bears maintenance and patching; limited scalability because growth requires more hardware. (2 marks)
2. Cloud ERP runs on the vendor's remote servers and is accessed over the internet by subscription. Advantages: low upfront cost; highly scalable; automatic updates by the vendor; accessible from anywhere; fast to deploy. Disadvantages: depends on internet connectivity; data security concerns because data is held offsite; less customisation as it is built for a broad market. (2 marks)
3. Hybrid ERP keeps sensitive data or functions on-premise and runs other functions in the cloud. Advantages: flexible deployment (choose what goes where); risk mitigation as sensitive data stays local; gradual migration to the cloud without abandoning existing investment. Disadvantages: integration complexity and data synchronisation between the two environments; the organisation must manage both infrastructures. (2 marks)
(2 marks per type including two valid advantages and two disadvantages, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate ERP deployment type for GSL, justifying your recommendation with reference to its circumstances.
parts.answer:
Recommendation: hybrid ERP.
1. Plant functions (production planning, cold storage, quality testing) should run on-premise at Gwadar: the intermittent internet would make a cloud-only system unusable during outages, and on-premise runs locally with no internet reliance. (1 mark)
2. On-premise also gives complete control over production and quality records, as export customers require, and a high degree of customisation for GSL's unique grading and freezing processes; the plant's IT team can handle maintenance. (1 mark)
3. Sales, CRM and related functions should run in the cloud: travelling staff in Karachi and Dubai need access from anywhere, those offices have no IT staff so automatic vendor updates and maintenance are valuable, and subscription costs are low upfront and scalable. (1 mark)
4. Hybrid therefore gives control and customisation where GSL needs them and flexibility everywhere else. (1 mark)
(Credit a reasoned alternative only if it addresses connectivity, control and remote access, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Discuss the main challenges GSL will face with the recommended deployment and how it should manage them.
parts.answer:
1. Integration complexity: the on-premise plant system and the cloud sales system must exchange orders, stock and shipment data. GSL should plan integration early and use middleware and APIs (and choose an ERP with pre-built connectors). (1 mark)
2. Data synchronisation: when the Gwadar link is down, orders and stock updates will be held in the separate environments and must be synchronised when it is restored. GSL should design queued transfers with reconciliation of stock and order data after each outage. (1 mark)
3. Managing two infrastructures: GSL must maintain the on-premise servers (patching, backups) and manage the cloud vendor relationship and contract, so it should define responsibilities clearly and include both in its IT support arrangements. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.topic: Total cost of ownership and ERP selection
secb.scenario: Faisalabad Home Textiles Limited (FHTL) has shortlisted two ERP vendors. The IT manager recommends Vendor X because 'its licence fee is less than half of Vendor Y's price'. The finance team has summarised what each offer involves:

tables.caption: Summary of the two ERP offers
rows: One-off licence fee, less than half of Vendor Y's first-year fee
FHTL must buy new servers and network equipment
Large consulting team; heavy customisation to match FHTL's processes
Smaller consulting team; mostly standard functionality
Annual maintenance fee; FHTL's IT team applies updates and patches
Included in the subscription; vendor applies updates
Training for all users; annual technical support contract
Training for all users; support included

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what is meant by total cost of ownership (TCO) and, using the information in the table, comment on the IT manager's recommendation.
parts.answer:
1. Total cost of ownership means assessing the full cost of an ERP over its life, including direct and indirect costs, not just the initial purchase price. (1 mark)
2. Its components are: initial implementation costs (software licences, hardware infrastructure for on-premise ERP, and consulting fees for set-up); maintenance and upgrades (system maintenance, software updates and possible hardware upgrades); and training and support (training staff and ongoing technical support). (1 mark)
3. Applied to Vendor X: although the licence is cheaper, FHTL must also pay for new servers and network equipment, a large consulting team, heavy customisation, an annual maintenance fee with its own IT staff applying patches, and a separate support contract. Excessive customisation also adds complexity, cost and delay. (1 mark)
4. Applied to Vendor Y: there is no hardware cost, implementation is lighter because mostly standard functionality is used, and maintenance, updates and support are included in the subscription, which is a recurring cost every year. (1 mark)
5. Comment: the IT manager has compared licence prices only, which is not a sound basis for the decision. A cheap licence can be the more expensive option once hardware, consulting, customisation, maintenance, training and support are included. FHTL should obtain full cost estimates for every TCO component of both offers over the same period before choosing. (1 mark)
(1 mark per point, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Apart from cost, explain three other key considerations FHTL should evaluate before choosing between the two vendors.
parts.answer:
1. System flexibility: can the ERP handle more users, regions and product lines as FHTL grows (scalability), and can it fit FHTL's processes through configuration? The PKR 15 million customisation for Vendor X suggests a poorer fit; excessive customisation adds complexity, cost and delay and makes upgrades difficult. (2 marks)
2. Integration capabilities: the ERP will not operate in isolation. FHTL should check for robust APIs and pre-built connectors, and compatibility with existing systems it may keep, such as dyeing machine controllers, the payroll attendance system or buyers' electronic ordering portals. (2 marks)
3. Vendor support: the vendor's track record of implementation assistance in similar textile companies, post-implementation support (helpdesk, troubleshooting, response times) and regular upgrades and security patches to keep the system current. For the cloud option, FHTL should also consider service availability and data security commitments in the contract. (2 marks)
(2 marks per consideration explained and applied, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Advise FHTL on any additional factors arising from the deployment type of each option that should be weighed alongside the TCO.
parts.answer:
1. Vendor Y (cloud) depends on reliable internet connectivity at FHTL's mills, raises data security concerns because data is held offsite on the vendor's servers, and offers less customisation because it is built for a broad market. FHTL should assess its connectivity and the vendor's security arrangements. (1 mark)
2. Vendor X (on-premise) gives complete control over data and works without reliance on the internet, but FHTL must bear maintenance and patching itself, needs in-house IT resources, and has limited scalability because growth requires more hardware. If these factors are not decisive, the option with the lower full TCO should be preferred. (1 mark)
(max 2)

secb.scenario:
Hyderabad Sugar Mills Limited (HSML) started an ERP implementation eight months ago. The project steering committee has received the following report from the internal auditor:
(i) Clerks in the cane procurement yard, supported by the workers' union, refuse to use the new weighbridge screens and continue to keep handwritten registers, fearing that the system will be used to reduce staff.
(ii) The project has already spent 80% of its budget, largely because servers and licences were bought for all eight modules at the start, even though only finance and procurement are needed for the coming crushing season.
(iii) Heads of the production and sales departments were not invited to requirement meetings and have now rejected the system design, demanding changes.
(iv) There is no schedule of milestones, and the steering committee only learned of a three-month delay from the vendor's invoice.
(v) Users at the mill were not informed when the go-live date was moved, and several turned up for training sessions that had been cancelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the issues (i) to (v), identify the ERP implementation challenge or success factor involved and recommend what HSML should do.
parts.answer:
1. Issue (i) - Resistance to change. Employees are reluctant to adopt new processes, leading to delays and under-utilisation. HSML should apply change management: communicate the benefits clearly (faster, accurate weighing and grower payments), involve union representatives and key users early, give comprehensive hands-on training, and demonstrate how the system makes their work easier. (2 marks)
2. Issue (ii) - High implementation costs. HSML should prioritise the most critical functionality (finance and procurement for the crushing season) and adopt a phased approach for the other modules, and consider cloud ERP for later modules to reduce upfront hardware and infrastructure costs. (2 marks)
3. Issue (iii) - Lack of stakeholder buy-in. Key people should be engaged from the beginning so they understand and support the project. HSML should involve the production and sales heads in reviewing requirements now, and the requested changes should be assessed through the gap analysis, using standard functionality where possible rather than costly customisation. (2 marks)
4. Issue (iv) - Weak budget and timeline management. ERP projects overrun notoriously, so realistic goals should be set and milestones monitored. HSML should approve a milestone plan and require regular progress and cost reports to the steering committee so delays are known before invoices arrive. (2 marks)
5. Issue (v) - Poor communication. The project team, users and management must be kept informed throughout. HSML should set up a communication plan (notices, briefings, a project contact at the mill) so changes to dates and training are announced promptly. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each challenge or success factor correctly identified and 1 for an applied recommendation, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend the implementation approach HSML should follow for the remaining rollout, explaining its benefits.
parts.answer:
1. HSML should use a phased implementation, starting with a pilot: go live with finance and procurement first (for example at the cane yard and head office), stabilise, and then roll out production, sales and other modules in planned stages. (1 mark)
2. Benefits: it reduces risk because problems affect only part of the business and can be isolated; lessons from the pilot (configuration errors, data problems, training gaps) are applied in later phases. (1 mark)
3. It spreads cost and training effort over time, which eases the budget pressure and allows the resistance in the yard to be dealt with before wider rollout. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Thar Microfinance Bank Limited (TMBL) is expanding its branch network in Sindh and southern Punjab. Its board has approved the purchase of an ERP system. A director has suggested that, to save money, the ERP should also be customised to handle customer savings accounts, cash deposits and withdrawals, and loan instalment collection, so that the bank does not need a separate core banking system.
The following activities take place at TMBL:
(i) A customer withdraws PKR 15,000 from her savings account at the Mithi branch.
(ii) The bank processes monthly salaries for its 900 employees.
(iii) A loan instalment is received from a borrower and applied to his loan account.
(iv) The bank pays its quarterly rent for branch premises.
(v) The bank prepares regulatory financial returns for the State Bank of Pakistan.
(vi) A mobile wallet payment is made from a customer's account to a merchant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between an ERP system and a Core Banking System (CBS), and identify which system would normally process each of the activities (i) to (vi).
parts.answer:
1. ERP: supports the bank's back office: corporate finance, procurement, compliance, HR and strategic planning; its purpose is financial control, regulatory reporting and planning. Examples SAP and Oracle. (1 mark)
2. CBS: a specialised platform for the front line: account management, deposits, withdrawals, payments, transaction processing and loan servicing, i.e. the day-to-day banking operations the customer touches. Examples Temenos and Finacle. (1 mark)
3. Classification: (i) withdrawal - CBS; (iii) loan instalment applied to loan account - CBS (loan servicing); (vi) customer payment to merchant - CBS (payments and transaction processing). (2 marks)
4. (ii) staff salaries - ERP (HR and payroll); (iv) rent for branch premises - ERP (procurement and accounts payable); (v) regulatory financial returns - ERP (regulatory reporting and corporate finance, drawing on data fed from the CBS). (2 marks)
(max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the director's suggestion to customise the ERP to perform core banking functions.
parts.answer:
1. The ERP and CBS serve different functions and neither is a substitute for the other. A general-purpose ERP is not built for the volume, real-time demands and specialised functionality of retail banking transactions such as deposits, withdrawals, payments and loan servicing. (1 mark)
2. Customising the ERP to do this would require extensive customisation. Excessive customisation causes increased complexity, higher costs and longer implementation timelines, and makes future upgrades difficult; any saving in licence cost is likely to be lost on a TCO basis. (1 mark)
3. The recommended response to customisation needs is to use standard, out-of-the-box functionality wherever possible and limit customisation to genuinely critical processes; for customer operations the standard solution is a CBS, built for that purpose. (1 mark)
4. Conclusion: the suggestion should be rejected; TMBL should run a CBS for customer-facing operations and the ERP for the back office. (1 mark)
(max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain why TMBL should integrate its ERP with the CBS and how the integration could be achieved.
parts.answer:
1. Why: integration allows financial data to flow seamlessly from the CBS (where customer transactions occur) into the ERP general ledger, so that the financial statements and SBP returns reflect the underlying banking activity without manual re-entry. (1 mark)
2. It also enables centralised risk management and consistent reporting across the enterprise, and reduces reconciliation differences between the two systems. (1 mark)
3. How: integration should be planned early, assessing every system that must connect, and middleware and APIs should be used to bridge the CBS and ERP, with reconciliation controls over the data transferred. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.topic: AI features, machine learning and LiDAR
secb.scenario:
BazaarHub (Private) Limited (BHL) is an online marketplace based in Lahore. Its technology team has introduced the following systems over the past year:
(i) A chatbot that answers customer questions typed in Urdu, Roman Urdu or English, and replies in the same language.
(ii) A system that reviews every cash-on-delivery order and flags orders whose characteristics differ from normal buying behaviour, such as unusual quantities sent to newly created addresses.
(iii) A pricing engine that recommends discount levels; its recommendations have become noticeably more accurate as it has been fed more months of sales data.
(iv) A warehouse system that decides on its own which orders to pick first, based on delivery deadlines, stock locations and courier pick-up times, without a supervisor's involvement.
BHL now plans to trial small self-navigating robots in its warehouse and delivery drones in Defence Housing Authority areas, both equipped with LiDAR.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the key feature of Artificial Intelligence demonstrated by each of the systems (i) to (iv) and explain how the feature operates in each case.
parts.answer:
1. System (i) - Natural Language Processing (NLP). NLP enables machines to understand, interpret and generate human language. The chatbot interprets the customer's question in whichever language it is written and generates a reply, handling routine enquiries 24/7 without human agents. (2 marks)
2. System (ii) - Pattern recognition. AI identifies patterns and anomalies in large datasets. The system learns what normal orders look like and flags those that deviate, which is how AI is used for fraud detection. (2 marks)
3. System (iii) - Learning and adaptation. AI continuously improves over time through exposure to new data; the pricing engine is self-improving, which is why its accuracy rises as more sales data is supplied. (2 marks)
4. System (iv) - Autonomous decision-making. AI makes decisions on its own from data and rules, simulating human cognition and automating repetitive, time-consuming decisions; the system sequences picking without a supervisor. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each feature and 1 for applied explanation, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, using one of BHL's systems as an illustration.
parts.answer:
1. AI is the development of computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as perception, decision-making and language understanding. Machine Learning is a subset of AI that focuses on algorithms allowing machines to learn from data, identify patterns and make decisions with minimal human intervention. Every ML system is AI, but not every AI system is ML. (1 mark)
2. Illustration: the pricing engine in (iii) is an ML system because it improves by learning from accumulated sales data; a system that only applied fixed rules written by programmers would not be ML. (1 mark)
(max 2)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain how LiDAR works and discuss one operational limitation BHL should consider before the drone trial.
parts.answer:
1. LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) emits laser (infrared light) pulses and times their reflection to measure distances, building a 3D map of the surroundings with centimetre-level precision. (1 mark)
2. This allows the robots and drones to detect shelves, people, buildings and obstacles and navigate without human control; it works in darkness, so night-time operation is possible. (1 mark)
3. Limitation: LiDAR can be disrupted by fog and rain. Lahore experiences heavy winter fog and monsoon rain, so BHL should plan for drone operations to be suspended or supported by other sensors (cameras, radar) in such weather. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Okara Dairies Limited (ODL) collects milk from about 3,000 farmers and transports it in chilled tankers to its processing plant. To reduce spoilage, ODL ran a pilot in which temperature sensors were fitted in 40 tankers and 25 village collection centres. When the temperature of milk rises above 4 degrees Celsius, a device in the tank automatically switches on additional cooling. Readings are sent over the mobile network and managers monitor all tankers on a web dashboard and a mobile app.
The pilot review identified the following matters:
(i) Sensors bought from two different manufacturers send data in different formats, and readings from one manufacturer's sensors do not appear on the dashboard.
(ii) An external tester logged into several collection-centre devices using the user name and password printed in the manufacturer's manual.
(iii) The existing database server has become slow because the sensors send a reading every ten seconds, and storage is nearly full after three months.
(iv) ODL plans to extend the system to all 400 tankers and 600 collection centres next year, but the IT team already finds it difficult to keep track of devices, their locations and firmware versions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the four components of an IoT system with reference to ODL's pilot.
parts.answer:
1. Sensors and actuators: a sensor captures data from the environment and an actuator does something physical in response. ODL's temperature probes are sensors; the device that switches on extra cooling when the milk exceeds 4 degrees Celsius is an actuator. (2 marks)
2. Connectivity: how devices communicate, for example Wi-Fi, 4G/5G, Bluetooth or wired Ethernet. ODL's devices use the mobile network to transmit readings. (1 mark)
3. Data processing: the collected data must be processed, either on the device itself (edge computing) or in centralised data centres or the cloud. The cooling decision is taken on the device in the tank, while readings are stored and analysed centrally on ODL's server. (2 marks)
4. User interface: how humans monitor and control the system, through a web dashboard, mobile app or voice interface. ODL's managers use the dashboard and mobile app. (1 mark)
(max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the matters (i) to (iv), identify the IoT challenge involved and recommend how ODL should address it.
parts.answer:
1. Matter (i) - Interoperability. Devices from different manufacturers use different protocols and standards, making integration difficult. ODL should use middleware to translate both data formats into one standard, and in future standardise on devices that support common protocols. (2 marks)
2. Matter (ii) - Security and privacy. IoT devices are attractive targets, and devices are often left running factory default passwords that were never changed. ODL should change all default credentials to strong unique passwords before deployment, restrict remote access, update firmware, and keep the devices on a network segment separated from its core systems. (2 marks)
3. Matter (iii) - Data overload. The volume of data generated can overwhelm existing storage and processing; this is a Big Data problem. ODL should move storage to scalable (for example cloud) infrastructure, process routine readings at the edge and send only summaries or exceptions centrally, and archive old readings. (2 marks)
4. Matter (iv) - Scalability. As the number of devices grows, managing the infrastructure becomes increasingly complex. ODL should maintain a central inventory of devices, use remote device-management tools for monitoring and firmware updates, and roll out in phases so that the management processes are proven before full expansion. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each challenge and 1 for an applied recommendation, max 8)

secb.topic: Blockchain features, smart contracts and limits of immutability
secb.scenario:
The Basmati Growers and Exporters Association (BGEA), based in Gujranwala, represents rice mills that export to the Middle East and Europe. Overseas buyers have complained that some consignments labelled as premium aged basmati have been mixed with cheaper varieties somewhere between the farm and the port, and that certificates of origin have occasionally been forged. Payments to mills are also delayed because buyers' banks wait for paper documents to arrive by courier.
BGEA proposes a shared blockchain platform in which farmers, mills, testing laboratories, shipping agents and buyers record each stage of a consignment's journey. It also proposes that payment be released to the mill automatically once the buyer's port records that a container has been received and its laboratory test meets the agreed grade.
At a meeting, the association's chairman said: 'Once our certificates are on the blockchain, buyers will never need to test the rice again, because the blockchain guarantees that whatever is recorded is true.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the four key features of blockchain and discuss how each would help address BGEA's problems.
parts.answer:
1. Decentralisation: the ledger operates without a central authority; all participants (nodes) maintain it, so it is resistant to central points of failure or control. No single mill, agent or official can rewrite the record of a consignment. (2 marks)
2. Immutability: once a block is added it cannot be altered, so the history of the consignment (harvest, milling, testing, loading) is permanent. A forged or retrospectively changed certificate of origin cannot replace the original entry. (2 marks)
3. Security: cryptographic algorithms secure each transaction, preventing unauthorised changes and ensuring data integrity, so only authorised participants can record entries and tampering is detectable. (2 marks)
4. Transparency: every participant sees the same version of the ledger, making it fully auditable. Buyers can trace each consignment through every stage, which ensures authenticity and reduces fraud in the supply chain, a recognised blockchain application. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each feature and 1 for application to BGEA, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the concept of a smart contract and how it would operate in BGEA's proposed payment arrangement.
parts.answer:
1. A smart contract is a self-executing contract with the terms of the agreement written directly into code; it executes automatically when predefined conditions are met (platforms such as Ethereum support them). (1 mark)
2. For BGEA, the conditions would be coded as: container received at buyer's port, and laboratory result recorded as meeting the agreed grade. When both entries are recorded on the blockchain, the contract automatically releases payment to the mill. (1 mark)
3. Benefits: payment no longer waits for couriered paper documents, reducing delays and bureaucracy and improving mills' cash flow; the terms are applied consistently without manual intervention. (1 mark)
(max 3)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the chairman's statement.
parts.answer:
1. The chairman confuses 'cannot be altered' with 'is true'. Immutability guarantees that a record has not been changed since it was written; it does not guarantee that the record was accurate when it was written. (1 mark)
2. If a mill or laboratory records a false grade or the rice is mixed before testing, the false entry becomes permanent; immutability then makes the error harder to correct rather than preventing it. (1 mark)
3. Buyers will therefore still need controls over what goes onto the chain, such as independent accredited laboratories and periodic sample testing on arrival. Blockchain secures the integrity of the record, not the validity of the underlying fact. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Karakoram Health Network (KHN) runs a specialist hospital in Islamabad and twelve small clinics in Gilgit-Baltistan. KHN plans two initiatives:
(i) Remote consultation and robot-assisted procedures, in which a specialist surgeon in Islamabad guides a robotic instrument and views high-definition video from a clinic in real time. Trials over the existing 4G network failed because of delays between the surgeon's movement and the instrument's response, and the video froze.
(ii) Wearable heart monitors for 2,000 cardiac patients living in remote valleys. The monitors will analyse the heart rhythm on the device itself and send an alert to the clinic only when an irregular pattern is detected, instead of streaming every reading to the Islamabad data centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the four key features of 5G technology and discuss how each is relevant to initiative (i).
parts.answer:
1. Increased network speed: download speeds up to 100 times faster than 4G, allowing the high-definition video from the clinic to be transmitted without freezing. (1.5 marks)
2. Low latency: latency as low as 1 millisecond compared with 30 to 50 milliseconds on 4G. This is critical for real-time applications such as remote surgery, because the instrument must respond to the surgeon's movement without perceptible delay; it directly addresses the failure of the 4G trial. (1.5 marks)
3. Greater capacity: far more connected devices are supported within a small area, so the video equipment, robotic instrument and monitoring devices at a clinic (and other users) can all be connected simultaneously. (1.5 marks)
4. Improved reliability: better coverage and performance, including in high-traffic areas, which matters because a dropped connection during a procedure is unacceptable. (1.5 marks)
(1.5 marks per feature with application, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the technology described in initiative (ii) and explain three of its features that make it suitable for KHN.
parts.answer:
Technology: edge computing, which brings data processing, storage and computation closer to where the data is generated instead of sending it to a distant centralised data centre. (1 mark)
1. Reduced latency: the rhythm is analysed on the device, so an irregular pattern is detected and the alert raised immediately, without waiting for a round trip to Islamabad. (1 mark)
2. Bandwidth efficiency: only alerts are transmitted rather than continuous readings from 2,000 patients, reducing strain on the limited mountain network and cutting bandwidth cost. (1 mark)
3. Enhanced privacy and security: sensitive health data stays on the device near its source, reducing exposure during transmission, which is important in healthcare. (Scalability, since processing is distributed across devices, is also acceptable.) (1 mark)
(max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Discuss three challenges KHN should expect in managing initiative (ii) and how it could respond to each.
parts.answer:
1. Complexity of management: updating and patching software on 2,000 distributed wearables is difficult. KHN should use central remote management for updates and keep an inventory of devices. (1 mark)
2. Security risks: the edge devices themselves are vulnerable if not secured. KHN should change default settings, encrypt stored and transmitted data and restrict who can configure the devices. (1 mark)
3. Data synchronisation: data processed on the devices must be kept consistent with central patient records. KHN should schedule periodic uploads of summaries to the hospital system when connectivity allows and reconcile them with patient files. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Crescent Homes Developers (CHD) builds apartment towers in Karachi and Lahore. It is evaluating three proposals from a technology vendor:
(i) Overseas Pakistanis in the Gulf and the United Kingdom would put on a headset and 'walk through' a fully simulated apartment in a tower that has not yet been built.
(ii) Site engineers would point a tablet at an unfinished wall and see, on the live camera image, the planned positions of electrical conduits and water pipes drawn over the real wall.
(iii) New tower-crane operators would practise lifting heavy loads in high winds in a fully simulated crane cabin before operating a real crane.
The finance director is concerned about cost and has asked whether there are any other drawbacks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the proposals (i) to (iii) as Augmented Reality (AR) or Virtual Reality (VR), explaining the distinction between the two and justifying each classification.
parts.answer:
Distinction: AR overlays digital elements on the real world; the user remains aware of physical surroundings and it works on ordinary smartphones, tablets or AR glasses. VR creates a fully simulated environment that replaces the real world; the user is completely absorbed and it requires specialised hardware such as headsets, controllers and sensors. (2 marks)
1. Proposal (i) - VR: the buyer is immersed in a simulated apartment that does not yet exist, using a headset; the real surroundings are shut out. Virtual property tours are a recognised VR application. (1.5 marks)
2. Proposal (ii) - AR: the engineer still sees the real wall, with the planned services overlaid on it using an ordinary tablet; reality is augmented, not replaced. (1 mark)
3. Proposal (iii) - VR: the operator trains in a fully simulated crane cabin, similar to flight simulation; no real crane or load is involved. (1.5 marks)
(max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss the benefits CHD could obtain from the proposals and respond to the finance director's question about drawbacks.
parts.answer:
Benefits
1. Enhanced user experience: overseas buyers understand layout and finishes far better than from drawings, supporting sales off-plan. (1 mark)
2. Remote interaction: virtual property tours allow buyers abroad to view apartments without travelling to Pakistan. (1 mark)
3. Cost-effective and safe training: crane operators can practise dangerous situations such as high winds without risk to life or equipment, reducing accidents; AR on site reduces errors such as drilling into hidden pipes. (1 mark)
Drawbacks
4. Expensive specialised hardware: VR headsets, controllers and sensors are costly and limit accessibility, for example buyers may need to visit a sales centre abroad to use them. (1 mark)
5. Costly content development: building accurate 3D models of each apartment type and crane simulation scenarios is expensive and time-consuming, and must be updated when designs change. (1 mark)
6. User discomfort: extended VR use can cause motion sickness and eye strain, so training sessions must be limited in length and buyers may find the experience uncomfortable. (1 mark)
(1 mark per applied point, max 6)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how a quantum computer differs from a classical computer, and describe the three key features of quantum computing.
parts.answer:
1. A classical computer processes information in bits, each of which is either 0 or 1, and evaluates possibilities one after another. A quantum computer uses qubits, which can be 0 and 1 at the same time, allowing many possibilities to be evaluated in parallel rather than sequentially. (2 marks)
2. Superposition: a qubit exists in multiple states at once (part 0 and part 1), enabling parallel processing of exponentially more possibilities. For example, a classical computer solves a maze one path at a time, while a quantum computer explores all paths simultaneously. (1.5 marks)
3. Entanglement: the state of one qubit depends on another even when they are physically separated, allowing qubits to be linked in complex ways so that multiple variables in, say, an optimisation problem are evaluated together. (1.5 marks)
4. Quantum tunnelling: allows the computer to bypass barriers that stop classical computation, solving problems that would otherwise be impossible. (1 mark)
(max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss the potential applications of quantum computing for a bank and for a logistics company, and explain why the technology is also considered a threat to the banking sector.
parts.answer:
1. Bank - financial modelling: risk analysis and portfolio optimisation by running many market simulations simultaneously. (1 mark)
2. Logistics company - optimisation: solving complex routing and supply chain problems, such as optimal delivery routes, far faster than classical computers. (1 mark)
3. Threat: encryption such as RSA is secure because factoring very large numbers would take a classical computer an impractically long time. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could do it far more efficiently and so break the encryption that protects banking transactions, e-commerce and confidential communications. (1 mark)
4. Response: post-quantum cryptography, meaning encryption methods designed to resist quantum attack. Banks should monitor developments and plan migration, since data encrypted today may still be sensitive when the capability arrives. (1 mark)
(Drug discovery, for example modelling protein folding, may be credited as a further application but not for the bank or logistics company; max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain three challenges that currently limit the commercial use of quantum computing.
parts.answer:
1. High error rates: qubits are extremely sensitive to temperature and electromagnetic interference, so calculations are prone to errors. (1 mark)
2. Hardware in its infancy: scaling up the number of qubits and maintaining coherence is difficult, so machines of the size needed for practical problems are not yet available. (1 mark)
3. Cost and accessibility: the equipment is expensive and specialised, so the technology is not yet commercially widespread and few organisations can use it directly. (1 mark)
(max 3)

secb.scenario:
Mehran Group Shared Services (MGSS) provides finance and HR processing to six companies in the Mehran Group. The group's ERP system was installed fifteen years ago and the IT department cannot fund changes to it for at least two years. MGSS's head has proposed automating the following processes using Robotic Process Automation (RPA):
(i) Matching 6,000 supplier invoices a month to purchase orders and goods received notes in the ERP, and preparing payment for invoices that match and are approved.
(ii) Calculating monthly salaries, deductions and withholding tax for 4,500 employees, and generating payslips.
(iii) Deciding the credit limit to grant to new distributors, which senior credit officers currently set after weighing financial statements, market reputation and their experience of similar businesses.
(iv) Handling complaints from distributors, which arrive by email in free text and vary widely; each is resolved differently depending on the circumstances.
(v) Transferring ten years of customer and vendor master data into the systems of a company the group has just acquired.
Staff in MGSS have heard about the project and many fear losing their jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Evaluate whether each of the processes (i) to (v) is suitable for RPA, giving reasons, and recommend an alternative where it is not.
parts.answer:
1. Process (i) - Suitable. Invoice processing is a typical RPA application: the bot extracts invoice data, matches it to purchase orders and GRNs using predefined rules, and generates payment for approved, matched invoices. It is repetitive, high-volume and rule-based. Exceptions (mismatches) should be routed to staff. (2 marks)
2. Process (ii) - Suitable. Payroll management is a recognised application: bots calculate salaries and deductions, generate payslips and support tax filings by applying defined rules. Accuracy improves and processing is faster. (2 marks)
3. Process (iii) - Not suitable. Setting credit limits requires judgment, weighing qualitative information and experience. RPA follows rules and does not think, judge or learn. AI (machine learning, using pattern recognition on past distributor data) is more appropriate, supporting the credit officers rather than replacing their approval. (2 marks)
4. Process (iv) - Not suitable. RPA works only on well-documented, standardised, rule-based processes; ambiguous tasks that vary case by case are unsuitable. Complaints should remain with staff; AI with NLP could help classify and route emails, and RPA could later automate any standard steps (for example logging the complaint). (2 marks)
5. Process (v) - Suitable. Data migration, transferring data between systems during an upgrade or merger, is a recognised RPA application; bots copy the data quickly and consistently. The data should be cleansed and the transfer reconciled. (2 marks)
Note for all suitable processes: because RPA is non-invasive, the bots work through the existing ERP screens without any change to the underlying system, so the IT department's funding constraint does not prevent automation.
(1 mark for each correct suitability conclusion and 1 for justification or alternative, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss the challenges MGSS should expect when introducing RPA and recommend how each should be managed.
parts.answer:
1. Change management: employees may resist, fearing job displacement, as is already happening. MGSS should communicate the purpose early, explain that bots take over monotonous work, and retrain staff for exception handling, review and analysis. (1.5 marks)
2. Process standardisation: RPA only works on well-documented, rule-based processes. MGSS should document and standardise each process (for example common invoice matching rules across the six companies) before automating. (1 mark)
3. Security risks: bots access sensitive data such as salaries and bank details. Each bot should have its own user ID with access limited to what its task requires, its credentials should be protected, and its activity logs reviewed. (1.5 marks)
4. Ongoing maintenance: bots must be updated whenever the underlying systems or rules change (for example a new tax rate or a changed ERP screen). MGSS should assign owners for each bot and include bots in change control. (1 mark)
(max 5)

secb.topic: Selecting emerging technologies for business needs
secb.scenario:
Sukkur Agro Industries Limited (SAIL) operates sugar, flour and edible oil plants in Sindh. Its innovation committee has received five requests from different departments:
(i) The customer service manager wants a system that can hold conversations with farmers and distributors over WhatsApp in Sindhi and Urdu and understand what they are asking.
(ii) The finance manager wants software that logs into the bank's website each morning, downloads statements for 14 accounts and posts them into the old accounting system, which cannot be modified.
(iii) The plant engineer wants vibration and temperature readings from the boilers analysed so that a fault is predicted and repaired before the boiler fails.
(iv) The supply chain manager wants a tamper-proof shared record of each consignment of edible oil imported, which the shipping line, customs agent, bank and SAIL can all view.
(v) The IT security manager has warned that the encryption protecting SAIL's long-term contracts and bank communications may become breakable within the next decade.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate emerging technology for each of the requests (i) to (v), justifying each recommendation.
parts.answer:
1. Request (i) - AI with Natural Language Processing (chatbot). NLP enables machines to understand, interpret and generate human language; an AI chatbot can answer routine queries 24/7 in the farmers' languages without human agents. (2 marks)
2. Request (ii) - Robotic Process Automation. The task is repetitive and rule-based (log in, download, post), needing no judgment. RPA is non-invasive: the bot mimics a human using the existing screens, so the old accounting system does not need to be modified. Bots also keep an audit trail of their actions. (2 marks)
3. Request (iii) - Industrial IoT combined with AI for predictive maintenance. IoT sensors on the boilers continuously capture vibration and temperature; AI pattern recognition analyses the readings to detect anomalies that precede failure, so repairs are planned before breakdown, avoiding costly unplanned stoppage of production. (2 marks)
4. Request (iv) - Blockchain. A decentralised, distributed ledger shared by all parties gives immutability (records cannot be altered), transparency (all see the same version) and cryptographic security; supply chain tracking is a recognised application that ensures authenticity and reduces fraud. (2 marks)
5. Request (v) - Post-quantum cryptography. The threat comes from quantum computing, which could break encryption such as RSA that relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers. SAIL should plan to migrate to encryption methods designed to resist quantum attack, starting with data that must stay confidential for many years. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each correct technology and 1 for justification, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why the technology recommended for request (iii) does not operate in isolation, identifying the other technologies it depends on.
parts.answer:
1. An IoT system needs connectivity to transmit readings from many sensors across a large plant, which 5G supports through its greater capacity and reliability; and the readings may need to be processed close to the boilers by edge computing so that urgent alerts are not delayed by sending data to a distant data centre. (1 mark)
2. Continuous readings generate very large volumes of data (the IoT data overload challenge, a Big Data issue), and AI is needed to interpret them. The technologies therefore form a stack: IoT senses, 5G connects, edge processes and AI interprets. (1 mark)
(max 2)

secb.scenario:
