Rohtas Microfinance Bank Limited (RMBL) lends small business loans to shopkeepers and farmers across rural Punjab. RMBL has decided to develop an AI model that will predict the probability of a borrower defaulting, so that loan officers can price and approve loans more consistently.
The project manager has drafted the following plan:
(i) Use only the loan files of the Multan branch for the last six months, because that data is already in one spreadsheet.
(ii) Start training the model immediately on the spreadsheet as it is, even though some records are duplicated, some CNIC numbers are missing and loan amounts are recorded in a mix of PKR and PKR thousands.
(iii) Measure the accuracy of the model on the same loan files that were used to train it.
(iv) Once the model goes live, leave it unchanged for at least five years to save cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the five stages of the AI learning cycle in the correct sequence, briefly stating what each stage involves.
parts.answer:
1. Data collection: gathering large volumes of relevant, accurate, high-quality data from all available sources.
2. Data pre-processing: cleaning, transforming and organising the collected data, e.g. removing duplicates, fixing missing values and standardising formats.
3. Model training: applying algorithms to the pre-processed data so that the model identifies patterns and relationships.
4. Results evaluation: testing the accuracy of the trained model on unseen (test) data before it is trusted with real decisions.
5. Model deployment: implementing the trained and tested model in a live business application.
(1 mark per stage correctly explained and in the correct order, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the weaknesses (i) to (iv) in the project manager's plan, identify the stage of the AI learning cycle that has been compromised and recommend how RMBL should correct it.
parts.answer:
(i) Data collection: six months of data from one branch is neither large in volume nor representative of RMBL's rural borrowers across Punjab, so the model would learn patterns of only one city and one season. RMBL should collect several years of loan, repayment and customer-profile data from all branches (covering harvest and non-harvest periods) from every available source.
(ii) Data pre-processing: training on duplicated records, missing CNICs and inconsistent units would teach the model wrong patterns (e.g. treating PKR 500 thousand as PKR 500). RMBL should first remove duplicates, fill or exclude records with missing values and standardise all amounts to one unit before training.
(iii) Results evaluation: accuracy measured on the training data is overstated because the model has already seen those records. RMBL should hold back a separate set of unseen test loans and measure accuracy (and wrongly approved / wrongly rejected cases) on that set before approving go-live.
(iv) Deployment and the iterative nature of the cycle: the AI learning cycle is iterative. After deployment the model's performance should be monitored, new repayment data collected and the model periodically retrained, otherwise its predictions will deteriorate as borrower behaviour and economic conditions change.
(1 mark for each stage correctly identified and 1 mark for each appropriate recommendation, max 8)

secb.scenario:
Shifa Care Pharmacies (SCP) operates 140 pharmacy outlets in Karachi, Hyderabad and Sukkur. SCP's board has approved the following AI initiatives for the coming year:
(i) A tool that studies three years of point-of-sale data to show which medicines sold most in each outlet during the last dengue season.
(ii) A model that estimates how many units of each antibiotic every outlet will need in the next quarter, so that purchase orders can be placed in advance.
(iii) A tool that writes product descriptions and Urdu and English health-awareness posts for SCP's social-media pages.
(iv) A system that examines last year's refund transactions to identify cashiers whose refund patterns were unusual compared to their colleagues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the three functional types of AI, stating the core question that each type answers.
parts.answer:
1. Analytical AI answers 'What happened?'. It analyses historical and current data to identify patterns and relationships, supporting data-driven decisions about the past and present.
2. Predictive AI answers 'What will happen?'. It uses past data together with regression, time-series and machine learning models to forecast future outcomes.
3. Generative AI answers 'Can you create something new?'. It learns patterns from large datasets and uses them to produce new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
(1 mark for each type explained and 1 mark for each correct core question, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the initiatives (i) to (iv) into the appropriate type of AI, giving a brief justification for each classification.
parts.answer:
(i) Analytical AI: the tool explains what has already happened by analysing historical point-of-sale data from the last dengue season; it does not forecast or create anything.
(ii) Predictive AI: the model uses past sales data to forecast future demand for antibiotics in the next quarter, which is a 'what will happen' question.
(iii) Generative AI: the tool creates brand-new content (descriptions and bilingual posts) based on patterns learnt from large volumes of text; staff should review it before publishing.
(iv) Analytical AI: the system examines last year's refund transactions to uncover unusual patterns that have already occurred, in the same way a bank analyses past transactions to detect fraud patterns.
(0.5 mark for each correct classification and 1 mark for each justification, max 6)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the meaning of Artificial Intelligence and identify the types of human intelligence it attempts to simulate.
parts.answer:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human intelligence by machines. It enables machines to perform tasks such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception and understanding natural language. AI systems analyse data, make decisions and improve their performance over time without needing continuous human intervention, e.g. a facial-recognition kiosk verifying a person's identity against a CNIC photo or a tax system flagging an unusual return.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for the abilities simulated, 1 mark for improvement over time without continuous human intervention / example, max 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the four subfields of AI and give one business application of each.
parts.answer:
1. Machine Learning (ML): algorithms that learn patterns from data and improve without being explicitly reprogrammed. Application: a bank detecting abnormal transaction patterns that may indicate fraud.
2. Deep Learning: a specialised subset of ML that uses multi-layered neural networks to handle complex, unstructured data. Application: analysing thousands of medical scans to flag possible tumours.
3. Natural Language Processing (NLP): enables machines to understand, interpret and generate human language. Application: a customer-service chatbot that understands queries typed in Urdu and English.
4. Computer Vision: enables machines to interpret and analyse visual data such as images and video. Application: automatically scanning and validating a CNIC or passport photo during customer onboarding.
(1 mark for each subfield explained and 1 mark for each relevant application, max 8)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: State the relationship between Machine Learning and Deep Learning.
parts.answer:
Deep Learning is not a separate field alongside Machine Learning; it is a specialised subset of Machine Learning. Both learn from data, but Deep Learning uses neural networks with many hidden layers, which makes it suitable for complex, unstructured data such as images, audio and free text.
(1 mark for stating that deep learning is a subset of ML using multi-layered neural networks)

secb.scenario:
Sutlej Electric Supply Company (SESC) distributes electricity to domestic, commercial and industrial consumers in southern Punjab. SESC wants to apply machine learning to three problems:
(i) SESC's vigilance team has records of 18,000 past meter inspections, each already marked as 'theft confirmed' or 'no theft'. SESC wants a model that will predict whether a newly inspected meter is likely to have been tampered with.
(ii) SESC holds hourly consumption readings for two million smart meters but has no predefined consumer categories. It wants the system to discover groups of consumers with similar usage behaviour so that tariffs and awareness campaigns can be designed for each group.
(iii) SESC wants its mobile app to suggest a 'best next offer' to each consumer (for example, an off-peak discount or an instalment plan for arrears) and to keep improving these suggestions according to whether consumers accept or ignore them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the most appropriate machine learning technique for each of the problems (i) to (iii) and explain how the identified technique learns.
parts.answer:
(i) Supervised learning. The inspection records are labelled data because the correct output ('theft confirmed' or 'no theft') is already known for each case. The model is trained on these examples to learn the relationship between meter characteristics and the known outcome, and is then used for classification of new meters. This is similar to learning with an answer key.
(ii) Unsupervised learning. The consumption readings are unlabelled; there are no predefined categories. The model finds hidden structure in the data by itself and clusters consumers with similar usage behaviour into segments, which SESC can then name and target.
(iii) Reinforcement learning. The system learns by interacting with its environment (the consumers) and receiving a reward when an offer is accepted and a penalty when it is ignored. Through this trial and error it improves its sequential decisions about which offer to make next.
(1 mark for each correct technique, 1 mark for explaining how it learns and 1 mark for applying it to SESC's problem, max 9)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the typical uses of each of the three machine learning techniques identified in (a).
parts.answer:
1. Supervised learning is typically used for classification (assigning an item to a known category, e.g. spam or not spam, theft or no theft) and regression (predicting a numerical value from labelled past examples).
2. Unsupervised learning is typically used for clustering (grouping similar records, such as customer segments) and association (discovering items or behaviours that tend to occur together).
3. Reinforcement learning is typically used for sequential decision-making, where a system must choose a series of actions and improve them based on the rewards or penalties received, e.g. recommendation engines and robotics.
(1.5 marks each for supervised and unsupervised uses, 1 mark for reinforcement learning, max 4)

secb.topic: Custom ML model vs off-the-shelf solution
secb.scenario:
Kohinoor General Insurance Limited (KGIL) writes motor, health and crop insurance in Pakistan. KGIL's management wants to use machine learning for two purposes:
(i) Pricing crop insurance for cotton and wheat farmers using KGIL's own 15 years of claims history, district-level rainfall records and its own field surveyors' reports. No vendor product on the market covers crop risk in Pakistan's districts.
(ii) Summarising lengthy hospital discharge reports received with health claims and producing standard monthly management reports.
KGIL has a small IT department with no data scientists. Its Chief Financial Officer is concerned about the cost and time of building models internally, while the Chief Risk Officer wants KGIL to retain control over how premiums are calculated because the pricing logic must be explained to SECP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Compare a custom-built machine learning model with an off-the-shelf machine learning solution under four criteria.
parts.answer:
1. Customisation: a custom model is fully tailored to the organisation's unique data and needs, whereas an off-the-shelf solution offers limited customisation because it is built for general use across many customers.
2. Cost and time: a custom model has higher development and maintenance cost and takes longer to build, whereas an off-the-shelf solution is cost-effective and quick to implement.
3. Technical expertise: a custom model requires in-house data science / ML skills, whereas an off-the-shelf solution needs minimal in-house expertise.
4. Control and maintenance: a custom model gives the organisation full control over algorithms, data and outputs but needs continuous monitoring by the organisation, whereas an off-the-shelf solution is vendor-dependent and its maintenance is largely the vendor's responsibility.
(1 mark for each side of each criterion correctly explained, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend, with justification, the most appropriate approach for each of KGIL's two purposes, taking into account the concerns of the CFO and the CRO.
parts.answer:
1. Crop insurance pricing (i): a custom ML model is recommended. KGIL's claims history, rainfall data and surveyor reports are unique to KGIL, and no generic product covers district-level crop risk, so an off-the-shelf tool could not meet the need. A custom model also gives KGIL full control over the algorithm and outputs, addressing the CRO's requirement to explain premium calculations to SECP. Because KGIL has no data scientists, it must hire or contract ML expertise and budget for continuous monitoring and retraining, which addresses the CFO's concern by limiting custom development to this high-value area only.
2. Summarising discharge reports and management reporting (ii): an off-the-shelf solution is recommended. These are general, lower-risk tasks for which ready-made text-summarisation and reporting tools already exist; they are cheaper and quicker to implement, need minimal in-house expertise and are maintained by the vendor, which meets the CFO's cost and time concern.
3. Overall, KGIL should adopt a hybrid approach, which is how most organisations use ML in practice.
(1 mark for each correct recommendation, up to 2 marks for each justification linked to the scenario, 1 mark for the hybrid conclusion, max 6)

secb.topic: Generative AI algorithms and neural networks
secb.scenario:
Chenab Creative Studios (CCS) is an advertising agency in Lahore. It plans to introduce Generative AI for the following client work:
(i) Producing realistic photographs of models wearing a client's new lawn collection, without arranging a photo shoot.
(ii) Drafting advertising scripts and translating them between English and Urdu, where the meaning of each word depends on the rest of the sentence.
(iii) A bank client has customer survey data in which 12% of income fields are blank. The client wants the missing values filled in and wants unusual survey responses flagged before analysis.
(iv) Composing short background jingles for radio advertisements, where each note must follow logically from the notes played much earlier in the tune.
CCS's creative director has also asked for a simple explanation of how the neural networks behind these tools learn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the structure of a neural network and the process through which it learns.
parts.answer:
1. Structure: a neural network is loosely modelled on the human brain. The input layer receives the raw data, one or more hidden layers perform calculations and extract patterns, and the output layer produces the prediction.
2. Learning through backpropagation: the network makes a prediction, measures the error against the correct answer, and then adjusts its internal weights backwards through the network to reduce that error.
3. This process is repeated over many training cycles (epochs) until the error is acceptably small.
(1 mark for each layer description up to 2, 1 mark for backpropagation, 1 mark for repetition over epochs, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the requirements (i) to (iv), identify the most appropriate Generative AI algorithm and explain how it works.
parts.answer:
(i) Generative Adversarial Network (GAN): two neural networks are trained against each other. The generator creates synthetic images, while the discriminator tries to distinguish real photographs from the fakes. Both improve until the generator's images are realistic enough to fool the discriminator, which suits realistic image generation.
(ii) Transformer model: it uses a self-attention mechanism that weighs the importance of every word relative to every other word in the sequence simultaneously, rather than one word at a time. This allows it to understand context and makes it suitable for text generation and translation; GPT is the best-known example.
(iii) Variational Autoencoder (VAE): a single network in which an encoder compresses the input into a compact latent space representing the essence of the data, and a decoder reconstructs it or generates new, similar data by sampling from that space. VAEs are particularly useful for data imputation (filling missing values) and anomaly detection.
(iv) Recurrent Neural Network with Long Short-Term Memory (RNN/LSTM): it processes sequential data one step at a time while retaining a memory of earlier inputs. A basic RNN tends to forget information from far back in the sequence, so an LSTM, whose memory cells retain relevant information over long sequences, is appropriate for music generation.
(1 mark for each correct algorithm and 1 mark for each explanation, max 8)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Briefly explain the type of data for which a Convolutional Neural Network and a Feedforward Neural Network are best suited.
parts.answer:
1. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN): best suited to image and spatial data. It uses filters to detect visual patterns such as edges, shapes and textures, which is why it underpins computer vision tasks.
2. Feedforward Neural Network (FNN): best suited to simple classification and regression problems. Data flows in one direction only, from the input layer through the hidden layers to the output layer, with no loops or memory of earlier inputs.
(1.5 marks for each network type correctly explained, max 3)

secb.topic: Agenting AI and types of intelligent agents
secb.scenario:
Margalla Smart Logistics (MSL) operates a large automated warehouse near Islamabad and a fleet of delivery vans. MSL has deployed several AI agents that operate without waiting for staff instructions:
(i) A cold-room agent that sounds an alarm whenever the temperature reading rises above 8 degrees Celsius. It has no record of earlier readings.
(ii) A routing agent whose objective is to deliver each parcel to its destination address, choosing among alternative routes those that bring the van closer to the destination.
(iii) A dock-scheduling agent that keeps an internal record of which loading docks are occupied, which vans are expected and how long each type of van has historically taken to unload, and uses this together with current sensor input to allocate docks.
(iv) A delivery-pricing agent that selects a delivery charge offering the best trade-off between revenue, van availability and the risk of losing the customer.
(v) A packing agent that refines its box-selection decisions after every week by learning from feedback on damaged parcels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what is meant by Agenting AI and how it differs from a conventional chatbot.
parts.answer:
Agenting AI refers to systems that operate autonomously within an environment to achieve a goal. An autonomous agent continuously perceives its environment, decides and acts, often without being prompted for each step. A conventional chatbot is reactive: it only answers when a user asks it something. MSL's agents, by contrast, are proactive, monitoring the warehouse and fleet and acting on their own to achieve their objectives.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for perceive-decide-act without prompting, 1 mark for contrast with a reactive chatbot, max 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain any four key features of autonomous agents, relating each to MSL's agents.
parts.answer:
1. Autonomy: operates independently without human input for every action, e.g. the cold-room agent raises an alarm without a supervisor checking the reading.
2. Goal-orientation: designed to work towards a specific objective, e.g. the routing agent's objective of delivering each parcel.
3. Adaptability: learns from experience and adjusts its strategy over time, e.g. the packing agent changing box selection after damage feedback.
4. Interactivity: communicates and coordinates with other agents or systems, e.g. the dock-scheduling agent using information about vans expected from the routing system.
5. Perception and action: senses its environment through data and acts on what it perceives, e.g. temperature and dock sensors.
(1 mark for each feature explained and related to MSL, any four, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the agents (i) to (v) into the appropriate type of intelligent agent, explaining how each type makes its decisions.
parts.answer:
(i) Simple reflex agent: acts only on its current perception using fixed IF-THEN rules (IF temperature > 8 degrees THEN alarm) and has no memory of past readings.
(ii) Goal-based agent: evaluates which available actions bring it closer to a specific goal, here reaching the delivery address, and chooses routes accordingly.
(iii) Model-based reflex agent: maintains an internal model of the world (dock occupancy, expected vans, historical unloading times) and decides using both current input and this history.
(iv) Utility-based agent: maximises a utility function, choosing the option that gives the best trade-off among competing objectives (revenue, van availability and customer retention), rather than merely achieving a single goal.
(v) Learning agent: improves its performance over time from experience and feedback, here using damage reports to refine future packing decisions.
(0.5 mark for each correct classification and 1 mark for each explanation of how that type decides, max 7)

secb.scenario:
Pak Agri Machinery Limited (PAML) manufactures tractors and threshers in Sheikhupura and buys components from about 600 local suppliers. Its accounts payable process works as follows:
(i) Suppliers email invoices in different formats: some as structured PDF forms, many as scanned photographs of handwritten invoices, and some with free-text notes about price changes.
(ii) Clerks key invoice data into the ERP, match each invoice with the purchase order and goods received note, and post it.
(iii) A senior accountant reviews invoices where the price or quantity differs from the purchase order and decides whether the difference is acceptable.
(iv) Approved invoices are scheduled for payment through the bank's corporate portal.
PAML's IT team has proposed deploying RPA bots for the whole process. The finance director doubts that RPA alone can handle it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the meaning of Intelligent Automation and justify the finance director's doubt by comparing what RPA alone and AI alone can and cannot do in PAML's process.
parts.answer:
1. Intelligent Automation (IA) combines Robotic Process Automation (RPA), which handles structured, rule-based tasks, with AI, which handles judgement, unstructured data and learning, so that an entire workflow can be automated end to end.
2. RPA alone: it performs structured, rule-based tasks very well, such as keying data from standard PDF forms into the ERP, performing fixed three-way matching and logging into the bank portal to schedule payments. However, it cannot read handwritten scanned invoices or free-text notes (unstructured data), it cannot judge whether a price difference is acceptable, and its fixed rules do not learn or improve.
3. AI alone: it can interpret scanned images and free text and can learn to assess whether a variance looks acceptable, but on its own it cannot log in to the ERP and bank portal and click through the posting and payment steps.
4. Therefore the finance director is right: only the combination (IA) can automate PAML's process from inbox to payment, including the parts needing judgement.
(1 mark for IA definition, up to 2 marks each for RPA-only and AI-only limitations applied to PAML, 1 mark for conclusion, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Describe how an Intelligent Automation solution would handle steps (i) to (iv) of PAML's process.
parts.answer:
1. Step (i): an RPA bot collects invoices from the supplier email inbox; an AI component (computer vision for scanned / handwritten invoices and NLP for free-text notes) extracts supplier, quantity, price and other data from unstructured documents.
2. Step (ii): an RPA bot enters the extracted data into the ERP and performs rule-based matching with the purchase order and goods received note.
3. Step (iii): an AI model assesses variances using patterns learnt from past decisions, recommending approval of routine, low-risk differences; unusual or high-value differences are escalated to the senior accountant (human-in-the-loop).
4. Step (iv): an RPA bot logs in to the bank's corporate portal and schedules payment for approved invoices, completing the end-to-end workflow.
(1 mark for each step correctly described with the right RPA / AI component, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain the 'human-in-the-loop' feature of Intelligent Automation and why it is important for PAML.
parts.answer:
Human-in-the-loop design means people remain involved in high-stakes or ambiguous cases while the system handles routine work and continues to learn. For PAML, the senior accountant would still decide on large or unusual price or quantity differences, so that incorrect or fraudulent supplier invoices are not paid automatically. The accountant's decisions also act as feedback from which the AI component learns, improving the accuracy of its future recommendations, while staff time is reserved only for the exceptions that genuinely need judgement.
(1 mark for the meaning, 1 mark for control over high-risk cases, 1 mark for learning feedback / efficiency, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Tezz Bites (Private) Limited (TBL) runs a food-delivery app in Lahore, Faisalabad and Islamabad. TBL moved its app to a cloud service provider (CSP) last year. TBL's Chief Technology Officer made the following observations in his annual report to the board:
(i) During Ramadan iftar hours the number of orders rises nearly tenfold. The app's capacity now grows automatically within minutes when orders spike and shrinks again after iftar, so TBL no longer pays for idle servers.
(ii) When TBL launched in Islamabad, its developers set up a new database and test servers themselves through the CSP's web console within an hour, without raising a request to the CSP's staff.
(iii) Riders, restaurant partners and TBL's head-office staff all use the same system through smartphones, tablets and laptops from wherever they are.
(iv) The monthly CSP invoice is itemised by the exact storage used and the compute hours consumed by TBL during the month.
(v) The CSP's data centre also serves many other unrelated companies on the same physical hardware, while each customer's data and workloads remain logically separate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what is meant by cloud computing and how it differs from traditional on-premise IT.
parts.answer:
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services such as servers, storage, databases, networking, software and analytics over the internet ('the cloud'), instead of the organisation owning and maintaining physical infrastructure. Under traditional on-premise IT, an organisation buys enough hardware to meet its peak demand and runs it itself, so much of it sits idle for the rest of the year. Cloud computing lets an organisation access and store data remotely, scale operations dynamically and pay for what it uses, reducing cost compared to on-premise IT.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for contrast with owning infrastructure, 1 mark for remote access / dynamic scaling / cost, max 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the cloud computing characteristic illustrated by each of the observations (i) to (v) and explain each identified characteristic.
parts.answer:
(i) Rapid elasticity: resources can be scaled up or down almost instantly in response to demand and released once no longer needed. TBL's capacity expands for iftar peaks and contracts afterwards.
(ii) On-demand self-service: users provision computing resources automatically, without contacting the provider's staff. TBL's developers created the database and servers themselves through the console.
(iii) Broad network access: services are accessible from any device and any location over the internet. Riders, partners and staff use the same system from phones, tablets and laptops.
(iv) Measured service: usage is monitored and billed on a pay-as-you-go basis, so the customer pays only for what it consumes. TBL's bill is based on actual storage and compute hours.
(v) Resource pooling (multi-tenancy): the provider's infrastructure is shared among many customers at the same time, with each customer logically isolated. TBL shares hardware with other companies while its data remains separate.
Note: observation (i) is elasticity (one customer scaling over time), not resource pooling (many customers sharing at the same time).
(1 mark for each correct characteristic and 1 mark for each explanation linked to the observation, max 10)

secb.scenario:
Ravi Group (RG) is a diversified group in Pakistan with three businesses, each with a different IT requirement:
(i) Ravi Steel Limited (RSL) runs a specialised production-planning application that requires a particular operating system version and custom security settings. RSL's experienced IT team wants full control over the operating system and applications but no longer wants to buy and maintain physical servers.
(ii) Ravi Digital (RD) is a small team of developers building a customer loyalty app for the group. RD wants to spend its time writing and deploying code and does not want to configure servers, operating systems, databases or middleware.
(iii) Ravi Foods (RF) has 40 sales offices with mostly non-technical staff. RF needs standard email, video-conferencing and customer relationship management software, accessed through a web browser, with nothing to install or maintain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate cloud service model for each of RSL, RD and RF, justifying each recommendation.
parts.answer:
(i) RSL: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). IaaS provides virtualised computing resources (virtual machines, storage and networking) over the internet while the customer controls the operating system and applications. This allows RSL's skilled IT team to install the required OS version and security settings, without owning physical hardware.
(ii) RD: Platform as a Service (PaaS). PaaS provides a ready-made platform of development tools, databases, middleware and operating systems, so developers can build, deploy and manage applications without managing the infrastructure. RD's small team can concentrate on its code.
(iii) RF: Software as a Service (SaaS). SaaS delivers fully functional, ready-to-use applications over the internet, usually on subscription, with the provider managing everything. RF's non-technical staff simply log in through a browser; there is nothing to install or maintain at the 40 offices.
(1 mark for each correct model and 1 mark for each justification, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the three service models, explain what the provider supplies and what remains the customer's responsibility.
parts.answer:
1. IaaS: the provider supplies and manages the physical infrastructure and provides virtual machines, storage and networking. The customer manages the operating system, middleware, runtime, applications and data.
2. PaaS: the provider supplies a development platform including tools, databases, middleware and operating systems, and manages everything underneath. The customer manages only its application code and data.
3. SaaS: the provider supplies a complete, ready-to-use application and manages the hardware, operating system and application. The customer simply uses it through a browser or API, with nothing to install, update or maintain locally.
(1 mark for the provider side and 1 mark for the customer side of each model, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Rank the three service models in order of the level of control given to the customer.
parts.answer:
From highest to lowest customer control: IaaS (high control, since the customer manages the OS and everything above it), then PaaS (medium control, since the customer manages only code and data), then SaaS (low control, since the provider manages the whole application). As control falls, so does the management burden on the customer, which is why RF, with no technical staff, is suited to SaaS while RSL, which needs control, is suited to IaaS.
(1 mark for the correct order, 1 mark for explanation, max 2)

secb.scenario:
The following organisations are each deciding how their cloud infrastructure should be deployed:
(i) Bolan Commercial Bank Limited (BCBL) processes customer deposits and loans. It must keep core banking data under strict control to satisfy SBP's regulatory requirements and wants maximum customisation of security settings.
(ii) GharSe (Private) Limited, a two-year-old online home-decor start-up, has a limited budget, no sensitive data beyond order details, and sales that jump sharply during the wedding season.
(iii) Indus Valley Hospitals (IVH) wants to keep patients' medical records in a dedicated environment, but its online appointment-booking portal faces unpredictable traffic and needs to scale cheaply.
(iv) Five general insurance companies have agreed to share common infrastructure for a KYC verification service that all of them require, so that they can split the cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate cloud deployment model for each of the organisations (i) to (iv) and justify your recommendation.
parts.answer:
(i) BCBL: Private cloud. A private cloud is dedicated to a single organisation and offers the greatest security, control and customisation, which suits a bank with strict SBP compliance requirements. It may be hosted on-premises or by a third party.
(ii) GharSe: Public cloud. Shared infrastructure delivered over the public internet is low cost and highly scalable and is fully managed by the provider. It suits a start-up with a limited budget, non-sensitive data and seasonal spikes.
(iii) IVH: Hybrid cloud. Medical records, being sensitive, stay on the private side, while the booking portal with variable demand runs on the public cloud where it can scale. This balances security with cost and flexibility.
(iv) The insurers: Community cloud. Infrastructure is shared by several organisations with similar requirements, which split the cost, e.g. shared KYC services among insurers.
(1 mark for each correct model and 1 mark for each justification linked to the scenario, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Compare the public, private and community cloud models in terms of ownership, security, cost and scalability, and explain how IVH's hybrid model balances these factors.
parts.answer:
1. Ownership: a public cloud is owned and operated by a third-party provider and shared by many tenants; a private cloud is dedicated to a single organisation, hosted on-premises or by a third party; a community cloud is shared by several organisations with common interests and managed internally or by a third party.
2. Security: public cloud security is moderate because infrastructure is shared broadly; private cloud security is high because resources are dedicated; community cloud security is high for the specific compliance needs of its members.
3. Cost: the public cloud is lowest cost because cost is spread across many users; the private cloud is higher cost because of dedicated resources; in a community cloud the cost is shared among the member organisations.
4. Scalability: the public cloud is highly scalable; a private cloud is limited by internal resources; a community cloud has moderate scalability depending on community needs.
5. IVH's hybrid model keeps medical records in the private part (high security and compliance) while the booking portal uses the public part (low cost, high scalability), so IVH pays a moderate combined cost while getting security where it is needed and scalability where demand varies.
(1 mark for each factor correctly compared across the models, 1 mark for the hybrid explanation applied to IVH, max 5)

secb.topic: Benefits of cloud migration and business case
secb.scenario:
Hala Ceramics Limited (HCL) manufactures tiles and sanitaryware in Hyderabad. It runs its ERP, email and file servers in a small on-premise server room. The following facts were noted during a recent IT review:
(i) The servers are seven years old and the vendor quotes PKR 85 million to replace them, payable upfront.
(ii) The server room is in the same building as the factory. Last monsoon season, water entered the building and HCL was unable to invoice customers for four days. Backups are taken to tape and kept in the same room.
(iii) Order volumes double between March and June every year, when ERP response times become very slow.
(iv) HCL's sales team, who travel across Sindh and Balochistan, can access the ERP only when they are physically in the office.
(v) HCL's marketing department wants to try AI-based demand analytics, but the IT department estimates that buying and setting up suitable hardware would take nine months.
HCL's directors are considering moving these systems to the cloud.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the benefits that cloud computing would offer to HCL, relating each benefit to the facts (i) to (v).
parts.answer:
(i) Cost efficiency: pay-as-you-go pricing removes the large upfront capital investment in hardware. Instead of spending PKR 85 million at once, HCL would pay a recurring subscription or pay-per-use charge based on what it consumes, and would also save on maintenance and upgrade costs because the provider maintains the infrastructure.
(ii) Disaster recovery: the cloud allows data and systems to be automatically replicated across regions or data centres. A flood at the Hyderabad building would no longer stop invoicing, and backups would not be lost together with the servers.
(iii) Scalability: capacity can be adjusted quickly to match demand. HCL can increase ERP capacity for the March to June peak and reduce it afterwards, avoiding slow response without paying for peak capacity all year.
(iv) Flexibility: employees can work from anywhere on any device over the internet, so the travelling sales team can enter orders and check stock while in the field.
(v) Faster innovation: new tools and platforms such as AI and analytics are available on demand without lengthy procurement, so marketing could begin its analytics trial within days rather than waiting nine months for hardware.
(1 mark for each benefit and 1 mark for relating it to the relevant fact, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss two challenges of cloud computing that HCL's directors should consider before approving the migration.
parts.answer:
Any two of the following:
1. Security and privacy: HCL's ERP data would be held on shared, multi-tenant infrastructure, which creates a different risk profile from data kept fully in-house; HCL must assess the provider's security and its own access controls.
2. Vendor lock-in: once HCL builds heavily on one provider's proprietary tools, switching to another provider later may be difficult and costly.
3. Downtime: even major providers occasionally suffer outages, and HCL's invoicing would depend on both the provider and its internet connectivity.
4. Cost management: it is easy to over-provision resources; without monitoring, HCL's monthly bill could exceed the budget used in the business case.
5. Technical expertise: HCL's small IT department may lack cloud architecture, security and DevOps skills.
(1 mark for each challenge identified and 1 mark for relating it to HCL, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Zarghun Telecom Services (ZTS) moved its billing, customer analytics and development systems to a public cloud two years ago. ZTS's internal audit department has reported the following issues:
(i) Several large virtual machines created for a one-month analytics project were never switched off, and the cloud bill for the last quarter was 60% above budget.
(ii) ZTS built its billing system using many proprietary database and messaging services of its current provider. When a cheaper provider offered better terms, ZTS found that moving would require rewriting much of the system.
(iii) A six-hour outage at the provider's regional data centre stopped ZTS's online bill payment, and ZTS had no arrangement to continue operating elsewhere.
(iv) A storage area holding customer call records was configured by a junior employee so that it could be accessed without authentication.
(v) ZTS has only one employee with cloud architecture skills, and several configuration changes have been delayed while waiting for him.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the cloud computing challenge illustrated by each of the issues (i) to (v) and explain each identified challenge.
parts.answer:
(i) Cost management: because resources can be provisioned so easily, it is equally easy to over-provision or forget to decommission resources, and unmonitored usage leads to unexpectedly large bills.
(ii) Vendor lock-in: after building heavily on one provider's proprietary tools and formats, it becomes difficult and costly to move to another provider. This is a technical dependency, not merely a long-term contract.
(iii) Downtime: even major providers occasionally suffer outages, which disrupt dependent business operations such as ZTS's bill payment.
(iv) Security and privacy: storing data on shared, multi-tenant infrastructure creates a different risk profile from in-house storage, and misconfiguration can expose sensitive customer data.
(v) Technical expertise: cloud architecture, security and DevOps skills are specialised and often in short supply, creating key-person dependency.
(1 mark for each challenge correctly identified and 1 mark for each explanation, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend one control that ZTS should implement to address each of the issues (i) to (v).
parts.answer:
(i) Set automated budget alerts that notify IT and finance as spending approaches defined thresholds, apply auto-shutdown for project and test instances after a period of inactivity, and assign a named owner to review and justify all active resources periodically.
(ii) Prefer open, portable formats and standard services where possible, and maintain a documented exit / migration plan so that dependency on proprietary services is a deliberate, approved decision.
(iii) Replicate critical systems across multiple data centres or regions and use the provider's failover options, so that services shift automatically to alternative servers, and test failover regularly so that bill payment can continue during a regional outage.
(iv) Restrict configuration rights, require authentication and encryption for all storage holding customer data, and perform regular configuration reviews of access settings.
(v) Train additional staff in cloud architecture and security, document configurations, and consider engaging a specialist partner to remove the single-person dependency.
(1 mark for each appropriate control, max 5)

secb.scenario:
The Provincial Land Revenue Department (PLRD) maintains land ownership records, citizens' CNIC details and mutation histories for millions of landowners. PLRD plans to replace its ageing on-premise systems with a new digital land-records platform.
During planning, the following proposals were made by different officials:
(i) The IT director proposes buying new physical servers for a PLRD-owned data centre because 'that is how government systems have always been built'.
(ii) A consultant proposes hosting all land and CNIC data with a low-cost cloud provider whose only data centres are outside Pakistan.
(iii) The finance officer is concerned that PLRD's staff have no experience in managing cloud services or cloud security.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the core mandate of Pakistan's Cloud First Policy (PCFP) and how it applies to proposal (i).
parts.answer:
The PCFP, issued by the Ministry of IT and Telecommunication (MoITT), makes cloud adoption the default option for all new public-sector ICT investments. Public Sector Entities must justify why a system should not be cloud-based, rather than justifying cloud adoption. Applied to proposal (i), PLRD cannot simply buy new servers out of habit; as this is a new ICT investment, it should adopt the cloud unless it can document a clear justification for an on-premise solution.
(1 mark for issuing body / default-to-cloud mandate, 1 mark for burden of justification, 1 mark for application to proposal (i), max 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate proposal (ii) in the light of the PCFP's data sovereignty and localisation objective and the utilisation of local cloud service providers.
parts.answer:
1. Data sovereignty and localisation: critical and sensitive government data must be hosted within Pakistan, so that it remains subject to Pakistani law rather than a foreign jurisdiction.
2. PLRD's land ownership records and citizens' CNIC details are critical and sensitive. If hosted only abroad, they would fall under the legal jurisdiction of another country, creating a risk of foreign access to the data and a national-security and privacy exposure.
3. Local hosting also enables faster local incident response and supports compliance audits under domestic legal frameworks.
4. The PCFP gives priority to cloud service providers that maintain physical data centres within Pakistan.
5. Conclusion: proposal (ii) should be rejected despite its low cost; PLRD should select a CSP with data centres inside Pakistan for this data.
(1 mark for each valid point, max 5)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain how the other objectives of the PCFP would support PLRD's project, including the concern raised in (iii).
parts.answer:
1. Digital transformation: adopting cloud for new ICT investments streamlines operations and speeds up digitisation of citizen services, e.g. online land-record verification for citizens.
2. Cost optimisation: shifting from capital expenditure on hardware to scalable, shared, pay-as-you-go services reduces the need for PLRD to fund a new data centre.
3. Standardisation: common rules for data classification, access control and audit / compliance (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO 22301), aligned with PECA 2016 and the National Cyber Security Policy 2021, give PLRD a ready framework for securing land records.
4. Capacity building: the policy provides for training government personnel in cloud computing, cybersecurity and data governance, which directly addresses the finance officer's concern in (iii).
5. Utilisation of local CSPs: priority for providers with data centres in Pakistan supports both the sovereignty requirement and local support.
(1 mark for each objective explained and applied to PLRD, max 5)

secb.scenario:
Sabz Kisan Agritech (SKA) provides farm advisory services to cotton and sugarcane growers in Sindh. SKA's management has listed the following needs for the next two years:
(i) Collecting and processing readings from 50,000 soil-moisture sensors installed on farms.
(ii) Training a machine learning model on several years of satellite images to predict crop yields; this requires GPU computing for a few weeks each year.
(iii) Analysing very large datasets of weather, sensor and market price data without investing in expensive hardware.
(iv) Allowing agronomists in Sukkur, Larkana and Mirpurkhas to share documents and hold video meetings with head office in Karachi.
(v) Building and testing a new farmer mobile app with frequent releases.
(vi) Ensuring that farmer records survive a local disaster such as flooding at the Karachi office.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the application of cloud computing relevant to each of SKA's needs (i) to (vi) and explain how the cloud supports it.
parts.answer:
(i) IoT management: the cloud manages and processes data from very large numbers of connected devices centrally, so the 50,000 sensor feeds can be received and processed in one place.
(ii) AI and machine learning: ML models can be trained and deployed using cloud compute power such as GPUs on demand; SKA rents GPUs for the few weeks needed instead of buying them.
(iii) Big Data analytics: massive datasets can be processed and analysed without investing in expensive on-premise hardware.
(iv) Collaboration tools: cloud email, video conferencing and shared documents allow distributed teams to communicate and work together.
(v) Software development and testing: on-demand infrastructure, including CI/CD pipelines, is used to build, test and deploy applications quickly and frequently.
(vi) Disaster recovery (with data storage and backup): data and systems are replicated across regions so operations can continue after a local outage or disaster.
(0.5 mark for each correct application and 1 mark for each explanation, max 9)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the cloud characteristics that make the cloud particularly cost-effective for SKA's need (ii), and explain why.
parts.answer:
1. Rapid elasticity: SKA can scale up GPU capacity sharply for the few weeks of model training and release it immediately afterwards.
2. Measured service: SKA is billed on a pay-as-you-go basis only for the GPU hours actually consumed, rather than owning expensive hardware that would be idle for most of the year.
3. On-demand self-service: SKA's data team can provision the GPU instances itself whenever training begins, without lengthy procurement or a request to the provider's staff.
(1 mark for each characteristic explained in context, max 3)

secb.topic: Service model responsibilities, cloud providers and key terms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Using a suitable analogy, explain how responsibility is divided between the cloud provider and the customer under on-premise IT, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
parts.answer:
A pizza analogy illustrates the division:
1. On-premise: like buying the oven, flour and cheese and cooking everything yourself, the organisation owns and manages all hardware, OS, applications and data.
2. IaaS: like renting a kitchen with an oven and cooking your own pizza, the provider supplies the physical infrastructure (virtual machines, storage, networking) while the customer manages the OS, middleware, runtime, application and data.
3. PaaS: like being given a part-baked base and toppings and only finishing and baking it, the provider manages the platform and infrastructure while the customer manages only its application code and data.
4. SaaS: like ordering a pizza that arrives ready to eat, the provider manages the whole application; the customer simply uses it.
5. As a result, customer control and flexibility fall from high (IaaS) to medium (PaaS) to low (SaaS), while the management burden carried by the provider rises in the same order.
(1 mark for each point, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Briefly describe what each of the following cloud providers is particularly known for: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Oracle Cloud.
parts.answer:
1. Amazon Web Services (AWS): the world's largest and most comprehensive cloud platform, offering a broad set of global services including computing power, storage and databases in a flexible, scalable environment for businesses of all sizes.
2. Microsoft Azure: a leading enterprise-grade cloud platform known for seamless integration with Microsoft products and a broad set of services covering computing, analytics, storage and networking.
3. Oracle Cloud: a strong enterprise player offering cloud infrastructure, platform services and enterprise applications, especially for database management and ERP, known for performance and reliability for mission-critical workloads.
(1 mark for each provider correctly described, max 3)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between rapid elasticity and resource pooling, and explain why vendor lock-in should not be confused with a long-term contract or a security breach.
parts.answer:
1. Rapid elasticity is about one customer's resources being scaled up or down over time in response to demand, e.g. a streaming platform growing from 20 to 200 servers during a live match and back again.
2. Resource pooling (multi-tenancy) is about many different customers sharing the same underlying infrastructure at the same time, each logically isolated.
3. Vendor lock-in means difficulty moving to a different provider because of deep dependency on one provider's proprietary tools, formats or services. A long-term contract is a legal commitment that ends at expiry, whereas lock-in persists as a technical and cost barrier even when no contract binds the customer.
4. A security breach is unauthorised access to data; lock-in involves no breach, only dependency.
(1 mark for each point, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Basmati Exporters Association (BEA) represents rice exporters in Gujranwala and Sheikhupura. Exporters currently prove the quality and origin of each consignment through paper certificates issued by laboratories, which buyers in the Gulf sometimes suspect of being altered. BEA proposes a shared blockchain ledger on which laboratories, exporters, the inspecting agency and buyers' banks would each run a computer that holds a copy of the ledger.
At a briefing, BEA members asked:
(i) 'If a laboratory employee later changes a test result already recorded on the ledger, how would anyone know?'
(ii) 'Who decides whether a new certificate is genuine before it is added?'
(iii) 'What happens to the record if one member's computer is switched off or damaged?'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the meaning of blockchain and describe the four key components of a blockchain.
parts.answer:
Blockchain is a decentralised, distributed ledger technology (DLT) that records and verifies transactions across a peer-to-peer network of computers in a secure, transparent and immutable manner, removing the need for an intermediary.
1. Blocks: the building units of the chain; each block contains transaction data plus a header (metadata), including the hash of the previous block.
2. Hashing: converts data into a fixed-size, unique digital fingerprint; even a tiny change to the input produces a completely different hash, so tampering is detectable.
3. Consensus mechanisms: protocols such as Proof of Work or Proof of Stake that let the network agree which transactions are valid, preventing fraud or unauthorised changes.
4. Nodes: the computers in the network that validate transactions, store a copy of the ledger and participate in consensus.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for each component explained, 1 mark for explaining that blocks are linked through the previous block's hash, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Using the components explained in (a), answer each of the BEA members' questions (i) to (iii).
parts.answer:
(i) Tampering is detectable through hashing and chaining. Changing a recorded test result would change that block's hash; because every following block contains the hash of the block before it, every subsequent link would break, and all other nodes holding copies would immediately detect the mismatch. A change could only be forced by controlling the majority of the network, which is practically impossible, so the record is immutable.
(ii) The decision is made by the consensus mechanism, not by any single party. The new certificate is broadcast to the participating nodes, which verify it (e.g. that the laboratory is registered and the details match the consignment). Only once a majority agrees it is valid is it grouped into a new block and added.
(iii) Every node keeps a full copy of the ledger, so the record does not depend on one member's computer. If a node is switched off or damaged, the other nodes continue to hold and validate the ledger, and the node can resynchronise its copy when it returns.
(2 marks for each question answered correctly with reference to the relevant component, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain why blockchain removes the need for a single trusted intermediary in BEA's arrangement.
parts.answer:
Because every participant holds a copy of the same ledger and new records are added only by network consensus, the parties do not need to rely on one central authority (such as a single certifying office or bank) to maintain and vouch for the records. Trust comes from the shared, verifiable and tamper-evident ledger itself, so a Gulf buyer can verify a certificate's history directly.
(1 mark for shared ledger / consensus replacing a central party, 1 mark for application to BEA, max 2)

secb.scenario:
Thar Renewables Cooperative (TRC) is a group of 300 households and small businesses in Mithi that have installed solar panels. TRC plans to set up a blockchain platform on which members will sell excess solar electricity directly to their neighbours, without the electricity distribution company acting as intermediary for each sale.
TRC's technical adviser has proposed using Proof of Work for validating transactions because 'it is what the first cryptocurrency used'. Several members object that the computers needed would consume a large share of the very electricity they are trying to sell, and that the platform must be able to handle a high number of small trades every hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how Proof of Work and Proof of Stake consensus mechanisms operate and compare their energy requirements.
parts.answer:
1. Proof of Work (PoW): miners compete to solve cryptographic puzzles; the first to solve the puzzle validates the block and adds it to the chain. Solving the puzzles requires massive computing power.
2. Proof of Stake (PoS): validators are selected on the basis of what they have staked (the digital assets they hold and lock up in the network) rather than by solving puzzles.
3. Both ensure that only valid transactions are added to the ledger and prevent unauthorised changes.
4. Energy: PoW requires significant computing power and electricity, which is a key challenge of PoW blockchains; PoS uses far less energy and is therefore considerably more energy-efficient.
(1.5 marks each for PoW and PoS operation, 1 mark for common purpose, 1 mark for energy comparison, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the technical adviser's proposal and recommend a more suitable approach for TRC, with justification.
parts.answer:
1. The proposal is unsuitable. PoW's high energy consumption directly conflicts with TRC's purpose of selling surplus solar electricity, as members have pointed out.
2. Scalability is also a challenge: many blockchains process far fewer transactions per second than centralised systems, and PoW mining creates a bottleneck for the large number of small hourly trades.
3. Recommendation: TRC should use a Proof of Stake based platform, which is far more energy-efficient while still ensuring that only valid trades are recorded. Since high volumes of small transactions are expected and full public decentralisation is not needed, TRC could also consider a DAG-based DLT, which eliminates mining and is faster and more scalable.
(1 mark for each valid point, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain how peer-to-peer energy trading on a blockchain would benefit TRC's members.
parts.answer:
1. Members could sell excess solar energy directly to neighbours without a utility acting as intermediary for each sale, reducing intermediary costs and giving sellers a better price.
2. Every trade would be recorded on a shared, immutable ledger visible to members, so disputes about how many units were sold and at what price are reduced.
3. Smart contracts could automatically trigger payment to the seller once the meter confirms that the agreed units have been delivered, avoiding manual billing and collection delays.
(1 mark for each benefit, max 3)

secb.scenario:
The following organisations are each considering a blockchain solution:
(i) Indus Pharma Limited (IPL) wants to record internal batch-production and quality-control data, which must remain confidential, while also allowing patients to scan a QR code on each pack and verify publicly that the medicine is genuine.
(ii) Six commercial banks in Pakistan want a shared ledger to record trade-finance transactions among themselves. Each bank wants a role in governing the ledger, and the data must not be visible to the public.
(iii) Chiniot Furniture Works (CFW) wants to track movement of timber and finished goods between its own factories and showrooms. Only CFW's authorised staff should have access, and CFW wants full control of the ledger.
(iv) A non-profit group of software developers is launching a digital token that anyone in the world should be able to hold, read the transaction history of, and help validate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend the most appropriate type of blockchain for each of the organisations (i) to (iv), justifying each recommendation.
parts.answer:
(i) IPL: Hybrid blockchain. It combines public and private elements: a public chain allows any patient to verify the pack through a QR code, while a private chain keeps batch-production and quality data restricted to authorised users.
(ii) The banks: Consortium blockchain. It is controlled jointly by a pre-approved group of organisations and is semi-decentralised, giving each bank a governance role while keeping transactions private from the public (e.g. platforms such as R3 Corda are used by groups of banks).
(iii) CFW: Private blockchain. Access is restricted to authorised users and the ledger is controlled by a single organisation, which meets CFW's need for confidentiality and full control over internal supply-chain tracking.
(iv) The developers: Public blockchain. It is open, so anyone can join, read and participate in validation, and it is fully decentralised, as with Bitcoin and Ethereum.
(1 mark for each correct type and 1 mark for each justification, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why a private blockchain would be inappropriate for the banks in (ii), and why a public blockchain would be inappropriate for CFW in (iii).
parts.answer:
1. Private blockchain for the banks: a private blockchain is controlled by a single organisation. If one bank controlled the ledger, the other five would have to trust it in the same way as a central intermediary and would have no role in governance, defeating the purpose of a shared ledger among separate, independent organisations. A consortium spreads control among the pre-approved group.
2. Public blockchain for CFW: a public chain is open for anyone to join and read, so CFW's internal stock movements, volumes and showroom details would become visible to competitors, and CFW would lose control over who participates in validation.
3. Public chains also tend to have lower transaction speeds and, where Proof of Work is used, higher energy consumption, neither of which CFW needs to accept for an internal application.
(2 marks each for points 1 and 2, 1 mark for point 3, max 5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), its relationship with blockchain, and how it differs from a centralised database.
parts.answer:
1. DLT is a digital system for recording transactions in which the data is distributed across multiple locations rather than stored on one central server, and in which there is no single central authority.
2. Blockchain is the best-known type of DLT but not the only one; other DLT types exist to solve problems such as speed, scalability and energy use that classic blockchain struggles with.
3. In a centralised database, one party owns and controls the single copy of the data and can alter it unilaterally, whereas in a DLT participants share the records and changes require agreement across the network.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for relationship with blockchain, 2 marks for contrast with centralised database, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Describe the structure and key advantage of DAG, Hashgraph and Holochain, and suggest a suitable use for each.
parts.answer:
1. Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG): uses a non-linear, graph-like structure in which each new transaction validates earlier transactions directly, rather than grouping transactions into a linear chain of blocks. Key advantage: it eliminates mining, so it is faster and more scalable. Suitable use: high-volume IoT micro-transactions, e.g. smart meters or vehicle sensors paying tolls (IOTA's 'Tangle').
2. Hashgraph: spreads transaction information across the network using a gossip protocol and reaches agreement through 'virtual voting'. Key advantage: very fast and fair consensus. Suitable use: applications needing high transaction speed with fair ordering (e.g. Hedera Hashgraph).
3. Holochain: each user (agent) keeps their own chain of interactions, so no global consensus is required. Key advantage: highly scalable with low overhead. Suitable use: decentralised social or collaborative applications.
(1 mark each for structure, advantage and suitable use of each DLT type, max 9)

secb.scenario:
Saadat Bank Limited (SBL), a mid-sized commercial bank, has approved a digital strategy containing the following initiatives:
(i) A mobile wallet allowing customers, including people without a traditional bank account, to send money, pay utility bills and pay shopkeepers by scanning a QR code.
(ii) Small loans to gig workers and street vendors who have no formal credit history, assessed using their wallet transaction patterns and utility-bill payment history.
(iii) An automated investment platform that builds a mutual-fund portfolio for each customer according to his or her goals and risk tolerance and rebalances it automatically as markets move.
(iv) A partnership with an insurer to offer motor insurance whose premium is based on a driver's actual driving behaviour recorded by a sensor in the car, with simple claims settled by an AI chatbot.
(v) A system that screens every new customer against sanctions lists, politically exposed persons and adverse media, and monitors transactions for suspicious activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the meaning of fintech.
parts.answer:
Fintech (financial technology) is the use of advanced technology in financial services to improve processes, increase efficiency and improve the customer experience. It is transforming traditional financial institutions such as SBL by making financial activities faster, more accessible, more secure and more customer-friendly.
(1 mark for definition, 1 mark for its effect on financial services, max 2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the key area of fintech to which each of the initiatives (i) to (v) belongs and explain one benefit of each initiative to SBL or its customers.
parts.answer:
(i) Digital payments: mobile wallets and contactless (QR / NFC) payments let users store payment details and pay with their phones, protected by encryption and tokenisation. Benefit: instant, convenient payments without an intermediary, extending services to the unbanked.
(ii) Lending and credit (alternative credit scoring): non-traditional data such as transaction patterns and utility-bill history is used to assess creditworthiness. Benefit: expanded access to credit for underserved people and faster approval than traditional loan processing.
(iii) Wealth management (robo-advisor): an automated, algorithm-based platform builds and manages portfolios based on the user's goals and risk tolerance. Benefit: lower fees than a traditional adviser, personalised strategies and automated rebalancing.
(iv) Insurance (InsurTech): AI, IoT and big data are used to personalise policies and automate claims. Benefit: premiums priced on the driver's real risk profile rather than broad demographic categories, and faster, more accurate claims processing.
(v) RegTech: technology that automates compliance and risk management, including AML / KYC monitoring and name screening. Benefit: reduced manual effort and cost, faster and more consistent detection of suspicious activity, and a stronger audit trail for SBP.
(1 mark for each correct area and 1 mark for each relevant benefit, max 10)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain two overall benefits that fintech brings to the financial sector.
parts.answer:
Any two of: improved accessibility of credit, payments and investment for previously underserved populations; enhanced efficiency through automation; cost reduction from fewer intermediaries; personalisation of products through data analytics; and greater transparency through real-time visibility of balances and transaction history.
(1 mark for each benefit explained, max 2)

secb.scenario:
Qila Digital Finance (QDF) is a Pakistani fintech start-up planning a blockchain-based platform with the following features:
(i) A PKR 900 million shopping plaza in Islamabad will be divided into 90,000 digital units, so that salaried investors can buy and sell small shares of it.
(ii) Travel insurance sold on the platform will automatically pay compensation to a passenger's wallet as soon as data from the airline confirms that a flight was delayed by more than three hours.
(iii) Overseas Pakistanis will send money home directly to family members' wallets, avoiding the chain of correspondent banks that currently takes two to three days.
(iv) A customer's verified identity credentials will be held by the customer, who can share only the details needed when opening an account with any participating institution.
(v) Users will be able to lend and borrow digital assets with each other through decentralised applications, without a bank acting as intermediary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the blockchain and fintech synergy illustrated by each of the features (i) to (v) and explain how each works.
parts.answer:
(i) Tokenization: a real-world asset (the plaza) is converted into digital tokens on a blockchain, enabling fractional ownership and easier trading, which improves liquidity of an otherwise indivisible property.
(ii) Smart contracts: self-executing contracts written into blockchain code automatically trigger an action, here payment of compensation, once pre-defined conditions (delay over three hours) are confirmed, with no manual claim or enforcement.
(iii) Cross-border payments: blockchain enables direct peer-to-peer transfers across borders, reducing intermediaries and settlement time compared to correspondent banking.
(iv) Identity verification through self-sovereign identity (SSI): individuals control their own verified credentials and share only what is necessary, supporting faster, more secure onboarding across institutions and reducing repeated KYC checks.
(v) Decentralised Finance (DeFi): lending, borrowing and trading services are built on blockchain and run through decentralised applications (dApps) without a bank as intermediary, reducing cost and widening access.
(1 mark for each correct synergy and 1 mark for each explanation applied to QDF, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss the challenges that QDF is likely to face in implementing this platform.
parts.answer:
1. Regulatory uncertainty: laws on cryptocurrencies, DeFi and digital assets such as property tokens are still evolving, so QDF's features may require approvals or change as regulation develops.
2. Security risks at the edges: although the ledger is hard to tamper with, wallets, exchanges and smart-contract code can still be hacked or exploited; a coding error in the insurance smart contract could pay out wrongly.
3. Scalability: many blockchains process far fewer transactions per second than centralised systems, which could create bottlenecks for high volumes of remittances.
4. Integration complexity: connecting the platform with banks' legacy systems, airline data feeds and property registries requires significant effort.
5. Energy consumption: if a Proof of Work blockchain is used, high electricity use and cost would arise.
6. Compliance obligations: QDF must still meet SBP's AML / KYC requirements for its wallet, remittance and lending users, for example by using RegTech name screening and transaction monitoring alongside the platform.
(1 mark for each challenge explained and related to QDF, max 5)

secb.scenario:
The trade-finance unit of Hyderi Bank Limited (HYBL) reviewed the import and export transactions of its customer Lyallpur Fabrics (Private) Limited (LFPL). The review found the following:
(i) LFPL exported grey cloth invoiced at PKR 2,400 per metre, while comparable exports from other customers were invoiced at about PKR 600 per metre.
(ii) Two separate letters of credit at two different banks were supported by invoices for what appears to be the same consignment.
(iii) Payments were received for a shipment for which no shipping line could confirm that any goods had actually been loaded.
The bank's KYC team also notes that LFPL's directors had to submit the same identity documents separately to each of the four banks the company deals with, and that each bank holds only its own fragment of the trade paperwork.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the meaning of trade-based money laundering (TBML) and identify the TBML technique indicated by each of the findings (i) to (iii).
parts.answer:
TBML is the disguising of illicit funds by manipulating trade transactions, so that value is moved under the cover of apparently genuine trade.
(i) Over-invoicing: goods are invoiced at a value far above their true worth (four times the market rate), allowing excess funds to be moved as apparent export proceeds.
(ii) Multiple invoicing: more than one invoice is issued for the same shipment, so payment is obtained more than once for a single consignment.
(iii) Phantom shipment: payment is made for a shipment where no goods actually move.
(2 marks for explaining TBML, 1 mark for each technique correctly identified, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why TBML is difficult to detect using traditional documentation.
parts.answer:
Global trade networks are complex and opaque. Each party, such as the buyer, seller, shipping line, customs and several banks, holds only its own fragment of the paperwork, with no shared, verifiable single source of truth. As in LFPL's case, one bank cannot see that another bank has financed the same consignment, or confirm independently that goods were actually shipped.
(1 mark for complexity / opacity, 1 mark for fragmented records applied to the scenario, max 2)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain how a blockchain-based trade platform and blockchain-based KYC records could help HYBL address the issues identified.
parts.answer:
1. Transparency: a shared ledger among the banks, exporter, shipping lines and customs would give every party visibility of the same shipment and invoice records, so a second invoice for the same consignment (finding ii) would be visible to all banks.
2. Immutability: records are tamper-evident; once an invoice or shipment record is added it cannot be altered, so documents cannot be changed afterwards to cover up discrepancies.
3. End-to-end traceability: the actual movement of goods would be recorded on the ledger at each stage, making phantom shipments (finding iii) and unusual invoice values compared with shipment details (finding i) easier to detect.
4. Smart contracts: payment could be released only once verified shipment milestones (e.g. confirmed loading and customs clearance) are recorded on-chain, removing the opportunity to receive funds for goods never shipped.
5. AML / KYC: verified customer information could be stored securely on a blockchain and shared across the participating banks, so LFPL's directors would not have to resubmit documents to each bank; this reduces repeated identity checks, speeds onboarding and gives all banks a consistent view of the customer.
(1 mark for each point applied to the scenario, max 6, with at least 1 mark available for the KYC point)

secb.topic: Blockchain vs centralised systems: evaluation and challenges
secb.scenario:
Sindh Cooperative Housing Authority (SCHA) maintains ownership records of 40,000 residential plots in a centralised database managed by its own IT department. Several cases have come to light where plot ownership records were altered by an insider, and the change could not be traced. A consultant has recommended moving the ownership records to a blockchain shared between SCHA, the registration office and participating banks that lend against plots.
SCHA's board has asked for an independent view before approving the project. Some board members believe that 'once we are on blockchain, nothing can ever be hacked', while others are worried about cost and about whether the new system can work with SCHA's existing billing and banking interfaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how a blockchain would address the weaknesses of SCHA's current centralised ownership records.
parts.answer:
1. No single point of control: in the centralised database the IT department controls the single copy and an insider can alter it unilaterally. On a blockchain, every node (SCHA, the registration office and the banks) holds a copy, and a change requires network consensus.
2. Immutability through hashing: each block contains the hash of the previous block, so altering a recorded ownership entry would change its hash and break every later link, which all nodes would detect.
3. Traceable history: a transfer of ownership is added as a new transaction rather than overwriting the old record, so the complete history of each plot remains visible and verifiable.
4. Transparency for lenders: banks can verify ownership directly from the shared ledger before lending against a plot, reducing the risk of lending against fraudulent records.
5. Consensus: only transactions validated by the participating nodes are added, preventing unauthorised changes.
(1 mark for each point applied to SCHA, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the view that 'once we are on blockchain, nothing can ever be hacked'.
parts.answer:
The view is overstated. The ledger itself is very hard to tamper with because of hashing, chaining and consensus. However, security risks remain at the edges: wallets or user credentials, interfaces and applications connected to the ledger, and smart-contract code can still be hacked or exploited.
