In addition, blockchain only guarantees that recorded data is not altered afterwards; if incorrect or fraudulent data is entered by an authorised user in the first place, it will be faithfully preserved. SCHA must therefore still enforce access controls and validation of data at the point of entry.
(1 mark for each valid point, max 3)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Discuss the challenges SCHA's board should consider before approving the project.
parts.answer:
1. Integration complexity: connecting the blockchain to SCHA's existing billing system and the banks' legacy systems will require significant effort and cost.
2. Scalability: many blockchains process far fewer transactions per second than centralised systems; SCHA should confirm that the platform can handle its volumes of transfers and enquiries.
3. Energy consumption: a Proof of Work design would require significant computing power and electricity; a permissioned design with a more energy-efficient mechanism would be more appropriate.
4. Regulatory uncertainty: laws on digital records and digital assets are still evolving, so the legal standing of blockchain ownership records should be confirmed.
5. Security at the edges: user access and connected applications must still be secured.
(1 mark for each challenge explained in SCHA's context, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Kitab Mahal Limited (KML) has operated a chain of 22 bookshops across Lahore, Islamabad and Multan for over thirty years. KML's management has always focused on improving its existing operations, for example by upgrading its point-of-sale software and redesigning its store layouts. Over the last three years, however, KML's sales have fallen by 35%.
An internal review has highlighted the following developments in KML's market:
(i) A newly launched online book marketplace uses artificial intelligence to recommend titles and cloud-based systems to process thousands of orders an hour.
(ii) Customers, particularly students, now expect to compare prices on their phones, order at midnight and receive books the next day.
(iii) The marketplace records every search, click and purchase made by its users and uses this information to decide which titles to stock and promote.
(iv) New FBR requirements for real-time integration of retail sales invoices have forced KML's competitors to digitise their billing systems.
(v) Using widespread 4G mobile coverage, the marketplace sells to customers in small towns and to Pakistanis living abroad, markets KML has never been able to reach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'digital disruption'. Also explain why management's past initiatives at KML would NOT be regarded as a response to digital disruption.
parts.answer:
1. Digital disruption occurs when emerging technologies or innovative business models fundamentally alter the value proposition, operations or competitive landscape of an industry. It introduces radical change that redefines how value is created, delivered and consumed. (1 mark)
2. The concept grew out of Clayton Christensen's 1997 idea of 'disruptive innovation', where low-end entrants gradually displaced incumbents; it now describes technology-driven upheaval across whole industries at every market level. (1 mark)
3. KML's initiatives (upgrading point-of-sale software, redesigning store layouts) are incremental improvements: they make the existing bookshop model slightly better but do not change how KML creates or delivers value. (1 mark)
4. The online marketplace, by contrast, has changed the way books are discovered, bought and delivered, so KML is facing radical change rather than a competitor that is merely a little more efficient. Incremental upgrades alone cannot protect KML's position. (1 mark)
(1 mark per well-explained point, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the driver of digital disruption illustrated by each of the developments (i) to (v) above, and briefly explain how each driver is affecting KML's industry.
parts.answer:
(i) Technological Advancements: AI and cloud computing give the marketplace capabilities such as automated recommendations and high-volume real-time order processing that were not previously possible, so it can serve customers at a scale and speed KML's shops cannot match.
(ii) Consumer Expectations: digital-native customers demand faster, more convenient and personalised experiences (price comparison on phones, midnight ordering, next-day delivery), which forces booksellers to keep innovating or lose customers.
(iii) Data Explosion: the marketplace harnesses vast amounts of customer data (searches, clicks, purchases) to make better stocking and promotion decisions, a level of insight KML does not have from its shop sales alone.
(iv) Regulatory Changes: new FBR invoice-integration requirements compel retailers to adopt digital billing simply to remain compliant, pushing the whole industry towards digitisation.
(v) Global Connectivity: the internet and mobile networks allow the marketplace to operate across geographic boundaries, reaching small-town and overseas customers who were previously inaccessible to a shop-based retailer.
(1 mark for each correctly identified driver and 1 mark for each explanation applied to the scenario, max 10)

secb.topic: Impact of disruption on business dimensions
secb.scenario:
Sutlej Dairy Foods Limited (SDFL) is a milk and yoghurt producer based in Sahiwal that sells its products across Punjab. Over the last two years SDFL has carried out a digital transformation programme. The following changes have resulted:
(i) An AI chatbot on SDFL's WhatsApp line now answers most routine queries from retailers about order status and prices, and the call centre has been reduced from 30 to 8 staff.
(ii) SDFL's mobile app remembers each household's usual order and sends personalised reminders and offers before the customer runs out of milk.
(iii) Instead of only selling through shops, SDFL now offers a monthly home-delivery subscription, which has become a new and growing revenue stream.
(iv) IoT temperature sensors in SDFL's chilled vans transmit real-time data, allowing managers to track every consignment and re-route vans when delays occur.
(v) Clerks who previously keyed in retailer orders have been retrained as data analysts and customer relationship officers.
(vi) A start-up with no factory of its own has entered the market by selling milk from independent farmers through an app, at a much lower cost of entry than SDFL faced when it was established.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the dimension of business impact of digital disruption illustrated by each of the changes (i) to (vi), giving a brief justification for each.
parts.answer:
(i) Operational Efficiency: automation and AI have streamlined the handling of routine queries, reducing call-centre cost (from 30 to 8 staff) and improving productivity.
(ii) Customer Experience: data and AI are used to deliver personalised, real-time interactions (remembered orders, reminders, tailored offers), which improves customer satisfaction and retention.
(iii) Business Model Innovation: the subscription model creates an entirely new revenue stream that did not exist under SDFL's traditional shop-based sales model.
(iv) Supply Chain Transformation: IoT data gives SDFL real-time visibility of its chilled distribution and the agility to re-route vans, making the supply chain more efficient.
(v) Workforce Dynamics: automation has shifted employees from repetitive operational tasks (keying orders) towards more strategic roles, which required reskilling and upskilling.
(vi) Competitive Landscape: a digital-first start-up is challenging an established incumbent directly, at a fraction of the traditional cost of entry, because it uses a platform rather than owning production assets.
(1 mark for each correct dimension and 1 mark for each justification linked to the scenario, max 12)
Note: candidates should match the dimension to the business effect described, not to the technology used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: SDFL's chief executive believes that change (vi) is not a serious threat because the start-up 'does not even own a factory'. Comment on this view.
parts.answer:
1. The view is flawed. The start-up is using a platform-based model: it connects independent farmers directly with customers through a digital platform and earns revenue by facilitating that connection, without owning the heavy physical assets itself. (1 mark)
2. Because the physical assets belong to others, such competitors can scale much faster and more cheaply than an asset-heavy incumbent such as SDFL, so not owning a factory is actually a source of competitive strength, not weakness. (1 mark)

secb.scenario:
Hamraaz Home Services (HHS) is a Karachi-based company that has provided electricians, plumbers and air-conditioner technicians to households for fifteen years. HHS directly employs 180 technicians, owns a fleet of 60 service vans and operates a telephone booking centre. Its fixed costs are high and expanding to a new city requires HHS to recruit staff, buy vans and rent premises in that city.
Last year, a mobile app called 'FixKaro' was launched. FixKaro does not employ any technicians and owns no vans. Independent technicians register on the app, customers book jobs through it, and FixKaro keeps 15% of each job's value. FixKaro has already launched in Karachi, Lahore, Rawalpindi and Peshawar, and its ratings system allows customers to choose technicians based on reviews from other users.
HHS's board is considering whether to launch its own app-based service.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the key features of a platform-based business model, with reference to FixKaro.
parts.answer:
1. A platform-based business model does not own the physical assets involved in delivering the service. FixKaro owns neither vans nor employs technicians; these belong to the independent providers. (1 mark)
2. Instead, the company builds a digital platform (the FixKaro app) that connects independent providers (technicians) directly with customers (households). (1 mark)
3. Revenue is earned by facilitating the connection and taking a share of each transaction, here a 15% cut of each job's value, rather than by selling its own labour or products. (1 mark)
4. The platform is a form of business model innovation: it creates a new revenue model that did not exist under the traditional owned-workforce model used by HHS. (1 mark)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the ability of HHS and FixKaro to expand into new cities, explaining why FixKaro has been able to grow faster.
parts.answer:
1. HHS is asset-heavy: each new city requires recruitment of employed technicians, purchase of vans and rental of premises, so expansion is slow, capital-intensive and increases fixed costs. (1 mark)
2. FixKaro is asset-light: because the heavy physical assets (vehicles, tools, labour) belong to independent technicians, entering a new city mainly requires onboarding providers onto an existing app. (1 mark)
3. FixKaro's costs therefore rise mainly with activity on the platform rather than with fixed investment, so it can scale much faster and more cheaply than HHS, as shown by its launch in four cities within one year. (1 mark)
4. Digital-first entrants such as FixKaro can challenge established incumbents at a fraction of the traditional cost of entry, changing the competitive landscape of the home-services industry. (1 mark)
5. Global connectivity (internet and mobile access) allows the app to reach customers wherever there is mobile coverage, without HHS-style physical booking centres. (1 mark)
(1 mark per relevant comparative point, max 5)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A director of FixKaro has told the press that the company 'has permanently won the home-services market'. Discuss this claim in the context of the nature of digital disruption.
parts.answer:
1. Digital disruption is rarely a one-time event. A business that disrupts an industry can itself be disrupted later as new technologies become commercially available. (1 mark)
2. For example, ride-sharing apps disrupted the traditional taxi industry using mobile apps and GPS, yet that same industry is now being disrupted again by AI-driven autonomous ride-hailing (robotaxis). FixKaro could similarly face a newer platform or technology that changes how home services are delivered. (1 mark)
3. Because platform models have low costs of entry, other digital-first competitors (including HHS if it launches its own app with an established brand) can challenge FixKaro quickly. FixKaro must therefore keep innovating; its current position is not permanent. (1 mark)

secb.scenario:
Margalla Mobile Limited (MML) is a mobile network operator with 9 million subscribers across Pakistan. MML's newly appointed Chief Data Officer has presented the following four proposals to the board:
(i) Analyse subscribers' data usage, complaints and social-media feedback to design new bundles aimed at students and freelancers, segments where demand appears unmet.
(ii) Use each subscriber's usage history to offer individually tailored bundle recommendations through the MML app.
(iii) Use real-time network traffic data from cell towers to identify congested sites and schedule engineers' maintenance visits more efficiently.
(iv) Sell anonymised, aggregated footfall data showing movements of people between areas of Rawalpindi to the city development authority to support transport planning.
Some board members have argued that data is 'simply a by-product of operations, looked after by the IT department'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the way in which data is being used as a strategic asset in each of the proposals (i) to (iv), and explain the benefit MML could obtain from each.
parts.answer:
(i) Data-driven innovation: analysing customer preferences and market trends (usage, complaints, social-media feedback) to identify new opportunities. Benefit: MML can launch student and freelancer bundles that match real, unmet demand, increasing revenue and market share.
(ii) Personalisation and customer engagement: understanding individual preferences to deliver personalised recommendations and tailored services. Benefit: higher take-up of bundles, better customer satisfaction and lower churn to competing operators.
(iii) Operational optimisation: identifying inefficiencies and making data-driven decisions using real-time data. Benefit: congestion is addressed faster and engineers' visits are scheduled efficiently, improving network quality and reducing maintenance cost.
(iv) Data monetisation: sharing or selling anonymised data insights as a new revenue stream. Benefit: MML earns additional income from data it already holds; because the data is anonymised and aggregated, individual subscribers are not identified.
(1 mark for each correct use and 1 mark for each benefit applied to MML, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view expressed by some board members that data is 'simply a by-product of operations, looked after by the IT department'.
parts.answer:
1. The view is outdated. IT and data management are no longer purely operational tools; they are strategic assets that drive innovation, decision-making and competitive advantage. (1 mark)
2. The four proposals show that MML's data can create new products, improve customer retention, cut costs and generate new revenue, all of which are strategic, board-level outcomes rather than technical IT matters. (1 mark)
3. Data initiatives deliver value only when they are aligned with business goals; if data is left solely to the IT department, initiatives may not support MML's strategy and opportunities may be missed. (1 mark)
4. Aligning IT and data initiatives with business strategy allows MML to remain agile, optimise operations and deliver value in a rapidly changing telecom market where competitors are also using data. The board should therefore take ownership of data strategy. (1 mark)

secb.topic: IT governance frameworks and best practices
secb.scenario:
Ravi Healthcare Group (RHG) operates five hospitals and twelve diagnostic laboratories in Punjab. The board has recently approved a five-year expansion plan. The IT steering committee has raised the following concerns:
(i) The board wants assurance that the PKR 600 million IT budget planned over the next five years will directly support the expansion strategy and that IT risks are managed at board level.
(ii) The patient appointment and laboratory reporting systems suffer frequent outages, and there is no standard process for logging, escalating and resolving service incidents.
(iii) A major insurance company will only empanel RHG's hospitals if RHG can obtain certification showing how patient data is protected.
(iv) Each hospital has built its own systems over the years, resulting in duplicated applications and databases that cannot share patient records; RHG wants a single, unified design for its business, data, application and technology layers.
Currently, each hospital's administrator decides on IT purchases independently and the success of IT projects is not measured after they go live.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend the most appropriate IT governance framework for addressing each of the concerns (i) to (iv), giving reasons for your recommendation.
parts.answer:
(i) COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology): its primary focus is aligning IT with business goals and managing IT risk, with governance distinguished from management. It suits the board's need to ensure the IT budget supports the expansion strategy and that IT risk is governed at board level.
(ii) ITIL (IT Infrastructure Library): it standardises and optimises IT service delivery and supports continual service improvement, so it provides structured processes for logging, escalating and resolving the outages affecting appointment and laboratory systems.
(iii) ISO/IEC 27001: the international standard for building and maintaining an Information Security Management System (ISMS). Certification against it gives the insurer recognised evidence of how patient data is protected.
(iv) TOGAF (The Open Group Architecture Framework): it designs and aligns enterprise IT architecture across the business, data, application and technology layers with organisational goals, so it suits the need for a unified group-wide architecture replacing duplicated hospital systems.
(1 mark for each correct framework and 1 mark for each justification, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: With reference to the last paragraph of the scenario, recommend FOUR best practices that RHG should adopt to strengthen its IT governance.
parts.answer:
1. Establish clear IT governance structures: define roles, responsibilities and decision-making authority between the central IT function and the hospitals, replacing the current practice of each administrator buying IT independently. (1.5 marks)
2. Align IT with business strategy: require every IT investment, including hospital-level purchases, to be approved against the five-year expansion plan so that spending directly supports long-term goals. (1 mark)
3. Implement risk management processes: continuously assess IT risks such as cybersecurity, patient-data privacy and service availability of clinical systems, and mitigate them. (1 mark)
4. Focus on continuous improvement: set KPIs for each IT initiative (e.g. system uptime, incident resolution time) and measure projects after go-live, regularly reviewing and updating processes as technology and business needs evolve. (1.5 marks)
(Marks as indicated for each best practice applied to RHG, max 5)

secb.topic: Adequacy and improvement of ICT processes
secb.scenario: Chenab Microfinance Bank Limited (CMBL) uses a Loan Origination System (LOS) at its 45 branches to process small business and agricultural loans. The internal audit department has carried out a review of the ICT processes supporting the LOS. Extracts from its findings are given below:

tables.caption: Internal audit findings - Loan Origination System
rows: Average loan approval time is 6 working days against a management target of 2 days.
Loan application forms are printed at branches, couriered to head office and re-keyed into the LOS.
Security patches for the LOS database server are four months overdue.
Credit officers at several branches use a single shared supervisor login to approve loans.
A survey shows only 38% of branch staff are satisfied with the LOS; many say screens are confusing.
Branch staff maintain parallel Excel records of loans because they do not trust LOS reports.
The latest SBP inspection report contains observations on IT access management that remain open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess the adequacy of CMBL's ICT processes supporting the LOS, using the three dimensions normally used for such an assessment.
parts.answer:
1. Process Efficiency: this asks whether ICT processes are fast, cost-effective and resource-efficient. Loan approval takes 6 working days against a 2-day target, and printing and re-keying forms at head office adds manual effort and cost. The process is inefficient. (2 marks)
2. Security and Compliance: this asks whether ICT processes meet security standards and regulatory requirements such as SBP's IT risk framework. Security patches are four months overdue, credit officers share one supervisor login to approve loans, and the regulator's inspection raised observations. The process is not adequate from a security and compliance perspective. (2 marks)
3. User Satisfaction: this asks whether the people who rely on the system day to day find it usable, reliable and fit for purpose. Only 38% of branch staff are satisfied, and staff maintain parallel Excel records, indicating they do not trust or find the LOS fit for purpose. (2 marks)
Conclusion: the ICT processes are inadequate on all three dimensions and require improvement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend appropriate improvements for the weaknesses identified, clearly linking each improvement to the relevant finding(s).
parts.answer:
1. Automation: replace printing and re-keying of loan forms with automated electronic workflow from branch to head office. This reduces manual work, improves accuracy and helps bring approval time towards the 2-day target (findings 1 and 2). (2 marks)
2. Enhanced security controls: apply the overdue security patches and introduce regular patching; withdraw the shared supervisor login and issue individual user IDs with access rights matching each officer's role (findings 3 and 4). (2 marks)
3. Targeted training: train branch staff on LOS features and correct procedures so that they can rely on the system rather than maintaining parallel Excel records, which should also improve user satisfaction (findings 5 and 6). (1.5 marks)
4. Regular audits and monitoring: carry out periodic reviews of LOS processing times, access rights and patch status, and track the remediation of SBP inspection observations until closed, so that weaknesses are detected early in future (findings 3, 4 and 7). (1.5 marks)
(Marks as indicated for each improvement clearly linked to findings, max 7)

secb.scenario:
Kohat Cement Limited (KCL) is evaluating a proposal to implement a cloud-based analytics and plant-monitoring platform at a total investment of PKR 45 million, payable at the start of the project. The finance team has estimated the following annual benefits:
- Reduction in fuel and power costs from better kiln monitoring: PKR 9 million per year
- Reduction in unplanned maintenance downtime: PKR 5 million per year
- Reduction in manual reporting effort: PKR 2 million per year
In addition, the platform is expected to enable KCL to offer real-time order tracking to its large construction customers, which management believes will strengthen customer relationships, although this has not been quantified.
One board member has stated: 'I will only approve the project if it pays back all PKR 45 million within the first year. Once it is approved, there is no need to look at it again.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the costs and benefits that KCL should include in a cost-benefit analysis of the proposed platform, with reference to the scenario.
parts.answer:
1. Costs: the cost-benefit analysis should include all costs of implementing the platform, i.e. the PKR 45 million investment in hardware and software, plus related costs such as staff training. (1 mark)
2. Financial benefits: increased efficiency and reduced operational costs, i.e. the estimated savings in fuel and power from better kiln monitoring and the savings from reduced unplanned maintenance downtime. (1 mark)
3. Productivity gains and strategic value: the time and resources saved through reduced manual reporting effort, and the longer-term strategic value of real-time order tracking for large construction customers, which should be weighed even though it has not been quantified. (1 mark)
(1 mark per relevant category applied to KCL, max 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Critically evaluate the board member's statement.
parts.answer:
1. Requiring full payback within one year is too narrow. Not every valuable ICT investment shows an immediate financial return; some strategic investments build competitive advantage over time rather than an instant payback. (1 mark)
2. KCL's estimated benefits arise year after year rather than all at once, so a test requiring the full PKR 45 million to be recovered within the first year could lead KCL to reject a worthwhile investment. (1 mark)
3. The evaluation should use cost-benefit analysis including productivity gains, such as reduced manual reporting effort and less unplanned downtime, which free staff and plant capacity. (1 mark)
4. Longer-term strategic value must also be weighed, e.g. real-time order tracking that may strengthen relationships with large construction customers and improve competitiveness, even though it is difficult to quantify. (1 mark)
5. The second part of the statement is also wrong: ROI should be continuously monitored and reassessed rather than evaluated once and forgotten. Actual benefits may differ from estimates, and KCL may need to upgrade outdated technology or reallocate resources as circumstances change. (2 marks)
(Marks as indicated, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Recommend how KCL should monitor the investment after the platform goes live.
parts.answer:
1. Set measurable KPIs at approval stage for each expected benefit, e.g. fuel and power cost per tonne, hours of unplanned downtime and staff hours spent on reporting. (1 mark)
2. Periodically compare actual results against the annual benefits estimated in the business case (fuel and power, downtime and reporting effort) and report variances to the board. (1 mark)
3. Track the non-financial, strategic benefits too, e.g. customer feedback and repeat orders from construction customers using real-time order tracking. (1 mark)
4. Use the results to take action: if benefits fall short, investigate causes, upgrade or reconfigure the technology, or reallocate resources, as part of continuous reassessment of the investment. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Digital disruption and the accounting profession
secb.scenario:
Pak Fabrics Group (PFG) is a textile group with five subsidiaries. Its group finance department of 40 accountants currently spends most of its time on manual work. The CFO has announced the following initiatives for the next two years:
(i) Software 'bots' and optical character recognition will read supplier invoices received by email, post them to the ledger and perform daily bank reconciliations.
(ii) All subsidiaries will move to a single cloud-based ERP, giving the CFO a dashboard of cash, sales and costs that updates continuously instead of a monthly management pack prepared on spreadsheets.
(iii) PFG and its major cotton suppliers will record purchase transactions on a shared blockchain ledger that external auditors can access directly.
(iv) A RegTech tool will continuously scan contracts and export documents to check compliance with tax and export regulations, replacing a quarterly manual review.
(v) Accountants will build predictive models in Power BI to forecast cotton prices and advise the board on purchasing and pricing decisions.
Several accountants have expressed concern that 'there will be nothing left for accountants to do'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the initiatives (i) to (v), identify the impact of digital disruption on the accounting and finance profession that it represents, and explain the benefit PFG is likely to obtain.
parts.answer:
(i) Automation of routine tasks: RPA and OCR automate repetitive work such as data entry, ledger posting and bank reconciliations. Benefit: faster processing, fewer human errors, and staff time released for judgement-based work.
(ii) Real-time financial reporting: cloud computing and big data move reporting from periodic to real time. Benefit: the CFO can see cash and performance continuously and adjust budgets within hours of a market change, instead of waiting weeks for a monthly spreadsheet pack.
(iii) Compliance and audit enhancement (blockchain): blockchain creates immutable, independently verifiable records. Benefit: auditors can verify purchase transactions in seconds rather than tracing paper trails over weeks, and the risk of altered records is reduced.
(iv) Compliance and audit enhancement (RegTech): RegTech scans very large volumes of documents continuously. Benefit: compliance breaches are identified promptly instead of waiting for a labour-intensive quarterly manual review.
(v) Strategic advisory role: analytics and predictive modelling allow accountants to guide business decisions rather than simply reporting what has already happened. Benefit: better-informed purchasing and pricing decisions in a volatile cotton market.
(1 mark for each correct impact and 1 mark for each benefit applied to PFG, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Respond to the accountants' concern, explaining how their role and the skills required of them are likely to change.
parts.answer:
1. The concern is understandable but misplaced: digital disruption is turning accountants into strategic advisors who use real-time data and predictive tools to guide decisions, ensure compliance and manage risk, rather than eliminating their role. (1 mark)
2. Workforce dynamics: as bots take over routine posting and reconciliations, accountants shift from operational, repetitive tasks towards analysis, interpretation and advisory work, e.g. the cotton price forecasting in initiative (v). (1 mark)
3. Skill transformation: the expected skill set has moved over time from arithmetic, to ledgers and calculators, to Excel by the 2000s, and now to comfort with AI, blockchain and analytics tools. PFG's accountants will need skills in tools such as Power BI, working with cloud ERP data and understanding blockchain-based records. (1 mark)
4. This mirrors the profession's adaptation to computers in the 1960s, but the pace is much faster, so continuous, lifelong learning is essential rather than optional. (1 mark)
5. PFG should therefore invest in upskilling and reskilling its finance team through structured training so that staff can move into the new roles. (1 mark)

secb.scenario:
Saffron Asset Management Limited (SAML) is an SECP-licensed asset management company that manages mutual funds for over 200,000 investors. SAML plans to launch an online investment portal and a mobile app over the next year. At a recent board meeting, the directors raised the following concerns about SAML's IT environment:
(i) The server room at the Karachi head office has no access log, and last year a contractor was found inside it unaccompanied.
(ii) Unit prices of funds were published incorrectly on two occasions because figures had been changed in the valuation database without any record of who changed them.
(iii) Investors complained that they could not redeem units for most of a working day when the investor services system stopped responding.
(iv) Several staff received emails containing malicious attachments, and one employee's laptop was infected.
(v) The SECP has issued new cybersecurity guidelines, and SAML has not yet assessed whether its IT practices comply.
The chief executive has commented that IT risk management 'is a cost of doing business that adds no strategic value'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the terms 'risk' and 'risk management', and list the stages of the risk management process.
parts.answer:
1. Risk is the possibility of an event or condition that could lead to harm, loss or disruption. It is assessed in terms of two dimensions: probability (how likely the event is) and impact (how much harm it would cause). (1 mark)
2. Risk management is a systematic process of identifying, assessing and controlling risks to minimise their potential negative impact on an organisation, with the goal of ensuring business continuity, protecting assets and maintaining operational resilience. (1 mark)
3. Its stages are: Risk Identification, Risk Assessment, Risk Mitigation (treatment), and Monitoring and Review. (1 mark)

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each of the concerns (i) to (v), identify the objective of IT risk management that is NOT being achieved, giving a brief explanation.
parts.answer:
(i) Protect IT infrastructure: hardware, software and networks must be protected from physical damage, technical failure and unauthorised access; an unlogged server room entered by an unaccompanied contractor shows infrastructure is not protected.
(ii) Ensure data integrity: data must remain accurate, consistent and trustworthy throughout its lifecycle; untracked changes to valuation data produced incorrect unit prices.
(iii) Maintain system availability: IT systems must be accessible without interruption for operations and customers; investors could not redeem units for most of a day.
(iv) Mitigate cybersecurity threats: the organisation must defend against malware, phishing and similar threats; malicious attachments reached staff and infected a laptop.
(v) Support regulatory compliance: IT practices must be aligned with legal and industry standards; SAML has not assessed compliance with the SECP's new guidelines.
(1 mark per objective correctly identified and explained, max 5)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the chief executive's comment, explaining the strategic importance of IT risk management to SAML.
parts.answer:
The comment is incorrect; IT risk management has strategic value in several ways:
1. Supporting digital transformation: the new portal and app can be launched safely only if vulnerabilities are identified early, so innovation does not come at the cost of undue exposure. (1 mark)
2. Enabling business continuity: effective risk management keeps operations, such as unit redemptions, running through cyberattacks or system failures, protecting revenue and investor trust. (1 mark)
3. Fostering trust and compliance: aligning IT practices with the SECP guidelines and data-protection requirements builds stakeholder trust and reduces legal and regulatory exposure. (1 mark)
4. Enhancing agility and resilience: proactive risk management helps SAML adapt quickly to market shifts and recover faster when incidents occur. (1 mark)
5. Driving competitive advantage: an asset manager that can demonstrate strong management of IT risk attracts investors and partners who prioritise data protection and stability. (1 mark)
(1 mark per point applied to SAML, max 5)

secb.topic: Risk identification, assessment and the risk matrix
secb.scenario:
Sabz Bazaar (Private) Limited (SBL) operates an online grocery platform in Lahore and Islamabad. SBL has never carried out a formal IT risk exercise. The newly appointed risk manager plans to identify and assess the company's IT risks before the platform is expanded to Karachi.
SBL's board has set an IT risk appetite of PKR 12 million of potential loss per year for any single risk. The risk manager has prepared the following preliminary list of risks:

tables.caption: Preliminary IT risk list
rows: Attack on the payment page exposing customers' card data
Delivery riders' app crashing for short periods
Flooding of the single data centre in Lahore
Fault in the printer driver used for warehouse picking slips

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend THREE techniques that SBL's risk manager could use to identify IT risks, explaining how each would be applied at SBL.
parts.answer:
1. Risk workshops: bring together cross-functional teams such as IT, finance, warehouse operations, customer service and HR, so that each contributes its own perspective on what could go wrong with the platform and its expansion. (2 marks)
2. Threat modelling: create hypothetical models of how an attacker might exploit SBL's systems, e.g. how card data or customer accounts on the platform could be targeted, to find weaknesses before they are exploited. (2 marks)
3. Historical incident analysis: review SBL's past incidents (outages, complaints, security events) and incidents at other online retailers in the industry to spot recurring risks. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each technique and 1 mark for its application to SBL)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the three phases through which SBL's risk assessment should proceed.
parts.answer:
1. Risk Analysis: examine the nature and source of each identified risk and the existing controls over it, and estimate its likelihood and impact, ideally using a structured framework such as NIST SP 800-30 or ISO 31000. (1 mark)
2. Risk Evaluation: compare the analysed risk against SBL's risk appetite (PKR 12 million per risk) and any compliance requirements. (1 mark)
3. Decision Phase: decide whether each risk should be mitigated, transferred, accepted or monitored (or avoided if it is too severe). (1 mark)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using a risk matrix approach and the board's risk appetite, prioritise risks R1 to R4 and state whether each risk requires active treatment or may be accepted/monitored.
parts.answer:
A risk matrix combines probability and impact: high-probability, high-impact risks are critical and demand immediate action, while low-probability, low-impact risks can be monitored or accepted.
1. R1 (payment page attack): high probability and high impact (PKR 40 million), well above the PKR 12 million appetite. Highest priority; requires immediate treatment (mitigation). (1.5 marks)
2. R3 (data centre flood): low probability but high impact (PKR 30 million), exceeding appetite. Second priority; requires treatment, e.g. mitigation through a disaster recovery site/offsite backups or transfer through insurance. (1.5 marks)
3. R2 (delivery app crashes): high probability but low impact (PKR 3 million), within appetite. May be accepted and monitored, with documentation and periodic review. (1 mark)
4. R4 (printer driver fault): low probability and low impact (PKR 0.5 million), well within appetite. Lowest priority; accept and monitor. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Risk treatment strategies and risk appetite
secb.scenario:
Indus Pharma Distributors Limited (IPDL) distributes medicines to pharmacies across Sindh and Balochistan. IPDL's board has defined a risk appetite of PKR 5 million of expected annual loss for any single IT risk. The IT risk committee has made the following decisions during the year:
(i) After a penetration test found that IPDL's online ordering portal was vulnerable to SQL injection, a web application firewall was installed and the portal's code was corrected.
(ii) IPDL purchased a cyber insurance policy covering losses up to PKR 50 million arising from data breaches.
(iii) A proposal to let pharmacies pay through a new, unregulated digital-token scheme was rejected because no controls could bring its regulatory and fraud risk within tolerance.
(iv) Occasional formatting glitches in an internal staff-canteen ordering tool, with an estimated annual loss of PKR 20,000, were documented and will be reviewed annually rather than fixed.
(v) IPDL's only warehouse management server has no backup power. The estimated annual loss from power cuts is PKR 9 million. The committee has documented this risk and decided to 'live with it' because a UPS and generator would cost PKR 2 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the risk treatment strategy adopted in each of the decisions (i) to (v).
parts.answer:
(i) Mitigation (reduction): controls (web application firewall and code fixes) were applied to reduce the likelihood of exploitation.
(ii) Transfer: the financial consequence of a data breach has been shifted to an insurer.
(iii) Avoidance: IPDL decided not to undertake the activity at all because no feasible mitigation could bring the risk within tolerance.
(iv) Acceptance: a low-impact, low-likelihood risk is documented and periodically reviewed because the cost of fixing it outweighs the benefit.
(v) Acceptance: the committee has chosen to document the risk and live with it.
(1 mark per correctly identified strategy, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether each decision is consistent with IPDL's risk appetite and recommend any changes needed.
parts.answer:
1. Decisions (i) and (iii) are consistent: a serious vulnerability above appetite was reduced through controls, and a risk that could not be reduced to tolerance was avoided. (1 mark)
2. Decision (ii) is consistent for the financial consequence of a breach, which cannot be reduced to zero by technical controls alone. (1 mark)
3. Decision (iv) is consistent: an expected loss of PKR 20,000 is far below the PKR 5 million appetite and fixing the tool would cost more than the risk itself. (1 mark)
4. Decision (v) is NOT consistent: an expected loss of PKR 9 million exceeds the PKR 5 million appetite, so acceptance is not appropriate. Acceptance is meant for risks within appetite where mitigation costs outweigh benefits; here the mitigation cost (PKR 2 million) is well below the expected loss. (2 marks)
5. Recommendation: IPDL should mitigate risk (v) by installing a UPS and backup generator (regularly tested), bringing the risk within appetite. (1 mark)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A committee member has suggested that the cyber insurance in decision (ii) means IPDL no longer needs to invest in security controls over customer data. Discuss this suggestion.
parts.answer:
1. Transfer shifts only the financial consequence of a breach to the insurer; it does not reduce the likelihood of a breach occurring. (1 mark)
2. Insurance will not restore system availability, recover customer trust or prevent reputational damage and regulatory consequences after a breach, and losses above the PKR 50 million limit remain with IPDL. (1 mark)
3. Transfer should therefore be used alongside mitigation controls (encryption, access controls, network segmentation) that keep the risk within appetite, not as a replacement for them. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Risk monitoring, incident response planning and documentation
secb.scenario:
Kohinoor Takaful Limited (KTL) is a takaful operator regulated by the SECP. Following a security incident in which a hacker accessed a server holding participants' policy details, an internal review identified the following:
(i) Security logs from KTL's firewalls, servers and applications are stored separately on each device and are only examined after a problem is reported.
(ii) The last security audit and vulnerability assessment were carried out three years ago, although KTL has since moved several systems to new servers.
(iii) The help-desk officer who first noticed the suspicious activity did not know whether it was serious or whom to inform, and the matter reached the IT head only two days later.
(iv) Affected participants and the regulator were informed late and inconsistently, because nobody knew who was responsible for notifications.
(v) After the server was restored, no investigation was carried out into how the hacker gained access.
(vi) KTL's list of IT risks is an old spreadsheet that does not show which risks have been treated, and there is no formal record of the incident itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend appropriate tools or approaches that KTL should use to improve its risk monitoring, with reference to findings (i) and (ii).
parts.answer:
1. SIEM (Security Information and Event Management): aggregate and analyse security data from firewalls, servers and applications across the network in real time, so suspicious activity is detected automatically rather than only after a problem is reported (finding i). (1.5 marks)
2. Real-time monitoring tools: deploy intrusion detection systems (IDS), firewalls and endpoint detection and response (EDR) to track behaviour for anomalies continuously (finding i). (1 mark)
3. Audits and assessments: carry out regular security audits to confirm compliance, and regular vulnerability assessments to catch new weaknesses as infrastructure changes, particularly after the move to new servers (finding ii). (1.5 marks)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the three core components of an Incident Response Plan, relating each to the weaknesses identified in findings (iii) to (v).
parts.answer:
1. Incident classification: the plan should define severity levels and escalation steps. This would have told the help-desk officer how serious the activity was and to escalate it immediately to the IT head, avoiding the two-day delay (finding iii). (2 marks)
2. Communication protocols: the plan should define who notifies employees, customers and regulators, and how. Clear responsibility would have ensured that participants and the SECP were informed promptly and consistently (finding iv). (2 marks)
3. Post-incident review: after recovery, a root-cause analysis and lessons-learned exercise must be performed. This would identify how the hacker gained access so that the weakness can be closed and a repeat prevented (finding v). (2 marks)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how KTL should improve its reporting and documentation of IT risks, with reference to finding (vi).
parts.answer:
1. Risk register: maintain a current risk register that tracks each identified risk, its assessment (probability and impact) and its mitigation status, replacing the outdated spreadsheet. (1.5 marks)
2. Incident reports: prepare a formal report for every incident, including this breach, recording what happened, the response and the outcome. (1 mark)
3. Compliance records: keep records evidencing adherence to standards such as ISO 27001 and to SECP requirements. (1 mark)
4. Such documentation supports transparency, internal and external audit, regulatory compliance and continuous improvement of KTL's risk management. (0.5 mark)

secb.scenario:
Faisalabad Weaving Mills Limited (FWML) is a large textile exporter. Its IT manager has reported the following incidents to the audit committee for the year:
(i) During monsoon rains, water entered the basement server room and damaged two servers.
(ii) A laptop containing export pricing data was stolen from a sales manager's car.
(iii) Ransomware encrypted files on the design department's file server after exploiting a software flaw for which no patch was yet available.
(iv) A network administrator accidentally opened a firewall port to the internet while making a routine change.
(v) A storekeeper who had been refused a promotion used his authorised access to delete stock-movement records.
(vi) A nationwide breakdown of the electricity grid stopped production systems for several hours.
(vii) FWML's cloud-based payroll provider suffered a 24-hour outage on salary day, delaying payment to 4,000 workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the incidents (i) to (vii) into the appropriate category of IT risk, giving a brief reason.
parts.answer:
(i) Physical risk (natural disaster): flooding damaged tangible IT infrastructure (servers).
(ii) Physical risk (theft): tangible hardware was removed without authorisation.
(iii) Digital risk (malware/ransomware, zero-day exploit): software was exploited before a patch existed.
(iv) Human risk (negligence): an accidental mistake by an employee misconfigured the firewall.
(v) Human risk (malicious insider): an authorised user deliberately misused his access.
(vi) Environmental risk (power grid failure): an external factor beyond FWML's direct control affected IT operations.
(vii) Third-party risk (service interruption): an outside vendor's outage disrupted FWML's own operations.
(1 mark per correct classification with reason, max 7)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend one appropriate mitigation for each of the incidents (i) to (vii).
parts.answer:
(i) Prepare a Disaster Recovery Plan with offsite backups and a DR site in a second city; relocate servers out of the flood-prone basement.
(ii) Provide secure storage arrangements for portable devices and encrypt laptop data so that a stolen device does not expose pricing data.
(iii) Deploy antivirus/EDR and intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS), apply timely patch management once patches are released, and maintain regular backups for restoration.
(iv) Use change checklists and dual approval for sensitive actions such as firewall changes, supported by security awareness training.
(v) Apply role-based access control and least privilege, monitor behaviour with User and Entity Behaviour Analytics (UEBA), and follow exit procedures promptly when staff leave.
(vi) Install UPS systems and backup generators, tested regularly.
(vii) Agree contractual safeguards (SLAs) with the payroll provider, assess the vendor periodically and arrange redundancy (an alternative provider or fallback process) where feasible.
(1 mark per relevant mitigation, max 7)

secb.scenario:
Ravi Securities Limited (RSL) is a stock brokerage company with 120 staff in Lahore and Karachi. RSL's external auditors have reported the following weaknesses in access to its trading and back-office systems:
(i) Access rights are set up individually for each user on request from line managers, so staff in the same job often have very different rights.
(ii) Employees who move between departments keep their old access rights; a dealer who moved from the settlements department can still approve payments to clients.
(iii) Staff, including those working from home, log in with a password only. Two staff passwords were recently captured through a fake login page.
(iv) The database administrator uses a permanent 'admin' account with unrestricted rights; its activities are not recorded and the password has not changed for two years.
RSL's systems also treat any device connected to the office network as trusted, without further checks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the weaknesses (i) to (iv), recommend the most appropriate access control measure, explaining how it would address the weakness.
parts.answer:
(i) Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): access rights should be assigned according to a user's role rather than individually. Defining standard rights for each job ensures consistency and makes rights easier to review. (2 marks)
(ii) Principle of least privilege: users should be restricted to only the access necessary for their current role. When the dealer moved, his settlements rights should have been removed; rights should be reviewed whenever staff transfer, reducing the attack surface and fraud risk. (2 marks)
(iii) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): identity should be verified through more than one factor, e.g. password plus OTP token or biometric, so a captured password alone is not enough to log in. (2 marks)
(iv) Privileged Access Management (PAM): admin credentials should be held in a vault, sessions recorded and commands filtered, with admin access granted just-in-time and expiring automatically, rather than a permanent unmonitored account. (2 marks)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a Zero Trust Architecture would differ from RSL's current approach to devices on its network, and the benefit it would bring.
parts.answer:
1. RSL currently trusts any device once it is on the office network. Zero Trust assumes no user or device is automatically trustworthy, even inside the network perimeter. (1 mark)
2. Under Zero Trust, every access request is continuously authenticated and verified, regardless of where it originates, including from remote staff. (1 mark)
3. The network is micro-segmented, so access to one part of the network does not give access to everything. (1 mark)
4. Benefit: if an attacker compromises one device or account (e.g. using a captured password), the reach of the breach is limited and further access attempts are challenged. (1 mark)

secb.scenario:
Noor Diagnostic Laboratories (NDL) operates 30 collection centres across Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. NDL is reviewing the protection of its data and has identified the following needs:
(i) Patients' test results stored on NDL's servers and in nightly backup files held with a cloud provider must remain unreadable if the files are stolen.
(ii) Patients log in to NDL's website to download their reports and must be confident that they are connected to NDL's genuine site and that their data cannot be read while it travels over the internet.
(iii) Pathologists approve reports electronically, and doctors receiving the reports by email need assurance that each report was approved by the named pathologist and has not been altered.
NDL's IT officer has suggested using 'one password-protected key for everything' to keep things simple.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
parts.answer:
1. Encryption converts data into an unreadable format that can be read only with the correct key, protecting confidentiality and integrity at rest and in transit. (0.5 mark)
2. Symmetric encryption (e.g. AES-256) uses one key both to encrypt and to decrypt. It is fast and efficient and is typically used for data at rest, such as files stored on servers or in the cloud. (1.5 marks)
3. Asymmetric encryption, as used in Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), uses a pair of keys: a public key to encrypt and a private key, held only by the recipient, to decrypt. PKI adds digital certificates to prove identity. (1.5 marks)
4. It is typically used for data in transit: secure websites (HTTPS), email and digital signatures. (0.5 mark)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend the most appropriate type of encryption for each of NDL's needs (i) to (iii), with justification.
parts.answer:
(i) Symmetric encryption (AES-256): the stored results and backup files are data at rest; AES-256 is fast and efficient for large volumes of stored data, so stolen files would be unreadable without the key. (2 marks)
(ii) Asymmetric encryption/PKI (HTTPS): this is data in transit over the internet. NDL's website should use a digital certificate so patients' browsers can confirm the site is genuinely NDL's (the padlock icon), and data travelling between patient and site is encrypted. (2 marks)
(iii) Asymmetric encryption/PKI digital signatures: PKI supports digital signatures on documents to prove they have not been changed, and its digital certificates prove identity, so doctors can confirm that each report was approved by the named pathologist and has not been altered. (2 marks)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the IT officer's suggestion.
parts.answer:
1. A single shared key would mean that anyone who obtains it could decrypt all of NDL's data at rest and in transit, creating a single point of failure. (1 mark)
2. A single symmetric key cannot meet needs (ii) and (iii): proving the identity of NDL's website and of each individual pathologist requires key pairs and digital certificates under PKI, where the private key is held only by its owner. (1 mark)
3. NDL should therefore use AES-256 for stored data and PKI for data in transit and signatures, with keys properly protected. The suggestion should be rejected. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Incident response steps and advanced security technologies
secb.scenario:
Multan Agro Chemicals Limited (MACL) distributes fertilisers and pesticides to dealers across southern Punjab. On a Friday night, ransomware entered MACL's network through an infected email attachment opened by an accounts clerk. By Saturday morning, the ERP file server and two branch servers had been encrypted and a ransom demand appeared on their screens.
MACL had no documented incident response plan. The IT team learnt of the attack only when staff arrived on Saturday. Different staff members restarted and reconnected servers on their own initiative, which spread the infection further. The most recent backups were stored on a drive permanently connected to the ERP server and were also encrypted. MACL's IT team reviews system logs manually once a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the actions MACL should have taken at each of the six steps of an Incident Response Plan.
parts.answer:
1. Preparation: before any incident, MACL should have had a trained incident response team, defined roles, the necessary tools and clean backups held offline/offsite, so that they would not be encrypted with the live servers. (2 marks)
2. Detection: the attack should have been spotted early, e.g. through SIEM or endpoint alerts on unusual file-encryption activity, rather than when staff arrived the next morning. (2 marks)
3. Analysis: the team should determine what has happened and how serious it is: which ransomware, how it entered (the email attachment), and which servers and data are affected. (2 marks)
4. Containment: affected servers and the clerk's computer should be isolated from the network immediately and compromised credentials revoked to stop the spread. Staff should not reconnect servers on their own initiative, as happened at MACL. (2 marks)
5. Eradication: the ransomware should be fully removed from all affected machines and the exploited weakness closed, e.g. patching and strengthening email filtering. (2 marks)
6. Recovery: systems should be restored from clean backups, data integrity validated, and normal operations resumed in a controlled way, followed by a post-incident review of root cause and lessons learned. (2 marks)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how SIEM and AI/machine-learning-based security tools could have reduced the impact of this attack.
parts.answer:
1. SIEM aggregates and correlates security logs across the whole organisation in real time and issues alerts. It would have replaced MACL's monthly manual log review and alerted the team to the attack on Friday night. (1.5 marks)
2. AI/ML tools analyse large volumes of data in real time and learn normal behavioural patterns rather than relying on static rules. They could flag the abnormal behaviour of the clerk's account and the mass encryption of files as anomalies, allowing faster detection and response and limiting the spread. (1.5 marks)

secb.topic: CIA triad and why cybersecurity matters
secb.scenario:
SehatLink (Private) Limited (SLPL) is an Islamabad-based telemedicine company. Patients book video consultations with doctors through SLPL's app, upload their medical reports and pay online. Doctors issue electronic prescriptions that partner pharmacies use to dispense medicines. SLPL's 60 staff mostly work remotely and all its systems are hosted in the cloud.
At a board meeting, a director remarked: 'Cybersecurity is a technical matter for the IT team. Nobody would bother attacking a small company like ours.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain each element of the CIA triad, illustrating each with an example from SLPL's operations.
parts.answer:
1. Confidentiality: only authorised people can access data. At SLPL, patients' medical reports and consultation records should be visible only to the patient and the treating doctor/authorised staff. (2 marks)
2. Integrity: data is accurate and has not been tampered with. Electronic prescriptions must not be altered without authorisation, e.g. a changed dosage could harm a patient when the pharmacy dispenses it. (2 marks)
3. Availability: systems are accessible when needed by authorised users. The app must be available when patients need urgent consultations and when pharmacies need to verify prescriptions. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each explanation and 1 mark for each relevant SLPL example)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the director's remark, explaining why cybersecurity is now regarded as a top-tier organisational risk.
parts.answer:
The remark is incorrect; cybersecurity ranks alongside financial, operational and reputational risk because of:
1. Increased dependence on technology: SLPL's whole business runs on its app and cloud systems, so a breach could halt core business functions instantly. (1 mark)
2. Sophistication of threat actors: cybercriminals, state-sponsored hackers and insiders use AI-driven malware, ransomware and social engineering, and do not target only large companies. (1 mark)
3. Sensitive data everywhere: SLPL holds medical and payment data, which makes it a prime target regardless of its size. (1 mark)
4. Remote work and cloud use: SLPL's remote staff and cloud hosting significantly expand its attack surface. It is a board-level risk, not only an IT matter. (1 mark)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the potential consequences for SLPL of a successful cyber attack.
parts.answer:
1. Financial loss: theft of funds, ransom payments, and lost revenue during downtime when consultations cannot be booked. (1 mark)
2. Reputational damage: patients and doctors may lose trust in a telemedicine provider that cannot protect medical data, and move to competitors. (1 mark)
3. Regulatory penalties: if SLPL is found not to comply with the laws and regulations that apply to it, such as data-protection requirements for patient data, it may face fines or legal action. (1 mark)
4. Operational disruption: if systems are unavailable, consultations, prescriptions and pharmacy dispensing would stop, possibly affecting patient care. (1 mark)

secb.scenario:
Qadri Engineering Consultants (QEC) is a Lahore-based firm of 150 engineers. Following complaints of slow computers, QEC appointed an IT security firm to examine its network. The security firm reported the following findings:
(i) Several computers constantly displayed pop-up advertisements, some of which redirected users to suspicious websites.
(ii) A program hidden on the finance manager's laptop had been recording passwords and banking details and sending them to an external server.
(iii) An engineer had downloaded a 'free drawing converter' which, while appearing to work normally, had opened a backdoor allowing an outsider to access the network.
(iv) A malicious program had copied itself from one computer to another across the network without any user opening a file.
(v) Malicious code was attached to a legitimate project-costing spreadsheet template and spread to other files whenever the template was used.
(vi) Staff saw messages claiming 'Your PC is infected with 47 viruses - buy CleanPro now for PKR 4,999'.
(vii) The files of the drawings department were encrypted and a message demanded payment in cryptocurrency for the decryption key.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of malware illustrated in each of the findings (i) to (vii), giving a brief reason.
parts.answer:
(i) Adware: floods users with unwanted advertisements, sometimes leading to malicious sites.
(ii) Spyware: covertly collects personal data such as credentials and financial information.
(iii) Trojan horse: malware disguised as legitimate software that creates a backdoor for unauthorised access.
(iv) Worm: self-replicating malware that spreads across networks without user action.
(v) Virus: malicious code attached to legitimate software/files, spreading and corrupting files when the host is used.
(vi) Scareware: tricks users into believing their system is infected in order to sell fake software or services.
(vii) Ransomware: encrypts the victim's data and demands payment for the decryption key.
(1 mark per correct identification with reason, max 7)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend a layered set of cybersecurity defences that QEC should implement to protect against such threats in future.
parts.answer:
1. Preventive measures: strong authentication (MFA) so captured passwords alone cannot be used; encryption of data at rest and in transit (e.g. AES-256); and next-generation firewalls with deep packet inspection to control network traffic. (1.5 marks)
2. Detection and monitoring: up-to-date antivirus, intrusion detection systems and a SIEM to detect abnormal activity (e.g. data being sent to an external server, or a worm spreading) in real time. (1.5 marks)
3. Incident response: a rehearsed plan to contain, investigate and recover from attacks, including restoring the encrypted drawings from clean backups and a post-incident review. (1 mark)
4. Automation: automated vulnerability scanning and patch management to close weaknesses quickly and reduce human error. (1 mark)
5. User education: train engineers not to download unapproved software and to recognise suspicious pop-ups and messages. (1 mark)
(Marks as indicated, max 6)

secb.scenario:
Khyber Commercial Bank Limited (KCBL) has completed a fraud and security investigation which identified the following:
(i) A programmer amended the profit-calculation routine so that fractions of a paisa on every depositor's monthly profit were rounded down and credited to an account opened in a relative's name. Over two years, the account accumulated PKR 3.8 million.
(ii) A payroll officer increased the overtime hours of three colleagues in the input file before it was processed, in exchange for a share of the extra payment.
(iii) The treasury department received an email apparently from 'ceo@khybercommerciaI.com.pk' instructing an urgent transfer to a new supplier. On close inspection, the lowercase letter 'l' in the domain had been replaced with an uppercase 'I'.
(iv) A contractor's code was found in the core banking system that would have deleted customer loan records on the first day of the month after his contract ended.
(v) Investigators found that an external group had remained hidden in KCBL's network for eight months, quietly collecting information.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of attack illustrated in each of the situations (i) to (iv) and explain how each attack works.
parts.answer:
(i) Salami attack: tiny, unnoticeable amounts are stolen repeatedly, here fractions of a paisa from each depositor's profit, and aggregate into a large total (PKR 3.8 million) over time. (2 marks)
(ii) Data diddling: data is altered before it is processed, causing incorrect outputs, here inflated overtime hours in the payroll input file leading to excess payments. (2 marks)
(iii) Email spoofing: the sender's address is forged so that a message appears to come from a trusted source, often by changing just one character in the domain name, as with the 'l' replaced by 'I'. (2 marks)
(iv) Logic bomb: malicious code that remains dormant until triggered by a specific event, here a date after the contractor's contract ends, when it would delete loan records. (2 marks)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between insider and external threats, classifying situations (i), (ii), (iv) and (v) accordingly.
parts.answer:
1. Insider threats come from employees or contractors with authorised access. They may be malicious (deliberate misuse or leakage) or negligent (harm through carelessness or lack of training). External threats come from outsiders, from independent cybercriminals up to state-sponsored attackers, using malware, phishing and Advanced Persistent Threats. (1 mark)
2. (i) Insider threat (malicious): the programmer abused his authorised access to the profit routine. (0.75 mark)
3. (ii) Insider threat (malicious): the payroll officer deliberately altered data the officer was authorised to handle. (0.75 mark)
4. (iv) Insider threat (malicious): the contractor had authorised access to the system and planted the code. (0.75 mark)
5. (v) External threat, specifically an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT): a prolonged, targeted intrusion designed to remain undetected. (0.75 mark)

secb.scenario:
Swift Cargo Services Limited (SCSL) is a courier company with an online parcel-booking website and 70 branches. SCSL's IT auditor has reported the following findings:
(i) The software vendor of SCSL's booking website released a patch for a critical vulnerability ten weeks ago. The patch has not been applied because 'the website is working fine'.
(ii) The company that maintains SCSL's air-conditioning and generators connects remotely using a user account that can reach every server on SCSL's network, including the payments system.
(iii) SCSL's network is a single flat network: branch computers, warehouse scanners and the payments database all sit on the same network.
(iv) A widely publicised, actively exploited vulnerability in the operating system of SCSL's branch computers was patched by the vendor two months ago, but the patch has been installed on only 10 of the 70 branches.
(v) The IT department has no complete list of SCSL's servers and the software running on them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Briefly describe the Equifax (2017), Target (2013) and WannaCry (2017) incidents, explaining the root cause of each.
parts.answer:
1. Equifax (2017): personal data of about 147 million people was stolen. Root cause: a known vulnerability in Apache Struts had a patch available but it was not applied for over two months; asset inventory and vulnerability management were weak. (2 marks)
2. Target (2013): payment-card data of over 40 million customers was stolen. Root cause: attackers entered using compromised credentials of a third-party HVAC (heating, ventilation and air-conditioning) vendor and moved laterally to the point-of-sale systems because the network was not segmented. (2 marks)
3. WannaCry (2017): ransomware encrypted more than 200,000 computers in 150 countries. Root cause: it exploited a known Windows vulnerability (EternalBlue) for which Microsoft had already released a patch that had not been applied. (2 marks)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Relate each of SCSL's findings to the most similar incident, and recommend a corrective action for each finding.
parts.answer:
(i) Similar to Equifax: a known website vulnerability with an available patch is being left unpatched. Recommendation: introduce formal patch management with defined timelines, applying critical patches within days, supported by automated patch deployment. (1.5 marks)
(ii) Similar to Target: a maintenance vendor has access far beyond what it needs. Recommendation: restrict vendor access to only the systems strictly necessary (least privilege), e.g. the building-management systems only. (1.5 marks)
(iii) Similar to Target: a flat network allows an attacker to move laterally to the payments database. Recommendation: segment the network so that branch, scanner and payments systems are isolated from one another. (1.5 marks)
(iv) Similar to WannaCry: a widely known, actively exploited operating-system vulnerability remains unpatched on most machines. Recommendation: deploy the patch to all branches promptly, within days, and verify installation. (1.5 marks)
(v) Similar to Equifax: weak asset inventory makes it impossible to know what needs patching. Recommendation: build and maintain a complete asset inventory to support vulnerability management. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Cybersecurity defence strategies and best practices
secb.scenario:
Bolan Foods Limited (BFL) is a Quetta-based food processing company with 400 employees. BFL's chief executive believes that the company is well protected because 'we have antivirus on every computer and a firewall on our internet connection'. An external review has made the following observations:
(i) Staff log in with passwords only, and many passwords are simple words such as 'bolan123'.
(ii) Customer and supplier data on servers and on staff laptops is not encrypted.
(iii) The firewall is an old model that only checks which addresses traffic comes from, not the content of the traffic.
(iv) Nobody reviews system activity, so a suspicious login from abroad last month went unnoticed for three weeks.
(v) BFL has no plan for responding to an attack.
(vi) Security patches are installed manually by one IT officer when he has time.
(vii) Staff have never received any training on phishing or safe device use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the chief executive's belief, explaining the concept of layered security (defence in depth).
parts.answer:
1. The belief is mistaken. Antivirus and a basic firewall are only two individual controls; if either fails or is bypassed, BFL has no other protection. (1 mark)
2. Layered security (defence in depth) means multiple overlapping layers of protection, such as encryption, firewalls and monitoring, so that a single failure does not expose the whole organisation. (1 mark)
3. The observations show that BFL lacks most layers (authentication, encryption, monitoring, incident response, training), so it is exposed even though antivirus and a firewall exist. (1 mark)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend the cybersecurity defence measures BFL should implement, relating each to observations (i) to (vi).
parts.answer:
1. Authentication (preventive) - observation (i): enforce strong passwords and implement Multi-Factor Authentication, using biometrics where appropriate, so weak or stolen passwords alone cannot give access. (1.5 marks)
2. Encryption (preventive) - observation (ii): encrypt data at rest on servers and laptops and data in transit using standards such as AES-256. (1.5 marks)
3. Firewalls (preventive) - observation (iii): replace the old firewall with a next-generation firewall that monitors and controls traffic using deep packet inspection. (1 mark)
4. Detection and monitoring - observation (iv): deploy intrusion detection systems and a SIEM tool to track activity across the network in real time and alert on abnormal patterns such as foreign logins; AI/ML features can reduce false positives. (1.5 marks)
5. Incident response - observation (v): develop and rehearse an incident response plan to contain, investigate and recover from attacks, including restoration from backups and post-incident review. (1.5 marks)
6. Automation - observation (vi): use automated vulnerability scanning and patch management tools, reducing reliance on one officer and reducing human error. (1 mark)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from layered security and automation, explain the other best practices for cybersecurity that BFL should adopt, including in response to observation (vii).
parts.answer:
1. User education - observation (vii): train employees to recognise phishing, use strong passwords and follow secure device-usage policies, since staff are often the first target of attackers. (1 mark)
2. Compliance: adhere to legal and regulatory standards (e.g. PECA 2016 and applicable data-protection requirements) to protect data and avoid penalties. (1 mark)
3. Proactive defence: continuously monitor the threat landscape, run regular risk assessments and use threat intelligence to stay ahead of attackers rather than reacting only after an incident. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Emerging AI, IoT and cloud cybersecurity risks
secb.scenario:
Kissan Dost Finance Limited (KDFL) is an SECP-licensed non-bank finance company that provides small loans to farmers in Sindh and southern Punjab. KDFL has introduced three new initiatives:
(I) An AI model, trained on loan data from the last ten years, now decides loan applications automatically. Loan officers no longer review the decisions. Field staff report that applicants from certain districts are almost always rejected, even when their repayment history is good, and nobody at KDFL can explain why the model reached a particular decision.
(II) KDFL has supplied 5,000 soil-moisture and crop-monitoring sensors to borrowers so that it can monitor crop condition. The sensors are connected to KDFL's main network, still use the manufacturer's default passwords and have never received a firmware update. The sensors also transmit borrowers' farm locations.
(III) KDFL has moved its customer database to one public cloud provider and its accounting system to another. KDFL's IT manager believes that 'security is now the cloud providers' job'. Last month, a storage folder containing scanned copies of borrowers' CNICs was found to be publicly accessible on the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify and explain TWO AI-related risks arising from initiative (I), and recommend a mitigation for each.
parts.answer:
1. Algorithmic bias: the model has inherited bias from its historical training data and consistently rejects applicants from certain districts despite good repayment histories, producing unfair, discriminatory decisions. Mitigation: carry out regular bias audits and apply ethical AI guidelines. (2 marks)
2. Lack of transparency ('black box') / over-reliance on autonomous AI: nobody can explain the decisions, which hinders trust and auditability, and removing loan officers' review risks unforeseen or inappropriate outcomes. Mitigation: use Explainable AI (XAI) techniques and reinstate mandatory human oversight of loan decisions. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each risk and 1 mark for each mitigation)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify and explain THREE IoT-related risks arising from initiative (II), and recommend a mitigation for each.
parts.answer:
1. Inadequate device security: the sensors still use default passwords and have not had firmware updates, making them easy to compromise. Mitigation: change default credentials immediately on deployment, use strong authentication and apply regular firmware updates. (2 marks)
2. Increased attack surface / botnet attacks: each of the 5,000 sensors is a potential entry point into KDFL's main network, and unsecured devices can be hijacked into botnets (as with Mirai) to launch DDoS attacks. Mitigation: network segmentation, isolating sensors from KDFL's critical systems. (2 marks)
3. Data privacy concerns: the sensors transmit borrowers' farm locations and crop data, which may be poorly protected in transmission or storage. Mitigation: encrypt device data in transit and at rest. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each risk and 1 mark for each mitigation)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the shared responsibility model and evaluate the IT manager's view. Also identify the cloud risks illustrated in initiative (III) and recommend appropriate mitigations.
parts.answer:
1. Shared responsibility model: security in the cloud is split between the provider, which secures the underlying infrastructure, and the customer, which secures its own data, access and applications. Misunderstanding this split creates gaps in coverage. (1 mark)
2. The IT manager's view is therefore wrong: KDFL remains responsible for configuring access to its own data, and the exposed CNIC folder is a direct result of this gap. (1 mark)
3. Misconfigured cloud settings: a publicly accessible storage folder is one of the most common cloud risks. Mitigation: regular cloud configuration audits and encryption of all cloud data with strict access controls. (1.5 marks)
4. Lack of visibility and control: using two different cloud providers (multi-cloud) can create blind spots in which threats or policy violations go undetected. Mitigation: use a Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) for visibility and policy enforcement, and a multi-cloud governance framework so the same security policy applies across providers. (1.5 marks)

secb.scenario:
Gulshan Bank Limited (GBL) is a mid-sized commercial bank. Its Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) has identified the following needs for the coming year:
