(i) The security team wants to learn exactly how attackers are trying to break into the bank's systems, without exposing genuine customer data.
(ii) Corporate customers send payment instructions electronically; GBL needs to be sure that each instruction really came from the named customer and was not altered on the way.
(iii) The 300 relationship managers use bank-issued smartphones to access customer information while visiting clients.
(iv) Laptops and desktops across 150 branches need to be monitored continuously for threats, and the team needs to be able to investigate exactly what happened on a device after an incident.
(v) The security team is small and attacks often take place at night; GBL wants security measures that adjust and respond to threats immediately without waiting for an analyst.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend the most appropriate advanced cybersecurity technology for each of the needs (i) to (v), explaining how it would meet the need.
parts.answer:
(i) Decoy systems (honeypots): deliberately vulnerable-looking systems that attract attackers, letting the team study attack methods without exposing real assets or customer data. (2 marks)
(ii) Digital signatures: provide cryptographic proof of the authenticity and integrity of a digital communication, confirming who sent the payment instruction and that it has not been altered. (2 marks)
(iii) Smartphone security: encryption of device data, VPNs for secure connections to the bank, and biometric authentication to protect mobile devices that hold as much sensitive data as a laptop. (2 marks)
(iv) Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR): continuously monitors laptops, desktops and phones for threats, enabling rapid response and forensic investigation of what happened on a device. (2 marks)
(v) Automated defences using AI and machine learning: dynamically adjust security measures and respond to threats in real time without waiting for a human analyst. (2 marks)
(1 mark for each correct technology and 1 mark for each explanation applied to GBL)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The CISO also proposes to adopt a Zero Trust Architecture. Explain this approach and how it would benefit GBL's relationship managers' remote access.
parts.answer:
1. Zero Trust assumes that no user or device is automatically trustworthy, even inside the network perimeter. (1 mark)
2. Every access request is continuously authenticated and verified, so a relationship manager's smartphone is checked each time it requests customer information, rather than being trusted once connected. (1 mark)
3. Benefit: if a smartphone is lost or an account is compromised, the attacker cannot freely access other systems, limiting the reach of any breach. (1 mark)

secb.topic: Cyber regulations and the security talent shortage
secb.scenario:
Zarghoon Digital Lending Limited (ZDLL) is an SECP-licensed non-bank finance company operating a mobile lending app with 1.2 million users in Pakistan. A foreign investor that recently bought 30% of ZDLL has asked the board to demonstrate that ZDLL complies with relevant cybersecurity laws and standards, and to obtain internationally recognised certification of its information security management.
ZDLL's entire security function consists of two IT officers, neither of whom holds a security certification. Security alerts are reviewed only during office hours. ZDLL has advertised for experienced security analysts for six months without success, and the board is unwilling to fund a full in-house Security Operations Centre (SOC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify and briefly explain the Pakistan-specific and global laws, regulations and standards that are relevant to ZDLL's cybersecurity.
parts.answer:
Pakistan-specific:
1. Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016: provides legal cover to investigate and penalise cybercrime, so attacks on ZDLL's app and customer data can be investigated and the attackers prosecuted. (1 mark)
2. SECP Guidelines for Cyber Security: outline minimum controls and reporting mechanisms to ensure cyber resilience in SECP-regulated entities; as an SECP-licensed NBFC, ZDLL is expected to follow them. (1 mark)
3. Cyber Security Policy of Pakistan (2021): sets out the national strategy for critical information infrastructure protection, within which ZDLL's own cybersecurity arrangements operate. (1 mark)
4. Electronic Transaction Ordinance (ETO) 2002: gives legal recognition to digital documents, records and signatures, which supports the loan agreements and records ZDLL creates through its app. (1 mark)
(Credit may also be given for noting that SBP's Enterprise Technology Governance and Risk Management Framework mandates strong IT governance, data protection and cybersecurity mechanisms for the financial institutions it regulates, although ZDLL's own regulator is the SECP.)
Global:
5. ISO/IEC 27001: the international standard for building, running and continually improving an Information Security Management System (ISMS); certification would meet the investor's request for recognised certification. (1 mark)
6. NIST Cybersecurity Framework: a widely recognised framework that ZDLL can use as a reference for structuring its security governance and controls. (1 mark)
(1 mark per relevant item explained, max 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ZDLL is struggling to recruit, and recommend strategies ZDLL could adopt to strengthen its cybersecurity capability without building a full in-house SOC.
parts.answer:
1. Reason: global demand for skilled cybersecurity professionals significantly outstrips supply, and the shortage is well documented in Pakistan, leaving many organisations under-resourced against an escalating threat landscape. (1 mark)
2. Leverage a Managed Security Service Provider (MSSP): outsource security operations to a specialist provider to obtain 24/7 monitoring and response, addressing the office-hours-only alert review without hiring an internal team. (2 marks)
3. AI and automation: deploy tools that use AI for threat detection and automated response, such as SOAR platforms, reducing the manual workload on the two IT officers. (1.5 marks)
4. Upskill internal talent: fund industry certifications such as CISSP, CISM, CEH or CompTIA Security+ for the two IT officers to build in-house capability. (1.5 marks)
5. Public-private partnerships: partner with universities offering cybersecurity programmes (bootcamps, scholarships, fast-track certifications) to develop a future recruitment pipeline. (1 mark)
6. Inclusive hiring strategies: broaden recruitment to diverse backgrounds and offer flexible or remote work to attract under-represented talent. (1 mark)
(Marks as indicated, max 8)

secb.scenario:
Ravi Pharma Distributors Limited (RPDL) distributes medicines to pharmacies across Punjab using a sales order application. The application contains a built-in rule that blocks any sales order where the discount exceeds 8% of the list price unless a regional manager approves it online.
During the year-end audit, the auditor found that several orders carried discounts of 20% to 25% with no regional manager approval. Investigation revealed the following:
(i) An IT support officer holds database administrator rights on the production database and used them, at the request of a sales manager, to edit the discount field directly in the database tables after the orders had been approved.
(ii) Six months ago, a programmer changed the discount rule to allow 'temporary promotional discounts'. The change was moved to the live system the same day without approval or testing, and no record of the change exists.
(iii) Database activity on the production server is not logged or reviewed by anyone.
RPDL's Finance Director comments: 'Our discount control is built into the software, so it cannot fail. The auditor should simply test the application rule.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the difference between IT General Controls (ITGCs) and application controls with reference to scope, focus and the relationship between them. Use RPDL's discount rule to illustrate your answer.
parts.answer:
1. Scope: ITGCs are broad-based controls that apply organisation-wide to all IT systems, whereas application controls are specific to one application. At RPDL, controls over who can access the production database or move changes to the live system apply to every system, while the 8% discount rule exists only inside the sales order application.
2. Focus: ITGCs focus on the IT infrastructure, processes and environment (access, change management, backups, physical security). Application controls focus on data input, processing and output within a single application, for example the discount limit check and online approval on each sales order.
3. Relationship: ITGCs are the foundation. Application controls depend on ITGCs being effective to work as designed; if ITGCs fail, application controls may become unreliable even if well designed.
4. Illustration: the discount rule (application control) secures the process; RPDL's access and change controls (ITGCs) secure the environment in which that rule runs.
(1 mark per well-explained point, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the Finance Director's comment.
parts.answer:
The Finance Director's view is incorrect.
1. An application control is only reliable if the ITGCs around it are effective. At RPDL the discount rule was bypassed without the application ever being 'broken'.
2. Issue (i): the IT support officer used database administrator access to edit the discount field directly in the database tables, completely bypassing the application rule and the regional manager approval. This is an access control (privileged access) failure.
3. Issue (ii): the rule itself was altered without approval, testing or documentation, so the auditor cannot even be sure the rule operating today is the rule management designed. This is a change management failure.
4. Issue (iii): with no logging or review of database activity, such direct edits go undetected.
5. Therefore the auditor cannot rely on testing the application rule alone; the auditor must first test the ITGCs (access and change management) to conclude whether the application control operated throughout the year.
(1 mark per valid point, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Recommend ITGCs that RPDL should implement to address each of the issues (i) to (iii).
parts.answer:
Issue (i) - Privileged database access:
1. Apply Privileged Access Management (PAM): restrict database administrator rights to a minimum number of authorised staff, and monitor all use of those rights.
2. Apply Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): an IT support officer's job role does not require write access to sales data in production, so those rights should be removed.
Issue (ii) - Unauthorised program change:
3. Introduce formal change management: every change to the discount rule must be formally approved (e.g. by the Finance Director and business owner) before work starts.
4. Require testing and validation before implementation, with documented test results, and proper documentation of every change, so no change can reach production without an approved, tested change record.
Issue (iii) - No monitoring:
5. Under IT operations controls, implement continuous monitoring by logging all database activity on the production server (audit logs) and having an independent person review the logs regularly, with alerts on direct changes to sales tables.
(1 mark per appropriate recommendation linked to the issue, max 5)

secb.scenario:
Sutlej Foods Limited (SFL) is a listed food processing company in Lahore. It is a subsidiary of a US-listed group, and the group's external auditors require SFL to demonstrate that its IT environment supports reliable financial reporting.
The following events occurred at SFL during the last financial year:
(i) A junior accountant deleted several months of supplier ledger entries by mistake. The entries had to be re-keyed from paper files and some amounts were re-entered incorrectly.
(ii) The ERP system was unavailable for three working days during the peak Ramzan season because a failed server could not be brought back into service, delaying dispatches to distributors.
(iii) The salary file for all employees, including directors' remuneration, was saved on a shared network folder that every employee could open.
(iv) SFL was unable to provide the group auditors with evidence that its IT controls over financial reporting had operated during the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the events (i) to (iv), identify the key objective of ITGCs that was not achieved and briefly explain why.
parts.answer:
(i) Ensure Data Integrity: this objective requires preventing unauthorised or erroneous modification or deletion of data so that it remains accurate and reliable throughout its lifecycle. The deletion of supplier ledger entries and the incorrect re-keying mean the ledger is no longer accurate or reliable.
(ii) Maintain System Availability: ITGCs should ensure that IT systems are operational and accessible when needed to support business continuity. The ERP was down for three days in the busiest season and dispatches were delayed.
(iii) Safeguard Confidentiality: sensitive information should be protected from unauthorised disclosure through access controls, encryption and data classification. Salary and directors' remuneration data was open to all employees.
(iv) Support Regulatory Compliance: IT practices must align with legal and industry standards. As part of a US-listed group, SFL is affected by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX), which requires reliable ITGCs over financial reporting; failure to evidence them exposes SFL and the group to penalties and reputational harm.
(1 mark for each correct objective and 1 mark for each relevant explanation, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain the importance of ITGCs in SFL's risk management, giving one example relevant to SFL for each point you make.
parts.answer:
1. Risk mitigation: ITGCs act as a first line of defence by establishing standardised processes that reduce vulnerabilities, e.g. role-based access would have stopped all employees from opening the salary file.
2. Financial accountability: ITGCs ensure the reliability of data used in financial reporting, a requirement under SOX; strong change and access controls would give the group auditors evidence that SFL's ledgers can be relied on.
3. Operational continuity: ITGCs such as backup and recovery procedures help keep systems available for critical functions like supply chain and customer service, avoiding a repeat of the three-day ERP outage during Ramzan.
4. Trust and reputation: protecting sensitive data and privacy builds the confidence of employees, distributors, the parent group and investors in a listed company.
(1 mark per point with a relevant SFL example, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Chenab Life Assurance Limited (CLAL) is an insurance company with its head office in Faisalabad. An internal audit of CLAL's policy administration and claims system reported the following findings:
(i) Branch staff log in with a user ID and a four-digit numeric password that never expires. The system does not lock an account after repeated failed attempts.
(ii) To save time, all new joiners in the claims department are given the same access profile as the Claims Manager, including the right to approve claims of any amount.
(iii) Three IT staff share one 'sysadmin' account. Nobody can tell which individual made particular changes to user rights.
(iv) Seven user accounts belonged to agents whose contracts ended more than four months ago; two of these accounts were used after the contract end date.
(v) No review of user access rights has been performed since the system went live two years ago.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the findings (i) to (v), identify the access control weakness and recommend an appropriate control.
parts.answer:
(i) Weak user authentication: a short numeric password that never expires and no lockout makes identity verification unreliable and allows guessing. Recommend: strengthen user authentication by introducing multi-factor authentication (e.g. password plus a one-time code sent to the user's mobile) for system access, supported by stronger passwords.
(ii) Access not based on job role: giving every joiner the Claims Manager's profile grants excessive rights, including claim approval. Recommend: implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) so access is granted strictly according to each person's job role and responsibilities, with claim approval limits restricted to authorised managers.
(iii) Uncontrolled privileged access and no accountability: a shared administrator account cannot be traced to an individual. Recommend: Privileged Access Management (PAM) - issue individual named administrator accounts, restrict the number of privileged users and monitor and log all privileged activity.
(iv) Failure to remove leavers' access: ex-agents' accounts remained active and were used. Recommend: link account deactivation to the termination of agent contracts, ideally automated from HR or agency records, and investigate the two post-termination logins.
(v) No periodic access review: inappropriate rights and inactive accounts go unnoticed. Recommend: periodic (e.g. quarterly) user access reviews in which business owners confirm each user's rights, with exceptions removed and documented.
(1 mark for each weakness and 1 mark for each appropriate recommendation, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between RBAC and PAM, giving an example of each from CLAL's environment.
parts.answer:
1. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) grants access based on a user's job role and responsibilities, so every user gets only what the role requires. Example: a CLAL branch officer can enter policy details and register claims, but cannot approve claims.
2. Privileged Access Management (PAM) restricts and monitors users who have high-level system access, such as system or database administrators, because misuse of these accounts can bypass all other controls. Example: only named IT staff hold administrator rights on the claims system, and all their actions on user rights are logged and reviewed.
3. RBAC therefore controls ordinary users' rights across the organisation, while PAM adds tighter restriction and monitoring for the small group of powerful accounts.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Kohat Cement Limited (KCL) has an in-house IT team that maintains its ERP system and is also developing a new dealer portal through which dealers will place orders and view their account balances.
The IT auditor selected a sample of five changes made to the ERP during the year:

tables.caption: Table 1: Sample of ERP changes
rows: New sales tax rate for FBR return
New cement bag size in item master

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the sample in Table 1 and identify the deficiencies in KCL's change management controls. Explain the risk each deficiency creates for KCL.
parts.answer:
Change management controls require (1) formal approval of changes, (2) testing and validation before implementation and (3) proper documentation of all changes. CH-011 and CH-052 meet all three elements. Deficiencies:
1. CH-027 - no approval, no proper testing and no documentation: a change to the credit-limit calculation could allow dealers to exceed credit limits, increasing bad-debt exposure, and no one can show what was changed or why.
2. CH-034 - approved and documented, but no test evidence (deficiency in the testing and validation element): an untested overtime formula could cause payroll overpayments or underpayments.
3. CH-041 - no approval, testing or documentation for an 'urgent' fix: being 'urgent' does not exempt a change from formal approval, testing and documentation; an untested change to invoicing may cause errors in customer invoices and revenue.
4. Overall: 3 of 5 sampled changes (60%) are deficient, indicating a control weakness, not an isolated error, so the auditor cannot rely on the integrity of ERP calculations without further work.
(1.5 marks per deficiency with risk explained; max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend improvements to KCL's change management process.
parts.answer:
1. Formal approval: every change, including urgent fixes, must be raised on a change request and approved by the business owner and IT management before deployment, so that changes are necessary, appropriate and properly authorised.
2. Testing and validation: changes must be tested in a controlled test (sandbox) environment, not a developer's laptop, and user-accepted, with test results documented and reviewed.
3. Documentation: maintain a complete change log recording why each change was made, who approved it, the testing results and any issues encountered during implementation.
4. Hard control gate: no change can be moved to production unless the change record contains approval and reviewed test evidence, removing the possibility of undocumented deployment.
(1 mark per recommendation, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain the program development controls KCL should apply while developing the new dealer portal.
parts.answer:
Program development controls apply when new systems are developed, to ensure they are secure and meet business needs:
1. Requirement analysis: define business and technical requirements before development begins, e.g. which dealer data each user may see, order limits, link to credit limits and security requirements for internet access.
2. Code reviews: peer review of the portal's code before it is merged or deployed, to catch security flaws and errors early, which is important because the portal will be exposed to external dealers.
3. Comprehensive testing: unit and integration testing of the portal, followed by User Acceptance Testing (UAT) with sales staff and selected dealers, to confirm it works correctly under realistic conditions.
4. Go-live only after issues found in testing are resolved and UAT is formally signed off.
(1 mark per point, max 4)

secb.topic: IT operations: backup, RPO and RTO
secb.scenario:
Thal Textile Exports Limited (TTEL) is a garments exporter in Faisalabad. Its export order system processes orders from European buyers around the clock. Management has set the following targets for the system: a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of 2 hours and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of 6 hours.
Current IT operations arrangements are as follows:
(i) A full backup of the export order database is taken once a day at 11:00 p.m. to an external hard disk, which the IT officer takes home.
(ii) Backups have never been restored to test whether they work. The IT officer estimates that rebuilding the server and restoring the backup would take about two days.
(iii) When users report problems, they phone the IT officer directly. No record is kept of the problems reported or how they were resolved.
(iv) Nobody monitors server disk space, performance or error messages. Last month the server stopped because its disk was full, and this was only discovered when buyers complained.
Yesterday the server failed at 7:00 p.m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the terms RPO and RTO and evaluate whether TTEL's current arrangements meet its targets, using yesterday's failure to illustrate your answer.
parts.answer:
1. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time - it answers 'how much data can we afford to lose?'. TTEL's RPO of 2 hours means no more than 2 hours of order data should ever be lost.
2. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime - it answers 'how long can we afford to be down?'. TTEL's RTO of 6 hours means the system must be restored within 6 hours of failure.
3. RPO evaluation: the last backup before yesterday's 7:00 p.m. failure was taken at 11:00 p.m. the night before, so about 20 hours of orders are lost. Daily backups can lose up to 24 hours of data, far exceeding the 2-hour RPO.
4. RTO evaluation: estimated recovery takes about two days (48 hours), far beyond the 6-hour RTO, and because backups have never been tested, recovery may fail altogether.
5. The off-site copy is kept at the IT officer's home, so it may not be available at the time of failure, further lengthening recovery.
Conclusion: neither target is met.
(1 mark per valid point, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Recommend improvements to TTEL's backup and recovery procedures so that the RPO and RTO targets can be achieved.
parts.answer:
1. Backup frequency: take backups at least every 2 hours, or replicate data continuously to a secure offsite or cloud location, so that data loss never exceeds the 2-hour RPO.
2. Secure off-site storage: store backup copies in a secure off-site location or cloud backup controlled by the company, not at an employee's home, with access restricted and logged.
3. Restoration testing: perform regular documented restore tests to prove that backups are complete and can be restored, and measure the actual recovery time against the 6-hour RTO.
4. Recovery capability: prepare documented recovery procedures and keep standby hardware or a cloud recovery option ready so the system can be brought back within 6 hours.
(1 mark per recommendation, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Recommend incident management and system monitoring controls to address issues (iii) and (iv).
parts.answer:
1. Incident management (issue iii): introduce a formal incident management process in which every reported problem is logged with a reference, prioritised, assigned, resolved and closed, with records kept so recurring problems can be analysed and escalated.
2. Continuous system monitoring (issue iv): implement monitoring of disk space, performance and error logs, with automatic alerts to IT staff when thresholds (e.g. 80% disk usage) are reached, so problems are fixed before buyers are affected.
3. Monitoring reports and incident logs should be reviewed regularly by IT management to confirm that IT operations controls support business continuity.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Gwadar Port Logistics Limited (GPLL) hosts its own servers in a small data centre on the ground floor of its Karachi office. During a site visit, the IT auditor observed the following:
(i) The data centre door is opened with an ordinary key. Copies of the key are held by the IT team, the admin department and the office cleaners. No record is kept of who enters.
(ii) Visitors, including vendor engineers, are allowed into the data centre unaccompanied.
(iii) The room is cooled by a household split air conditioner. Room temperature regularly rises above 35°C during load-shedding, when the air conditioner stops.
(iv) Servers are connected directly to the main electricity supply. Two servers were damaged last month by a power surge when electricity was restored.
(v) There is no fire detection or suppression system in the room; a carton of printer paper is stored next to the server rack.
(vi) A CCTV camera covers the corridor outside the data centre, but footage is overwritten after 24 hours and is never reviewed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the physical security weakness in each of (i) to (vi) and recommend an appropriate control for each.
parts.answer:
(i) Uncontrolled physical access: ordinary keys held by many people and no entry record. Recommend restricted physical access using biometric scans or security badges limited to authorised IT staff, with logs tracking who enters and exits.
(ii) Unescorted visitors: vendors could tamper with or remove equipment. Recommend that visitors sign a visitor log and are escorted by authorised IT staff at all times.
(iii) Inadequate temperature control: overheating can damage servers and cause failures. Recommend environmental controls - proper temperature control (a dedicated cooling unit with a backup unit) powered from a generator or UPS, with temperature sensors and alarms.
(iv) No power protection: surges and sudden outages damage hardware. Recommend Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS) with surge protection, backed by a generator for long load-shedding.
(v) No fire protection and combustible material near servers. Recommend fire detection and an appropriate fire suppression system, and removal of paper and other combustibles from the room.
(vi) Ineffective surveillance: CCTV only covers the corridor and footage is not reviewed. Recommend CCTV inside the data centre with footage retained for a reasonable period and reviewed regularly, plus alarm systems that trigger an immediate security response to unauthorised entry.
(0.5 mark per weakness and 1 mark per appropriate recommendation, max 9)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain why physical security controls are treated as part of ITGCs, with reference to the objectives of ITGCs.
parts.answer:
1. ITGCs are broad-based controls protecting the whole IT environment; every system GPLL runs depends on the hardware in this one room, so a physical weakness affects all applications at once.
2. Physical security supports the System Availability objective: fire, overheating or power surges can make all systems unavailable and halt port logistics operations.
3. It also supports Data Integrity and Confidentiality: an unauthorised person with physical access can steal, damage or tamper with servers and storage media, bypassing logical access controls.
4. Strong physical controls also support regulatory compliance and the trust of customers whose shipment data GPLL holds.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Zarghun Microfinance Bank Limited (ZMBL) provides small loans and mobile wallet services in Balochistan and Sindh. During an ITGC review, the following controls were observed in operation:
(i) Customers must enter a one-time password sent to their registered mobile number before a wallet transfer is processed.
(ii) A SIEM tool raised an alert when an employee's account downloaded 40,000 customer records at 2:00 a.m.
(iii) After the alert in (ii), the IT team immediately disabled the employee's account.
(iv) Every week the finance team reconciles the loan disbursements recorded in the core banking system with the bank statement and investigates differences.
(v) A firewall blocks all inbound internet traffic to the core banking servers except from approved addresses.
(vi) Following a ransomware infection at one branch, the branch server was restored from the previous night's clean backup.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the controls (i) to (vi) as preventive, detective or corrective, giving a brief justification for each.
parts.answer:
(i) Preventive: the one-time password stops an unauthorised transfer before it happens, even if the wallet PIN has been stolen.
(ii) Detective: the mass download had already occurred; the SIEM alert identifies the anomaly quickly so it can be investigated.
(iii) Corrective: disabling the compromised account acts after the event to stop further damage and restore normal, secure operation.
(iv) Detective: the reconciliation identifies errors or unauthorised disbursements after they have been recorded, for investigation.
(v) Preventive: the firewall blocks unauthorised traffic before it reaches the core banking servers.
(vi) Corrective: restoring from a clean backup restores normal operations after the ransomware attack has occurred.
(1 mark per correct classification with justification, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: ZMBL is concerned about the risk of unauthorised changes to customer loan limits in the core banking system. Recommend one preventive, one detective and one corrective control for this risk.
parts.answer:
1. Preventive: restrict the right to change loan limits through role-based access control (RBAC) to a small number of authorised credit officers, protect their logins with multi-factor authentication, and manage privileged database accounts under PAM so limits cannot be edited directly in tables.
2. Detective: generate an audit log of all loan-limit changes and have an independent person (e.g. credit risk) review a daily exception report of changes against approved credit files; SIEM alerts on direct database changes.
3. Corrective: when an unauthorised change is found, reverse it to the approved limit, disable or restrict the account responsible, and execute the incident response procedure, including investigating loans disbursed under the changed limit.
(1 mark for each correctly typed and relevant control, plus 1 mark for overall linkage to the risk, max 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain why ZMBL should rely on all three types of control rather than only on preventive controls.
parts.answer:
1. Preventive controls reduce the likelihood of an incident but cannot guarantee it will never occur; for example, the OTP and firewall did not stop the insider download in (ii).
2. Detective controls are needed to catch what gets through preventive controls, including insider actions, so that the bank learns of an incident quickly rather than months later.
3. Corrective controls are needed because some incidents will still cause damage, such as the ransomware at the branch, and operations must be restored and recurrence prevented.
4. Used together, they form a layered defence, so if one layer fails ZMBL still has a chance to catch and recover from the incident.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain the five steps involved in implementing IT General Controls in an organisation, stating the key activities and the output of each step.
parts.answer:
1. Risk assessment: identify IT risks (cyber, physical, human and compliance), analyse vulnerabilities and assess the likelihood and impact of each risk. Output: a risk register prioritising risks.
2. Control design: select preventive, detective and/or corrective controls for each risk, align them with business objectives and carry out a cost-benefit analysis so controls are proportionate. Output: a control framework mapping each risk to its designed control.
3. Implementation: deploy the controls across systems, applications and networks using formal change management (authorise, test, document). Output: deployed, configured and tested controls.
4. Training and awareness: train employees on the controls relevant to their role, build IT security awareness and engage vendors and partners on ITGC requirements. Output: trained staff and documented training records.
5. Monitoring and review: continuously monitor controls using tools such as SIEM, conduct regular audits, refine controls as risks evolve and encourage incident reporting. Output: ongoing audit reports and an updated risk register.
The process is structured and continuous, aligned to the organisation's risk management framework.
(1 mark for activities and 0.5 mark for output of each step, plus 0.5 mark for correct sequence, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Discuss the challenges an organisation may face in managing ITGCs, and suggest how each may be addressed.
parts.answer:
1. Complexity of IT environments: multiple platforms, applications and devices (cloud, on-premise, mobile, IoT) make consistent controls hard to design and enforce. Address by using a single control framework that maps each of the five ITGC components across every environment.
2. Resource constraints: limited budgets, staff and expertise can result in incomplete or weak controls. Address by prioritising the highest risks in the risk register and using cost-benefit analysis, phased implementation or managed services.
3. Evolving cybersecurity threats: new and sophisticated threats can make existing controls obsolete. Address through continuous monitoring and regular review and updating of controls.
4. Regulatory changes: keeping pace with changing requirements, especially across jurisdictions, is difficult for multinational organisations. Address by assigning responsibility for tracking regulatory change and updating controls accordingly.
5. Balancing flexibility and security: overly rigid controls stifle innovation and frustrate users, while lax controls expose the organisation to risk. Address by aligning controls with business needs and reviewing the balance regularly, since it is an ongoing challenge, not a one-time decision.
(1 mark for each challenge explained with a suitable response, max 6)

secb.scenario:
Jhelum Agro Group (JAG) operates a sugar mill, a chain of farm-supply stores and an online fertiliser ordering service. JAG's risk committee recorded the following events during the last quarter:
(i) A store employee copied the group's customer database, including farmers' CNIC numbers and mobile numbers, onto a personal USB drive before resigning.
(ii) The warehouse management system at the sugar mill crashed for a full day, and no sugar could be dispatched to customers.
(iii) JAG's monthly sales tax return was filed with FBR after the due date because figures had to be compiled manually from three systems, and a penalty was imposed.
(iv) An accounts clerk created a fictitious supplier and paid PKR 4.5 million to a bank account he controlled.
(v) A new agri-technology start-up launched a mobile app offering farmers free crop advice and doorstep fertiliser delivery, and JAG's online orders fell by 30% in two months.
(vi) Imported fertiliser prices rose sharply due to rupee depreciation, and JAG's margins on fixed-price dealer contracts were wiped out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Classify each of the events (i) to (vi) into the appropriate risk category faced by modern organisations, giving a brief reason for each classification.
parts.answer:
(i) Cybersecurity risk: an insider threat leading to a data breach of sensitive customer data.
(ii) Operational risk: a system failure causing downtime and disruption to the supply chain (dispatches).
(iii) Compliance risk: failure to meet a regulatory requirement (FBR filing deadline), resulting in a legal penalty.
(iv) Financial risk: insider fraud resulting in direct financial loss.
(v) Strategic risk: competitive disruption threatening JAG's long-term market position, not a technical failure.
(vi) Financial risk: market volatility (currency and price movements) affecting profitability.
(1 mark per correct classification with reason, max 6)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: For each of the events (i) to (vi), explain how ICT could help JAG manage the risk in future.
parts.answer:
(i) ICT is both the target and the defence: risk mitigation tools such as encryption of the customer database so that copied data is unreadable to unauthorised users, with real-time monitoring (SIEM) alerting on bulk data copying by a user.
(ii) Real-time monitoring of system health and predictive maintenance to warn of failure, plus business continuity and disaster recovery (backup and redundant systems) to restore the warehouse system quickly.
(iii) Regulatory compliance tools that pull data automatically from the three systems, generate the return in the required format, track filing deadlines and maintain an audit trail.
(iv) Real-time transaction monitoring and fraud detection analytics that flag new suppliers, unusual payments or supplier bank accounts matching employee details.
(v) Competitive intelligence and market analytics tools to detect the start-up's impact early, and scenario-planning tools to evaluate responses such as JAG's own advisory app.
(vi) Financial modelling and forecasting tools to model the effect of rupee movements on margins before fixed-price contracts are signed.
(1 mark per relevant ICT tool explained, max 6)

secb.topic: ICT's dual role and the risk management cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain what is meant by the 'dual role' of ICT in risk management, giving suitable examples.
parts.answer:
1. ICT is often a SOURCE of risk: digital transformation exposes organisations to cyberattacks (ransomware, phishing, data breaches) and to system failures and downtime that would not exist in a manual environment.
2. At the same time, ICT is the main TOOL used to identify, report on and mitigate risk, including the risks ICT itself creates. For example, a bank's online channel creates the risk of hacking, while firewalls, encryption and SIEM monitoring are ICT tools that defend against it.
3. In cybersecurity risk in particular, ICT is both the primary target and the primary defence.
4. ICT also helps manage non-technology risks, e.g. analytics for fraud detection (financial risk) or automated compliance reporting (compliance risk).
(1 mark per point, max 4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Explain ICT's role in risk identification, risk reporting and risk mitigation, describing two ICT tools for each stage.
parts.answer:
Risk identification (the first step, as an organisation cannot manage what it does not know about):
1. Real-time monitoring: tools such as Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and SIEM give real-time alerts on suspicious activity as it happens.
2. Predictive modelling: historical data and predictive algorithms forecast risks, such as supply chain disruption, before they materialise. (Data analytics/AI and automated risk scanners are also acceptable.)
Risk reporting (getting risk information to the right people, in the right format, in time):
3. Dashboards and visualisation tools present risk data visually for faster, better-informed decisions.
4. Automated reporting systems generate and distribute risk reports on time and consistently without manual compilation. (Centralised risk repositories and regulatory compliance tools are also acceptable.)
Risk mitigation:
5. Risk mitigation tools such as firewalls, encryption and antivirus protect directly against cyber threats.
6. Business continuity and disaster recovery: backups, redundant networks and cloud-based recovery enable rapid recovery after an outage or attack. (Incident response systems and automated risk control systems are also acceptable.)
(1 mark per tool correctly explained under the right stage, max 6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Required: Explain how ICT changes risk management from a reactive exercise into a continuous discipline.
parts.answer:
1. Traditionally, risk identification was a periodic, manual exercise, so risks were often found only after they had caused damage.
2. ICT makes identification continuous and automated: data analytics, real-time monitoring and automated scanners detect anomalies and weaknesses as they arise, and predictive models flag risks before they occur.
3. Automated reporting and incident response systems mean that risk information reaches decision-makers immediately and responses can be triggered automatically, minimising damage and downtime.
4. As a result, organisations can stay ahead of emerging threats and maintain business continuity, rather than only reacting after the event.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

secb.scenario:
Bazaar-e-Lahore (Private) Limited (BEL) operates an online marketplace where 2,000 small sellers sell clothing and household goods to customers across Pakistan. BEL's newly appointed Head of Risk has raised the following concerns:
(i) Fraudsters are placing cash-on-delivery orders using fake addresses and then refusing delivery. The pattern is only noticed months later when courier charges are reconciled.
(ii) BEL has no idea whether its web servers contain unpatched software or misconfigurations, because no one has checked since the website was launched.
(iii) Last Eid, demand for certain products was far higher than expected; popular items went out of stock and sellers lost sales.
(iv) BEL found out about an attempted break-in to its seller payment system only when a seller complained that his bank details had been changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the concerns (i) to (iv), recommend the most appropriate ICT tool for risk identification and explain how it would help BEL.
parts.answer:
(i) Data analytics and monitoring: ICT systems using AI and machine learning can analyse large volumes of order data to detect anomalies, such as repeated orders to unverified addresses or customers with high refusal rates, and flag likely fraudulent orders before dispatch rather than months later.
(ii) Automated risk scanners: vulnerability scanners and penetration testing tools (e.g. Nessus, OpenVAS) scan BEL's web servers for unpatched software and misconfigurations, enabling weaknesses to be fixed proactively before attackers exploit them.
(iii) Predictive modelling: historical sales data from previous Eid seasons and predictive algorithms forecast demand and the risk of stock-outs before they occur, so sellers can stock up in advance.
(iv) Real-time monitoring: an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and SIEM would generate real-time alerts on suspicious activity, such as repeated failed logins or unusual changes to seller bank details, as it happens, instead of BEL relying on seller complaints.
(1 mark for the correct tool and 1 mark for the explanation applied to BEL, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between real-time monitoring and predictive modelling as methods of risk identification, using BEL's concerns to illustrate.
parts.answer:
1. Real-time monitoring identifies risk events while they are happening, by continuously watching activity and alerting on suspicious behaviour, e.g. an IDS/SIEM alert when someone attempts to change seller bank details in concern (iv).
2. Predictive modelling looks forward: it uses historical data and algorithms to forecast risks that have not yet happened, e.g. predicting the Eid stock-out risk in concern (iii).
3. Real-time monitoring therefore shortens the time between an event and its detection, minimising damage, whereas predictive modelling allows action before the risk materialises at all.
4. Both support a proactive approach and are complementary: BEL needs prediction to plan and monitoring to catch what still happens.
(1 mark per point, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Pothohar Leasing Modaraba (PLM) is regulated by SECP and has eight branches. The Board Risk Committee has expressed dissatisfaction with risk reporting:
(i) The quarterly risk report reaches the Committee about six weeks after quarter end because the risk officer compiles it manually from branch e-mails and spreadsheets.
(ii) The report is a 90-page set of tables, and directors find it difficult to see which risks are increasing.
(iii) Each branch keeps its own risk log in a different format; the head office and branch figures for overdue lease rentals frequently do not agree.
(iv) PLM submitted two periodic returns to SECP late this year, and the auditors could not trace some figures in the returns back to source records.
Management plans to automate risk reporting immediately by connecting the existing branch spreadsheets to a new reporting tool.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend appropriate ICT tools for risk reporting to address each of the issues (i) to (iv), explaining how each tool would help.
parts.answer:
(i) Automated reporting systems: ICT automates the generation and distribution of risk reports to the Committee on a defined schedule, ensuring timely, consistent updates without six weeks of manual compilation.
(ii) Dashboards and visualisation tools: interactive dashboards present key risk indicators visually (e.g. trends and colour-coded ratings), so directors can see at a glance which risks are increasing and make faster, better-informed decisions.
(iii) Centralised risk repository: a cloud-based platform storing all branch and head office risk data in one place, in one format, provides a single transparent source accessible across the organisation, removing the conflicting branch logs.
(iv) Regulatory compliance tools: ICT systems automate compliance reporting, pulling data from source systems to produce SECP returns in the required format, tracking deadlines and maintaining a clear audit trail back to source records.
(1 mark for each appropriate tool and 1 mark for each explanation linked to the issue, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate management's plan to connect the existing branch spreadsheets to a new reporting tool, and recommend how PLM should ensure data accuracy and integrity.
parts.answer:
Evaluation:
1. Risk decisions are only as good as the data behind them. Automating reports from inconsistent branch spreadsheets will simply produce inaccurate reports faster, giving the Committee false confidence.
2. The head office/branch differences in (iii) show the source data is already unreliable, so it must be fixed before or alongside automation.
Recommendations:
3. Data validation and quality checks: standardise data formats and apply validation rules at input, with checks to catch errors and inconsistencies before data feeds reports.
4. Audit trails: maintain audit trails recording who entered or changed risk data and when, so figures can be traced to source - important for SECP returns and the auditors. Where a tamper-proof record is critical, blockchain can provide an immutable audit trail.
5. Move branch risk data into the centralised repository rather than linking separate spreadsheets, so there is one source of truth.
(1 mark per valid point, max 5)

secb.scenario:
Sindhu Diagnostic Centres Limited (SDCL) operates 15 medical laboratories in Karachi and Hyderabad. All test results are stored on servers at its head office. During the last monsoon season the following incidents occurred:
(i) Malware arrived through an e-mail attachment opened by a receptionist, spread to the head office servers and encrypted patient files.
(ii) It took the IT team six hours to notice the malware and a further day to decide what to do, as there was no defined response procedure.
(iii) Urban flooding damaged the head office server room. Because all data and systems were held only at head office, laboratories could not issue reports for four days.
(iv) When the main internet link to one laboratory failed, staff had to wait until an IT engineer manually switched the laboratory to a backup connection the next morning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Recommend the ICT tool for risk management and mitigation most appropriate to each of the incidents (i) to (iv), and explain how it would have reduced the impact.
parts.answer:
(i) Risk mitigation tools: up-to-date antivirus/endpoint protection, e-mail filtering at the firewall and encryption of patient data would have blocked the attachment or contained the malware closer to the point of entry, and encrypted data would remain protected from disclosure.
(ii) Incident response systems: automated incident response mechanisms would detect the malware and immediately trigger predefined steps (isolating infected machines, alerting the response team), minimising damage and downtime instead of losing over a day.
(iii) Business continuity and disaster recovery: backup systems, redundant networks and cloud-based disaster recovery replicate data and systems offsite, so laboratories could have switched to the offsite copy and resumed issuing reports quickly after the flood.
(iv) Automated risk control systems: a self-healing network would automatically detect the failed link and reroute traffic to the backup connection without manual intervention.
(1 mark for the correct tool and 1 mark for explanation applied to SDCL, max 8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Distinguish between incident response systems and automated risk control systems, and explain why SDCL needs both.
parts.answer:
1. Incident response systems are mechanisms that let the organisation react quickly once a risk event has occurred, coordinating containment and recovery to minimise damage and downtime (e.g. isolating infected computers and alerting the response team).
2. Automated risk control systems, such as self-healing networks and intelligent threat-detection tools, proactively detect, prevent and respond to risks without manual intervention, often before users notice a problem (e.g. rerouting traffic away from a failing link).
3. Automated controls handle known, routine conditions instantly, but not every incident can be resolved automatically; serious events like the malware outbreak need a structured, coordinated response.
4. Using both reduces the number of incidents that cause disruption and shortens recovery from those that still occur, supporting SDCL's business continuity.
(1 mark per point, max 4)

secb.scenario:
Kirthar Telecom Limited (KTL) is a mobile network operator. Over the past year, KTL has taken the following actions to integrate ICT into its risk management:
(i) KTL feeds tower power-consumption and weather data into an analytics model that forecasts which sites are likely to fail during heatwaves, and sends maintenance crews in advance.
(ii) Validation rules now reject subscriber records with missing or invalid CNIC numbers, and every change to subscriber records is logged in an audit trail.
(iii) The legal, network operations and finance teams now record and update risks on one cloud-based GRC platform, where each team can see the others' actions in real time.
(iv) Security patches are deployed automatically to servers, and an independent firm performs penetration testing every six months.
(v) All call-centre staff complete phishing simulation exercises each quarter, and supervisors receive role-specific training on the fraud monitoring tool.
(vi) Software robots now perform the daily check of new SIM activations against the biometric verification records, a task previously done manually by four staff.
KTL's Chief Risk Officer notes that, after a major billing outage last year, the team restored service but never studied why the outage happened.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Identify the best practice for integrating ICT into risk management illustrated by each of the actions (i) to (vi), and explain the benefit KTL obtains from each.
parts.answer:
(i) Adopt a proactive approach: predictive analytics identifies sites likely to fail before they fail, so KTL prevents outages rather than reacting after customers lose service.
(ii) Ensure data accuracy and integrity: validation and quality checks catch errors and inconsistencies, and the audit trail records changes, so risk and compliance decisions are based on reliable subscriber data.
(iii) Foster collaboration across teams: a shared GRC platform lets several departments see and update the same risk information in real time, eliminating information silos and out-of-sync departmental records.
(iv) Regularly update and test systems: automated patch management closes known security flaws in outdated systems, and penetration testing verifies that controls actually work rather than being assumed to work.
(v) Train employees on ICT tools: human error remains a major risk factor; phishing simulations and role-specific training ensure staff recognise attacks and use the fraud tool correctly.
(vi) Leverage automation: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) performs repetitive compliance checks, reducing manual effort and speeding up detection of irregular SIM activations.
(1 mark for each correct best practice and 1 mark for each benefit, max 12)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Identify the best practice that KTL has not applied, as indicated by the Chief Risk Officer's note, and explain how KTL should apply it.
parts.answer:
1. The missing best practice is 'Continuously improve risk management processes'. Risk management must evolve as technology and threats evolve.
2. KTL should carry out a post-incident analysis after every significant incident, such as the billing outage, reviewing exactly how and why the failure occurred and how it was detected and resolved.
3. The findings should be fed back to refine predictive models, response strategies and controls, so the same failure becomes both less likely to recur and faster to catch next time.
(1 mark per point, max 3)

secb.topic: End-to-end ICT support for fraud risk
secb.scenario:
Ravi Commercial Bank Limited (RCBL) issues debit cards to 1.2 million customers. Card fraud losses have tripled in two years. At present, suspicious transactions are identified only when customers complain, a monthly fraud report is compiled manually in spreadsheets and sent to senior management, and blocking a compromised card requires a branch officer to complete a paper form.
The CEO has proposed purchasing an AI-based fraud detection system and states: 'Once the AI system is in place, we can stop spending money on staff training and data clean-up, because the system will learn by itself.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: Explain how ICT could support RCBL in identifying, reporting and mitigating its card fraud risk.
parts.answer:
Card fraud is a financial risk (digital fraud) which ICT helps manage through real-time transaction monitoring and fraud detection.
Identification:
1. Data analytics and monitoring using AI/machine learning to analyse card transactions and detect anomalies, e.g. unusual locations, amounts or times compared to the customer's normal pattern.
2. Real-time monitoring that raises alerts while the suspicious transaction is happening, rather than waiting for customer complaints.
3. Predictive modelling using historical fraud data to forecast which cards, merchants or channels are at higher risk.
Reporting:
4. Dashboards showing fraud alerts, losses and trends visually to senior management for faster decisions.
5. Automated reporting systems producing the fraud report daily or weekly without manual spreadsheet compilation.
6. Regulatory compliance tools to generate any fraud-related reports required by SBP with a clear audit trail.
Mitigation:
7. Automated risk control systems that block or hold a high-risk transaction or card immediately, without manual intervention.
8. Incident response systems that trigger predefined steps - notify the customer, block the card, open a fraud case - in place of the paper form.
9. Risk mitigation tools such as encryption of card data and multi-factor authentication for online card use.
(1 mark per valid point, at least 2 under each stage, max 9)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: Evaluate the CEO's statement.
parts.answer:
The CEO's statement is not valid.
1. Data accuracy and integrity: an AI system learns from RCBL's data; risk decisions are only as good as the data behind them. Poor-quality or incomplete data would produce inaccurate fraud scores, either missing real fraud or blocking genuine customers. Data validation, quality checks and audit trails remain essential.
2. Training employees on ICT tools: the effectiveness of any ICT tool depends on how well its users understand it. Human error remains a major risk factor; fraud staff must be trained to investigate and act on alerts, and customer-facing staff to recognise social engineering.
3. Integrating ICT into risk management requires more than simply buying tools; the system also needs regular updating and testing and continuous improvement through post-incident review of fraud cases that were missed.
4. The investment in training and data quality should therefore be continued, not stopped.
(1 mark per valid point, max 4)

secb.topic: Recommending ICT best practices after audit
secb.scenario:
Tarbela Power Distribution Company Limited (TPDC) distributes electricity in northern Pakistan. An internal audit of its risk management arrangements reported the following findings:
(i) Transformer failures are recorded only after customers report outages; the large volume of historical failure and load data held in the billing and maintenance systems is never analysed.
(ii) The customer billing server runs an operating system that the vendor stopped supporting three years ago, and the last security test of the network was performed in 2021.
(iii) Meter readings are typed manually from handheld devices into the billing system; several thousand readings each month contain obvious keying errors which flow into risk and loss reports.
(iv) Line losses are tracked by the operations department in one spreadsheet, while finance uses a different spreadsheet for revenue-at-risk; the two never agree, and each department is unaware of the other's actions.
(v) Monthly line-loss reports for the regulator are compiled by three staff over ten working days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Required: For each of the findings (i) to (v), recommend the most appropriate best practice for integrating ICT into risk management, and explain how TPDC should implement it.
parts.answer:
(i) Adopt a proactive approach: apply predictive analytics to historical failure and load data, together with real-time monitoring of transformers, to forecast which transformers are likely to fail and schedule maintenance before outages occur.
(ii) Regularly update and test systems: replace or upgrade the unsupported operating system, introduce automated patch management to keep systems current, and perform regular penetration testing to verify that security controls actually work.
(iii) Ensure data accuracy and integrity: apply data validation and quality checks (e.g. range checks against previous readings) and, where possible, transfer readings electronically from the handheld devices, with audit trails of corrections, so risk and loss reports are based on reliable data.
(iv) Foster collaboration across teams: replace the separate spreadsheets with a shared cloud-based GRC platform so operations and finance see and update the same risk information in real time, eliminating information silos.
(v) Leverage automation: automate the regulatory line-loss report so data is pulled from source systems and the report generated automatically, and use RPA for repetitive data-collection tasks, reducing manual effort and time.
(1 mark for each correct best practice and 1 mark for each implementation explained, max 10)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Required: TPDC's management argues that recommending new technology is enough and that no further action is needed once the tools are installed. Discuss two other best practices that TPDC must also adopt for the ICT tools to remain effective.
parts.answer:
1. Train employees on ICT tools: the effectiveness of any ICT-based risk tool depends on how well its users understand it. TPDC should give role-specific training to meter readers, operations and finance staff on the new devices, analytics and GRC platform, and run ongoing awareness such as phishing simulations, since human error remains a major risk factor.
2. Continuously improve risk management processes: risk management must evolve as technology and threats evolve. TPDC should perform post-incident analysis of major outages or breaches to understand exactly how they occurred, and feed the findings back into refining predictive models, response strategies and controls, so failures become less likely and are caught faster next time.
(1 mark for each best practice identified and 1 mark for each explanation applied to TPDC, max 4)
